chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man with a large fortune must be looking for a wife.

No matter how little is known about such a man's feelings or intentions when he first moves into a neighborhood, this truth is so firmly established in the minds of the surrounding families that he is considered the rightful property of one or another of their daughters.
"My dear Mr. Bennet," his wife said to him one day, "have you heard that Netherfield Park has finally been rented?"
Mr. Bennet replied that he had not.
"But it has," she returned. "Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it."
Mr. Bennet made no answer.
"Don't you want to know who has taken it?" cried his wife impatiently.
"_You_ want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it."
This was invitation enough.

"Well, my dear, you must know that Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been taken by a young man with a large fortune from the north of England. He came down on Monday in a carriage and four to see the place, and was so delighted with it that he came to terms with Mr. Morris immediately. He is to move in before the end of September, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week."
"What is his name?"
"Bingley."
"Is he married or single?"
"Oh, single, my dear, of course! A single man with a large fortune—four or five thousand a year. What a wonderful thing for our girls!"
"How so? How can it affect them?"
"My dear Mr. Bennet," replied his wife, "how can you be so tiresome? You must know that I am thinking of him marrying one of them."
"Is that his reason for settling here?"
"His reason? Nonsense, how can you say such things! But it is very likely that he _may_ fall in love with one of them, and so you must visit him as soon as he arrives."

"I see no need for that. You and the girls may go—or you may send them by themselves, which might be even better, since you are as handsome as any of them, and Mr. Bingley might like you best of all."

"My dear, you flatter me. I certainly _have_ had my share of beauty, but I don't pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown-up daughters, she ought to stop thinking about her own looks."
"In such cases, a woman doesn't often have much beauty left to think about."
"But, my dear, you really must go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes into the neighborhood."
"That is more than I can promise you, I assure you."

"But think of your daughters. Just think what a match it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, purely for that reason—and you know they generally never visit newcomers. You really must go, because it will be impossible for _us_ to visit him if you don't."

"You are far too particular about these things. I'm sure Mr. Bingley will be very glad to see you, and I will send a note with you to assure him of my wholehearted consent to his marrying whichever of the girls he chooses—though I must put in a good word for my little Lizzy."
"I insist you do no such thing. Lizzy is no better than the others, and I am sure she is not half as pretty as Jane, nor half as cheerful as Lydia. But you are always giving _her_ the preference."
"None of them have much to recommend them," he replied. "They are all silly and ignorant like other girls. But Lizzy has a bit more sharpness than her sisters."
"Mr. Bennet, how can you insult your own children like that? You enjoy upsetting me. You have no compassion for my poor nerves."
"You misunderstand me, my dear. I have the deepest respect for your nerves. They are old friends of mine. I have heard you mention them with great feeling for at least twenty years."
"Oh, you have no idea what I suffer."
"But I hope you will get over it, and live to see many young men worth four thousand a year move into the neighborhood."
"It will be no use to us if twenty such men should come, since you won't visit any of them."
"You can count on it, my dear, that when there are twenty, I will visit them all."

Mr. Bennet was such a strange mix of sharp wit, sarcastic humor, reserve, and unpredictability that twenty-three years of marriage had not been enough for his wife to understand his character. _Her_ mind was easier to read. She was a woman of limited intelligence, little knowledge, and unreliable temper. When she was unhappy, she convinced herself she was ill. The purpose of her life was to get her daughters married; her comfort was gossip and visiting.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Mr. Bennet was among the first to call on Mr. Bingley. He had always intended to visit him, though he kept assuring his wife right up to the end that he would not go; and until the evening after the visit was paid, she had no idea. He revealed it in the following way. Noticing his second daughter busy trimming a hat, he suddenly said to her:
"I hope Mr. Bingley will like it, Lizzy."
"We have no way of knowing _what_ Mr. Bingley likes," said her mother resentfully, "since we are not to visit."
"But you forget, Mama," said Elizabeth, "that we will meet him at the local dances, and that Mrs. Long has promised to introduce him."
"I don't believe Mrs. Long will do any such thing. She has two nieces of her own. She is a selfish, hypocritical woman, and I have no respect for her."
"Neither do I," said Mr. Bennet, "and I am glad to find that you don't depend on her doing you any favors."
Mrs. Bennet did not bother to reply, but unable to contain herself, began scolding one of her daughters.
"Stop coughing like that, Kitty, for heaven's sake! Have a little compassion for my nerves. You tear them to pieces."
"Kitty has no sense of timing with her coughs," said her father. "She times them badly."
"I don't cough for my own amusement," replied Kitty irritably. "When is your next ball, Lizzy?"
"Two weeks from tomorrow."
"Yes, so it is," cried her mother, "and Mrs. Long doesn't come back until the day before, so it will be impossible for her to introduce him, since she won't know him herself."
"Then, my dear, you may have the advantage over your friend and introduce Mr. Bingley to _her_."
"Impossible, Mr. Bennet, impossible, when I am not acquainted with him myself! How can you be so annoying?"

"I admire your caution. Two weeks' acquaintance is certainly very little. You can't really know what a man is like after just two weeks. But if _we_ don't make the effort, someone else will. After all, Mrs. Long and her nieces must take their chances. And so, since she will consider it a kindness if you decline the duty, I will take it on myself."
The girls stared at their father. Mrs. Bennet said only, "Nonsense, nonsense!"

"What can be the meaning of that forceful exclamation?" he cried. "Do you consider the proper forms of introduction, and the importance placed on them, as nonsense? I can't quite agree with you _there_. What do you say, Mary? You are a young lady of deep thought, I know, and you read serious books and take notes."
Mary wished to say something very wise but didn't know how.
"While Mary is organizing her thoughts," he continued, "let us get back to Mr. Bingley."
"I am sick of Mr. Bingley," cried his wife.

"I am sorry to hear _that_—but why didn't you tell me so before? If I had known this morning, I certainly would not have called on him. It is very unfortunate, but since I have actually paid the visit, we can't avoid the acquaintance now."

The astonishment of the ladies was exactly what he had hoped for—Mrs. Bennet's perhaps exceeding everyone else's. Though when the first wave of joy had passed, she began to insist that it was what she had expected all along.

"How good of you, my dear Mr. Bennet! But I knew I would persuade you in the end. I was sure you loved your girls too much to neglect such an opportunity. Well, how pleased I am! And it is such a good joke, too, that you went this morning and never said a word about it until now."
"Now, Kitty, you may cough as much as you like," said Mr. Bennet; and as he spoke, he left the room, exhausted by his wife's raptures.

"What an excellent father you have, girls," she said when the door was shut. "I don't know how you will ever repay him for his kindness—or me either, for that matter. At our age, it is not so pleasant, I can tell you, to be making new acquaintances every day. But for your sakes we would do anything. Lydia, my love, though you _are_ the youngest, I'm sure Mr. Bingley will dance with you at the next ball."
"Oh," said Lydia boldly, "I am not afraid. Though I _am_ the youngest, I'm the tallest."
The rest of the evening was spent guessing how soon Mr. Bingley would return Mr. Bennet's visit and deciding when they should invite him to dinner.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Despite their best efforts, neither Mrs. Bennet nor her five daughters could get Mr. Bennet to give a satisfactory description of Mr. Bingley. They tried every approach—direct questions, clever guesses, and roundabout hints—but he dodged them all. In the end they had to settle for secondhand information from their neighbor, Lady Lucas. Her report was very favorable. Sir William had been delighted with him. Mr. Bingley was quite young, wonderfully handsome, extremely agreeable, and best of all, he intended to come to the next assembly with a large party. Nothing could be more exciting! To be fond of dancing was practically the first step toward falling in love, and their hopes for winning Mr. Bingley's heart ran high.
"If I can just see one of my daughters happily settled at Netherfield," said Mrs. Bennet to her husband, "and all the others equally well married, I shall have nothing left to wish for."

A few days later, Mr. Bingley returned Mr. Bennet's visit and spent about ten minutes with him in his library. He had hoped to get a glimpse of the young ladies, whose beauty he had heard so much about, but he saw only the father. The ladies were somewhat luckier—they managed to confirm, from an upper window, that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

A dinner invitation was promptly sent off, and Mrs. Bennet had already planned the menu that would showcase her skills as a hostess, when a reply arrived that put everything on hold. Mr. Bingley was obliged to be in town the following day and could not accept their kind invitation. Mrs. Bennet was thoroughly put out. She couldn't imagine what business he could have in town so soon after arriving in Hertfordshire, and she began to worry that he might always be running off from one place to another and never settle at Netherfield properly. Lady Lucas eased her fears somewhat by suggesting that he had

gone to London only to gather a large party for the ball. A rumor soon followed that Mr. Bingley was bringing twelve ladies and seven gentlemen with him to the assembly. The girls were dismayed at so many ladies, but were cheered the day before the ball by hearing that instead of twelve, he had brought only six from London—his five sisters and a cousin. And when the party actually entered the assembly room, it consisted of only five people altogether: Mr. Bingley, his two sisters, the husband of the eldest, and another young man.

Mr. Bingley was good-looking and well-mannered, with a pleasant face and easy, natural ways. His sisters were stylish women with an air of sophistication. His brother-in-law, Mr. Hurst, merely looked respectable. But his friend Mr. Darcy soon drew the attention of the entire room with his tall, striking figure, handsome features, and noble bearing—and the rumor, which was circulating within five minutes of his entrance, that he had an income of ten thousand a year. The men declared him a fine figure of a man; the ladies pronounced him much handsomer than Mr. Bingley; and he was admired with great enthusiasm for about half the evening—until his manners created a distaste that reversed the tide of his popularity. He was found to be proud, above his company, and above being pleased; and not even his large estate in Derbyshire could save him from being considered the most forbidding, disagreeable man present, and utterly unworthy of comparison with his friend.

Mr. Bingley had quickly introduced himself to all the important people in the room. He was lively and open, danced every dance, complained that the ball ended too early, and talked of hosting one himself at Netherfield. Such charming qualities spoke for themselves. What a contrast with his friend! Mr. Darcy danced only once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley, refused to be introduced to any other lady, and spent the rest of the evening walking around the room, occasionally speaking to someone in his own group. Everyone agreed: he was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world, and they all hoped he would never come again. Among his harshest critics was Mrs. Bennet, whose general dislike of his behavior was sharpened into personal resentment by his having slighted one of her daughters.

Elizabeth Bennet had been forced, by the shortage of gentlemen, to sit out two dances. During part of that time, Mr. Darcy had been standing close enough for her to overhear a conversation between him and Mr. Bingley, who had come away from the dance for a few minutes to urge his friend to join in.
"Come, Darcy," he said, "you must dance. I hate seeing you standing around by yourself like this. You really should dance."

"I certainly will not. You know how I hate it, unless I know my partner well. At a gathering like this, it would be unbearable. Your sisters are already dancing, and there is not another woman in the room whom it would not be a punishment for me to stand up with."

"I wouldn't be as fussy as you for anything in the world!" cried Bingley. "I swear I've never met so many pleasant girls in my life as I have tonight, and several of them, you can see, are uncommonly pretty."
"_You_ are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room," said Mr. Darcy, looking at the eldest Miss Bennet.

"Oh, she is the most beautiful woman I have ever seen! But there is one of her sisters sitting down just behind you who is very pretty, and I'm sure very pleasant. Let me ask my partner to introduce you."

"Which one do you mean?" Turning around, he looked at Elizabeth for a moment until, catching her eye, he looked away and said coldly, "She is passable, but not attractive enough to tempt _me_. And I am in no mood to pay attention to young ladies who are being ignored by other men. You had better go back to your partner and enjoy her smiles—you are wasting your time with me."

Mr. Bingley took his advice. Mr. Darcy walked off, and Elizabeth was left with no very warm feelings toward him. She told the story, however, with great spirit among her friends, for she had a lively, playful nature that delighted in anything ridiculous.

The evening overall was a pleasant one for the whole family. Mrs. Bennet had seen her eldest daughter much admired by the Netherfield party. Mr. Bingley had danced with her twice, and she had been singled out by his sisters. Jane was as pleased by this as her mother, though in a quieter way. Elizabeth shared in Jane's happiness. Mary had heard herself described to Miss Bingley as the most accomplished girl in the neighborhood. And Catherine and Lydia had been lucky enough to never lack for dance partners, which was all they had yet learned to care about at a ball. They all returned in high spirits to Longbourn, the village where they lived and where they were the principal family. They found Mr. Bennet still up. With a book in hand, he was indifferent to the time, and on this occasion he was quite curious about the evening's events, which had raised such grand expectations. He had rather hoped that his wife's fantasies about the stranger would be disappointed, but he soon found he had quite a different story to hear.

"Oh, my dear Mr. Bennet," she said as she entered the room, "we have had the most delightful evening, the most wonderful ball. I wish you had been there. Jane was so admired—nothing could compare! Everyone said how well she looked, and Mr. Bingley thought her absolutely beautiful, and danced with her twice. Just think of _that_, my dear—he actually danced with her twice! And she was the only woman in the room he asked a second time. First he asked Miss Lucas. I was so annoyed to see him dance with her, but he didn't admire her at all—nobody can, you know—and he seemed quite struck by Jane as she was moving through the dance. So he asked who she was, got introduced, and asked her for the next two dances. Then for the next pair he danced with Miss King, then with Maria Lucas, then with Jane again, then with Lizzy, and then the final dance—"

"If he had had any compassion for _me_," cried her husband impatiently, "he would not have danced half so much! For God's sake, say no more about his partners. I wish he had sprained his ankle in the first dance!"

"Oh, my dear," continued Mrs. Bennet, "I am absolutely delighted with him. He is so extraordinarily handsome! And his sisters are charming women. I never in my life saw anything more elegant than their dresses. I'm sure the lace on Mrs. Hurst's gown—"

Here she was interrupted again. Mr. Bennet refused to hear any description of their finery. She was forced to find another topic, and described, with considerable bitterness and some exaggeration, the shocking rudeness of Mr. Darcy.

"But I can assure you," she added, "that Lizzy doesn't lose much by not appealing to _his_ taste, because he is a most disagreeable, horrible man, not at all worth pleasing. So arrogant and conceited that there was no bearing him! He walked here, and he walked there, thinking himself so great! Not pretty enough to dance with! I wish you had been there, my dear, to give him one of your put-downs. I absolutely detest the man."

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: When Jane and Elizabeth were alone, Jane, who had been careful in her praise of Mr. Bingley around others, told her sister just how much she admired him.
"He is exactly what a young man should be," she said. "Sensible, cheerful, lively—and I have never seen such easy manners! So relaxed, with such perfect courtesy!"
"He is also handsome," replied Elizabeth, "which a young man ought to be as well, if he possibly can. That makes his character complete."
"I was very flattered that he asked me to dance a second time. I didn't expect such a compliment."

"Didn't you? _I_ did, on your behalf. But that is one great difference between us. Compliments always take _you_ by surprise, and _me_ never. What could be more natural than his asking you again? He couldn't help seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in the room. He deserves no credit for noticing that. Well, he is certainly very agreeable, and I give you permission to like him. You have liked many a more foolish man."
"Dear Lizzy!"

"Oh, you are far too inclined to like people in general. You never see a fault in anyone. Everyone is good and agreeable in your eyes. I have never heard you speak badly of a single person in my life."
"I would not wish to be hasty in judging anyone, but I always say what I think."

"I know you do—and that is exactly what makes it so remarkable. With _your_ good sense, to be so genuinely blind to the flaws and nonsense of others! Pretending to be fair-minded is common enough—you see it everywhere. But to truly be generous without any show or calculation, to find the best in everyone's character and make it even better, and say nothing of the worst—that belongs to you alone. And so, you like his sisters too, do you? Their manners are not equal to his."

"Not at first, certainly. But they are very pleasant women when you talk to them. Miss Bingley is going to live with her brother and manage his household, and I would be very surprised if we don't find her a charming neighbor."

Elizabeth listened in silence but was not convinced. Their behavior at the assembly had not been designed to please anyone in particular. With sharper observation and less flexibility of temperament than her sister, and with a judgment untouched by any attention paid to herself, she was not at all inclined to approve of them. They were, in fact, very grand ladies—not lacking in good humor when they were in the mood, nor in the ability to be charming when they chose to be, but proud and conceited. They were fairly attractive, had been educated at one of the top private schools in London, had a fortune of twenty thousand pounds, were in the habit of spending more than they should, and of associating with people of high rank. They therefore felt entitled, in every respect, to think well of themselves and poorly of others. They came from a respectable family in the north of England—a fact they remembered more vividly than the fact that their brother's fortune and their own had been made in trade.

Mr. Bingley had inherited property worth nearly a hundred thousand pounds from his father, who had intended to buy an estate but didn't live long enough to do it. Mr. Bingley had the same intention, and sometimes even picked out a county, but since he now had a fine house and the freedom to enjoy a gentleman's life, many who knew his easygoing nature doubted whether he might not spend the rest of his days at Netherfield and leave the next generation to buy the estate.

His sisters were very eager for him to have his own estate. But though he was presently only a tenant, Miss Bingley was perfectly willing to preside over his household, and Mrs. Hurst, who had married a man with more style than money, was no less inclined to treat his house as her own home whenever it suited her. Mr. Bingley had been of age barely two years when, through a chance recommendation, he was persuaded to look at Netherfield House. He looked at it, and through it, for half an hour, was pleased with the location and the main rooms, satisfied with the owner's description, and took it immediately.

Between him and Darcy there was a very solid friendship, despite their very different characters. Bingley's easygoing, open, and adaptable nature endeared him to Darcy, though no temperament could have offered a greater contrast to his own, and though Darcy never seemed dissatisfied with his own personality. Bingley had the firmest trust in Darcy's loyalty and the highest opinion of his judgment. In intellect, Darcy was the superior. Bingley was by no means lacking, but Darcy was clever. He was at the same time proud, reserved, and critical, and his manners, though polished, were not welcoming. In that regard, his friend had the clear advantage. Bingley was sure to be liked wherever he went; Darcy was constantly causing offense.

The way they each described the Meryton assembly was typical. Bingley had never met more pleasant people or prettier girls in his life. Everyone had been kind and attentive to him. There had been no pretension, no stiffness. He had quickly felt at ease with everyone in the room, and as for Miss Bennet, he could not imagine a more beautiful angel. Darcy, on the other hand, had seen a gathering of people with little beauty and no elegance, none of whom had sparked the slightest interest in him, and from none of whom he had received either attention or pleasure. He did acknowledge Miss Bennet to be pretty—but she smiled too much.

Mrs. Hurst and her sister agreed on that point, but they still admired Jane and liked her, calling her a sweet girl and one they wouldn't mind getting to know better. Miss Bennet was thus established as a sweet girl, and their brother felt authorized by their approval to think of her however he liked.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: A short walk from Longbourn lived a family with whom the Bennets were especially close. Sir William Lucas had formerly been in trade in Meryton, where he had made a decent fortune and earned a knighthood after giving an address to the king during his time as mayor. The distinction had perhaps gone to his head a little. It had given him a distaste for his business and for living in a small market town, and leaving both behind, he had moved with his family to a house about a mile from Meryton, known from that time on as Lucas Lodge. There he could reflect pleasantly on his own importance and, freed from business, devote himself entirely to being polite to everyone. For though he was proud of his title, it did not make him arrogant—on the contrary, he was attentive to everyone. By nature harmless, friendly, and obliging, his presentation at the royal court had made him courteous.

Lady Lucas was a very good sort of woman, not too clever to be a valuable neighbor to Mrs. Bennet. They had several children. The eldest, a sensible, intelligent young woman of about twenty-seven, was Elizabeth's closest friend.
It was absolutely necessary that the Lucas girls and the Bennet girls should meet to discuss the ball, and the morning after the assembly brought the former to Longbourn to hear and share the news.
"_You_ began the evening well, Charlotte," said Mrs. Bennet, with polite self-control, to Miss Lucas. "_You_ were Mr. Bingley's first choice."
"Yes, but he seemed to like his second choice better."

"Oh, you mean Jane, I suppose, because he danced with her twice. That certainly _did_ seem as if he admired her—I do rather think he _did_—I heard something about it—though I'm not sure what—something about Mr. Robinson."

"Perhaps you mean what I overheard between him and Mr. Robinson. Didn't I mention it to you? Mr. Robinson asked him how he liked our Meryton assemblies, and whether he didn't think there were a great many pretty women in the room, and _which_ he thought the prettiest. And he answered the last question immediately: 'Oh, the eldest Miss Bennet, without a doubt—there can't be two opinions on that.'"
"Really! Well, that was very definite indeed—that does seem as if—but still, it may all come to nothing, you know."
"_My_ eavesdropping was more useful than _yours_, Eliza," said Charlotte. "Mr. Darcy is not as worth listening to as his friend, is he? Poor Eliza—to be only just _tolerable_."

"Please don't put it into Lizzy's head to be upset by his rudeness, because he is such a disagreeable man that it would be a real misfortune to be liked by him. Mrs. Long told me last night that he sat next to her for half an hour without once opening his mouth."
"Are you quite sure, Mama? Isn't there some mistake?" said Jane. "I definitely saw Mr. Darcy speaking to her."
"Yes, because she finally asked him how he liked Netherfield, and he could hardly refuse to answer. But she said he seemed very annoyed at being spoken to."
"Miss Bingley told me," said Jane, "that he never talks much unless he is among close friends. With _them_ he is remarkably pleasant."

"I don't believe a word of it, my dear. If he had been so very pleasant, he would have talked to Mrs. Long. But I can guess how it was—everyone says he is consumed by pride, and I'm sure he had heard somehow that Mrs. Long doesn't keep a carriage and had to come to the ball in a hired one."
"I don't mind his not talking to Mrs. Long," said Miss Lucas, "but I wish he had danced with Eliza."
"Another time, Lizzy," said her mother, "I would not dance with _him_ if I were you."
"I think, Mama, I may safely promise you I will _never_ dance with him."

"His pride," said Miss Lucas, "doesn't offend _me_ as much as pride usually does, because there is an excuse for it. You can't wonder that such a fine young man, with family, fortune, and everything in his favor, should think highly of himself. If I may say so, he has a _right_ to be proud."
"That is very true," replied Elizabeth, "and I could easily forgive _his_ pride if he had not wounded _mine_."

"Pride," observed Mary, who prided herself on the depth of her reflections, "is a very common failing, I believe. From all that I have ever read, I am convinced that it is very common indeed—that human nature is particularly prone to it, and that very few of us do not harbor a feeling of self-satisfaction about some quality or other, real or imaginary. Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used interchangeably. A person may be proud without being vain. Pride has more to do with our opinion of ourselves; vanity with what we want others to think of us."
"If I were as rich as Mr. Darcy," cried a young Lucas boy who had come with his sisters, "I wouldn't care how proud I was. I would keep a pack of foxhounds and drink a bottle of wine every day."
"Then you would drink a great deal more than you should," said Mrs. Bennet, "and if I saw you at it, I would take your bottle away at once."
The boy protested that she would not; she kept insisting that she would; and the argument ended only when the visit did.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: The ladies of Longbourn soon paid a visit to those at Netherfield, which was returned in proper form. Jane's pleasing manners gradually won over Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley, and though the mother was found to be unbearable and the younger sisters not worth talking to, a desire for closer acquaintance with the two eldest was expressed. Jane received this attention with great pleasure, but Elizabeth still detected condescension in their treatment of everyone—hardly excepting even her sister—and could not bring herself to like them. Still, their kindness to Jane, such as it was, had some value, as it probably arose from the influence of their brother's admiration. It was obvious whenever they met that he _did_ admire her, and equally obvious to Elizabeth that Jane was giving in to the attraction she had felt for him from the start, and was well on her way to being very much in love. But she reflected with satisfaction that the world at large was unlikely to notice, since Jane combined deep feeling with an even temperament and a steady cheerfulness that would shield her from nosy speculation. She mentioned this to her friend Miss Lucas.

"It may be nice," replied Charlotte, "to be able to fool the public in such a case—but it can sometimes be a disadvantage to be so guarded. If a woman hides her feelings just as successfully from the man himself, she may lose the chance of securing him, and it will be cold comfort to know the rest of the world is equally in the dark. There is so much gratitude or vanity in almost every attachment that it is not safe to leave it to develop on its own. We can all _begin_ freely—a slight preference is natural enough—but very few of us have the courage to truly fall in love without encouragement. Nine times out of ten, a woman is better off showing _more_ affection than she feels. Bingley undoubtedly likes your sister, but he may never do more than like her if she doesn't help things along."
"But she does help things along, as much as her nature allows. If _I_ can see her feelings for him, he must be a fool not to see them too."
"Remember, Eliza, that he doesn't know Jane's character the way you do."
"But if a woman is attracted to a man and doesn't try to hide it, he must figure it out."

"Perhaps, if he sees enough of her. But though Bingley and Jane meet fairly often, it is never for many hours at a time, and since they always see each other at large social gatherings, they can't spend every moment talking to each other. Jane should therefore make the most of every half hour she has his attention. When she has secured him, there will be plenty of time to fall in love as deeply as she likes."

"Your plan is a good one," replied Elizabeth, "if the only goal is to marry well. If I were determined to land a rich husband, or any husband, I'm sure I would follow it. But those are not Jane's motives—she is not being strategic. She can't yet be certain how deep her own feelings run, or whether they are reasonable. She has known him only two weeks. She danced four dances with him at Meryton, saw him one morning at his own house, and has since dined in his company four times. That is hardly enough to understand his character."

"Not the way you put it. If she had merely _dined_ with him, she might only have learned whether he had a good appetite. But you must remember that four evenings have also been spent together—and four evenings can accomplish a great deal."
"Yes—those four evenings have enabled them to discover that they both prefer Vingt-un to Commerce. But as for any other significant trait, I doubt much has been revealed."

"Well," said Charlotte, "I wish Jane every success. And if she were to marry him tomorrow, I would think she had as good a chance of happiness as if she had spent a year studying his character. Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of luck. Even if two people know each other's dispositions perfectly, or are remarkably alike beforehand, it doesn't improve their chances one bit. They always end up growing different enough afterward to have their share of misery, and it is better to know as little as possible about the faults of the person you are going to spend your life with."
"You make me laugh, Charlotte. But that isn't sensible. You know it isn't sensible, and you would never act that way yourself."

Busy watching Mr. Bingley's attention to her sister, Elizabeth had no idea that she herself was becoming an object of interest to his friend. At first, Mr. Darcy had barely admitted she was pretty—he had looked at her without admiration at the ball, and when they next met, he looked at her only to find fault. But no sooner had he assured himself and his friends that she had hardly a single good feature in her face than he began to notice it was made remarkably intelligent by the beautiful expression of her dark eyes. This discovery was followed by others equally unwelcome. Though his critical eye had detected more than one flaw in the symmetry of her figure, he was forced to admit that it was light and pleasing. And despite his claim that her manners were not those of fashionable society, he found himself drawn to their easy playfulness. Of all this she was completely unaware. To her, he was simply the man who was pleasant to no one and who had not thought her pretty enough to dance with.

He began to want to know more about her, and as a first step toward speaking with her directly, he started listening to her conversations with others. She noticed this. It happened at Sir William Lucas's house, where a large party had gathered.
"What does Mr. Darcy mean," she said to Charlotte, "by listening to my conversation with Colonel Forster?"
"That is a question only Mr. Darcy can answer."
"But if he keeps doing it, I will certainly let him know I see what he is up to. He has a very sharp, mocking eye, and if I don't take the offensive first, I'll soon be afraid of him."

When he approached them shortly afterward, though without any apparent intention of speaking, Miss Lucas dared her friend to raise the subject with him. This immediately provoked Elizabeth to do it, and she turned to him and said:
"Didn't you think, Mr. Darcy, that I made my case uncommonly well just now, when I was pressuring Colonel Forster to give us a ball at Meryton?"
"With great energy—but it is a subject that always makes a lady energetic."
"You are hard on us."
"It will be _her_ turn soon to be put on the spot," said Miss Lucas. "I am going to open the piano, Eliza, and you know what comes next."

"You are a very strange kind of friend! Always wanting me to play and sing in front of anyone and everyone! If my vanity ran in a musical direction, you would have been invaluable. But as it is, I would really rather not perform before people who must be used to hearing the very best." When Miss Lucas insisted, however, she added, "Very well—if it must be, it must." And with a serious glance at Mr. Darcy: "There is a fine old saying that everyone here is surely familiar with: 'Save your breath to cool your porridge'—and I shall save mine to power my song."

Her performance was pleasant, though by no means exceptional. After a song or two, and before she could respond to several requests that she sing again, she was eagerly replaced at the piano by her sister Mary, who—being the only plain one in the family—had worked hard at her studies and accomplishments and was always eager to show them off.

Mary had neither natural talent nor good taste, and though her vanity had given her dedication, it had also given her a pedantic manner and a self-important air that would have diminished even greater skill than she possessed. Elizabeth, natural and unaffected, had been listened to with much more enjoyment despite being the lesser player. And Mary, at the end of a long piece, was glad to earn praise and gratitude by playing Scottish and Irish folk tunes at the request of her younger sisters, who along with some of the Lucases and two or three officers, eagerly joined in dancing at one end of the room.

Mr. Darcy stood near them in silent disapproval of this way of spending an evening—to the exclusion of all conversation—and was too absorbed in his own thoughts to notice that Sir William Lucas was standing beside him until Sir William spoke up:
"What a charming pastime for young people, Mr. Darcy! There is nothing quite like dancing, after all. I consider it one of the great refinements of civilized society."
"Certainly, sir. And it has the added advantage of being popular among less civilized societies as well—every savage can dance."
Sir William only smiled. "Your friend dances beautifully," he continued after a pause, seeing Bingley join the group. "And I have no doubt that you are quite the expert yourself, Mr. Darcy."
"You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir."
"Yes, indeed, and it gave me considerable pleasure. Do you often dance at the royal court?"
"Never, sir."
"Don't you think it would be a fitting tribute to the place?"
"It is a tribute I never pay to any place if I can help it."
"You have a house in town, I take it?"
Mr. Darcy bowed.
"I once thought of settling in town myself, as I am fond of good company. But I was not quite sure the London air would suit Lady Lucas."

He paused, hoping for a response, but his companion was not inclined to give one. At that moment Elizabeth happened to walk toward them, and Sir William was struck with the idea of doing something gallant. He called out to her:

"My dear Miss Eliza, why aren't you dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to present this young lady to you as a most desirable partner. You cannot refuse to dance, I am sure, when so much beauty is before you." And taking her hand, he would have placed it in Mr. Darcy's—who, though extremely surprised, was not unwilling to take it—when she instantly pulled back and said with some embarrassment to Sir William:
"Indeed, sir, I have no intention of dancing. Please don't imagine I came this way to look for a partner."
Mr. Darcy, with formal politeness, asked for the honor of her hand—but without success. Elizabeth was determined, and Sir William's attempts at persuasion did nothing to change her mind.

"You dance so beautifully, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you. And though this gentleman generally dislikes dancing, I am sure he would have no objection to obliging us for half an hour."
"Mr. Darcy is all politeness," said Elizabeth, smiling.
"He is indeed. But given the incentive, my dear Miss Eliza, we can hardly wonder at his willingness—for who would object to such a partner?"
Elizabeth gave a knowing look and turned away. Her refusal had not hurt her standing with the gentleman, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley approached him:
"I can guess what you are thinking about."
"I doubt it."

"You are considering how unbearable it would be to spend many evenings like this, in such company. And I completely agree with you. I have never been more bored! The dullness, and yet the noise—the emptiness, and yet the self-importance of all these people! What would I give to hear your criticisms of them!"
"Your guess is entirely wrong, I assure you. My mind was more pleasantly occupied. I have been reflecting on the very great pleasure that a pair of beautiful eyes in a pretty face can give."
Miss Bingley immediately fixed her eyes on his face and demanded to know which lady had inspired such thoughts. Mr. Darcy replied boldly:
"Miss Elizabeth Bennet."
"Miss Elizabeth Bennet!" repeated Miss Bingley. "I am astonished. How long has she been such a favorite? And when shall I congratulate you?"
"That is exactly the question I expected you to ask. A lady's imagination works fast—it leaps from admiration to love, from love to marriage, in an instant. I knew you would be congratulating me."
"Well, if you are serious about it, I shall consider the matter completely settled. You will have a charming mother-in-law, indeed, and of course she will always be at Pemberley with you."
He listened to her with perfect indifference while she chose to amuse herself in this way. And since his composure convinced her that all was safe, her wit flowed freely.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Mr. Bennet's wealth consisted almost entirely of an estate bringing in two thousand a year, which, unfortunately for his daughters, was entailed—in the absence of male heirs—to a distant relation. And their mother's fortune, though sufficient for her position in life, could hardly make up for this. Her father had been a lawyer in Meryton and had left her four thousand pounds.
She had a sister married to a Mr. Philips, who had been a clerk to their father and taken over his practice, and a brother settled in London in a respectable line of business.

The village of Longbourn was only a mile from Meryton—a very convenient distance for the young ladies, who were usually tempted to go there three or four times a week to visit their aunt and a hat shop just across the street. The two youngest, Catherine and Lydia, made these trips most frequently. Their minds were more empty than their sisters', and when nothing better presented itself, a walk to Meryton was necessary to fill their mornings and provide conversation for the evening. And however scarce the local news might be, they always managed to get some from their aunt. At present, they were well supplied with both news and excitement by the recent arrival of a militia regiment in the neighborhood, which was to stay for the whole winter, with Meryton as its headquarters.

Their visits to Mrs. Philips now produced the most fascinating information. Every day added to their knowledge of the officers' names and connections. Their lodgings were not long a secret, and eventually they began to know the officers themselves. Mr. Philips called on them all, which opened up for his nieces a source of happiness previously unknown. They could talk of nothing but officers, and Mr. Bingley's large fortune—the mention of which so excited their mother—was worthless in their eyes compared to the uniform of a junior officer.
After listening one morning to their gushing on this subject, Mr. Bennet calmly remarked:
"From everything I can gather from the way you talk, you must be two of the silliest girls in the country. I have suspected it for some time, but now I am convinced."

Catherine was flustered and said nothing, but Lydia, completely unfazed, continued to express her admiration for Captain Carter and her hope of seeing him that day, since he was leaving for London the next morning.
"I am astonished, my dear," said Mrs. Bennet, "that you are so ready to call your own children silly. If I were going to think poorly of anyone's children, it would not be my own."
"If my children are silly, I hope I will always be aware of it."
"Yes, but as it happens, they are all very clever."

"This is the only point, I flatter myself, on which we disagree. I had hoped our opinions were identical in every respect, but I must part company with you in thinking our two youngest daughters uncommonly foolish."

"My dear Mr. Bennet, you cannot expect such young girls to have the sense of their father and mother. When they reach our age, I'm sure they won't think about officers any more than we do. I remember when I found a red coat very appealing myself—and to be honest, I still do deep down. And if a sharp young colonel with five or six thousand a year should want one of my girls, I won't say no. I thought Colonel Forster looked very handsome the other night at Sir William's in his uniform."

"Mama," cried Lydia, "my aunt says that Colonel Forster and Captain Carter don't go to Miss Watson's house nearly as often as they did when they first arrived. She sees them quite often now standing around in Clarke's bookshop."

Mrs. Bennet was prevented from replying by the entrance of a servant with a note for Miss Bennet. It came from Netherfield, and the servant waited for an answer. Mrs. Bennet's eyes sparkled with pleasure, and she was eagerly calling out while her daughter read:
"Well, Jane, who is it from? What is it about? What does he say? Well, Jane, hurry up and tell us—hurry, my love!"
"It is from Miss Bingley," said Jane, and then read it aloud.
"My dear friend,

"If you are not kind enough to dine today with Louisa and me, we shall be in danger of hating each other for the rest of our lives, for a whole day alone together between two women can never end without a quarrel. Come as soon as you can after receiving this. My brother and the gentlemen are dining with the officers. Yours always,
"CAROLINE BINGLEY."
"With the officers!" cried Lydia. "I wonder why my aunt didn't tell us about _that_."
"Dining out," said Mrs. Bennet. "That is very unfortunate."
"Can I have the carriage?" said Jane.
"No, my dear, you had better go on horseback, because it looks like rain—and then you will have to stay the night."
"That would be a good plan," said Elizabeth, "if you were sure they wouldn't offer to send her home."
"Oh, but the gentlemen will have Mr. Bingley's carriage to go to Meryton, and the Hursts have no horses for theirs."
"I would much rather go in the coach."
"But, my dear, your father can't spare the horses, I'm sure. They are needed on the farm—aren't they, Mr. Bennet?"
"They are needed on the farm far more often than I can get them."
"But if you have them today," said Elizabeth, "my mother's purpose will be served."

She finally extracted from her father an admission that the horses were already spoken for. Jane was therefore obliged to go on horseback, and her mother saw her off at the door with many cheerful predictions of bad weather. Her hopes were fulfilled—Jane had not been gone long before it began to rain heavily. Her sisters were worried for her, but her mother was delighted. The rain continued all evening without stopping. Jane certainly could not come back.

"This was a clever idea of mine!" said Mrs. Bennet more than once, as if the credit for making it rain belonged entirely to her. Until the next morning, however, she did not realize the full success of her scheme. Breakfast was barely over when a servant from Netherfield brought the following note for Elizabeth:
"My dearest Lizzy,

"I find myself very unwell this morning, which I suppose is the result of getting soaked through yesterday. My kind friends won't hear of my going home until I'm better. They also insist I see Mr. Jones—so don't be alarmed if you hear he has been called for me—and apart from a sore throat and a headache, there is not much the matter with me.
"Yours, etc."

"Well, my dear," said Mr. Bennet, when Elizabeth had read the note aloud, "if your daughter should have a dangerous bout of illness—if she should die—it would be a comfort to know that it was all in pursuit of Mr. Bingley, and under your instructions."

"Oh, I am not at all afraid of her dying. People don't die from minor colds. She will be well taken care of. As long as she stays there, it's all perfectly fine. I would go and see her if I could have the carriage."
Elizabeth, genuinely worried, decided to go to her, even though the carriage was unavailable. Since she was no horsewoman, walking was her only option. She announced her plan.
"How can you be so silly," cried her mother, "as to think of such a thing, with the roads in this state! You won't be fit to be seen when you get there."
"I shall be perfectly fit to see _Jane_—which is all I want."
"Is this a hint, Lizzy," said her father, "that I should send for the horses?"
"No, not at all. I don't wish to avoid the walk. The distance is nothing when you have a reason—only three miles. I shall be back by dinner."
"I admire the energy of your kindness," observed Mary, "but every impulse of feeling should be guided by reason, and in my opinion, effort should always be proportionate to what is required."
"We will walk with you as far as Meryton," said Catherine and Lydia. Elizabeth accepted their company, and the three young ladies set off together.
"If we hurry," said Lydia as they walked, "perhaps we can catch a glimpse of Captain Carter before he leaves."

At Meryton they parted ways. The two youngest headed to the lodgings of one of the officers' wives, and Elizabeth continued her walk alone, crossing field after field at a quick pace, climbing over fences and jumping over puddles with restless energy, until she finally came within sight of the house, with tired ankles, muddy stockings, and a face glowing from the exercise.

She was shown into the breakfast room, where everyone except Jane was gathered, and where her appearance caused considerable surprise. That she should have walked three miles so early in the day in such miserable weather, and by herself, was almost unbelievable to Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley; and Elizabeth was certain they looked down on her for it. She was received, however, very politely by them, and in their brother's manner there was something better than politeness—there was genuine warmth and kindness. Mr. Darcy said very little, and Mr. Hurst said nothing at all. Darcy was torn between admiration for the glow that exercise had given her complexion and doubt about whether the occasion justified her coming so far alone. Mr. Hurst was thinking only of his breakfast.

Her questions about her sister were not answered very encouragingly. Miss Bennet had slept badly, was still very feverish, and was not well enough to leave her room. Elizabeth was glad to be taken to her immediately. And Jane, who had only held back from saying in her note how much she longed for such a visit for fear of causing alarm or inconvenience, was overjoyed to see her. She was not up to much conversation, though, and when Miss Bingley left them alone, could manage little more than expressions of gratitude for the extraordinary kindness she was being shown. Elizabeth sat quietly by her side.

After breakfast, they were joined by the sisters, and Elizabeth began to warm to them when she saw how much affection and concern they showed for Jane. The doctor came and, after examining his patient, said—as might be expected—that she had caught a severe cold and they must try to get her through it. He advised her to return to bed and promised to send some medicine. The advice was willingly followed, for the feverish symptoms were getting worse and her head ached badly. Elizabeth did not leave her room for a moment, and the other ladies were not often absent either—with the gentlemen out, they had nothing else to do.

When the clock struck three, Elizabeth felt she must go and very reluctantly said so. Miss Bingley offered her the carriage, and she needed only slight persuasion to accept, when Jane showed such distress at her leaving that Miss Bingley was obliged to turn the offer of the carriage into an invitation to stay at Netherfield for the time being. Elizabeth gratefully agreed, and a servant was sent to Longbourn to inform the family of her stay and bring back a change of clothes.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: At five o'clock the two ladies went upstairs to change for dinner, and at half past six Elizabeth was called down. To the polite inquiries that poured in—among which she was pleased to notice Mr. Bingley's far greater concern—she could not give a very encouraging answer. Jane was no better at all. The sisters, hearing this, repeated three or four times how sorry they were, how terrible it was to have a bad cold, and how much they hated being sick themselves—and then gave the matter no further thought. Their indifference toward Jane, when she was not directly in front of them, brought back all of Elizabeth's original dislike.

Their brother, in fact, was the only member of the party whom she could regard with any real warmth. His concern for Jane was obvious, and his attentions to Elizabeth herself were very kind, preventing her from feeling as much like an intruder as she believed the others considered her. She received very little notice from anyone but him. Miss Bingley was absorbed with Mr. Darcy, her sister nearly as much so; and as for Mr. Hurst, who sat next to Elizabeth, he was a lazy man who lived only to eat, drink, and play cards, and who, finding that she preferred a plain dish to a fancy one, had nothing more to say to her.

When dinner was over, she went straight back to Jane, and Miss Bingley began criticizing her as soon as she left the room. Her manners were pronounced to be terrible—a mixture of pride and rudeness. She had no conversation, no style, no taste, no beauty. Mrs. Hurst agreed and added:
"She has nothing, in short, to recommend her except being an excellent walker. I shall never forget her appearance this morning. She really looked almost wild."

"She really did, Louisa. I could barely keep a straight face. How ridiculous to come at all! Why must _she_ be tramping across the countryside because her sister had a cold? Her hair so messy, so windblown!"
"Yes, and her petticoat—I hope you noticed her petticoat, six inches deep in mud, I am absolutely certain—and the skirt that had been let down to cover it was doing no such thing."

"Your description may be perfectly accurate, Louisa," said Bingley, "but all of that was completely lost on me. I thought Miss Elizabeth Bennet looked remarkably well when she came into the room this morning. Her muddy petticoat escaped my notice entirely."
"_You_ noticed it, Mr. Darcy, I'm sure," said Miss Bingley, "and I'm inclined to think you would not wish to see _your_ sister make such a spectacle of herself."
"Certainly not."

"To walk three miles, or four miles, or five miles, or whatever it is, ankle-deep in mud, and alone—completely alone! What could she have been thinking? It seems to me to show a dreadful sort of conceited independence, a most country-town disregard for propriety."
"It shows a devotion to her sister that is very touching," said Bingley.
"I'm afraid, Mr. Darcy," observed Miss Bingley in a half whisper, "that this little adventure has somewhat dampened your admiration of her fine eyes."
"Not at all," he replied. "They were brightened by the exercise." A short silence followed, and then Mrs. Hurst began again:

"I am tremendously fond of Jane Bennet—she really is a very sweet girl—and I wish with all my heart she were well settled. But with such a father and mother, and such low connections, I'm afraid there is no chance of it."
"I think I've heard you say that their uncle is a lawyer in Meryton?"
"Yes, and they have another one who lives somewhere near Cheapside."
"How wonderful," added her sister, and they both laughed heartily.
"If they had enough uncles to fill _all_ of Cheapside," cried Bingley, "it would not make them one bit less agreeable."
"But it must considerably reduce their chance of marrying men of any standing," replied Darcy.
To this Bingley made no answer, but his sisters gave their wholehearted agreement and amused themselves for some time at the expense of their dear friend's common relatives.

With a revival of tenderness, however, they went to Jane's room after leaving the dining room and sat with her until they were called for coffee. She was still very unwell, and Elizabeth would not leave her until late in the evening, when she had the comfort of seeing her fall asleep. It seemed more like a duty than a pleasure to go downstairs herself. On entering the drawing room, she found the whole party playing cards and was immediately invited to join them. But suspecting they were playing for high stakes, she declined, and using her sister as an excuse, said she would amuse herself for the short time she could stay downstairs with a book. Mr. Hurst looked at her in astonishment.
"You prefer reading to cards?" he said. "That is rather unusual."
"Miss Eliza Bennet," said Miss Bingley, "looks down on cards. She is a great reader and takes pleasure in nothing else."
"I deserve neither such praise nor such criticism," cried Elizabeth. "I am _not_ a great reader, and I take pleasure in many things."
"In taking care of your sister I'm sure you find pleasure," said Bingley, "and I hope it will soon be increased by seeing her fully recovered."
Elizabeth thanked him sincerely, and then walked toward a table where a few books were lying. He immediately offered to bring her more—anything his library had to offer.
"And I wish my collection were larger, for your benefit and my own credit. But I am a lazy fellow, and though I don't have many books, I have more than I have ever looked into."
Elizabeth assured him that she could find something perfectly suitable from those in the room.
"I am amazed," said Miss Bingley, "that my father should have left so small a collection of books. What a wonderful library you have at Pemberley, Mr. Darcy!"
"It should be good," he replied. "It has been the work of many generations."
"And then you have added so much to it yourself—you are always buying books."
"I cannot understand the neglect of a family library in times like these."
"Neglect! I am sure you neglect nothing that can add to the splendor of that magnificent place. Charles, when you build _your_ house, I hope it may be half as wonderful as Pemberley."
"So do I."
"But I would really advise you to buy in that neighborhood, and use Pemberley as a model. There is no finer county in England than Derbyshire."
"With all my heart—I will buy Pemberley itself, if Darcy will sell it."
"I am talking about realistic possibilities, Charles."
"On my word, Caroline, I should think it more realistic to get Pemberley by buying it than by copying it."

Elizabeth was so entertained by this exchange that she had little attention left for her book. Soon setting it aside entirely, she moved closer to the card table and positioned herself between Mr. Bingley and his eldest sister to watch the game.
"Has Miss Darcy grown much since the spring?" said Miss Bingley. "Will she be as tall as I am?"
"I think she will. She is now about Miss Elizabeth Bennet's height, or perhaps a bit taller."
"How I long to see her again! I have never met anyone who delighted me so much. Such a face, such manners, and so extremely accomplished for her age! Her piano playing is exquisite."
"It amazes me," said Bingley, "how young ladies can have the patience to be so very accomplished, as they all seem to be."
"All young ladies accomplished! My dear Charles, what do you mean?"

"Yes, all of them, I think. They all paint tables, embroider screens, and knit purses. I hardly know anyone who can't do all this, and I'm sure I never heard a young lady mentioned for the first time without being told that she was very accomplished."

"Your list of common accomplishments," said Darcy, "has too much truth in it. The word is applied to many a woman who deserves it for nothing more than knitting a purse or embroidering a screen. But I am far from agreeing with your estimate of women in general. I cannot claim to know more than half a dozen, in the whole range of my acquaintance, who are truly accomplished."
"Nor can I, I'm sure," said Miss Bingley.
"Then," observed Elizabeth, "you must include a great deal in your idea of an accomplished woman."
"Yes, I do include a great deal."

"Oh, certainly," cried his faithful supporter, "no one can really be considered accomplished who does not far surpass the usual standard. A woman must have a thorough knowledge of music, singing, drawing, dancing, and modern languages to deserve the word; and besides all this, she must possess a certain something in her bearing and manner of walking, the tone of her voice, her conversation and expressions, or the word is only half deserved."
"All this she must possess," added Darcy, "and to all of it she must add something more substantial—the improvement of her mind through extensive reading."
"I am no longer surprised at your knowing _only_ six accomplished women. I rather wonder now that you know _any_."
"Are you so hard on your own sex as to doubt the possibility of all this?"
"_I_ have never seen such a woman. _I_ have never seen such talent, taste, dedication, and elegance, as you describe, all in one person."

Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley both protested at the unfairness of her implied doubt, and were both insisting that they knew many women who fit the description, when Mr. Hurst called them to order with bitter complaints about their inattention to the game. Since all conversation was thus ended, Elizabeth soon left the room.

"Eliza Bennet," said Miss Bingley when the door had closed behind her, "is one of those young ladies who try to make themselves attractive to men by putting down their own sex. And with many men, I dare say it works. But in my opinion, it is a cheap trick, a very low strategy."

"Without a doubt," replied Darcy, to whom this remark was mainly directed, "there is something low in _all_ the tricks that women sometimes resort to for the sake of attraction. Anything that hints at manipulation is contemptible."
Miss Bingley was not entirely satisfied with this reply, and dropped the subject.

Elizabeth rejoined them only to say that her sister was worse and that she could not leave her. Bingley urged that Mr. Jones be sent for immediately; while his sisters, convinced that no country doctor could be of any use, recommended sending an express to London for one of the most eminent physicians. Elizabeth would not hear of it, but she was not so unwilling to agree to their brother's suggestion. It was decided that Mr. Jones should be sent for early in the morning if Miss Bennet was not noticeably better. Bingley was quite upset. His sisters declared they were miserable. They comforted their unhappiness, however, by singing duets after supper, while he could find no better relief for his feelings than giving his housekeeper instructions that every possible care should be given to the sick young lady and her sister.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Elizabeth spent most of the night in her sister's room, and in the morning had the pleasure of being able to send a fairly good report in response to the inquiries she received very early from Mr. Bingley through a housemaid, and shortly afterward from the two elegant ladies who attended his sisters. Despite this improvement, however, she asked to have a note sent to Longbourn requesting her mother come and see Jane and judge her condition for herself. The note was sent immediately, and its request quickly fulfilled. Mrs. Bennet, accompanied by her two youngest daughters, arrived at Netherfield soon after the family had finished breakfast.

If she had found Jane in any apparent danger, Mrs. Bennet would have been very upset. But being satisfied upon seeing her that her illness was not serious, she had no wish for a quick recovery, since getting better would probably mean leaving Netherfield. She would not, therefore, agree to her daughter's suggestion of being taken home. Neither did the doctor, who arrived around the same time, think it advisable. After sitting a while with Jane, on Miss Bingley's appearance and invitation, the mother and three daughters all followed her into the breakfast room. Bingley greeted them with hopes that Mrs. Bennet had not found Miss Bennet worse than expected.
"Indeed I have, sir," was her answer. "She is far too ill to be moved. Mr. Jones says we must not think of moving her. We must impose on your kindness a little longer."
"Moved!" cried Bingley. "That must not be considered. My sister, I'm sure, will not hear of it."
"You may be assured, madam," said Miss Bingley with cool politeness, "that Miss Bennet will receive every possible attention while she remains with us."
Mrs. Bennet was full of thanks.

"I'm sure," she added, "that if it were not for such good friends, I don't know what would become of her, for she is very ill indeed and suffers terribly—though with the greatest patience in the world, which is always the way with her, for she has, without exception, the sweetest temperament I have ever known. I often tell my other girls they are nothing compared to _her_. You have a lovely room here, Mr. Bingley, and a charming view over that gravel walk. I don't know a place in the country equal to Netherfield. You won't think of leaving it in a hurry, I hope, even though you have only a short lease."

"Whatever I do is done in a hurry," he replied, "and so if I were to decide to leave Netherfield, I would probably be gone within five minutes. At present, however, I consider myself quite settled here."
"That is exactly what I would have guessed about you," said Elizabeth.
"You're beginning to understand me, are you?" cried he, turning toward her.
"Oh, yes—I understand you perfectly."
"I wish I could take that as a compliment, but being so easily read, I'm afraid, is rather pathetic."
"That depends on the circumstances. It does not necessarily follow that a deep, complex character is any more or less admirable than one like yours."
"Lizzy," cried her mother, "remember where you are and do not rattle on in the wild manner you are allowed to at home."
"I didn't know before," continued Bingley immediately, "that you were a student of character. It must be an entertaining study."
"Yes, but complex characters are the _most_ entertaining. They have at least that advantage."
"The countryside," said Darcy, "can generally supply few subjects for such a study. In a rural neighborhood, you move in a very limited and unchanging circle."
"But people themselves change so much that there is always something new to observe in them."
"Yes, indeed," cried Mrs. Bennet, offended by his dismissive mention of a country neighborhood. "I assure you there is quite as much of _that_ going on in the country as in town."
Everyone was surprised, and Darcy, after looking at her for a moment, turned silently away. Mrs. Bennet, who imagined she had won a complete victory over him, pressed on triumphantly:
"I can't see that London has any great advantage over the country, for my part, except the shops and public entertainments. The country is a great deal more pleasant, isn't it, Mr. Bingley?"
"When I am in the country," he replied, "I never wish to leave it, and when I am in town, it is pretty much the same. They each have their advantages, and I can be equally happy in either."
"Yes, that is because you have the right temperament. But _that_ gentleman," looking at Darcy, "seemed to think the country was nothing at all."

"Really, Mama, you are mistaken," said Elizabeth, blushing for her mother. "You completely misunderstood Mr. Darcy. He only meant that there is not such a variety of people to meet in the country as in town, which you must admit is true."
"Of course, my dear, nobody said there was. But as for not meeting many people in this neighborhood, I believe there are few neighborhoods larger. I know we dine with twenty-four different families."

Only concern for Elizabeth allowed Bingley to keep a straight face. His sister was less discreet, and directed a very knowing smile at Mr. Darcy. Elizabeth, hoping to redirect her mother's thoughts, asked whether Charlotte Lucas had been at Longbourn since she had been away.

"Yes, she called yesterday with her father. What an agreeable man Sir William is, Mr. Bingley—isn't he? Such a man of the world! So refined and so easy! He always has something to say to everyone. _That_ is my idea of good manners—and those people who think themselves very important and never open their mouths have it all wrong."
"Did Charlotte stay for dinner?"

"No, she had to go home. I imagine she was needed for the baking. For my part, Mr. Bingley, _I_ always keep servants who can do their own work; _my_ daughters are brought up differently. But everyone must judge for themselves, and the Lucas girls are very nice, I assure you. It is a pity they are not pretty! Not that _I_ think Charlotte so _very_ plain—but then she is our particular friend."
"She seems a very pleasant young woman," said Bingley.

"Oh yes, certainly. But you must admit she is very plain. Lady Lucas herself has often said so, and envied me Jane's beauty. I don't like to boast about my own child, but really—Jane—you don't often see anyone better looking. It is what everyone says. I don't trust my own bias. When she was only fifteen, there was a gentleman at my brother Gardiner's in town so much in love with her that my sister-in-law was certain he would propose before we left. But he didn't. Perhaps he thought her too young. However, he wrote some verses about her, and very pretty they were."
"And so ended his affection," said Elizabeth impatiently. "There have been many, I imagine, overcome in the same way. I wonder who first discovered how effective poetry is at killing love!"
"I have always considered poetry to be the _food_ of love," said Darcy.

"Of a strong, robust, healthy love, perhaps. Everything nourishes what is already strong. But if it is only a slight, fragile sort of attraction, I am convinced that one good sonnet will starve it to death."

Darcy only smiled, and the pause that followed made Elizabeth anxious that her mother might embarrass herself again. She wanted to speak but could think of nothing to say. After a short silence, Mrs. Bennet began repeating her thanks to Mr. Bingley for his kindness to Jane, with an apology for troubling him with Lizzy as well. Mr. Bingley was genuinely polite in his response, and forced his younger sister to be polite too, saying what the occasion required. She played her part without much grace, but Mrs. Bennet was satisfied and soon afterward called for her carriage. At this signal, the youngest daughter stepped forward. The two girls had been whispering to each other throughout the visit, and the result was that the youngest should challenge Mr. Bingley about his promise, made when he first arrived in the neighborhood, to host a ball at Netherfield.

Lydia was a sturdy, well-developed girl of fifteen, with a fine complexion and a cheerful face—a favorite of her mother, whose affection had launched her into society at an early age. She had high spirits and a natural sense of self-importance, which the attention of the officers—to whom her uncle's good dinners and her own easy manners recommended her—had boosted into real boldness. She was perfectly capable, therefore, of addressing Mr. Bingley on the subject of the ball, and she abruptly reminded him of his promise, adding that it would be the most shameful thing in the world if he didn't keep it. His answer was music to her mother's ears.

"I am perfectly ready, I assure you, to keep my promise. And when your sister has recovered, you may, if you like, name the very day of the ball. But you wouldn't want to be dancing while she is ill?"

Lydia declared herself satisfied. "Oh, yes—it would be much better to wait until Jane is well. And by that time, most likely, Captain Carter will be back in Meryton. And when you have given _your_ ball," she added, "I shall insist on their giving one too. I shall tell Colonel Forster it will be a disgrace if he doesn't."

Mrs. Bennet and her daughters then left, and Elizabeth returned immediately to Jane, leaving her own and her family's behavior to the comments of the two ladies and Mr. Darcy. The latter, however, could not be persuaded to join in their criticism of _her_, despite all of Miss Bingley's jokes about _fine eyes_.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: The day passed much as the one before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent some hours of the morning with the patient, who continued, though slowly, to improve. In the evening, Elizabeth joined their party in the drawing room. The card table, however, did not appear. Mr. Darcy was writing a letter, and Miss Bingley, seated near him, was watching its progress and repeatedly interrupting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst was watching their game.

Elizabeth took up some needlework and was sufficiently entertained by what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady's constant praise—of his handwriting, the evenness of his lines, the length of his letter—and the perfect indifference with which her compliments were received made for an amusing exchange, and matched perfectly with her opinion of each of them.
"How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!"
He made no answer.
"You write remarkably fast."
"You are mistaken. I write rather slowly."
"How many letters you must have to write in the course of a year! Business letters too! How tedious I would find them!"
"It is fortunate, then, that they fall to me instead of to you."
"Do tell your sister that I am longing to see her."
"I have already told her so once, at your request."
"I'm afraid you don't like your pen. Let me fix it for you. I fix pens remarkably well."
"Thank you—but I always fix my own."
"How do you manage to write so evenly?"
He was silent.

"Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and please let her know that I am absolutely in love with her beautiful little design for a table, and I think it infinitely superior to Miss Grantley's."
"Will you allow me to save your raptures for my next letter? At present I don't have room to do them justice."
"Oh, it doesn't matter. I shall see her in January. But do you always write such charmingly long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?"
"They are generally long, but whether always charming is not for me to judge."
"It is my rule that a person who can write a long letter easily cannot write badly."
"That won't work as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline," cried her brother, "because he does _not_ write easily. He agonizes over four-syllable words. Don't you, Darcy?"
"My writing style is very different from yours."
"Oh," cried Miss Bingley, "Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable. He leaves out half his words and smudges the rest."
"My ideas flow so fast that I don't have time to express them properly, which means my letters sometimes convey no ideas at all to the people I write to."
"Your humility, Mr. Bingley," said Elizabeth, "must disarm any criticism."
"Nothing is more deceptive," said Darcy, "than the appearance of humility. It is often just carelessness of opinion, and sometimes an indirect boast."
"And which of the two do you call _my_ little recent display of modesty?"

"The indirect boast. You are actually proud of your defects in writing, because you see them as the result of rapid thinking and careless execution, which, if not admirable, you consider at least very interesting. The ability to do anything quickly is always highly valued by the person who has it, and often without any attention to how poorly the thing is done. When you told Mrs. Bennet this morning that if you ever decided to leave Netherfield you would be gone in five minutes, you meant it as a sort of self-congratulation. And yet what is so praiseworthy about a recklessness that must leave important business undone, and can be of no real benefit to yourself or anyone else?"

"Come now," cried Bingley, "this is too much—to remember at night all the foolish things that were said in the morning. And yet, on my honor, I believed what I said about myself to be true, and I believe it at this moment. At least, then, I did not pretend to be impulsive just to show off in front of the ladies."

"I dare say you believed it. But I am by no means convinced you would actually leave so quickly. Your behavior would be just as dependent on chance as any man's I know. And if, as you were mounting your horse, a friend were to say, 'Bingley, you had better stay till next week,' you would probably do it—you would probably not go—and at another word, might stay a month."
"You have only proved by this," cried Elizabeth, "that Mr. Bingley did not do justice to his own character. You have shown him off far better than he did himself."

"I am extremely grateful," said Bingley, "that you turn what my friend says into a compliment on my good nature. But I'm afraid you are giving it a meaning that gentleman by no means intended, for he would certainly think better of me if, in such a situation, I were to give a flat refusal and ride off as fast as I could."
"Would Mr. Darcy then consider the rashness of your original intention to be redeemed by your stubbornness in sticking to it?"
"On my word, I can't quite explain the matter—Darcy must speak for himself."

"You expect me to justify opinions that you choose to call mine but that I have never claimed. However, accepting your version of events, you must remember, Miss Bennet, that the friend who supposedly wanted him to return to the house and delay his plan merely asked for it—without offering a single argument in its favor."
"To give in readily—easily—to the _persuasion_ of a friend holds no value for you."
"To give in without being convinced is no compliment to either person's judgment."

"You seem to me, Mr. Darcy, to allow nothing for the influence of friendship and affection. Regard for the person asking would often make one readily agree to a request, without waiting to be argued into it. I am not specifically talking about the case you have imagined with Mr. Bingley. We might as well wait until such a situation actually arises before we debate the wisdom of his behavior. But in general, ordinary cases between friends, where one asks the other to change a decision of no great importance—would you think badly of that person for agreeing without waiting to be persuaded by arguments?"
"Would it not be wise, before we continue, to establish more precisely the level of importance attached to this request, as well as the degree of closeness between the parties?"

"By all means," cried Bingley. "Let us hear all the details—not forgetting their respective heights and builds, for that will carry more weight in the argument, Miss Bennet, than you may realize. I assure you that if Darcy were not such a tall, imposing fellow compared to me, I would not defer to him half as much. I swear I do not know a more intimidating sight than Darcy on certain occasions and in certain settings—at his own house especially, on a Sunday evening when he has nothing to do."

Mr. Darcy smiled, but Elizabeth thought she could detect that he was somewhat offended, and so she suppressed her laugh. Miss Bingley hotly resented the insult to him, scolding her brother for talking such nonsense.
"I see what you're doing, Bingley," said his friend. "You dislike an argument and want to end this one."
"Perhaps I do. Arguments are too much like quarrels. If you and Miss Bennet will save yours until I am out of the room, I would be very grateful—and then you may say whatever you like about me."
"What you ask," said Elizabeth, "is no sacrifice on my part. And Mr. Darcy had better finish his letter."
Mr. Darcy took her advice and finished his letter.

When that was done, he asked Miss Bingley and Elizabeth if they would favor him with some music. Miss Bingley moved eagerly to the piano, and after a polite request that Elizabeth go first—which she politely but firmly declined—she sat down to play.
