Mrs. Hurst sang with her sister, and while they were occupied, Elizabeth could not help noticing, as she turned through some music books on the piano, how frequently Mr. Darcy's eyes were fixed on her. She could hardly believe she could be an object of admiration to such a man, and yet the idea that he looked at her because he disliked her was even stranger. She could only suppose, in the end, that she drew his attention because there was something about her more wrong and objectionable, by his standards, than in anyone else present. The thought did not bother her. She liked him too little to care about his approval.
After playing some Italian songs, Miss Bingley changed the mood with a lively Scottish tune. Soon afterward, Mr. Darcy moved closer to Elizabeth and said:
"Don't you feel a strong urge, Miss Bennet, to take this opportunity to dance a reel?"
She smiled but made no answer. He repeated the question, somewhat surprised by her silence.

"Oh," she said, "I heard you the first time, but I couldn't immediately decide what to say in reply. You wanted me, I know, to say 'Yes,' so you could have the pleasure of looking down on my taste. But I always enjoy foiling that kind of scheme and denying someone their premeditated contempt. I have therefore made up my mind to tell you that I do _not_ want to dance a reel at all—and now look down on me if you dare."
"Indeed I do not dare."

Elizabeth, who had rather expected to offend him, was amazed by his gallantry. But there was a mixture of sweetness and mischief in her manner that made it hard for her to offend anyone, and Darcy had never been so captivated by any woman as he was by her. He truly believed that, were it not for her inferior connections, he would be in some danger.
Miss Bingley saw, or suspected, enough to be jealous, and her great concern for the recovery of her dear friend Jane was considerably helped along by her desire to be rid of Elizabeth.
She often tried to provoke Darcy into disliking her guest by talking about their supposed marriage and planning his happiness in such a match.

"I hope," she said, as they were walking together in the garden the next day, "you will give your mother-in-law a few hints, when this happy event takes place, about the advantage of holding her tongue. And if you can manage it, try to cure the younger girls of chasing after the officers. And, if I may mention so delicate a subject, try to correct that certain something, bordering on conceit and rudeness, that your lady possesses."
"Is there anything else you'd like to suggest for my domestic happiness?"

"Oh yes. Do have the portraits of your uncle and aunt Philips hung in the gallery at Pemberley. Put them next to your great-uncle the judge. They are in the same profession, you know, only in different branches. As for your Elizabeth's portrait, you must not attempt to have it painted, for what artist could do justice to those beautiful eyes?"
"It would not be easy, indeed, to capture their expression. But their color and shape, and the eyelashes, so remarkably fine, might be copied."
At that moment they were met from another path by Mrs. Hurst and Elizabeth herself.
"I did not know that you intended to walk," said Miss Bingley, somewhat flustered, in case they had been overheard.
"You treated us terribly," answered Mrs. Hurst, "running off without telling us you were going outside."
Then, taking Mr. Darcy's free arm, she left Elizabeth to walk by herself. The path was only wide enough for three. Mr. Darcy noticed their rudeness and immediately said:
"This path is not wide enough for all of us. We had better go to the main walk."
But Elizabeth, who had no desire whatsoever to stay with them, laughingly replied:
"No, no—stay where you are. You are charmingly arranged and look wonderful together. The picture would be spoiled by adding a fourth. Goodbye."

She then ran off cheerfully, delighting, as she wandered about, in the hope of being home again in a day or two. Jane was already so much recovered that she planned to leave her room for a couple of hours that evening.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: When the ladies left the dining room after dinner, Elizabeth hurried up to her sister and, seeing her well wrapped up against the cold, accompanied her into the drawing room. She was welcomed by the two ladies with many expressions of pleasure, and Elizabeth had never seen them so agreeable as they were during the hour before the gentlemen appeared. Their conversation was lively—they could describe a party with precision, tell a story with humor, and make fun of their acquaintances with spirit.

But when the gentlemen entered, Jane was no longer the center of attention. Miss Bingley's eyes turned instantly toward Darcy, and she had something to say to him before he had taken many steps. He went directly to Miss Bennet with a polite congratulation on her recovery. Mr. Hurst also gave her a slight bow and said he was "very glad." But it was Bingley who greeted her with real warmth and enthusiasm. He was full of joy and attentiveness. The first half hour was spent building up the fire, in case she should suffer from the change of room, and at his suggestion she moved to the other side of the fireplace, farther from the door. He then sat down beside her and spoke to hardly anyone else. Elizabeth, sewing in the opposite corner, watched it all with great delight.

When tea was over, Mr. Hurst reminded his sister-in-law of the card table—but in vain. She had learned privately that Mr. Darcy did not want to play cards, and Mr. Hurst soon found even his direct request rejected. She assured him that no one intended to play, and the silence of the rest of the party on the subject seemed to back her up. Mr. Hurst therefore had nothing to do but stretch out on one of the sofas and go to sleep. Darcy picked up a book. Miss Bingley did the same, and Mrs. Hurst, mainly occupied with playing with her bracelets and rings, joined now and then in her brother's conversation with Miss Bennet.

Miss Bingley's attention was quite as much taken up with watching Mr. Darcy's progress through _his_ book as with reading her own, and she was constantly either asking him questions or glancing at his page. She could not draw him into any conversation, however—he merely answered her question and read on. At last, completely unable to enjoy her own book, which she had only chosen because it was the second volume of his, she gave a big yawn and said, "How pleasant it is to spend an evening like this! Really, there is no enjoyment like reading! How much sooner one tires of anything else! When I have a house of my own, I shall be miserable if I don't have an excellent library."
No one replied. She yawned again, tossed her book aside, and looked around the room for some amusement. Hearing her brother mention a ball to Miss Bennet, she turned suddenly toward him and said:

"By the way, Charles, are you really serious about hosting a dance at Netherfield? I would advise you, before you decide, to consider the wishes of the present company. I am much mistaken if there are not some among us for whom a ball would be more of a punishment than a pleasure."

"If you mean Darcy," cried her brother, "he can go to bed before it starts, if he likes. But as for the ball, it is quite settled, and as soon as the cook has made enough white soup, I shall send out my invitations."

"I would like balls infinitely better," she replied, "if they were conducted in a different way. There is something unbearably tedious about the usual routine. Surely it would be much more sensible if conversation, instead of dancing, were the main activity."
"Much more sensible, my dear Caroline, I dare say—but it would hardly feel like a ball."

Miss Bingley made no answer and soon got up and walked about the room. Her figure was elegant and she walked gracefully, but Darcy, at whom it was all aimed, remained stubbornly absorbed in his book. In desperation, she resolved on one more effort. Turning to Elizabeth, she said:
"Miss Eliza Bennet, let me persuade you to follow my example and take a turn about the room. I assure you it is very refreshing after sitting so long in one position."

Elizabeth was surprised but agreed at once. Miss Bingley also succeeded in her real objective: Mr. Darcy looked up. He was just as struck by this unexpected attention as Elizabeth herself, and he unconsciously closed his book. He was immediately invited to join them, but he declined, remarking that he could imagine only two reasons for their choosing to walk up and down the room together, and his joining them would interfere with either one. What could he mean? She was desperate to know—and asked Elizabeth whether she could make any sense of it.
"Not at all," was her answer. "But you can be sure he means to be harsh on us, and our best way of disappointing him will be to ask nothing about it."
Miss Bingley, however, was incapable of disappointing Mr. Darcy in anything and insisted on an explanation of his two motives.

"I have no objection whatsoever to explaining them," he said, as soon as she let him speak. "You either chose this way of passing the evening because you are close confidantes and have secrets to discuss, or because you are aware that your figures look best when you are walking. If it is the first, I would be completely in the way; and if it is the second, I can admire you much better from where I sit by the fire."
"Oh, shocking!" cried Miss Bingley. "I never heard anything so outrageous. How shall we punish him for such a remark?"
"Nothing easier, if you are so inclined," said Elizabeth. "We can all torment and punish one another. Tease him—laugh at him. As close as you are, you must know how to do it."

"But on my honor, I do _not_. I assure you that our closeness has not yet taught me _that_. Tease his calm temperament and composure! No, no—I think he could defy us there. And as for laughter, we will not embarrass ourselves, if you please, by trying to laugh without a reason. Mr. Darcy can congratulate himself."

"Mr. Darcy is not to be laughed at!" cried Elizabeth. "That is an uncommon advantage, and I hope it will stay that way, for it would be a great loss to _me_ to have many such acquaintances. I dearly love a laugh."

"Miss Bingley," said he, "has given me more credit than I deserve. The wisest and best of men—and even the wisest and best of their actions—can be made to look ridiculous by a person whose first aim in life is a joke."

"Certainly," replied Elizabeth, "there are such people, but I hope I am not one of _them_. I hope I never make fun of what is wise or good. Follies and nonsense, whims and inconsistencies _do_ amuse me, I admit, and I laugh at them whenever I can. But those, I suppose, are precisely what you are free of."
"Perhaps that is not possible for anyone. But it has been the purpose of my life to avoid those weaknesses that often make even a strong mind look ridiculous."
"Such as vanity and pride."
"Yes, vanity is a weakness indeed. But pride—where there is a genuine superiority of mind—pride will always be kept in check."
Elizabeth turned away to hide a smile.
"Your examination of Mr. Darcy is over, I assume," said Miss Bingley. "And what is the result?"
"I am entirely convinced that Mr. Darcy has no faults. He admits it himself without hesitation."

"No," said Darcy, "I have made no such claim. I have plenty of faults, but I hope they are not faults of understanding. My temperament I cannot guarantee. It is, I believe, too unforgiving—certainly too much so for the world's liking. I cannot forget the follies and vices of others as quickly as I should, nor offenses against myself. My feelings are not easily swayed by every attempt to manipulate them. My temperament might perhaps be called resentful. My good opinion, once lost, is lost forever."
"_That_ is a failing indeed!" cried Elizabeth. "Unforgiving resentment _is_ a flaw in anyone's character. But you have chosen your fault well. I really cannot _laugh_ at it. You are safe from me."
"There is, I believe, in every temperament a tendency toward some particular vice—a natural defect that not even the best upbringing can overcome."
"And _your_ defect is a tendency to hate everybody."
"And _yours_," he replied with a smile, "is to deliberately misunderstand them."
"Do let us have some music," cried Miss Bingley, tired of a conversation in which she had no part. "Louisa, you won't mind my waking Mr. Hurst."
Her sister had no objection at all, and the piano was opened. Darcy, after a few moments' reflection, was not sorry. He was beginning to feel the danger of paying Elizabeth too much attention.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Following an agreement between the sisters, Elizabeth wrote to her mother the next morning, asking that the carriage be sent for them that day. But Mrs. Bennet, who had counted on her daughters staying at Netherfield until the following Tuesday—which would round out Jane's full week there—could not bring herself to welcome them home before then. Her reply, therefore, was not what Elizabeth had hoped for, though Elizabeth was eager to get home. Mrs. Bennet sent word that they could not possibly have the carriage before Tuesday, and in a postscript added that if Mr. Bingley and his sister pressed them to stay longer, she could easily do without them. Elizabeth, however, was absolutely resolved against staying longer, nor did she much expect to be asked. Fearful, on the contrary, of being thought to have overstayed their welcome, she urged Jane to borrow Mr. Bingley's carriage immediately. At last it was agreed that they would mention their original plan to leave Netherfield that morning and make the request.

This announcement drew many expressions of concern, and enough was said about wishing them to stay at least until the next day to work on Jane, so their departure was postponed by a day. Miss Bingley then regretted having suggested the delay, for her jealousy and dislike of one sister far exceeded her affection for the other.

The master of the house heard with genuine regret that they were leaving so soon, and repeatedly tried to persuade Miss Bennet that it would not be safe—that she was not sufficiently recovered. But Jane was firm when she knew she was right.

To Mr. Darcy it was welcome news. Elizabeth had been at Netherfield long enough. She attracted him more than he liked, and Miss Bingley was rude to _her_ and more provocative than usual toward himself. He wisely resolved to be especially careful that no sign of admiration should _now_ escape him—nothing that could give her hope of influencing his happiness. He was aware that, if such an idea had been suggested to her, his behavior during this last day would carry significant weight in either confirming or crushing it. Holding firm to his purpose, he spoke barely ten words to her through the whole of Saturday. And though they were once left alone together for half an hour, he stuck conscientiously to his book and would not even look at her.

On Sunday, after the morning church service, the parting—welcome to almost everyone—took place. Miss Bingley's politeness to Elizabeth increased very rapidly at the end, as did her affection for Jane. When they separated, after assuring Jane that it would always give her pleasure to see her at either Longbourn or Netherfield, and embracing her tenderly, she even shook hands with Elizabeth. Elizabeth took leave of the whole party in the highest spirits.

They were not welcomed home very warmly by their mother. Mrs. Bennet was surprised at their coming, thought them very wrong to cause so much trouble, and was sure Jane would catch cold again. But their father, though very brief in expressing his pleasure, was genuinely glad to see them. He had felt their importance in the family circle. The evening conversation, when they were all gathered together, had lost much of its liveliness and almost all its sense during the absence of Jane and Elizabeth.

They found Mary, as usual, deep in the study of music theory and human nature, and had some new passages to admire and some new observations of well-worn morality to listen to. Catherine and Lydia had news of a different kind. Much had happened and much had been said in the regiment since the previous Wednesday. Several of the officers had recently dined with their uncle, a soldier had been flogged, and it had actually been hinted that Colonel Forster was going to be married.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: "I hope, my dear," said Mr. Bennet to his wife over breakfast the next morning, "that you have ordered a good dinner today, because I have reason to expect an addition to our party."
"Who do you mean, my dear? I don't know of anyone coming, unless Charlotte Lucas happens to stop by—and I hope _my_ dinners are good enough for her. I don't think she often sees the like at home."
"The person I speak of is a gentleman, and a stranger."

Mrs. Bennet's eyes sparkled. "A gentleman and a stranger! It must be Mr. Bingley. Why, Jane—you never said a word about this, you sly thing! Well, I shall be extremely glad to see Mr. Bingley. But—good heavens, how unlucky! There isn't a bit of fish to be had today. Lydia, my love, ring the bell. I must speak to Hill this instant."
"It is _not_ Mr. Bingley," said her husband. "It is a person whom I have never seen in my entire life."
This caused general astonishment, and he had the pleasure of being eagerly questioned by his wife and five daughters at once.

After amusing himself for a while with their curiosity, he explained: "About a month ago I received this letter, and about two weeks ago I answered it, for I thought it was a delicate matter that required prompt attention. It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house whenever he pleases."

"Oh, my dear," cried his wife, "I cannot bear to hear that mentioned. Please do not talk about that horrible man. I think it is the most unjust thing in the world that your estate should be taken away from your own children. And I am sure, if I had been you, I would have tried long ago to do something about it."

Jane and Elizabeth tried to explain to her the nature of an entail. They had often tried before, but it was a subject on which Mrs. Bennet was beyond the reach of reason. She continued to complain bitterly about the cruelty of settling an estate away from a family of five daughters in favor of a man nobody cared about.

"It certainly is a most unjust arrangement," said Mr. Bennet, "and nothing can clear Mr. Collins of the guilt of inheriting Longbourn. But if you will listen to his letter, you may perhaps be somewhat softened by his way of expressing himself."

"No, I'm sure I won't be. And I think it was very presumptuous of him to write to you at all, and very hypocritical. I hate such false friends. Why couldn't he keep on fighting with you, as his father did before him?"
"Well, indeed, he does seem to have had some family scruples on that point, as you will hear."
"Hunsford, near Westerham, Kent, _October 15th_.
"Dear Sir,

"The disagreement between yourself and my late honored father always caused me great uneasiness, and since I had the misfortune of losing him, I have frequently wished to heal the rift. For some time, however, I held back, fearing it might seem disrespectful to his memory for me to be on good terms with anyone with whom he had always chosen to be at odds."—'There, Mrs. Bennet.'—"My mind, however, is now made up on the matter. Having been ordained at Easter, I have been so fortunate as to be distinguished by the patronage of the Right Honorable Lady Catherine de Bourgh, widow of Sir Lewis de Bourgh, whose generosity and kindness has given me the valuable parish of this village, where it shall be my earnest effort to conduct myself with grateful respect toward her Ladyship, and to be always ready to perform those services that the Church of England requires. As a clergyman, moreover, I feel it my duty to promote and establish the blessing of peace in all families within my influence, and on these grounds I flatter myself that my present gesture of goodwill is highly commendable, and that the fact of my being next in line for the Longbourn estate will be kindly overlooked on your side, and will not lead you to reject this olive branch. I cannot help but feel concerned at being the means of disadvantaging your lovely daughters, and I beg leave to apologize for it, as well as to assure you of my willingness to make them every possible amends—but more on this later. If you have no objection to receiving me in your house, I propose to have the pleasure of calling on you and your family on Monday, November 18th, by four o'clock, and shall probably impose on your hospitality until the following Saturday week, which I can do without any inconvenience, as Lady Catherine is far from objecting to my occasional absence on a Sunday, provided that another clergyman covers the services. I remain, dear sir, with respectful regards to your wife and daughters, your well-wisher and friend,
"WILLIAM COLLINS."

"At four o'clock, then, we may expect this peacemaking gentleman," said Mr. Bennet, folding up the letter. "He seems to be a most conscientious and polite young man, upon my word, and I have no doubt he will prove a valuable acquaintance—especially if Lady Catherine should be kind enough to let him visit us again."
"There is some sense in what he says about the girls, though, and if he is willing to make them some kind of amends, I shall not be the one to discourage him."
"Though it is difficult," said Jane, "to guess how he could mean to make the reparations he thinks we are owed, the wish is certainly to his credit."
Elizabeth was chiefly struck by his extraordinary reverence for Lady Catherine, and his kind intention of baptizing, marrying, and burying his parishioners whenever required.

"He must be very odd, I think," she said. "I cannot figure him out. There is something very pompous in his writing style. And what can he mean by apologizing for being next in the entail? We can hardly suppose he would change it if he could. Can he be a sensible man, Father?"
"No, my dear, I think not. I have great hopes of finding him quite the opposite. There is a mixture of groveling and self-importance in his letter that is very promising. I can't wait to see him."
"In terms of composition," said Mary, "his letter does not seem faulty. The olive branch metaphor is perhaps not entirely original, but I think it is well expressed."

To Catherine and Lydia, neither the letter nor its writer were the least bit interesting. It was practically impossible that their cousin would arrive in a red coat, and it had been some weeks since they had found any pleasure in the company of a man in any other color. As for their mother, Mr. Collins's letter had done away with much of her ill feeling, and she was preparing to see him with a degree of calm that astonished her husband and daughters.

Mr. Collins arrived exactly on time and was received very politely by the whole family. Mr. Bennet said little, but the ladies were ready enough to talk, and Mr. Collins seemed neither to need encouragement nor to be inclined toward silence himself. He was a tall, heavy-looking young man of twenty-five. His manner was solemn and stiff, and his behavior very formal. He had not been seated long before he complimented Mrs. Bennet on having such a fine family of daughters, said he had heard much of their beauty, but that in this case, reputation had fallen short of the truth, and added that he had no doubt she would see them all properly married in due time. This flattery was not much to the taste of some of his listeners, but Mrs. Bennet, who never turned down a compliment, answered readily:
"You are very kind, sir, I'm sure, and I wish with all my heart it may turn out that way—because otherwise they will be left with very little. Things are arranged so strangely."
"You are referring, perhaps, to the entail of this estate."

"Oh yes, sir, I am indeed. It is a terrible thing for my poor girls, you must admit. Not that I mean to blame _you_, for such things, I know, are all a matter of chance in this world. There is no telling where estates will end up once they are entailed."

"I am very aware, madam, of the hardship to my fair cousins, and could say much on the subject, but I am careful not to appear too forward. I can assure the young ladies, however, that I have come prepared to admire them. At present I will not say more, but perhaps, when we are better acquainted—"

He was interrupted by a call to dinner, and the girls exchanged knowing smiles. They were not the only objects of Mr. Collins's admiration. The entrance hall, the dining room, and all its furniture were examined and praised, and his approval of everything would have warmed Mrs. Bennet's heart, if not for the irritating suspicion that he was viewing it all as his own future property. The dinner, too, was highly praised, and he asked to know which of his fair cousins was responsible for the excellent cooking. But here he was set straight by Mrs. Bennet, who informed him somewhat sharply that they were perfectly capable of keeping a good cook, and that her daughters had nothing to do in the kitchen. He begged her pardon for having offended her. In a softened tone she declared herself not at all offended, but he continued to apologize for about fifteen minutes.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: During dinner, Mr. Bennet hardly spoke at all, but when the servants had left, he thought it time for some conversation with his guest. He started a topic on which he expected Mr. Collins to shine, by remarking that he seemed very fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh's attention to his wishes and consideration for his comfort appeared quite extraordinary. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen better. Mr. Collins was eloquent in her praise. The subject raised him to even greater solemnity than usual, and with a very important air he declared that he had never in his life seen such behavior in a person of rank—such friendliness and gracious condescension as he had personally experienced from Lady Catherine. She had been kind enough to approve both the sermons he had already had the honor of preaching before her. She had also invited him to dine at Rosings twice, and had sent for him just the previous Saturday to fill out her card table for the evening. Lady Catherine was considered proud by many people, he knew, but _he_ had never seen anything but friendliness in her. She had always spoken to him as she would to any other gentleman. She had no objection to his mixing with the local community, nor to his leaving his parish occasionally for a week or two to visit relatives. She had even gone so far as to advise him to marry as soon as possible, provided he chose wisely, and had once paid a visit to his humble parsonage, where she had thoroughly approved all the changes he had made, and had even suggested a few of her own—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

"That is all very proper and polite, I'm sure," said Mrs. Bennet, "and I dare say she is a very pleasant woman. It's a pity that great ladies in general are not more like her. Does she live near you, sir?"
"The garden of my humble home is separated only by a lane from Rosings Park, her Ladyship's residence."
"I think you said she was a widow, sir? Does she have any family?"
"She has only one daughter, the heiress of Rosings, and of very extensive property."
"Ah," cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, "then she is better off than many girls. And what sort of young lady is she? Is she pretty?"

"She is a most charming young lady indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in terms of true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the best-looking women anywhere—because there is something in her features that marks her as a woman of distinguished birth. She is unfortunately of a delicate constitution, which has prevented her from making the progress in accomplishments that she would otherwise have certainly achieved, as I am told by the lady who oversaw her education and who still lives with them. But she is perfectly lovely, and often honors my humble home by driving past in her little carriage and ponies."
"Has she been presented at court? I don't recall her name among the ladies there."

"Her poor state of health unfortunately prevents her from going to London, and thereby, as I told Lady Catherine myself one day, has deprived the British Court of its brightest jewel. Her Ladyship seemed pleased with the idea, and you can imagine that I am happy at every opportunity to offer those little delicate compliments that are always welcome to ladies. I have more than once remarked to Lady Catherine that her charming daughter seemed born to be a duchess, and that the highest rank, instead of giving her prestige, would be graced by her. These are the sort of little things that please her Ladyship, and it is the kind of attention that I consider myself especially obliged to pay."

"You judge very wisely," said Mr. Bennet, "and it is fortunate for you that you have the talent for flattery with such delicacy. May I ask whether these charming remarks come from the impulse of the moment, or are the result of advance planning?"

"They arise mainly from whatever is happening at the time—though I do sometimes amuse myself by thinking up and arranging little elegant compliments that may suit ordinary occasions. I always try to give them as spontaneous an air as possible."

Mr. Bennet's expectations were fully met. His cousin was as ridiculous as he had hoped, and he listened to him with the keenest enjoyment while maintaining the most composed expression—requiring no partner in his amusement other than an occasional glance at Elizabeth.
By teatime, however, the dose had been enough, and Mr. Bennet was glad to bring his guest back into the drawing room. When tea was over, he was glad to invite him

to read aloud to the ladies. Mr. Collins readily agreed, and a book was produced. But upon seeing it—for everything about it proclaimed it to be a novel from a lending library—he recoiled and, begging their pardon, declared that he never read novels. Kitty stared at him, and Lydia exclaimed. Other books were produced, and after some deliberation he chose Fordyce's Sermons. Lydia's mouth fell open as he opened the volume, and before he had, in a very monotone and solemn voice, read three pages, she interrupted him with:

"Do you know, Mama, that Uncle Philips is talking about letting Richard go? And if he does, Colonel Forster will hire him. My aunt told me so herself on Saturday. I shall walk to Meryton tomorrow to hear more about it and to ask when Mr. Denny comes back from town."
Lydia was told by her two eldest sisters to be quiet, but Mr. Collins, very much offended, put aside his book and said:

"I have often noticed how little interest young ladies take in serious books, though written solely for their benefit. It amazes me, I confess, for surely there can be nothing so beneficial to them as moral instruction. But I will no longer impose on my young cousin."

Then, turning to Mr. Bennet, he offered himself as an opponent at backgammon. Mr. Bennet accepted the challenge, remarking that Mr. Collins acted very wisely in leaving the girls to their own trivial amusements. Mrs. Bennet and her daughters apologized most politely for Lydia's interruption and promised it would not happen again if he would resume his book. But Mr. Collins, after assuring them that he bore his young cousin no ill will and would never take her behavior as an insult, seated himself at another table with Mr. Bennet and prepared for backgammon.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Mr. Collins was not a clever man, and his natural limitations had been little helped by education or social experience—the greatest part of his life having been spent under the thumb of an ignorant and stingy father. Though he had attended one of the universities, he had merely served the required terms without making any useful connections. The strict upbringing his father had imposed had originally given him great meekness, but this was now considerably offset by the vanity of a feeble mind living in isolation, combined with the self-important feelings that came from early and unexpected success. A fortunate recommendation had brought him to Lady Catherine de Bourgh's notice when the parish of Hunsford became vacant, and the awe he felt for her high rank, his reverence for her as his patroness, combined with a very high opinion of himself, his authority as a clergyman, and his rights as a rector, made him altogether a peculiar mix of pride and groveling, self-importance and humility.

Now that he had a good house and a very comfortable income, he intended to marry. In seeking a reconciliation with the Longbourn family, he had a wife in mind, as he planned to choose one of the daughters—if he found them as attractive and pleasant as common report suggested. This was his plan for making amends for inheriting their father's estate, and he thought it an excellent one—perfectly suitable and appropriate, and extraordinarily generous and selfless on his part.

His plan did not change upon seeing them. Miss Bennet's lovely face confirmed his intentions and established all his strictest ideas about the rights of the eldest. For the first evening, _she_ was his definite choice. The next morning, however, brought a change, for in a fifteen-minute private conversation with Mrs. Bennet before breakfast—which began with his parsonage house and led naturally to his hope that a wife for it might be found at Longbourn—she produced, amid very encouraging smiles and general approval, a warning against the very Jane he had chosen. "As for her _younger_ daughters, she could not say—she could not be certain—but she did not _know_ of any attachment. Her _eldest_ daughter, however, she felt obliged to mention—she felt it her duty to hint—was likely to be engaged very soon."
Mr. Collins had only to switch from Jane to Elizabeth—and it was quickly done—done while Mrs. Bennet was poking the fire. Elizabeth, next to Jane in both age and beauty, naturally succeeded her.
Mrs. Bennet cherished this hint, trusting that she might soon have two daughters married. And the man she could not bear to hear mentioned the day before was now firmly in her good graces.

Lydia's plan to walk to Meryton was not forgotten. Every sister except Mary agreed to go, and Mr. Collins was to accompany them—at Mr. Bennet's request, for he was desperate to be rid of him and have his library to himself. Mr. Collins had followed him there after breakfast and had remained, supposedly reading one of the largest volumes in the collection, but in reality talking non-stop to Mr. Bennet about his house and garden at Hunsford. This greatly disturbed Mr. Bennet. In his library, he had always been assured of peace and quiet, and though he was prepared, as he told Elizabeth, to encounter foolishness and vanity in every other room in the house, he was used to being free of them there. His invitation for Mr. Collins to join his daughters on their walk was therefore very prompt. And Mr. Collins, being in fact much better suited to walking than reading, was extremely pleased to close his large book and go.

The time passed with pompous small talk on his side and polite agreement on that of his cousins, until they reached Meryton. The younger girls' attention was then no longer his to command. Their eyes immediately began scanning the street for officers, and nothing less than a very stylish hat or a genuinely new fabric in a shop window could distract them.

But every lady's attention was soon captured by a young man they had never seen before, very gentlemanly in appearance, walking with an officer on the other side of the street. The officer was the very Mr. Denny about whose return from London Lydia had come to inquire, and he bowed as they passed. Everyone was struck by the stranger's bearing, and everyone wondered who he could be. Kitty and Lydia, determined to find out if possible, led the way across the street on the pretense of wanting something in a shop opposite. They had fortunately just reached the pavement when the two gentlemen, turning back, arrived at the same spot. Mr. Denny addressed them directly and asked permission to introduce his friend, Mr. Wickham, who had returned with him from London the day before and, he was happy to say, had accepted a commission in their regiment. This was exactly as it should be—for the young man needed only a uniform to make him completely charming. His appearance was very much in his favor: he had all the best features of good looks, a fine face, a good figure, and very pleasing manners. The introduction was followed on his side by an easy readiness of conversation—perfectly proper and unassuming—and the whole group was still standing and talking together very pleasantly when the sound of horses drew their attention, and Darcy and Bingley were seen riding down the street. Recognizing the ladies in the group, the two gentlemen came directly toward them and exchanged the usual greetings. Bingley was the main speaker, and Miss Bennet the main focus. He was on his way to Longbourn, he said, specifically to ask about her health. Mr. Darcy confirmed this with a bow and was beginning to resolve not to stare at Elizabeth when his eyes were suddenly caught by the sight of the stranger. Elizabeth, happening to see both their faces as they looked at each other, was astonished at the effect of the meeting. Both changed color—one went white, the other red. Mr. Wickham, after a few moments, touched his hat in greeting—a gesture Mr. Darcy barely deigned to return. What could it mean? It was impossible to guess—and impossible not to want to know.
A minute later, Mr. Bingley, without seeming to have noticed what had passed, said goodbye and rode on with his friend.

Mr. Denny and Mr. Wickham walked with the young ladies to the door of Mr. Philips's house and then took their leave, despite Lydia's urgent pleas that they come in, and even despite Mrs. Philips throwing open the parlor window and loudly seconding the invitation.

Mrs. Philips was always glad to see her nieces, and the two eldest, given their recent absence, were especially welcome. She was eagerly expressing her surprise at their sudden return home—which, since their own carriage had not come for them, she would have known nothing about, had she not happened to see Mr. Jones's shop boy in the street, who told her they were not to send any more medicine to Netherfield because the Miss Bennets had left—when her attention was claimed for Mr. Collins, whom Jane introduced to her. She received him with her very best manners, which he returned with even more, apologizing for his intrusion without any previous acquaintance—though he could not help hoping, he said, that his relationship to the young ladies who introduced him might justify it. Mrs. Philips was quite overwhelmed by such excessive politeness. But her contemplation of one stranger was soon interrupted by questions and exclamations about the other, of whom she could only tell her nieces what they already knew—that Mr. Denny had brought him from London, and that he was to have a lieutenant's commission in the regiment. She had been watching him for the last hour, she said, as he walked up and down the street. Had Mr. Wickham appeared, Kitty and Lydia would certainly have continued this activity, but unfortunately no one now passed the windows except a few officers, who in comparison with the stranger had become "stupid, disagreeable fellows." Some of them were to dine with the Philipses the next day, and their aunt promised to have her husband call on Mr. Wickham and invite him too, if the Longbourn family would come in the evening. This was agreed to, and Mrs. Philips promised they would have a nice comfortable noisy game of lottery tickets and a little hot supper afterward. The prospect of such delights was very cheering, and they parted in high spirits. Mr. Collins repeated his apologies on leaving and was assured, with tireless politeness, that they were completely unnecessary.

As they walked home, Elizabeth told Jane what she had seen pass between the two gentlemen. But though Jane would have defended either or both had they appeared to be in the wrong, she could no more explain such behavior than her sister could.

Mr. Collins, on his return, greatly pleased Mrs. Bennet by praising Mrs. Philips's manners and politeness. He declared that, apart from Lady Catherine and her daughter, he had never seen a more elegant woman—for she had not only received him with the utmost courtesy but had even specifically included him in her invitation for the next evening, although she had never met him before. Something, he supposed, might be due to his connection with the family, but he had never in his entire life been treated with so much attention.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Since no one objected to the young people's evening engagement with their aunt, and all of Mr. Collins's reservations about leaving Mr. and Mrs. Bennet for a single evening during his visit were firmly overruled, the carriage conveyed him and his five cousins to Meryton at a suitable hour. The girls had the pleasure of learning, as they entered the drawing room, that Mr. Wickham had accepted their uncle's invitation and was already in the house.

Once this information was shared and they had all taken their seats, Mr. Collins was free to look around and admire. He was so impressed by the size and furnishings of the room that he declared he might almost have thought himself in the small summer breakfast room at Rosings—a comparison that did not at first mean much to anyone. But when Mrs. Philips learned from him what Rosings was and who owned it, and when she had listened to the description of just one of Lady Catherine's drawing rooms and discovered that the fireplace mantel alone had cost eight hundred pounds, she felt the full force of the compliment and would hardly have objected to a comparison with the housekeeper's room.

In describing to her all the grandeur of Lady Catherine and her mansion, with occasional detours to praise his own humble home and its improvements, Mr. Collins was happily occupied until the gentlemen joined them. He found in Mrs. Philips a very attentive listener, whose estimation of his importance grew with every word, and who was already planning to share it all with her neighbors as soon as possible. For the girls, who could not bear to listen to their cousin, and who had nothing to do but wish for a piano and examine their own mediocre imitation china on the mantelpiece, the wait seemed very long. At last, however, it was over. The gentlemen arrived, and when Mr. Wickham walked into the room, Elizabeth felt that she had neither been looking at him before nor thinking of him since with the slightest degree of unreasonable admiration. The officers of the regiment were generally a very respectable, gentlemanly group, and the best of them were at this party—but Mr. Wickham was as far above them all in looks, bearing, and manner as _they_ were above the broad-faced, stuffy Uncle Philips, breathing port wine, who followed them into the room.

Mr. Wickham was the lucky man toward whom nearly every female eye was turned, and Elizabeth was the lucky woman next to whom he finally sat down. The pleasant way he immediately fell into conversation—though it was only about the wet weather and the likelihood of a rainy season—made her feel that the most ordinary, dullest topic could be made interesting by a skilled speaker.

With such rivals for the ladies' attention as Mr. Wickham and the officers, Mr. Collins seemed to fade into insignificance. To the young ladies he was certainly nothing at all. But he still had a willing listener in Mrs. Philips, who kept him generously supplied with coffee and muffins.
When the card tables were set up, he had a chance to return the favor by sitting down to whist.
"I know little of the game at present," he said, "but I shall be glad to improve, for in my position in life—" Mrs. Philips was very grateful for his willingness but could not wait for his reason.

Mr. Wickham did not play whist, and was received with ready delight at the other table between Elizabeth and Lydia. At first there seemed a danger of Lydia monopolizing him entirely, for she was a most determined talker. But being equally passionate about lottery tickets, she soon became too absorbed in the game—too busy placing bets and exclaiming over prizes—to pay attention to anyone in particular. Allowing for the normal demands of the game, Mr. Wickham was therefore free to talk to Elizabeth, and she was very willing to listen, though what she most wanted to hear—the history of his acquaintance with Mr. Darcy—she could not expect to be told. She did not even dare mention that gentleman. Her curiosity, however, was unexpectedly satisfied. Mr. Wickham raised the subject himself. He asked how far Netherfield was from Meryton, and after receiving her answer, asked in a hesitant way how long Mr. Darcy had been staying there.
"About a month," said Elizabeth. Then, unwilling to let the subject drop, she added, "He is a man of very large property in Derbyshire, I understand."

"Yes," replied Wickham. "His estate there is a magnificent one. A clear ten thousand a year. You could not have met with a person better able to give you information on that subject than myself—for I have been connected with his family in a special way since infancy."
Elizabeth could not help looking surprised.
"You may well be surprised, Miss Bennet, at such a statement, after seeing, as you probably did, the very cold manner of our meeting yesterday. Are you well acquainted with Mr. Darcy?"
"As well as I ever wish to be," cried Elizabeth warmly. "I spent four days in the same house with him, and I find him very disagreeable."

"I have no right to give _my_ opinion," said Wickham, "on whether he is agreeable or not. I am not qualified to form one. I have known him too long and too well to be a fair judge. It is impossible for _me_ to be impartial. But I believe your opinion of him would generally astonish people—and perhaps you would not express it quite so strongly anywhere else. Here you are among your own family."

"I assure you I say no more _here_ than I would in any house in the neighborhood, except Netherfield. He is not at all liked in Hertfordshire. Everyone is disgusted by his pride. You will not find him spoken of favorably by anyone."

"I cannot pretend to be sorry," said Wickham after a brief pause, "that he or any man should not be valued beyond what he deserves. But with _him_ I believe it rarely happens. The world is blinded by his fortune and status, or intimidated by his haughty and imposing manner, and sees him only as he chooses to be seen."
"I would have judged him, even from _my_ slight acquaintance, to be a bad-tempered man."
Wickham only shook his head.
"I wonder," he said at the next opportunity, "whether he is likely to be in this area much longer."
"I don't know at all, but I _heard_ nothing about his leaving when I was at Netherfield. I hope your plans for the regiment won't be affected by his being in the neighborhood."

"Oh no—it is not for _me_ to be driven away by Mr. Darcy. If _he_ wishes to avoid seeing _me_, he must leave. We are not on friendly terms, and it always pains me to meet him, but I have no reason for avoiding _him_ that I couldn't declare to the whole world—a sense of being very badly used, and the most painful regret at his being what he is. His father, Miss Bennet, the late Mr. Darcy, was one of the best men who ever lived and the truest friend I ever had. I can never be in the company of this Mr. Darcy without being pierced to the heart by a thousand tender memories. His treatment of me has been outrageous. But I truly believe I could forgive him anything and everything rather than his betrayal of his father's wishes and disgrace to his father's memory."
Elizabeth found the subject more and more compelling and listened with all her heart. But its delicate nature prevented her from asking more.

Mr. Wickham began to speak on more general topics—Meryton, the neighborhood, the local society—appearing highly pleased with everything he had seen, and speaking of the latter with gentle but unmistakable charm.

"It was the prospect of constant society, and good society," he added, "that was my main reason for joining the regiment. I know it to be a most respectable, agreeable group, and my friend Denny tempted me further with his description of their present quarters and the excellent hospitality and fine acquaintances Meryton had provided them. Society, I admit, is necessary to me. I have been a disappointed man, and my spirits cannot bear solitude. I _must_ have activity and company. A military life is not what I was meant for, but circumstances have now made it the right choice. The church _ought_ to have been my profession—I was raised for it—and I should by now have been in possession of an extremely valuable parish, if it had pleased the gentleman we were just speaking of."
"Really!"

"Yes—the late Mr. Darcy left me the next appointment to the best parish in his gift. He was my godfather and was extraordinarily attached to me. I cannot do justice to his kindness. He meant to provide for me generously and believed he had done so. But when the parish became vacant, it was given to someone else."
"Good heavens!" cried Elizabeth. "But how could _that_ be? How could his will be ignored? Why didn't you seek legal recourse?"

"There was just enough informality in the wording of the bequest to give me no legal standing. An honorable man could not have doubted the intention, but Mr. Darcy chose to doubt it—or to treat it as merely a conditional recommendation, and to claim that I had forfeited all right to it through extravagance, recklessness—in short, anything or nothing. What is certain is that the parish became vacant two years ago, exactly when I was old enough to hold it, and it was given to another man. Equally certain is that I cannot accuse myself of having done anything to deserve losing it. I have a warm, unguarded temperament and may perhaps have sometimes spoken my opinion _of_ him, and _to_ him, too freely. I can think of nothing worse. But the fact is that we are very different sorts of men, and that he hates me."
"This is outrageous! He deserves to be publicly disgraced."
"Someday he _will_ be—but it will not be by _me_. As long as I remember his father, I can never defy or expose _him_."
Elizabeth admired him for such feelings, and thought him even more handsome as he expressed them.
"But what," she said after a pause, "could have been his motive? What could have made him behave so cruelly?"

"A deep, deliberate dislike of me—a dislike that I can only attribute in part to jealousy. Had the late Mr. Darcy liked me less, his son might have tolerated me better. But his father's extraordinary attachment to me irritated him, I believe, from a very early age. He did not have the temperament to bear the kind of rivalry between us—the kind of preference that was often shown to me."

"I had not thought Mr. Darcy as bad as this. Though I have never liked him, I had not thought so terribly of him. I had assumed he simply looked down on his fellow creatures in general, but I did not suspect him capable of such malicious revenge, such injustice, such inhumanity!"

After a few minutes' thought, however, she continued, "I _do_ remember him boasting one day at Netherfield about how unforgiving his resentments are—about having a temper that never relents. His character must be terrible."
"I will not trust myself on the subject," replied Wickham. "_I_ can hardly be fair to him."

Elizabeth was again deep in thought and after a time exclaimed, "To treat in such a way the godson, the friend, the favorite of his father!" She could have added, "A young man, too, like _you_, whose very face is proof of being good." But she contented herself with: "And someone who had probably been his companion from childhood, connected together, as I think you said, in the closest way."

"We were born in the same parish, within the same estate. The greatest part of our youth was spent together—living in the same house, sharing the same activities, the objects of the same fatherly care. _My_ father began life in the profession that your uncle, Mr. Philips, seems to do so much credit to, but he gave up everything to be of service to the late Mr. Darcy and devoted all his time to managing the Pemberley property. He was held in the highest regard by Mr. Darcy—the most intimate, trusted friend. Mr. Darcy often acknowledged that he owed a great debt to my father's active management. And when, just before my father's death, Mr. Darcy made him a voluntary promise to provide for me, I am convinced he felt it to be as much a debt of gratitude to _him_ as of affection to myself."

"How strange!" cried Elizabeth. "How despicable! I would have thought that Mr. Darcy's very pride would have made him honest with you. If for no better reason, he should have been too proud to be dishonest—for dishonest I must call it."

"It _is_ remarkable," replied Wickham, "for almost everything he does can be traced to pride—and pride has often been his best quality. It has brought him closer to virtue than any other feeling. But none of us are consistent, and in his treatment of me there were impulses even stronger than pride."
"Can such terrible pride as his ever have done him good?"

"Yes—it has often led him to be generous, to give his money freely, to offer hospitality, to help his tenants, and to aid the poor. Family pride, and _filial_ pride—for he is very proud of what his father was—have done this. The desire not to disgrace his family, not to fall below the standards expected, or to lose the influence of the Pemberley name, is a powerful motivator. He also has _brotherly_ pride, which, combined with _some_ brotherly affection, makes him a very devoted and careful guardian of his sister. You will generally hear him praised as the most attentive and best of brothers."
"What sort of girl is Miss Darcy?"

He shook his head. "I wish I could call her pleasant. It pains me to speak badly of a Darcy, but she is too much like her brother—very, very proud. As a child, she was affectionate and sweet and extremely fond of me, and I spent hours and hours entertaining her. But she is nothing to me now. She is a pretty girl, about fifteen or sixteen, and I understand she is very accomplished. Since her father's death, her home has been London, where a woman lives with her and oversees her education."
After many pauses and many attempts at other topics, Elizabeth could not help returning once more to the first, saying:

"I am amazed at his friendship with Mr. Bingley. How can Mr. Bingley, who seems like good nature itself and who I really believe is genuinely kind, be friends with such a man? How can they possibly get along? Do you know Mr. Bingley?"
"Not at all."
"He is a sweet-tempered, pleasant, charming man. He cannot possibly know what Mr. Darcy is really like."

"Probably not. But Mr. Darcy can be charming when he wants to be. He is not lacking in ability. He can be good company if he thinks it worth the effort. Among those who are his equals in status, he is a very different man from what he is to those less fortunate. His pride never leaves him, but with the wealthy he is open-minded, fair, sincere, sensible, honorable, and perhaps even agreeable—allowing something for fortune and appearance."

When the whist game broke up shortly afterward, the players gathered around the other table, and Mr. Collins positioned himself between his cousin Elizabeth and Mrs. Philips. The usual questions about how he had done were asked by Mrs. Philips. He had not done well at all—he had lost every hand. But when Mrs. Philips began to express her concern, he assured her with earnest solemnity that it was of no importance at all, that he considered the money a mere trifle, and begged her not to worry.

"I know very well, madam," he said, "that when people sit down to a card table they must accept these things. And fortunately I am not in circumstances where five shillings matters. There are, no doubt, many who cannot say the same—but thanks to Lady Catherine de Bourgh, I am far above the need to worry about such small amounts."
Mr. Wickham's attention was caught, and after watching Mr. Collins for a few moments, he asked Elizabeth in a low voice whether her relatives were closely acquainted with the de Bourgh family.
"Lady Catherine de Bourgh," she replied, "has very recently given him a parish. I hardly know how Mr. Collins first came to her attention, but he certainly has not known her long."
"You know, of course, that Lady Catherine de Bourgh and Lady Anne Darcy were sisters—which means she is aunt to the present Mr. Darcy."
"No, indeed, I did not. I knew nothing at all about Lady Catherine's connections. I had never heard of her existence until the day before yesterday."
"Her daughter, Miss de Bourgh, will have a very large fortune, and it is widely believed that she and her cousin will marry and unite the two estates."

This information made Elizabeth smile, as she thought of poor Miss Bingley. How useless all her attentions must be—useless her affection for his sister and her praise of himself—if he was already destined for another.

"Mr. Collins," she said, "speaks very highly of both Lady Catherine and her daughter. But from some details he has shared about her Ladyship, I suspect his gratitude is misleading him, and that despite her being his patroness, she is an arrogant, conceited woman."

"I believe she is both, to a great degree," replied Wickham. "I have not seen her for many years, but I remember well that I never liked her and that her manner was domineering and rude. She has a reputation for being remarkably clever and intelligent, but I rather think she owes part of that reputation to her rank and fortune, part to her commanding manner, and the rest to the pride of her nephew, who insists that everyone connected with him should be considered first-rate."

Elizabeth agreed that he had given a very reasonable account of it, and they continued talking together with mutual enjoyment until supper ended the card games and gave the other ladies their share of Mr. Wickham's attention. There was no possibility of conversation in the noise of Mrs. Philips's supper party, but his manners recommended him to everyone. Whatever he said was said well, and whatever he did was done gracefully. Elizabeth left with her head full of him. She could think of nothing but Mr. Wickham and what he had told her all the way home. But there was no time to even mention his name on the journey, for neither Lydia nor Mr. Collins were silent for a moment. Lydia talked constantly about lottery tickets, about the money she had lost and won; and Mr. Collins, describing the politeness of Mr. and Mrs. Philips, insisting that he did not in the least mind his losses at whist, listing every dish at supper, and repeatedly worrying that he was crowding his cousins, had more to say than he could manage before the carriage stopped at Longbourn House.

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The next day, Elizabeth told Jane what had passed between Mr. Wickham and herself. Jane listened with astonishment and concern—she could not believe that Mr. Darcy could be so unworthy of Mr. Bingley's friendship, and yet it was not in her nature to question the honesty of a young man as pleasant-looking as Wickham. The possibility that he had really suffered such cruelty was enough to touch all her tender feelings. Nothing remained, therefore, but to think well of them both, to defend each one's behavior, and to put down to accident or misunderstanding anything that could not otherwise be explained.

"They have both," she said, "been misled in some way, I'm sure, though we can't imagine how. Biased people have perhaps misrepresented each to the other. In short, it is impossible for us to guess the causes or circumstances that may have turned them against each other, without real fault on either side."

"Very true indeed. And now, my dear Jane, what do you have to say on behalf of the biased people who have probably been involved? Do clear _them_ too, or we shall be forced to think badly of somebody."

"Laugh all you like, but you won't laugh me out of my opinion. My dearest Lizzy, just think how disgracefully it reflects on Mr. Darcy to treat his father's favorite this way—someone his father had promised to provide for. It is impossible. No man with common decency, no man who valued his reputation, could be capable of it. Can his closest friends really be so thoroughly fooled by him? Oh, no."

"I can much more easily believe that Mr. Bingley has been deceived than that Mr. Wickham would invent the kind of history he told me last night—names, facts, everything stated openly. If it isn't true, let Mr. Darcy deny it. Besides, there was truth in his face."
"It is difficult indeed—it is distressing. One doesn't know what to think."
"Forgive me—one knows _exactly_ what to think."
But Jane could think with certainty on only one point: that Mr. Bingley, if he _had_ been deceived, would suffer greatly when the affair became public.

The two young ladies were called from the garden, where this conversation took place, by the arrival of some of the very people they had been discussing. Mr. Bingley and his sisters came to deliver their personal invitation to the long-expected ball at Netherfield, which was set for the following Tuesday. The two ladies were delighted to see their dear friend Jane again, said it felt like ages since they had met, and repeatedly asked what she had been doing since their last meeting. To the rest of the family they paid little attention—avoiding Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, saying not much to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. They were soon gone, rising from their seats with a haste that surprised their brother, and hurrying off as if eager to escape Mrs. Bennet's hospitality.

The prospect of the Netherfield ball was extremely exciting to every female in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to see it as given in honor of her eldest daughter, and was particularly flattered by receiving the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself rather than a formal card. Jane pictured a happy evening in the company of her two friends and their brother's attentions. Elizabeth thought with pleasure of dancing a great deal with Mr. Wickham, and of seeing confirmation of everything in Mr. Darcy's look and behavior. The happiness that Catherine and Lydia anticipated depended less on any single event or particular person—for though each of them, like Elizabeth, planned to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was by no means the only partner who could satisfy them, and a ball was, in any case, a ball. Even Mary could assure her family that she had no objection to it.

"As long as I can have my mornings to myself," she said, "that is enough. I think it is no sacrifice to occasionally join in evening entertainment. Society has claims on us all, and I consider myself someone who believes intervals of recreation and amusement are good for everyone."

Elizabeth's spirits were so high that, though she did not often speak to Mr. Collins unnecessarily, she could not help asking him whether he planned to accept Mr. Bingley's invitation, and if so, whether he would consider it proper to join in the dancing. She was rather surprised to find that he had no reservations whatever on that point, and was very far from fearing a scolding from either the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh for venturing to dance.

"I am by no means of the opinion, I assure you," he said, "that a ball of this kind, given by a young man of character for respectable people, can have any harmful tendency. And I am so far from objecting to dancing myself that I hope to have the honor of dancing with all my fair cousins during the evening. I take this opportunity to request yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances especially—a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the right reason, and not to any disrespect toward her."

Elizabeth felt completely trapped. She had fully intended to be asked by Wickham for those very dances, and to have Mr. Collins instead! Her liveliness had never been worse timed. There was nothing to be done about it, however. Mr. Wickham's happiness and her own must be put off a little longer, and Mr. Collins's request was accepted with as much grace as she could manage. She was not made any happier by his gallantry when it suggested something more. It now struck her for the first time that _she_ had been selected from among her sisters as worthy of being the mistress of Hunsford Parsonage, and of helping to fill a card table at Rosings when more desirable guests were unavailable. The idea quickly became a conviction as she observed his increasing attentions toward her and his frequent attempts to compliment her wit and liveliness. And though she was more astonished than flattered by the effect of her charms, it was not long before her mother let her know that the prospect of their marriage was extremely pleasing to _her_. Elizabeth, however, chose not to take the hint, knowing well that a serious argument would follow any reply. Mr. Collins might never actually propose, and until he did, it was pointless to fight about him.

If there had not been a Netherfield ball to prepare for and talk about, the younger Bennet sisters would have been in a sorry state at this time, for from the day of the invitation to the day of the ball, there was such a steady run of rain that they could not walk to Meryton once. No aunt, no officers, no news could be sought out; even the shoe decorations for Netherfield had to be obtained by someone else. Even Elizabeth might have found her patience tested by weather that completely prevented her from improving her acquaintance with Mr. Wickham. And nothing less than a dance on Tuesday could have made such a Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday bearable to Kitty and Lydia.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Until Elizabeth entered the drawing room at Netherfield and looked in vain for Mr. Wickham among the cluster of red coats assembled there, it had never occurred to her that he might not be present. The certainty of seeing him had not been shaken by any of the thoughts that might reasonably have worried her. She had dressed with more than usual care and arrived in the highest spirits, planning to conquer whatever remained unconquered of his heart—trusting that it was nothing more than could be won in the course of the evening. But instantly the terrible suspicion arose that he had been deliberately left out of the Bingleys' invitation to the officers for Mr. Darcy's benefit. Though this was not exactly the case, his actual absence was confirmed by his friend Mr. Denny, to whom Lydia eagerly applied, and who told them that Wickham had been obliged to go to town on business the day before and had not yet returned—adding, with a meaningful smile:
"I don't think his business would have called him away just now if he had not wanted to avoid a certain gentleman here."

This part of the information, though missed by Lydia, was caught by Elizabeth. Since it confirmed that Darcy was just as responsible for Wickham's absence as if her first guess had been right, every feeling of displeasure against Darcy was sharpened by immediate disappointment, and she could barely reply with tolerable politeness to the friendly inquiries he came to make shortly afterward. Attention, patience, civility toward Darcy was an injury to Wickham. She resolved against any sort of conversation with him and turned away with a degree of bad temper that she could not entirely overcome, even when speaking to Mr. Bingley, whose blind devotion to Darcy annoyed her.

But Elizabeth was not made for ill humor, and though every prospect of her own enjoyment was ruined for the evening, her spirits could not be dampened for long. After sharing all her grievances with Charlotte Lucas, whom she had not seen in a week, she was soon able to shift to the eccentricities of her cousin and point him out for Charlotte's particular attention. The first two dances, however, brought a return of misery—they were dances of humiliation. Mr. Collins, awkward and solemn, apologizing instead of paying attention, and often moving the wrong way without realizing it, gave her all the shame and torment that a terrible dance partner can inflict. The moment she was released from him was pure bliss.

She danced next with an officer and had the refreshment of talking about Wickham and hearing that he was universally liked. When those dances were over, she returned to Charlotte Lucas, and was talking with her when she found herself suddenly addressed by Mr. Darcy, who so took her by surprise in asking for her hand that, without knowing what she was doing, she accepted. He walked away immediately, and she was left to berate herself for her own lack of composure. Charlotte tried to console her.
"I dare say you will find him very agreeable."
"Heaven forbid! _That_ would be the greatest misfortune of all! To find agreeable a man one is determined to hate! Don't wish such a thing on me."

When the dancing resumed, however, and Darcy approached to claim her hand, Charlotte could not help whispering a warning not to be a fool and let her liking for Wickham make her seem unpleasant to a man ten times his social standing. Elizabeth made no answer and took her place in the set, amazed at the honor of being allowed to stand opposite Mr. Darcy, and reading in her neighbors' faces their equal amazement at seeing it. They stood for some time without speaking a word, and she began to think that their silence would last through both dances. At first she resolved not to break it—until she suddenly decided that it would be a greater punishment to her partner to force him to talk. She made a slight remark about the dance. He replied, and was silent again. After a pause of some minutes, she addressed him a second time:
"It is _your_ turn to say something now, Mr. Darcy. _I_ talked about the dance, and _you_ ought to make some kind of remark about the size of the room, or the number of couples."
He smiled, and assured her that whatever she wished him to say would be said.
"Very well—that reply will do for the moment. Perhaps later I may observe that private balls are much more enjoyable than public ones. But for _now_ we may be silent."
"Do you follow a set of rules when you talk while dancing?"

"Sometimes. One must say a little, you know. It would look strange to be completely silent for half an hour. And yet, for the benefit of _some_ people, conversation ought to be arranged so that they need say as little as possible."
"Are you speaking for your own feelings in this case, or do you imagine you are pleasing mine?"

"Both," replied Elizabeth mischievously. "For I have always seen a great similarity in the way our minds work. We are each unsociable and quiet by nature, unwilling to speak unless we expect to say something that will amaze the whole room and be passed down to future generations with all the brilliance of a proverb."
"This is no very accurate description of your own character, I'm sure," said he. "How close it may be to _mine_, I cannot say. _You_ think it a faithful portrait, no doubt."
"I must not judge my own work."

He made no answer, and they were silent again until they had moved down the dance, when he asked whether she and her sisters often walked to Meryton. She answered yes, and, unable to resist the temptation, added, "When you met us there the other day, we had just been making a new acquaintance."

The effect was immediate. A deeper shade of haughtiness spread over his features, but he said nothing. And Elizabeth, though blaming herself for her own weakness, could not go on. At length Darcy spoke, and in a strained manner said:
"Mr. Wickham is blessed with such charming manners that he is sure to _make_ friends easily. Whether he is equally capable of _keeping_ them is less certain."
"He has been so unlucky as to lose _your_ friendship," replied Elizabeth with emphasis, "and in a way that he is likely to suffer from for the rest of his life."

Darcy made no answer and seemed eager to change the subject. At that moment Sir William Lucas appeared nearby, intending to cross through the set to the other side of the room. But on seeing Mr. Darcy, he stopped, bowed with great courtesy, and complimented him on his dancing and his partner.

"I have been most gratified indeed, my dear sir. Such very superior dancing is not often seen. It is clear that you move in the highest circles. Allow me to say, however, that your lovely partner does you no discredit, and that I must hope to see this pleasure repeated often, especially when a certain happy event, my dear Miss Eliza"—glancing at her sister and Bingley—"takes place. What congratulations will pour in! I appeal to Mr. Darcy. But let me not keep you, sir. You will not thank me for detaining you from the enchanting conversation of that young lady, whose bright eyes are also scolding me for it."

The last part of this speech was barely heard by Darcy, but Sir William's reference to his friend seemed to strike him hard, and his eyes turned with a very serious expression toward Bingley and Jane, who were dancing together. Recovering himself shortly, however, he turned to his partner and said:
"Sir William's interruption has made me forget what we were talking about."

"I don't think we were talking at all. Sir William could not have interrupted any two people in the room who had less to say to each other. We have tried two or three subjects already without success, and what we should talk about next, I cannot imagine."
"What do you think of books?" he said, smiling.
"Books—oh no! I'm sure we never read the same ones, or not with the same reactions."
"I'm sorry you think so. But if that is the case, there can at least be no shortage of material. We could compare our different opinions."
"No—I cannot talk about books at a ball. My head is always full of other things."
"The _present_ always occupies you in such settings—does it?" he said, with a look of doubt.

"Yes, always," she replied without knowing what she said, for her thoughts had wandered far from the topic, as soon became clear when she suddenly exclaimed, "I remember hearing you once say, Mr. Darcy, that you hardly ever forgive—that your resentment, once formed, is permanent. You are very careful, I suppose, about what _creates_ it?"
"I am," he said with a firm voice.
"And you never allow yourself to be blinded by prejudice?"
"I hope not."
"It is especially important for those who never change their opinion to be sure of judging correctly the first time."
"May I ask where these questions are leading?"
"Simply to an understanding of _your_ character," she said, trying to shake off her seriousness. "I am trying to figure you out."
"And how is that going?"
She shook her head. "Not at all well. I hear such different reports of you that they puzzle me completely."

"I can easily believe," he answered gravely, "that reports about me may vary greatly. And I could wish, Miss Bennet, that you would not try to sketch my character at this particular moment, since there is reason to fear the result would do credit to neither of us."
"But if I don't capture your likeness now, I may never have another chance."

"I would by no means interfere with any pleasure of yours," he replied coldly. She said no more, and they finished the dance and parted in silence—each dissatisfied, though not equally so. In Darcy's heart there was a fairly powerful feeling toward her, which soon earned her his forgiveness and directed all his anger at another person.
They had not been long apart when Miss Bingley came toward her and, with an expression of polite disdain, addressed her:

"So, Miss Eliza, I hear you are quite delighted with George Wickham? Your sister has been talking to me about him and asking me a thousand questions. And I find that the young man forgot to tell you, among his other revelations, that he was the son of old Wickham, the late Mr. Darcy's steward. Let me advise you, however, as a friend, not to place blind trust in everything he says. As for Mr. Darcy treating him badly, it is completely false—on the contrary, he has always been remarkably kind to him, though George Wickham has treated Mr. Darcy in the most disgraceful way. I don't know the details, but I know very well that Mr. Darcy is not the least bit to blame, that he cannot bear to hear George Wickham's name mentioned, and that though my brother felt he could not easily exclude him from the invitation to the officers, he was extremely glad to find that Wickham had taken himself out of the way. His even coming into this area is a most insolent thing, and I wonder how he dared to do it. I pity you, Miss Eliza, for this discovery of your favorite's guilt—but really, considering his origins, one could not expect much better."

"His guilt and his origins appear, by your account, to be the same thing," said Elizabeth angrily, "for I have heard you accuse him of nothing worse than being the son of Mr. Darcy's steward—and of _that_, I can assure you, he told me himself."
"I beg your pardon," replied Miss Bingley, turning away with a sneer. "Excuse my interference. It was kindly meant."

"Insolent woman!" said Elizabeth to herself. "You are very much mistaken if you think you can influence me with such a feeble attack. I see nothing in it but your own willful ignorance and Mr. Darcy's malice." She then went to find her eldest sister, who had undertaken to make inquiries on the same subject with Bingley. Jane met her with a smile of such sweet contentment, a glow of such happiness, as clearly showed how well pleased she was with the evening. Elizabeth instantly read her feelings, and at that moment, concern for Wickham, resentment against his enemies, and everything else gave way to the hope that Jane was on the surest path to happiness.

"I want to know," she said, with a face no less smiling than her sister's, "what you have learned about Mr. Wickham. But perhaps you have been too happily occupied to think about anyone else—in which case you may be sure of my forgiveness."

"No," replied Jane, "I have not forgotten him, but I have nothing satisfying to tell you. Mr. Bingley does not know his whole history and is quite unaware of the circumstances that have especially offended Mr. Darcy. But he will vouch for the good character, integrity, and honor of his friend, and is perfectly convinced that Mr. Wickham has deserved much less attention from Mr. Darcy than he has received. And I am sorry to say that by his account, as well as his sister's, Mr. Wickham is by no means a respectable young man. I'm afraid he has been very reckless and has deserved to lose Mr. Darcy's regard."
"Mr. Bingley doesn't know Mr. Wickham himself."
"No, he had never seen him until the other morning in Meryton."
"Then this account is what he received from Mr. Darcy. I am perfectly satisfied. But what does he say about the parish?"
"He doesn't exactly recall the circumstances, though he has heard them from Mr. Darcy more than once, but he believes it was left to him only _conditionally_."
