"I have no doubt of Mr. Bingley's sincerity," said Elizabeth warmly, "but you must forgive me for not being convinced by second-hand assurances. Mr. Bingley's defense of his friend was very skillful, I'm sure, but since he is unfamiliar with several parts of the story and has heard the rest from that friend himself, I shall continue to think of both gentlemen exactly as I did before."

She then changed the subject to one more pleasant for them both, on which there could be no disagreement. Elizabeth listened with delight to the happy though modest hopes that Jane held for Bingley's regard, and did all she could to strengthen her confidence. When Mr. Bingley himself joined them, Elizabeth moved away to Miss Lucas. She had scarcely replied to Charlotte's inquiry about how she had enjoyed her last dance partner before Mr. Collins came up to them and told her with great excitement that he had just been fortunate enough to make a most important discovery.

"I have found out," he said, "by a remarkable coincidence, that there is now in this room a close relation of my patroness. I happened to overhear the gentleman himself mentioning to the young lady who is hosting this party the names of his cousin Miss de Bourgh, and of her mother, Lady Catherine. How wonderfully these things happen! Who would have thought I would meet—possibly—a nephew of Lady Catherine de Bourgh at this gathering! I am most grateful that I made this discovery in time to pay my respects to him, which I am now going to do. I trust he will excuse my not having done so earlier. My complete ignorance of the connection must serve as my apology."
"You are not going to introduce _yourself_ to Mr. Darcy?"

"Indeed I am. I shall beg his pardon for not having done it sooner. I believe him to be Lady Catherine's _nephew_. It will be in my power to assure him that her Ladyship was quite well a week ago Saturday."

Elizabeth tried hard to talk him out of it, assuring him that Mr. Darcy would consider being addressed by a stranger without a proper introduction as an impertinent liberty rather than a compliment to his aunt; that there was no need for any acknowledgment on either side; and that if there were, it should come from Mr. Darcy, as the person of higher standing. Mr. Collins listened with the determined air of someone who would follow his own inclination regardless, and when she finished, replied:

"My dear Miss Elizabeth, I have the highest opinion in the world of your excellent judgment in all matters within the scope of your understanding. But allow me to say that there must be a great difference between the social customs of ordinary people and those that govern the clergy. For, if you will permit me to observe, I consider the clerical office equal in dignity to the highest rank in the kingdom—provided, of course, that a proper humility of behavior is maintained. You must therefore allow me to follow my conscience on this occasion, which leads me to perform what I see as a point of duty. Forgive me for not taking your advice, which on every other subject shall be my constant guide—though in this case I consider myself better qualified by education and habitual study to judge what is right than a young lady like yourself." And with a low bow he left her to approach Mr. Darcy, whose reception of his advance she watched eagerly and whose astonishment at being so addressed was very evident. Her cousin began his speech with a solemn bow, and though she could not hear a word of it, she felt as if she heard everything, and saw in the motion of his lips the words "apology," "Hunsford," and "Lady Catherine de Bourgh." It pained her to see him expose himself to such a man. Mr. Darcy was staring at him in open amazement, and when at last Mr. Collins allowed him to speak, he replied with an air of cool civility. Mr. Collins, however, was not discouraged from speaking again, and Mr. Darcy's contempt seemed to grow steadily with the length of his second speech. At the end of it, Darcy merely gave him a slight bow and moved away. Mr. Collins then returned to Elizabeth.

"I have no reason, I assure you," he said, "to be dissatisfied with my reception. Mr. Darcy seemed very pleased with the attention. He answered me with the greatest courtesy and even paid me the compliment of saying that he was so confident in Lady Catherine's judgment that he was certain she could never bestow a favor unworthily. It was really a very handsome thought. On the whole, I am very pleased with him."

Since Elizabeth no longer had any interest of her own to pursue, she turned her attention almost entirely to her sister and Mr. Bingley. The pleasant train of thought that her observations inspired made her perhaps nearly as happy as Jane. She pictured her sister settled in that very house, enjoying all the happiness that a marriage of true affection could bring, and she felt capable, under such circumstances, of even trying to like Bingley's two sisters. Her mother's thoughts were plainly running in the same direction, and she resolved not to go near her, for fear of hearing too much. When they sat down to supper, therefore, she considered it a most unfortunate coincidence that placed them within earshot of each other. She was deeply upset to find that her mother was talking freely and openly to Lady Lucas about nothing but her expectation that Jane would soon marry Mr. Bingley. It was a thrilling subject, and Mrs. Bennet seemed tireless in listing the advantages of the match. His being such a charming young man, and so rich, and living only three miles away were the first points of self-congratulation. Then it was such a comfort to think how fond the two sisters were of Jane, and to be certain they must want the connection as much as she did. It was, moreover, so promising for her younger daughters, since Jane's marrying so well would surely bring them into contact with other rich men. And lastly, it was so pleasant at her age to be able to hand her single daughters over to their sister's care, so that she need not go out in society more than she liked. It was necessary to present this as a matter of pleasure, because etiquette demanded it—but no one was less likely than Mrs. Bennet to find comfort in staying at home at any point in her life. She concluded with many good wishes that Lady Lucas might soon be equally fortunate—though obviously and triumphantly believing there was no chance of it.

Elizabeth tried in vain to slow the torrent of her mother's words, or persuade her to express her joy in a quieter voice. To her inexpressible mortification, she could see that most of it was overheard by Mr. Darcy, who sat directly opposite them. Her mother only scolded her for being silly.
"What is Mr. Darcy to me, pray, that I should be afraid of him? I'm sure we owe him no such special courtesy that we must avoid saying anything _he_ might not want to hear."
"For heaven's sake, Mama, speak more quietly. What good can it do you to offend Mr. Darcy? You will never make yourself liked by his friend this way."

Nothing she could say, however, had any influence. Her mother continued to broadcast her views at the same clearly audible volume. Elizabeth blushed and blushed again with shame and frustration. She could not help frequently glancing at Mr. Darcy, though every glance confirmed her fears—for though he was not always looking at her mother, she was sure his attention was invariably fixed on her. The expression on his face changed gradually from angry contempt to a composed and steady gravity.

At length Mrs. Bennet had no more to say, and Lady Lucas, who had long been yawning at this recitation of delights she saw no chance of sharing, was left to the comforts of cold ham and chicken. Elizabeth now began to revive. But the respite was short. When supper was over, singing was suggested, and she had the mortification of seeing Mary, after very little persuasion, preparing to oblige the company. With many meaningful looks and silent pleas she tried to prevent this display—but in vain. Mary would not understand them. Such an opportunity to show off was delightful to her, and she began to sing. Elizabeth watched her with the most painful feelings and followed her progress through the verses with an impatience that was very poorly rewarded at the end—for Mary, on receiving among the polite thanks a hint that she might be persuaded to sing again, began another song after a half-minute pause. Mary's talents were by no means suited to such a performance—her voice was weak and her manner affected. Elizabeth was in agony. She looked at Jane to see how she was taking it, but Jane was calmly chatting with Bingley. She looked at his two sisters and saw them exchanging mocking glances with each other and at Darcy, who remained, however, impenetrably serious. She looked at her father to beg him to intervene before Mary sang all night. He took the hint, and when Mary had finished her second song, said aloud:
"That will do very well, child. You have delighted us long enough. Let the other young ladies have a turn."

Mary, though pretending not to hear, was somewhat flustered. Elizabeth, sorry for her and sorry for her father's bluntness, was afraid her anxiety had done no good. Others in the group were now asked to perform.

"If I," said Mr. Collins, "were fortunate enough to be able to sing, I should have great pleasure, I'm sure, in obliging the company with a song. For I consider music a perfectly innocent pastime, and entirely compatible with the profession of a clergyman. I do not mean to suggest, however, that we can be justified in devoting too much of our time to music, for there are certainly other things to attend to. The rector of a parish has much to do. First, he must come to an arrangement for tithes that is beneficial to himself and not offensive to his patron. He must write his own sermons, and the time that remains will not be too much for his parish duties and the care and improvement of his house, which he cannot be excused from making as comfortable as possible. And I do not think it a small matter that he should have attentive and conciliatory manners toward everyone, especially toward those to whom he owes his appointment. I cannot excuse him from that duty, nor could I think well of any man who missed an opportunity to show his respect toward anyone connected with the family." And with a bow to Mr. Darcy, he concluded his speech, which had been delivered so loudly that half the room could hear it. Many people stared, many smiled, but no one looked more amused than Mr. Bennet himself, while his wife seriously praised Mr. Collins for having spoken so sensibly and remarked, in a half whisper to Lady Lucas, that he was a remarkably clever, good sort of young man.

To Elizabeth it seemed that if her family had made a pact to embarrass themselves as thoroughly as possible during the evening, they could not have played their parts with more energy or greater success. She was glad for Bingley's sake and her sister's that some of the spectacle had escaped his notice, and that his feelings were not the sort to be greatly distressed by the foolishness he must have witnessed. That his two sisters and Mr. Darcy, however, should have had such an opportunity to mock her family was bad enough. And she could not decide whether the silent contempt of the gentleman or the insolent smiles of the ladies were more unbearable.

The rest of the evening brought her little enjoyment. She was pestered by Mr. Collins, who stayed stubbornly at her side, and though he could not persuade her to dance with him again, he made it impossible for her to dance with anyone else. She begged him in vain to ask someone else to dance and offered to introduce him to any young lady in the room. He assured her that as for dancing, he was perfectly indifferent to it—his chief purpose was, through delicate attentions, to recommend himself to her, and he would therefore make a point of staying close to her all evening. There was no arguing with such a plan. Her greatest relief came from her friend Miss Lucas, who often joined them and good-naturedly drew Mr. Collins's conversation to herself.

She was at least free from the annoyance of any further attention from Mr. Darcy. Though he often stood very near her, quite unoccupied, he never came close enough to speak. She felt this was probably the result of her references to Mr. Wickham, and was glad of it.

The Longbourn party was the last to leave, and through a maneuver of Mrs. Bennet's had to wait for their carriage a quarter of an hour after everyone else had gone—which gave them time to see how eagerly some of the household wished them away. Mrs. Hurst and her sister barely opened their mouths except to complain of tiredness, and were obviously impatient to have the house to themselves. They rebuffed every attempt by Mrs. Bennet at conversation, casting a pall over the whole group that was scarcely lightened by the long speeches of Mr. Collins, who was complimenting Mr. Bingley and his sisters on the elegance of their party and the hospitality and politeness they had shown their guests. Darcy said nothing at all. Mr. Bennet, equally silent, was enjoying the scene. Mr. Bingley and Jane stood a little apart from the rest, talking only to each other. Elizabeth maintained as steady a silence as either Mrs. Hurst or Miss Bingley, and even Lydia was too tired to do more than occasionally exclaim "God, I'm so tired!" followed by a huge yawn.

When they finally rose to leave, Mrs. Bennet was extremely pressing in her hope of seeing the whole family soon at Longbourn, and addressed herself particularly to Mr. Bingley, assuring him how happy he would make them by coming to a family dinner anytime, without the formality of a proper invitation. Bingley was all grateful pleasure, and readily promised to take the earliest opportunity of visiting her after his return from London, where he was obliged to go the next day for a short time.

Mrs. Bennet was perfectly satisfied, and left the house under the delightful conviction that, allowing for the necessary preparations of marriage settlements, new carriages, and wedding clothes, she would undoubtedly see her daughter settled at Netherfield within three or four months. She thought with equal certainty of having another daughter married to Mr. Collins—with considerable, though not equal, pleasure. Elizabeth was the least dear to her of all her children, and though the man and the match were quite good enough for _her_, the value of each was eclipsed by Mr. Bingley and Netherfield.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: The next day opened a new scene at Longbourn. Mr. Collins made his formal proposal. Having resolved to do it without delay—since his leave of absence lasted only until the following Saturday—and having no feelings of shyness to make the moment uncomfortable for himself, he went about it in a very organized way, with all the formalities he supposed to be a regular part of the process. Finding Mrs. Bennet, Elizabeth, and one of the younger girls together soon after breakfast, he addressed the mother with these words:
"May I hope, madam, for your support with your lovely daughter Elizabeth, when I request the honor of a private conversation with her this morning?"
Before Elizabeth had time for anything but a blush of surprise, Mrs. Bennet instantly answered:

"Oh dear! Yes, certainly. I'm sure Lizzy will be very happy—I'm sure she can have no objection. Come, Kitty, I need you upstairs." And gathering up her sewing, she was hurrying away when Elizabeth called out:
"Dear Mama, please don't go. I beg you not to go. Mr. Collins must excuse me. He can have nothing to say to me that everyone cannot hear. I am leaving myself."

"No, no, nonsense, Lizzy. I want you to stay where you are." And when Elizabeth seemed really about to escape, with an annoyed and embarrassed expression, she added, "Lizzy, I _insist_ that you stay and hear Mr. Collins."

Elizabeth could not resist such a command, and a moment's thought also made her realize it would be wisest to get it over with as quickly and quietly as possible. She sat down again and tried to hide, behind constant busyness with her needlework, feelings that were divided between dread and amusement. Mrs. Bennet and Kitty left, and as soon as they were gone, Mr. Collins began:

"Believe me, my dear Miss Elizabeth, that your modesty, far from doing you any harm, actually adds to your other perfections. You would have been less charming in my eyes if there had _not_ been this little reluctance. But allow me to assure you that I have your respected mother's permission for this address. You can hardly doubt the purpose of what I am about to say, however your natural modesty may lead you to pretend otherwise. My attentions have been too obvious to be mistaken. Almost as soon as I entered this house, I singled you out as the companion of my future life. But before I am carried away by my feelings on this subject, perhaps it would be wise for me to state my reasons for marrying—and moreover, for coming to Hertfordshire with the specific intention of choosing a wife, as I certainly did."

The idea of Mr. Collins, with all his solemn composure, being "carried away by his feelings" nearly made Elizabeth laugh, and she could not use the short pause he allowed for any attempt to stop him. He continued:

"My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it the right thing for every clergyman in comfortable circumstances, like myself, to set an example of marriage in his parish. Second, that I am convinced it will greatly increase my happiness. And third—which perhaps I should have mentioned first—that it is the particular advice and recommendation of the very noble lady whom I have the honor of calling my patroness. Twice she has condescended to give me her opinion (without being asked!) on this subject. And it was just the Saturday night before I left Hunsford—between hands at cards, while Mrs. Jenkinson was arranging Miss de Bourgh's footstool—that she said, 'Mr. Collins, you must marry. A clergyman like you must marry. Choose well—choose a gentlewoman for _my_ sake and for your _own_. Let her be an active, practical sort of person, not raised too high, but able to stretch a modest income. This is my advice. Find such a woman as soon as you can, bring her to Hunsford, and I will visit her.' Allow me, by the way, to observe, my fair cousin, that I do not consider the notice and kindness of Lady Catherine de Bourgh as the least of the advantages I can offer you. You will find her manners beyond anything I can describe, and your wit and liveliness, I think, must be acceptable to her, especially when balanced with the silence and respect that her rank will naturally inspire. So much for my general reasons for wanting to marry. It remains to explain why I looked to Longbourn rather than my own neighborhood, where I assure you there are many lovely young women. But the fact is that, being, as I am, the heir to this estate after the death of your honored father—who may, however, live many years longer—I could not rest until I resolved to choose a wife from among his daughters, so that their loss might be as small as possible when that sad event occurs—which, however, as I said, may not be for several years. This has been my motive, my fair cousin, and I flatter myself it will not lower me in your estimation. And now nothing remains but to assure you, in the strongest possible language, of the intensity of my affection. I am perfectly indifferent to money and shall make no financial demands on your father, since I am well aware they could not be met, and that one thousand pounds in government bonds, which will not be yours until after your mother's death, is all you may ever be entitled to. On that subject, therefore, I shall remain permanently silent, and you may rest assured that no ungracious reproach shall ever pass my lips when we are married."
It was absolutely necessary to interrupt him now.

"You are too hasty, sir," she cried. "You forget that I have not given you an answer. Let me do so without further delay. Thank you for the compliment you are paying me. I am very aware of the honor of your proposal, but it is impossible for me to do anything other than refuse it."

"I am well aware," replied Mr. Collins with a formal wave of the hand, "that it is customary for young ladies to reject the man they secretly mean to accept when he first proposes, and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second or even a third time. I am therefore not at all discouraged by what you have just said, and hope to lead you to the altar before long."

"Upon my word, sir," cried Elizabeth, "your hope is rather extraordinary after what I have said. I assure you that I am not one of those young ladies—if such young ladies exist—who are so bold as to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I am perfectly serious in my refusal. You could not make _me_ happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who could make _you_ happy. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine were to know me, I am sure she would find me in every way unsuitable for the position."

"If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so—" said Mr. Collins very seriously, "but I cannot imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you at all. And you may be sure that when I have the honor of seeing her again, I shall speak in the highest terms of your modesty, frugality, and other fine qualities."

"Really, Mr. Collins, all praise of me will be unnecessary. You must allow me to judge for myself, and pay me the compliment of believing what I say. I wish you every happiness and prosperity, and by refusing your hand, I do everything in my power to ensure both. In making me this offer, you must have satisfied any obligation you felt toward my family, and you may take possession of the Longbourn estate whenever it falls to you without any guilt. This matter may be considered, therefore, as finally settled." And rising as she spoke, she would have left the room had Mr. Collins not addressed her again:

"When I do myself the honor of raising this subject with you again, I hope to receive a more favorable answer than you have given me now. Though I am far from accusing you of cruelty at present, because I know it is the established custom of your sex to reject a man on his first proposal—and perhaps you have even now said as much to encourage me as would be consistent with the true delicacy of a woman's character."

"Really, Mr. Collins," cried Elizabeth with some heat, "you puzzle me completely. If what I have said so far can appear to you as encouragement, I do not know how to express my refusal in a way that would convince you it _is_ one."

"You must allow me to flatter myself, my dear cousin, that your refusal is merely a formality. My reasons for believing so are briefly these: it does not seem to me that my hand is unworthy of your acceptance, or that the life I can offer would be anything other than highly desirable. My position in life, my connections with the de Bourgh family, and my relationship to your own are all strongly in my favor. And you should further consider that, despite your many attractions, it is by no means certain that another proposal of marriage will ever be made to you. Your inheritance is unfortunately so small that it will in all probability cancel out the effect of your beauty and fine qualities. Since I must therefore conclude that you are not serious in rejecting me, I choose to attribute it to your wish to increase my love through suspense, according to the usual practice of sophisticated women."

"I assure you, sir, that I have no pretensions whatever to the kind of sophistication that consists of tormenting a respectable man. I would rather be paid the compliment of being believed sincere. I thank you again and again for the honor you have done me with your proposal, but to accept it is absolutely impossible. My feelings in every respect forbid it. Can I speak more plainly? Do not think of me now as a sophisticated woman trying to torment you, but as a rational person speaking the truth from her heart."
"You are unfailingly charming!" he cried with an air of clumsy gallantry. "And I am convinced that when authorized by both your excellent parents, my proposal will not fail to be accepted."

To such stubbornness in willful self-deception Elizabeth would make no reply, and she immediately and silently left the room—determined that if he continued to interpret her repeated refusals as flattering encouragement, she would appeal to her father, whose rejection could be delivered in a manner that must be decisive, and whose behavior at least could not be mistaken for the flirtation of a sophisticated woman.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Mr. Collins was not left long to the quiet contemplation of his successful love, for Mrs. Bennet, who had been hovering in the hallway waiting for the conference to end, no sooner saw Elizabeth open the door and hurry past her toward the stairs than she entered the breakfast room and warmly congratulated both him and herself on the happy prospect of their closer connection. Mr. Collins received and returned these congratulations with equal pleasure, and proceeded to share the details of the conversation, with the result of which he had every reason to be satisfied—since his cousin's firm refusal would naturally come from her bashful modesty and the genuine delicacy of her character.

This information, however, alarmed Mrs. Bennet. She would have been glad to be equally convinced that her daughter had meant to encourage him by protesting against his proposal, but she did not dare believe it, and could not help saying so.

"But rest assured, Mr. Collins," she added, "Lizzy shall be brought to reason. I will speak to her about it myself right away. She is a very stubborn, foolish girl who does not know what is good for her. But I will _make_ her see it."

"Forgive me for interrupting, madam," cried Mr. Collins, "but if she is really stubborn and foolish, I am not sure she would be a very desirable wife for a man in my position, who naturally looks for happiness in marriage. If, therefore, she truly persists in rejecting me, perhaps it would be better not to force her into accepting, because if she is prone to such defects of temperament, she could hardly contribute much to my happiness."

"Sir, you completely misunderstand me," said Mrs. Bennet, alarmed. "Lizzy is only stubborn about things like this. In everything else she is the most good-natured girl who ever lived. I will go directly to Mr. Bennet, and we shall settle it with her very quickly, I'm sure."
She would not give him time to reply, but hurried straight to her husband and called out as she entered the library:

"Oh, Mr. Bennet, you are needed at once! We are all in chaos. You must come and make Lizzy marry Mr. Collins, because she swears she will not have him—and if you don't hurry, he will change his mind and not have _her_."
Mr. Bennet raised his eyes from his book as she entered and fixed them on her face with calm indifference, which was not in the least changed by her announcement.
"I don't have the pleasure of understanding you," he said when she had finished. "What are you talking about?"
"About Mr. Collins and Lizzy. Lizzy declares she will not have Mr. Collins, and Mr. Collins is starting to say he will not have Lizzy."
"And what am I supposed to do about it? It seems a hopeless situation."
"Talk to Lizzy about it yourself. Tell her that you insist she marry him."
"Have her called down. She shall hear my opinion."
Mrs. Bennet rang the bell, and Miss Elizabeth was summoned to the library.
"Come here, child," cried her father when she appeared. "I have sent for you on an important matter. I understand that Mr. Collins has proposed to you. Is it true?"
Elizabeth replied that it was.
"Very well—and this proposal you have refused?"
"I have, sir."
"Very well. We now come to the point. Your mother insists that you accept it. Isn't that so, Mrs. Bennet?"
"Yes, or I will never see her again."

"An unhappy choice lies before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents. Your mother will never see you again if you do _not_ marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you _do_."
Elizabeth could not help smiling at such an ending to such a beginning, but Mrs. Bennet, who had convinced herself that her husband would see things her way, was bitterly disappointed.
"What do you mean, Mr. Bennet, by talking like this? You promised me you would _insist_ on her marrying him."

"My dear," replied her husband, "I have two small favors to ask. First, that you will allow me the free use of my own judgment on this occasion; and second, of my room. I would like to have the library to myself as soon as possible."

Despite her disappointment in her husband, however, Mrs. Bennet did not give up. She talked to Elizabeth again and again, alternately coaxing and threatening her. She tried to recruit Jane to her side, but Jane, with all possible gentleness, declined to interfere. Elizabeth, sometimes with genuine seriousness and sometimes with playful good humor, answered her attacks. Though her manner varied, her determination never did.

Mr. Collins, meanwhile, was reflecting in solitude on what had happened. He thought too well of himself to understand why his cousin could possibly refuse him, and though his pride was hurt, he suffered in no other way. His feelings for her were entirely imaginary, and the possibility that she deserved her mother's scolding prevented him from feeling any regret.

While the family was in this turmoil, Charlotte Lucas came to spend the day with them. She was met in the hall by Lydia, who flew to her and cried in a half whisper, "I'm so glad you're here—there's such excitement! What do you think happened this morning? Mr. Collins proposed to Lizzy, and she won't have him."

Charlotte barely had time to respond before Kitty joined them to share the same news. And no sooner had they entered the breakfast room, where Mrs. Bennet was alone, than she too launched into the subject, appealing to Miss Lucas for sympathy and begging her to persuade her friend Lizzy to go along with the family's wishes. "Please do, my dear Miss Lucas," she added in a sorrowful tone, "for nobody is on my side, nobody supports me. I am cruelly treated. Nobody feels for my poor nerves."
Charlotte was spared having to reply by the entrance of Jane and Elizabeth.

"Yes, there she comes," continued Mrs. Bennet, "looking as unconcerned as can be, and caring no more about us than if we were a hundred miles away, as long as she gets her own way. But I tell you what, Miss Lizzy—if you keep turning down every offer of marriage like this, you will never get a husband at all. And I am sure I don't know who is going to support you when your father is dead. _I_ won't be able to keep you—so I warn you. I am done with you from this very day. I told you in the library, you know, that I would never speak to you again, and you will find I keep my word. I have no pleasure in talking to disobedient children. Not that I have much pleasure in talking to anybody. People who suffer as I do from nervous complaints have no great desire for conversation. Nobody can imagine what I suffer! But it is always the same. Those who don't complain are never pitied."

Her daughters listened in silence to this outburst, knowing that any attempt to reason with or calm her would only make things worse. She talked on without interruption from any of them until they were joined by Mr. Collins, who entered with an air more solemn than usual. On seeing him, she said to the girls:
"Now, I insist that you all hold your tongues and let Mr. Collins and me have a little conversation."

Elizabeth quietly left the room, followed by Jane and Kitty, but Lydia held her ground, determined to hear everything she could. Charlotte, detained first by the politeness of Mr. Collins—whose detailed inquiries about her and her entire family were very thorough—and then by a little curiosity, contented herself with walking to the window and pretending not to listen. In a mournful voice, Mrs. Bennet began the planned conversation:
"Oh, Mr. Collins!"

"My dear madam," he replied, "let us be silent on this point forever. Far be it from me," he soon continued, in a voice that showed his displeasure, "to resent your daughter's behavior. Accepting inevitable misfortunes is the duty of us all—especially of a young man who has been as fortunate as I have, in receiving an early appointment. And I trust I am resigned. Perhaps all the more so because I have my doubts about whether I would truly have been happy had my fair cousin honored me with her hand—for I have often observed that resignation is never so complete as when the thing denied begins to lose some of its value in our estimation. I hope you will not consider me disrespectful to your family, my dear madam, by withdrawing my claim to your daughter's affection without having paid you and Mr. Bennet the compliment of asking you to use your authority on my behalf. My conduct may, I fear, be open to criticism for having accepted my dismissal from your daughter's lips rather than yours. But we are all prone to error. I have certainly meant well throughout. My aim has been to secure a pleasant companion for myself, with proper consideration for the benefit of your whole family. And if my _manner_ has been at all objectionable, I hereby beg to apologize."

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: The discussion of Mr. Collins's proposal was now nearly over, and Elizabeth had only to endure the uncomfortable feelings that naturally came with it, along with the occasional irritable remark from her mother. As for the gentleman himself, _his_ feelings were expressed not by embarrassment or sadness, or by trying to avoid her, but by stiff manners and resentful silence. He barely spoke to her, and the devoted attentions he had been so aware of giving were transferred for the rest of the day to Miss Lucas, whose willingness to listen to him was a welcome relief to everyone, especially Elizabeth.

The next day brought no improvement in Mrs. Bennet's bad mood or health. Mr. Collins was in the same state of angry pride. Elizabeth had hoped his resentment might shorten his visit, but his plans appeared unaffected. He had always meant to leave on Saturday, and on Saturday he still intended to go.

After breakfast, the girls walked to Meryton to find out whether Mr. Wickham had returned and to lament his absence from the Netherfield ball. He met them as they entered town and accompanied them to their aunt's, where his regret and frustration, and everyone's concern, were thoroughly discussed. To Elizabeth, however, he privately admitted that his absence had been his own decision.

"I found," he said, "as the time approached, that I had better not face Mr. Darcy—that to be in the same room, at the same party with him for so many hours, might be more than I could bear, and that scenes might arise that would be unpleasant for more than just myself."

She strongly approved of his restraint, and they had ample time for a full discussion of it, and for all the compliments they politely exchanged, as Wickham and another officer walked back with them to Longbourn. During the walk, he paid particular attention to her. His joining them was a double benefit: she felt the compliment it paid to herself, and it was a perfect chance to introduce him to her father and mother.

Soon after their return, a letter was delivered to Miss Bennet. It came from Netherfield and was opened at once. The envelope contained a sheet of elegant, fine-pressed paper, covered with a lady's graceful, flowing handwriting. Elizabeth saw her sister's face change as she read, and noticed her lingering on certain passages. Jane soon composed herself and, putting the letter away, tried to join in the general conversation with her usual cheerfulness. But Elizabeth felt a worry about it that drew her attention even from Wickham. No sooner had he and his companion taken their leave than a glance from Jane invited her to follow upstairs. When they reached their room, Jane took out the letter and said, "This is from Caroline Bingley. What it says has surprised me considerably. The entire party has already left Netherfield and is on their way to London, with no intention of coming back. Let me read you what she says."

She read the first sentence aloud, which announced that they had just decided to follow their brother to London immediately and would dine that day in Grosvenor Street, where Mr. Hurst had a house. The next part went: "'I don't pretend to regret anything I am leaving behind in Hertfordshire except your company, my dearest friend. But we may hope, at some future time, to enjoy many more of those delightful conversations we have shared, and in the meantime can ease the pain of separation through frequent and open correspondence. I count on you for that.'" Elizabeth listened to these extravagant expressions with all the skepticism of distrust. Though the suddenness of their departure surprised her, she saw nothing in it to really regret. There was no reason to suppose that their absence from Netherfield would keep Mr. Bingley away, and as for the loss of their company, she was sure Jane would soon stop missing it once she had his.

"It is unfortunate," she said after a short pause, "that you couldn't see your friends before they left. But may we not hope that the future happiness Miss Bingley looks forward to may arrive sooner than she expects—and that the delightful friendship you have known will be renewed with even greater pleasure as sisters? Mr. Bingley will not be kept in London by them."
"Caroline firmly says that none of the party will return to Hertfordshire this winter. Let me read it to you.

"'When my brother left us yesterday, he expected that his business in London would take three or four days. But since we are certain it cannot be settled that quickly, and at the same time convinced that once Charles gets to town he will be in no hurry to leave it, we have decided to follow him, so that he need not spend his free time in a dreary hotel. Many of my friends are already in town for the winter. I wish I could hear that you, my dearest friend, had any intention of joining the crowd, but I despair of that. I sincerely hope your Christmas in Hertfordshire will be full of the festivities the season usually brings, and that your admirers will be so numerous as to prevent your feeling the loss of the three of whom we shall deprive you.'
"It is obvious from this," added Jane, "that he will not come back this winter."
"It is only obvious that Miss Bingley does not intend him _to_."

"Why will you think that? It must be his own decision—he is his own master. But you don't know _everything_. I _will_ read you the passage that particularly hurts me. I will have no secrets from _you_. 'Mr. Darcy is eager to see his sister, and to tell the truth, _we_ are scarcely less eager to see her again. I really do not think Georgiana Darcy has her equal in beauty, elegance, and accomplishments; and the affection she inspires in Louisa and me is heightened into something still more exciting by the hope we dare to hold of her one day being our sister. I don't know whether I ever mentioned my feelings on this subject to you before, but I will not leave the country without sharing them, and I trust you will not think them unreasonable. My brother already admires her greatly; he will now have frequent opportunities to see her in the most intimate setting; her family all wish for the match as much as his own; and I don't think a sister's bias is misleading me when I call Charles most capable of winning any woman's heart. With all these circumstances in favor of an attachment, and nothing to prevent it, am I wrong, my dearest Jane, in hoping for an event that will secure the happiness of so many?' What do you think of _that_, my dear Lizzy?" said Jane as she finished. "Isn't it clear enough? Doesn't it plainly declare that Caroline neither expects nor wants me to be her sister? That she is perfectly convinced of her brother's indifference? And that if she suspects the nature of my feelings for him, she means—most kindly!—to warn me off? Can there be any other interpretation?"
"Yes, there can—for mine is completely different. Would you like to hear it?"
"Very much."

"I'll give it to you in a few words. Miss Bingley sees that her brother is in love with you and wants him to marry Miss Darcy. She follows him to London hoping to keep him there, and tries to convince you that he doesn't care about you."
Jane shook her head.

"Really, Jane, you must believe me. No one who has ever seen you together can doubt his feelings. Miss Bingley, I'm sure, cannot—she is no fool. If she had seen half as much love from Mr. Darcy for _herself_, she would have ordered her wedding dress already. But here is the situation: we are not rich enough or grand enough for them, and she is all the more eager to get Miss Darcy for her brother because she thinks that once there has been _one_ intermarriage between the families, she will have less difficulty arranging a second. There is certainly some cunning in that, and I dare say it would work if Miss de Bourgh were not in the way. But, my dearest Jane, you cannot seriously think that because Miss Bingley tells you her brother greatly admires Miss Darcy, he is even slightly less aware of _your_ worth than when he said goodbye to you on Tuesday—or that she has the power to convince him that instead of being in love with you, he is actually in love with her friend."

"If we thought alike about Miss Bingley," replied Jane, "your version of all this would put me completely at ease. But I know the assumption is unfair. Caroline is incapable of deliberately deceiving anyone. All I can hope in this case is that she is deceiving herself."
"Exactly right. You couldn't have hit on a better idea, since you won't take comfort in mine. By all means, believe she is mistaken. You have done your duty by her, and must worry no longer."
"But, my dear sister, can I really be happy—even assuming the best—in accepting a man whose sisters and friends are all wishing he would marry someone else?"

"You must decide that for yourself," said Elizabeth. "And if, after careful thought, you find that the pain of displeasing his two sisters outweighs the happiness of being his wife, I strongly advise you to refuse him."
"How can you talk like that?" said Jane with a faint smile. "You know that, though I would be deeply upset by their disapproval, I could not hesitate."
"I didn't think you would—and that being the case, I can't feel too sorry for you."
"But if he doesn't come back this winter, the choice may never be mine to make. A thousand things can happen in six months."

Elizabeth treated the idea of his not returning with utter contempt. It seemed to her nothing more than the product of Caroline's self-interested scheming, and she could not for a moment suppose that those wishes, however openly or cunningly expressed, could influence a young man so completely independent of everyone.

She argued her view to her sister as forcefully as she could, and soon had the pleasure of seeing it take effect. Jane's temperament was not naturally gloomy, and she was gradually led to hope—though her self-doubting affection sometimes overcame the hope—that Bingley would return to Netherfield and fulfill every wish of her heart.

They agreed that Mrs. Bennet should only be told that the family had left, without being alarmed about the gentleman's behavior. But even this partial news caused her great distress, and she lamented it as terribly unlucky that the ladies should happen to leave just when they were all becoming so close. After mourning it at length, however, she had the consolation of believing that Mr. Bingley would soon come back and soon be dining at Longbourn. And her final comfortable conclusion was that, though he had only been invited to a family dinner, she would make sure to have two full courses.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: The Bennets were invited to dine with the Lucases, and again, for most of the day, Miss Lucas was kind enough to listen to Mr. Collins. Elizabeth took the chance to thank her. "It keeps him in a good mood," she said, "and I am more grateful than I can say."

Charlotte assured her friend that she was happy to be helpful, and that it more than repaid her for the small sacrifice of her time. This was very kind—but Charlotte's purpose went further than Elizabeth had any idea. Her aim was nothing less than to prevent any return of Mr. Collins's attentions to Elizabeth by directing them toward herself. Such was Miss Lucas's plan, and appearances were so promising that when they parted that night, she would have felt almost sure of success if he had not been leaving Hertfordshire so soon. But here she underestimated the fire and independence of his character, for it led him to sneak out of Longbourn House the next morning with admirable stealth and hurry to Lucas Lodge to throw himself at her feet. He was anxious to avoid his cousins' notice, convinced that if they saw him leave they would surely guess his purpose, and he did not want the attempt known until its success was. Though he felt fairly confident—and with reason, for Charlotte had been reasonably encouraging—he was somewhat cautious after Wednesday's experience. His reception, however, was of the most flattering kind. Miss Lucas spotted him from an upstairs window as he walked toward the house and immediately set out to meet him "accidentally" in the lane. But she had hardly dared to hope that so much love and eloquence awaited her there.

In as short a time as Mr. Collins's long speeches would allow, everything was settled between them to the satisfaction of both. As they entered the house, he earnestly begged her to name the day that would make him the happiest of men. Though this request had to be put off for now, the lady felt no desire to play games with his happiness. The dullness that nature had bestowed on him would protect his courtship from any charm that could make a woman wish it to continue, and Miss Lucas, who accepted him purely from the practical and clear-headed desire for a stable home, did not care how soon that home was secured.

Sir William and Lady Lucas were quickly asked for their consent, which was given with the most joyful eagerness. Mr. Collins's current circumstances made it an excellent match for their daughter, to whom they could give little money, and his prospects for future wealth were extremely good. Lady Lucas immediately began to calculate, with more interest than the matter had ever

inspired before, how many years longer Mr. Bennet was likely to live. Sir William gave it as his firm opinion that whenever Mr. Collins came into possession of the Longbourn estate, it would be highly advisable for both him and his wife to be presented at the royal court. The whole family, in short, was suitably overjoyed. The younger girls began hoping they might be launched into society a year or two sooner than expected, and the boys were relieved of their fear that Charlotte would die an old maid. Charlotte herself was fairly calm. She had achieved her goal and had time to think about it. Her reflections were generally satisfactory. Mr. Collins, to be sure, was neither clever nor pleasant; his company was tedious, and his attachment to her must be imaginary. But he would still be her husband. Without thinking highly of either men or marriage, marriage had always been her goal. It was the only respectable option for well-educated young women with small fortunes, and however unlikely to bring happiness, it was their best protection against poverty. This protection she had now secured, and at twenty-seven, without ever having been pretty, she felt all the good fortune of it. The least pleasant aspect of the business was the surprise it would cause Elizabeth Bennet, whose friendship she valued above anyone else's. Elizabeth would be astonished, and would probably disapprove. And though her decision could not be shaken, her feelings would be hurt by such disapproval. She resolved to tell Elizabeth herself, and therefore instructed Mr. Collins, when he returned to Longbourn for dinner, to drop no hint of what had happened in front of the family. A promise of secrecy was of course dutifully given, but it could hardly be kept—for the curiosity aroused by his long absence erupted in such direct questions on his return that considerable ingenuity was needed to dodge them. At the same time, he was exercising great self-control, for he was desperate to announce his successful romance.

Since he had to begin his journey too early the next morning to see any of the family, the farewell ceremony was performed when the ladies retired for the night. Mrs. Bennet, with great politeness and warmth, said how happy they would be to see him at Longbourn again, whenever his other commitments allowed him to visit.

"My dear madam," he replied, "this invitation is particularly gratifying, because it is exactly what I have been hoping to receive. And you may be very certain that I shall take you up on it as soon as possible."
They were all astonished, and Mr. Bennet, who by no means wished for such a quick return, immediately said:
"But isn't there a danger of Lady Catherine disapproving, my good sir? You had better neglect your relatives than risk offending your patroness."
"My dear sir," replied Mr. Collins, "I am particularly grateful for this friendly warning, and you may count on my not taking so important a step without her Ladyship's approval."

"You cannot be too cautious. Risk anything rather than her displeasure. And if you think your coming to us again might provoke it—which I should think extremely likely—just stay quietly at home, and rest assured that _we_ shall take no offense."

"Believe me, my dear sir, my gratitude is warmly aroused by such affectionate concern. And rest assured, you will shortly receive from me a letter of thanks for this and for every other kindness shown during my stay in Hertfordshire. As for my fair cousins, though my absence may not be long enough to require it, I will now take the liberty of wishing them health and happiness—not excluding my cousin Elizabeth."

With proper goodbyes, the ladies then withdrew, all equally surprised to learn that he was planning a quick return. Mrs. Bennet liked to think he meant to propose to one of her younger girls, and Mary might have been persuaded to accept him. She rated his abilities much higher than any of the others did—there was a substance to his thoughts that often struck her—and though by no means as clever as herself, she thought that if encouraged to read and improve himself by her example, he might become a very agreeable companion. But the following morning put an end to all such hopes. Miss Lucas called soon after breakfast and, in a private conversation with Elizabeth, told her what had happened the day before.

The possibility that Mr. Collins might fancy himself in love with her friend had occurred to Elizabeth in the last day or two. But that Charlotte would encourage him seemed almost as impossible as encouraging him herself, and her astonishment was therefore so great that it at first broke through the bounds of good manners, and she could not help crying out:
"Engaged to Mr. Collins! My dear Charlotte—impossible!"

The composure that Miss Lucas had maintained while telling her story gave way to a momentary fluster at receiving so direct a reproach. But since it was no more than she expected, she soon recovered her calm and replied quietly:
"Why should you be surprised, my dear Eliza? Do you think it impossible that Mr. Collins could win any woman's good opinion, just because he was not lucky enough to succeed with you?"

But Elizabeth had collected herself, and with a strong effort was able to assure her, with reasonable steadiness, that the prospect of their closer relationship was very pleasing to her, and that she wished her every happiness imaginable.

"I see what you are feeling," replied Charlotte. "You must be surprised—very much surprised—since so recently Mr. Collins was wanting to marry you. But when you have had time to think it all over, I hope you will be satisfied with what I have done. I am not romantic, you know—I never was. I ask only for a comfortable home, and considering Mr. Collins's character, connections, and position, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as good as most people can claim when they enter marriage."

Elizabeth quietly answered, "Of course," and after an awkward pause, they rejoined the rest of the family. Charlotte did not stay much longer, and Elizabeth was left to reflect on what she had heard. It was a long time before she became at all reconciled to the idea of such an unsuitable match. The strangeness of Mr. Collins making two proposals within three days was nothing compared to his actually being accepted. She had always known that Charlotte's views on marriage were not exactly like her own, but she could not have believed it possible that, when put to the test, Charlotte would sacrifice every finer feeling for worldly advantage. Charlotte, the wife of Mr. Collins, was a deeply humiliating picture! And to the pain of a friend disgracing herself and falling in her estimation was added the distressing certainty that it was impossible for that friend to be even tolerably happy with the choice she had made.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Elizabeth was sitting with her mother and sisters, reflecting on what she had heard and wondering whether she was free to mention it, when Sir William Lucas himself appeared, sent by his daughter to announce her engagement to the family. With many compliments and much self-congratulation on the prospect of a connection between the two households, he shared the news—to an audience not just astonished but disbelieving. Mrs. Bennet, with more persistence than politeness, insisted he must be entirely mistaken, and Lydia, always blunt and often rude, loudly exclaimed:
"Good Lord! Sir William, how can you tell such a story? Don't you know that Mr. Collins wants to marry Lizzy?"

Nothing less than the graciousness of a courtier could have endured such treatment without anger. But Sir William's good manners carried him through it all, and though he insisted on the truth of his information, he listened to all their rudeness with the most patient courtesy.

Elizabeth, feeling it was her duty to rescue him from this unpleasant situation, stepped forward to confirm his account by mentioning that she already knew about it from Charlotte herself. She tried to put a stop to her mother's and sisters' exclamations through her warm congratulations to Sir William—in which Jane readily joined—and by making various comments about the happiness the match would bring, Mr. Collins's excellent character, and the convenient distance of Hunsford from London.

Mrs. Bennet was, in fact, too overwhelmed to say much while Sir William was there. But no sooner had he left than her feelings poured out. First, she persisted in disbelieving the whole thing. Second, she was certain Mr. Collins had been tricked. Third, she was confident they would never be happy together. And fourth, she hoped the engagement might be broken off. Two conclusions, however, were clearly drawn from the whole affair: one, that Elizabeth was the real cause of all the trouble; and the other, that she herself had been cruelly treated by all of them. On these two points she mainly dwelt for the rest of the day. Nothing could comfort or calm her. Nor did her resentment fade with that day. A week passed before she could see Elizabeth without scolding her. A month went by before she could speak to Sir William or Lady Lucas without being rude. And many months passed before she could forgive their daughter at all.

Mr. Bennet's feelings were much calmer on the occasion, and those he did experience he pronounced to be of a most agreeable kind—for it gratified him, he said, to discover that Charlotte Lucas, whom he had always considered reasonably sensible, was as foolish as his wife and more foolish than his daughter!

Jane admitted to being somewhat surprised by the match, but she said less about her surprise than about her sincere wish for their happiness, and Elizabeth could not persuade her to consider happiness improbable. Kitty and Lydia were far from envying Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman, and it affected them in no other way than as a piece of news to spread around Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not help feeling triumphant at being able to repay Mrs. Bennet with the satisfaction of having a daughter well married, and she called at Longbourn more often than usual to say how happy she was—though Mrs. Bennet's sour looks and nasty remarks might have been enough to drive away anyone's happiness.

Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there was a constraint that kept them both silent on the subject. Elizabeth felt certain that no real intimacy could ever exist between them again. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her turn with even greater affection to her sister, whose integrity and sensitivity she was sure she could never doubt, and for whose happiness she grew daily more anxious, since Bingley had now been gone a week and nothing was heard of his return.

Jane had sent Caroline an early reply to her letter and was counting the days until she could reasonably hope to hear again. The promised thank-you letter from Mr. Collins arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father and written with all the solemnity of gratitude that a yearlong stay with the family might have inspired. Having cleared his conscience on that point, he went on to inform them, with many rapturous expressions, of his happiness in winning the affection of their charming neighbor, Miss Lucas. He then explained that it was merely to enjoy her company that he had been so eager to accept their kind wish to see him again at Longbourn, where he hoped to return in two weeks' time on Monday. For Lady Catherine, he added, so heartily approved of his marriage that she wished it to take place as soon as possible—which he trusted would be an unanswerable argument for his dear Charlotte to set an early date for making him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins's return to Hertfordshire was no longer a source of pleasure to Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was as ready to complain about it as her husband. It was very strange that he should come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge. It was also very inconvenient and extremely annoying. She hated having visitors in the house when her health was so poor, and lovers were the most disagreeable visitors of all. Such were Mrs. Bennet's gentle complaints, and they gave way only to the greater distress of Mr. Bingley's continued absence.

Neither Jane nor Elizabeth was comfortable about this. Day after day passed without bringing any news of him other than the rumor that soon spread through Meryton that he would not return to Netherfield for the entire winter—a report that infuriated Mrs. Bennet and which she never failed to dismiss as a scandalous lie.

Even Elizabeth began to fear—not that Bingley was indifferent—but that his sisters would succeed in keeping him away. Unwilling as she was to accept an idea so destructive to Jane's happiness and so insulting to her suitor's constancy, she could not prevent it from coming back again and again. The combined efforts of his two heartless sisters and his domineering friend, aided by the attractions of Miss Darcy and the entertainments of London, might be too much, she feared, for the strength of his attachment.

As for Jane, _her_ anxiety under this uncertainty was naturally more painful than Elizabeth's. But whatever she felt, she wanted to hide it, and between herself and Elizabeth the subject was never mentioned. But since no such restraint held back their mother, an hour rarely passed without her talking about Bingley, expressing her impatience for his arrival, or even demanding that Jane admit that if he did not come back, she would consider herself very badly treated. It took all of Jane's steady gentleness to endure these attacks with reasonable calm.

Mr. Collins returned with perfect punctuality on the appointed Monday, but his reception at Longbourn was not quite as warm as on his first visit. He was too happy, however, to need much attention, and luckily for the others, the business of courtship spared them a great deal of his company. Most of each day was spent at Lucas Lodge, and he sometimes returned to Longbourn only in time to apologize for his absence before the family went to bed.

Mrs. Bennet was really in a most pitiable state. The slightest mention of anything connected with the match threw her into a fit of bad temper, and wherever she went she was sure to hear it discussed. The sight of Miss Lucas was hateful to her. As her future successor in the house, she regarded Charlotte with jealous loathing. Whenever Charlotte came to visit, she assumed she was counting the hours until she took possession. And whenever Charlotte spoke in a low voice to Mr. Collins, she was convinced they were discussing the Longbourn estate and planning to turn her and her daughters out of the house as soon as Mr. Bennet died. She complained bitterly about all this to her husband.

"Really, Mr. Bennet," she said, "it is very hard to think that Charlotte Lucas should ever be mistress of this house, that _I_ should be forced to make way for _her_, and live to see her take my place in it!"
"My dear, don't give in to such gloomy thoughts. Let us hope for better things. Let us comfort ourselves with the thought that _I_ may be the survivor."
This was not very comforting to Mrs. Bennet, and so instead of responding, she continued as before.
"I cannot bear to think that they should get all this property. If it were not for the entail, I would not mind."
"What wouldn't you mind?"
"I wouldn't mind anything at all."
"Let us be thankful that you are spared from a state of such indifference."

"I can never be thankful, Mr. Bennet, for anything about the entail. How anyone could have the conscience to entail an estate away from one's own daughters, I cannot understand—and all for the sake of Mr. Collins, too! Why should _he_ get it more than anyone else?"
"I leave that for you to work out," said Mr. Bennet.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: Miss Bingley's letter arrived and put an end to all doubt. The very first sentence confirmed that they were all settled in London for the winter, and concluded with her brother's regret at not having had time to pay his respects to his friends in Hertfordshire before leaving.

Hope was over—entirely over. And when Jane could focus on the rest of the letter, she found little besides the writer's professed affection that could give her any comfort. Praise of Miss Darcy filled most of it. Her many charms were dwelt on at length, and Caroline joyfully boasted of their growing closeness and ventured to predict the fulfillment of the hopes she had outlined in her previous letter. She also wrote with great pleasure of her brother staying at Mr. Darcy's house, and mentioned with delight some plans of Darcy's regarding new furniture.

Elizabeth, to whom Jane soon communicated the gist of all this, heard it in silent indignation. Her heart was divided between concern for her sister and resentment against everyone else. She gave no credit to Caroline's claim that her brother preferred Miss Darcy. That he was genuinely fond of Jane she doubted no more than she ever had. And much as she had always been inclined to like him, she could not think without anger—hardly without contempt—of his weak temperament and lack of proper resolve, which now made him the slave of his scheming friends and led him to sacrifice his own happiness to their whims. Had only his own happiness been at stake, he might have been free to play with it however he liked. But her sister's was involved too, and she felt he must know that. It was, in short, a subject on which she could reflect endlessly without getting anywhere. She could think of nothing else—and yet whether Bingley's feelings had truly faded, or were being suppressed by his friends' interference, whether he had known of Jane's attachment or it had escaped his notice—whichever was the case, though her opinion of him would be greatly affected by which it was, her sister's situation was the same, her peace equally damaged.

A day or two passed before Jane had the courage to speak of her feelings to Elizabeth. But at last, when Mrs. Bennet left them alone after a longer rant than usual about Netherfield and its master, she could not help saying:

"Oh, if only my dear mother had more self-control! She has no idea of the pain she causes me with her constant talk about him. But I will not complain. It cannot last long. He will be forgotten, and we shall all be as we were before."
Elizabeth looked at her sister with skeptical concern but said nothing.

"You doubt me," cried Jane, blushing slightly. "Indeed, you have no reason. He may live in my memory as the most agreeable man I have ever known, but that is all. I have nothing to hope or fear, and nothing to blame him for. Thank God I don't have _that_ pain. A little time, therefore—I shall certainly try to get over it—"
In a stronger voice she soon added, "I have this immediate comfort: that it has been nothing more than a mistake on my side, and has done no harm to anyone but myself."

"My dear Jane," exclaimed Elizabeth, "you are too good. Your sweetness and selflessness are truly angelic. I don't know what to say to you. I feel as if I have never done you justice, or loved you as you deserve."
Miss Bennet eagerly denied any special virtue and turned the praise back on her sister's warm affection.

"No," said Elizabeth, "this isn't fair. _You_ wish to think well of everyone, and are hurt if I speak badly of anyone. _I_ only want to think _you_ perfect, and you fight me on it. Don't worry about my going to extremes, or trespassing on your privilege of universal goodwill. You needn't. There are few people I truly love, and still fewer I think well of. The more I see of the world, the more dissatisfied I am with it, and every day confirms my belief in the inconsistency of all human character and how little you can trust the appearance of either goodness or sense. I have met with two instances lately—one I won't mention; the other is Charlotte's marriage. It's inexplicable! From every angle, it's inexplicable!"

"My dear Lizzy, don't give way to such feelings. They will ruin your happiness. You don't make enough allowance for differences in circumstances and temperament. Consider Mr. Collins's respectability, and Charlotte's sensible, steady character. Remember that she is one of a large family, and that in terms of money it is an excellent match. And be ready to believe, for everyone's sake, that she may feel something like respect and esteem for our cousin."

"To please you, I would try to believe almost anything. But no one else could benefit from such a belief, for if I were convinced Charlotte had any regard for him, I would only think worse of her judgment than I now do of her heart. My dear Jane, Mr. Collins is a conceited, pompous, narrow-minded, foolish man—you know he is, as well as I do—and you must feel, as well as I do, that the woman who marries him cannot have a sound way of thinking. You must not defend her, even though it is Charlotte Lucas. You must not, for the sake of one person, change the meaning of principle and integrity, or try to persuade yourself or me that selfishness is wisdom and blindness to danger is a guarantee of happiness."

"I think you are too harsh about both," replied Jane. "And I hope you will be convinced of it by seeing them happy together. But enough of this. You mentioned something else. You said _two_ instances. I cannot misunderstand you, but I beg you, dear Lizzy, not to hurt me by blaming _that person_ and saying your opinion of him has sunk. We must not be so quick to imagine we have been deliberately wronged. We must not expect a lively young man to always be so careful and cautious. Very often it is nothing but our own vanity that misleads us. Women imagine that admiration means more than it does."
"And men make sure that it should."
"If it is done deliberately, they cannot be excused. But I have no idea that there is as much scheming in the world as some people suppose."

"I am far from attributing any part of Mr. Bingley's behavior to scheming," said Elizabeth. "But without intending to do wrong or to make others unhappy, there can be mistakes and there can be misery. Thoughtlessness, failure to consider other people's feelings, and lack of resolve will do the job."
"And do you blame him for one of those?"
"Yes—the last. But if I go on, I shall upset you by saying what I think of people you respect. Stop me while you can."
"You still maintain, then, that his sisters are influencing him?"
"Yes—together with his friend."
"I cannot believe it. Why would they try to influence him? They can only wish for his happiness, and if he is attached to me, no other woman can secure it."

"Your first assumption is wrong. They may wish for many things besides his happiness—they may wish for an increase in his wealth and status. They may wish him to marry a girl who has all the advantages of money, important connections, and social standing."

"There is no doubt they wish he would choose Miss Darcy," replied Jane. "But this may come from better motives than you suppose. They have known her much longer than they have known me—no wonder if they love her better. But whatever their own wishes may be, it is very unlikely they would have opposed their brother. What sister would think herself free to do so, unless something was seriously wrong? If they believed he was attached to me, they would not try to separate us. And if he were attached to me, they could not succeed. By imagining such a scenario, you make everyone behave unnaturally and wrongly, and me most unhappy. Don't distress me with the idea. I am not ashamed of having been mistaken—or at least, it is slight, nothing compared to what I would feel if I thought badly of him or his sisters. Let me see it in the best light—in the way it may be understood."
Elizabeth could not resist such a wish, and from this time Mr. Bingley's name was hardly ever mentioned between them.

Mrs. Bennet still continued to wonder and fret about his not returning, and though Elizabeth explained it clearly almost every day, there seemed little chance of her ever viewing it with less bewilderment. Elizabeth tried to convince her of what she did not believe herself—that his attentions to Jane had been merely the effect of a common and passing attraction, which ended when he no longer saw her. But though the likelihood of this was admitted at the time, the same story had to be repeated every day. Mrs. Bennet's best comfort was that Mr. Bingley would surely come back in the summer.

Mr. Bennet dealt with the matter differently. "So, Lizzy," he said one day, "your sister is disappointed in love, I hear. I congratulate her. Next to being married, a girl likes to be disappointed in love a little now and then. It is something to think about, and gives her a sort of distinction among her friends. When is your turn? You will hardly bear to be outdone by Jane for long. Now is your time. There are enough officers at Meryton to disappoint all the young ladies in the country. Let Wickham be your man. He is a pleasant fellow, and would jilt you creditably."
"Thank you, sir, but a less agreeable man would satisfy me. We cannot all expect Jane's good fortune."
"True," said Mr. Bennet, "but it is a comfort to think that, whatever of that kind may happen to you, you have an affectionate mother who will always make the most of it."

Mr. Wickham's company was a real help in lifting the gloom that recent events had cast over much of the Longbourn family. They saw him often, and to his other attractions was now added that of total openness. Everything Elizabeth had already heard—his claims on Mr. Darcy, and all he had suffered from him—was now openly acknowledged and publicly discussed. And everyone was pleased to think how much they had always disliked Mr. Darcy even before they knew anything about it.

Miss Bennet was the only person who could imagine there might be circumstances that excused him, unknown to Hertfordshire society. Her gentle and steady fairness always argued for allowances and raised the possibility of misunderstanding. But by everyone else, Mr. Darcy was condemned as the worst of men.

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: After a week spent in declarations of love and plans for future happiness, Mr. Collins was called away from his dear Charlotte by the arrival of Saturday. The pain of separation, however, could be eased on his side by preparations for receiving his bride, as he had reason to hope that shortly after his next return to Hertfordshire, the date would be set for making him the happiest of men. He said goodbye to his relatives at Longbourn with as much solemnity as before, wished his fair cousins health and happiness again, and promised their father another letter of thanks.

The following Monday, Mrs. Bennet had the pleasure of welcoming her brother and his wife, who came as usual to spend Christmas at Longbourn. Mr. Gardiner was a sensible, well-mannered man, far superior to his sister in both natural ability and education. The Netherfield ladies would have had difficulty believing that a man who lived by trade, within sight of his own warehouses, could be so polished and pleasant. Mrs. Gardiner, who was several years younger than Mrs. Bennet and Mrs. Philips, was a likable, intelligent, elegant woman and a great favorite with her Longbourn nieces. Between the two eldest and herself especially there was a very close bond. They had frequently stayed with her in town.

Mrs. Gardiner's first order of business on arrival was to hand out her presents and describe the latest fashions. When that was done, she had a less active role to play—it became her turn to listen. Mrs. Bennet had many grievances to air and much to complain about. They had all been terribly treated since she last saw her sister. Two of her girls had been on the verge of marriage, and in the end nothing had come of it.

"I don't blame Jane," she continued, "for Jane would have got Mr. Bingley if she could. But Lizzy! Oh, sister! It is very hard to think that she might have been Mr. Collins's wife by now, if not for her own stubbornness. He proposed to her in this very room, and she refused him. The result is that Lady Lucas will have a daughter married before I do, and the Longbourn estate is just as entailed as ever. The Lucases are very cunning people indeed, sister. They are all about what they can get. I'm sorry to say it of them, but it's true. It makes me very anxious and unwell, to be thwarted so in my own family and to have neighbors who think of themselves before anyone else. However, your coming just at this time is the greatest comfort, and I am very glad to hear what you tell us about long sleeves."
Mrs. Gardiner, to whom most of this news had already been given through Jane and Elizabeth's letters, gave her sister a brief reply and, out of compassion for her nieces, changed the subject.

When alone with Elizabeth afterward, she spoke more on the topic. "It seems to have been a promising match for Jane," she said. "I'm sorry it fell through. But these things happen so often! A young man like your Mr. Bingley so easily falls in love with a pretty girl for a few weeks, and when circumstances separate them, so easily forgets her, that this kind of inconstancy is very common."

"An excellent consolation in its way," said Elizabeth, "but it won't do for _us_. We are not suffering by accident. It does not often happen that the interference of friends persuades a young man of independent fortune to stop thinking about a girl he was deeply in love with only a few days before."

"But the expression 'deeply in love' is so overused, so vague, so indefinite, that it gives me very little to go on. It is as often applied to feelings that arise from half an hour's acquaintance as to a real, strong attachment. Tell me—how _deep_ was Mr. Bingley's love?"

"I never saw a more promising attachment. He was growing quite oblivious to other people and wholly absorbed by her. Every time they met, it was more obvious and striking. At his own ball he offended two or three young ladies by not asking them to dance, and I spoke to him twice myself without getting an answer. Could there be clearer signs? Isn't general rudeness the very essence of love?"

"Oh yes—of the kind of love I suppose him to have felt. Poor Jane! I'm sorry for her, because with her temperament she may not get over it quickly. It would have been better if it had happened to _you_, Lizzy—you would have laughed yourself out of it sooner. But do you think she could be persuaded to come back with us? A change of scene might help, and perhaps a little break from home may do as much good as anything."
Elizabeth was extremely pleased with this idea and felt sure of her sister's willing agreement.

"I hope," added Mrs. Gardiner, "that no thought of this young man will influence her decision. We live in such a different part of town, all our connections are so different, and, as you well know, we go out so little that it is very unlikely they would ever meet, unless he specifically comes to see her."

"And _that_ is quite impossible, for he is now in the custody of his friend, and Mr. Darcy would never allow him to visit Jane in such a part of London! My dear aunt, how could you think it? Mr. Darcy may perhaps have _heard_ of such a place as Gracechurch Street, but he would hardly think a month's cleansing enough to purify him from its taint, were he ever to set foot there. And rest assured, Mr. Bingley never goes anywhere without him."
"So much the better. I hope they won't meet at all. But doesn't Jane write to his sister? _She_ won't be able to resist calling."
"She will drop the friendship entirely."

But despite the certainty with which Elizabeth pretended to settle this point—as well as the still more interesting question of Bingley being prevented from seeing Jane—she felt a concern about it that convinced her, on reflection, that she did not consider the situation entirely hopeless. It was possible, and sometimes she thought it probable, that his feelings might be revived, and the influence of his friends successfully overcome by the more natural pull of Jane's attractions.

Miss Bennet accepted her aunt's invitation with pleasure. The Bingleys were in her thoughts at the same time only insofar as she hoped that since Caroline was not living in the same house as her brother, she might occasionally spend a morning with her without any risk of seeing him.

The Gardiners stayed a week at Longbourn, and between the Philipses, the Lucases, and the officers, there was not a day without a social engagement. Mrs. Bennet had provided so carefully for her brother and sister's entertainment that they never once sat down to a family dinner. When the party was at home, some of the officers always made up part of the group—and Mr. Wickham was always one of them.
