On these occasions, Mrs. Gardiner, made suspicious by Elizabeth's warm praise of him, watched them both carefully. Without supposing from what she saw that they were very seriously in love, their preference for each other was obvious enough to make her a little uneasy. She resolved to speak to Elizabeth about it before leaving Hertfordshire, and to point out the imprudence of encouraging such an attachment.

Wickham had one means of pleasing Mrs. Gardiner that was unconnected with his general charm. About ten or twelve years ago, before her marriage, she had spent a considerable time in the very part of Derbyshire where he was from. They therefore had many acquaintances in common, and though Wickham had been there little since Darcy's father died five years before, he could still give her more recent news of her old friends than she had been able to get elsewhere.

Mrs. Gardiner had seen Pemberley and had known the late Mr. Darcy by reputation very well. Here, therefore, was an inexhaustible topic of conversation. In comparing her memories of Pemberley with the detailed description Wickham could provide, and in offering her tribute of praise to the character of its late owner, she was delighting both him and herself. On being told about the present Mr. Darcy's treatment of Wickham, she tried to recall something of that gentleman's reported character as a young boy that might fit. In the end she was confident that she remembered hearing Fitzwilliam Darcy spoken of as a very proud, ill-natured boy.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Mrs. Gardiner's warning to Elizabeth was delivered promptly and kindly at the first good opportunity to speak with her alone. After honestly telling her what she thought, she continued:

"You are too sensible a girl, Lizzy, to fall in love simply because you are warned against it—so I am not afraid to speak openly. Seriously, I want you to be careful. Do not get involved, or try to involve him, in a relationship that the lack of money would make very unwise. I have nothing to say against _him_—he is a most interesting young man, and if he had the fortune he should have, I would think you could not do better. But as things stand, you must not let your imagination run away with you. You have good sense, and we all expect you to use it. Your father would count on _your_ judgment and good behavior, I am sure. You must not disappoint your father."
"My dear aunt, this really is serious."
"Yes, and I hope to get you to take it seriously too."
"Well, then, you need not worry. I will take care of myself, and of Mr. Wickham too. He shall not be in love with me, if I can help it."
"Elizabeth, you are not being serious now."

"I beg your pardon. I will try again. At present I am not in love with Mr. Wickham—no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison, the most agreeable man I have ever seen—and if he becomes truly attached to me, I think it would be better if he did not. I see the imprudence of it. Oh, _that_ despicable Mr. Darcy! My father's good opinion of me does me the greatest honor, and I would be miserable to lose it. My father, however, is partial to Mr. Wickham. In short, my dear aunt, I would be very sorry to make any of you unhappy. But since we see every day that where there is affection, young people are rarely prevented by a lack of money from getting engaged, how can I promise to be wiser than so many others, if I am tempted? Or how am I even to know it would be wiser to resist? All I can promise, therefore, is not to rush into anything. I will not be quick to believe myself his first choice. When I am with him, I will not be hoping. In short, I will do my best."
"Perhaps it would be wise if you discouraged his coming here so often. At the very least, you should not _remind_ your mother to invite him."

"As I did the other day," said Elizabeth with a sheepish smile. "Very true—it would be wise of me to avoid _that_. But don't imagine he is always here this often. It is on your account that he has been so frequently invited this week. You know my mother's ideas about the necessity of constant company for her guests. But really, and on my honor, I will try to do what I think is wisest. And now I hope you are satisfied."
Her aunt assured her she was, and Elizabeth, having thanked her for the kindness of her advice, they parted—a remarkable instance of advice on such a subject being given without causing offense.

Mr. Collins returned to Hertfordshire soon after the Gardiners and Jane had left, but since he stayed with the Lucases, his arrival was no great inconvenience to Mrs. Bennet. His marriage was now fast approaching, and she had at last resigned herself enough to consider it inevitable, and even repeatedly said, in a spiteful tone, that she "_wished_ they might be happy." Thursday was to be the wedding day, and on Wednesday Miss Lucas paid her farewell visit. When she rose to leave, Elizabeth, ashamed of her mother's grudging good wishes and sincerely moved herself, accompanied her out of the room. As they went downstairs together, Charlotte said:
"I shall count on hearing from you very often, Eliza."
"_That_ you certainly will."
"And I have another favor to ask. Will you come and see me?"
"We shall often meet, I hope, in Hertfordshire."
"I'm not likely to leave Kent for some time. Promise me, therefore, to come to Hunsford."
Elizabeth could not refuse, though she expected little pleasure from the visit.
"My father and Maria are coming to see me in March," added Charlotte, "and I hope you will agree to join them. Really, Eliza, you will be as welcome to me as either of them."

The wedding took place. The bride and groom set off for Kent from the church door, and everyone had as much to say and hear about it as usual. Elizabeth soon heard from her friend, and their correspondence was as regular and frequent as it had ever been—though it could not be equally open. Elizabeth could never write to her without feeling that the comfort of real intimacy was gone. And though she was determined not to slack off as a correspondent, it was for the sake of what had been, rather than what was. Charlotte's first letters were received with considerable eagerness—there was natural curiosity about how she would speak of her new home, how she would like Lady Catherine, and how happy she would dare to claim to be. But when the letters were read, Elizabeth felt that Charlotte expressed herself on every point exactly as she might have predicted. She wrote cheerfully, seemed surrounded by comforts, and mentioned nothing she could not praise. The house, furniture, neighborhood, and roads were all to her taste, and Lady Catherine's behavior was most friendly and accommodating. It was Mr. Collins's picture of Hunsford and Rosings, just toned down to be more reasonable. Elizabeth realized she would have to wait for her own visit to learn the rest.
Jane had already written a few lines to her sister announcing their safe arrival in London, and when she wrote again, Elizabeth hoped she would be able to say something about the Bingleys.

Her impatience for this second letter was rewarded as impatience usually is. Jane had been a week in town without either seeing or hearing from Caroline. She explained it, however, by supposing that her last letter to her friend from Longbourn had been lost in the mail.
"My aunt," she continued, "is going tomorrow to that part of town, and I shall take the opportunity to call at Grosvenor Street."

She wrote again after the visit, having seen Miss Bingley. "I did not think Caroline was in good spirits," were her words, "but she was very glad to see me, and scolded me for not giving her any notice of my coming to London. So I was right—my last letter never reached her. I asked after their brother, of course. He was well, but so busy with Mr. Darcy that they hardly ever saw him. I learned that Miss Darcy was expected for dinner—I wish I could see her. My visit was not long, as Caroline and Mrs. Hurst were going out. I expect I shall see them here soon."
Elizabeth shook her head over this letter. It convinced her that only chance could reveal to Mr. Bingley that her sister was in town.

Four weeks passed, and Jane saw nothing of him. She tried to convince herself she did not regret it, but she could no longer ignore Miss Bingley's neglect. After staying home every morning for two weeks and inventing a fresh excuse for her every evening, the visitor finally appeared—but the brevity of her stay, and even more the change in her manner, would no longer let Jane deceive herself. The letter she wrote to her sister on this occasion shows what she felt:

"My dearest Lizzy will, I am sure, be incapable of gloating over her better judgment at my expense when I confess that I was completely wrong about Miss Bingley's regard for me. But, my dear sister, though events have proved you right, don't think me stubborn if I still maintain that, given her behavior, my trust was as natural as your suspicion. I cannot at all understand her reason for wanting to be close to me. But if the same circumstances arose again, I am sure I would be fooled again. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday, and not a note, not a line, did I receive in the meantime. When she did come, it was very clear she took no pleasure in it. She made a brief, formal apology for not calling sooner, said nothing about wanting to see me again, and was, in every way, so changed that when she left, I was perfectly resolved to end the friendship. I pity her, though I cannot help blaming her. She was very wrong to single me out as she did—I can safely say that every move toward intimacy began on her side. But I pity her because she must feel that she has been acting wrongly, and because I am quite sure that concern for her brother is the cause. I need not explain further. And though _we_ know this concern to be quite unnecessary, if she feels it, it easily explains her behavior toward me. And as genuinely dear as he is to his sister, whatever anxiety she feels on his behalf is natural and understandable. I cannot help wondering, however, that she should have any such fears now, because if he had cared about me at all, we would surely have met long, long ago. He knows I am in town, I am certain, from something she said herself. And yet it seems, from the way she talked, as if she wanted to convince herself that he is really attracted to Miss Darcy. I cannot understand it. If I were not afraid of being too harsh, I would be almost tempted to say that there is a strong appearance of dishonesty in all this. I will try to banish every painful thought and think only of what will make me happy—your love, and the unfailing kindness of my dear uncle and aunt. Write to me very soon. Miss Bingley said something about his never returning to Netherfield again, about giving up the house, but nothing definite. We had better not mention it. I am extremely glad you have such pleasant reports from our friends at Hunsford. Do go and see them with Sir William and Maria. I am sure you will be very comfortable there.
"Yours, etc."

This letter caused Elizabeth some pain, but her spirits returned when she considered that Jane would no longer be deceived, by the sister at least. All hope from the brother was now completely over. She would not even wish for any renewal of his attentions. His character sank with every review of it, and as a punishment for him—as well as a possible benefit to Jane—she seriously hoped he might really soon marry Mr. Darcy's sister, who, by Wickham's account, would make him bitterly regret what he had thrown away.

Around this time, Mrs. Gardiner reminded Elizabeth of her promise regarding that gentleman and asked for news. Elizabeth had information to send that would satisfy her aunt more than herself. His apparent interest had faded, his attentions were over, and he was now admiring someone else. Elizabeth was observant enough to see it all, but she could see it and write about it without serious pain. Her heart had been only slightly touched, and her vanity was satisfied by believing that _she_ would have been his only choice if fortune had allowed it. The sudden acquisition of ten thousand pounds was the most notable charm of the young lady he was now courting. But Elizabeth, perhaps less clear-sighted in this case than in Charlotte's, did not blame him for wanting financial security. Nothing, on the contrary, could be more natural, and while she could suppose it had cost him some struggle to give her up, she was ready to call it a wise and sensible decision for both, and could very sincerely wish him happy.

All this was shared with Mrs. Gardiner, and after describing the circumstances, she continued: "I am now convinced, my dear aunt, that I have never been deeply in love—for if I had really experienced that pure and powerful passion, I should at this moment detest his very name and wish him every kind of misfortune. But my feelings toward _him_ are not only friendly, they are even fair toward Miss King. I cannot find that I hate her at all, or that I am the least bit unwilling to think her a perfectly nice girl. There can be no love in all this. My vigilance has been effective. And though I would certainly be a more interesting figure to my acquaintances were I distractedly in love with him, I cannot say I regret my relative insignificance. Importance may sometimes be purchased too dearly. Kitty and Lydia take his defection much more to heart than I do. They are young in the ways of the world, and not yet open to the humbling truth that handsome young men must have something to live on, just like everyone else."

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: With no more exciting events than these in the Longbourn family, and otherwise varied by little beyond walks to Meryton—sometimes muddy, sometimes cold—January and February passed away. March was to take Elizabeth to Hunsford. She had not at first taken the plan very seriously, but Charlotte, she soon found, was counting on it, and she gradually came to look forward to it with more pleasure and more certainty. Distance had increased her desire to see Charlotte again and weakened her aversion to Mr. Collins. There was novelty in the plan, and since, with such a mother and such unsociable sisters, home could not be perfect, a little change was welcome for its own sake. The journey would also give her a chance to see Jane. And in short, as the time drew near, she would have been very sorry for any delay. Everything went smoothly, however, and was finally arranged according to Charlotte's original plan. She was to travel with Sir William and his second daughter. The added treat of spending a night in London was worked in, and the plan became as perfect as a plan could be.
The only pain was leaving her father, who would certainly miss her, and who, when it came down to it, so disliked her going that he told her to write to him and almost promised to write back.

Her farewell with Mr. Wickham was perfectly friendly—on his side, even more so. His current pursuit could not make him forget that Elizabeth had been the first to attract and deserve his attention, the first to listen and sympathize, the first to be admired. And in his manner of saying goodbye—wishing her every pleasure, reminding her of what to expect from Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and trusting that their opinion of her (their opinion of everybody) would always agree—there was a warmth and interest that she felt must always inspire her sincere regard. She parted from him convinced that, whether married or single, he must always be her model of charm and agreeableness.

Her traveling companions the next day were not the sort to make her think him less appealing. Sir William Lucas and his daughter Maria, a good-natured girl but as empty-headed as himself, had nothing to say worth hearing, and were listened to with about as much enjoyment as the rattle of the carriage. Elizabeth loved absurdity, but she had known Sir William's too long. He could tell her nothing new about the wonders of his presentation at court and his knighthood, and his compliments were as worn out as his stories.

It was a journey of only twenty-four miles, and they started so early that they were in Gracechurch Street by noon. As they drove up to Mr. Gardiner's door, Jane was at a drawing-room window watching for their arrival. When they entered the hall, she was there to welcome them, and Elizabeth, looking carefully at her face, was pleased to see it healthy and lovely as ever. On the stairs was a troop of little boys and girls, whose eagerness for their cousin's arrival would not let them wait in the drawing room, and whose shyness, after not seeing her for a year, prevented them from coming any lower. All was joy and warmth. The day passed most pleasantly—the morning in bustle and shopping, the evening at the theater.

Elizabeth managed to sit by her aunt. Their first topic was her sister, and she was more saddened than surprised to hear, in reply to her detailed questions, that though Jane always tried to keep her spirits up, there were periods of dejection. It was reasonable, however, to hope they would not last. Mrs. Gardiner also gave her the details of Miss Bingley's visit to Gracechurch Street and reported various conversations between Jane and herself, which proved that Jane had, from her heart, given up the friendship.
Mrs. Gardiner then teased her niece about Wickham's desertion, and complimented her on bearing it so well.
"But, my dear Elizabeth," she added, "what sort of girl is Miss King? I should be sorry to think our friend was money-motivated."

"Tell me, my dear aunt, what is the difference in marriage matters between a mercenary motive and a prudent one? Where does good judgment end and greed begin? Last Christmas you were afraid he would marry me because it would be imprudent. And now, because he is pursuing a girl with only ten thousand pounds, you want to decide he is mercenary."
"If you will only tell me what sort of girl Miss King is, I shall know what to think."
"She is a perfectly nice girl, I believe. I know nothing bad about her."
"But he paid her not the slightest attention until her grandfather's death made her the owner of this fortune?"
"No—why should he? If it was not acceptable for him to win _my_ affections because I had no money, what point would there have been in courting a girl he didn't care about, who was equally poor?"
"But there seems something tasteless about turning his attention to her so soon after her grandfather's death."
"A man in difficult circumstances doesn't have time for all the polite niceties that others can observe. If _she_ doesn't mind, why should _we_?"
"_Her_ not minding doesn't justify _him_. It only shows a deficiency in her—either sense or feeling."
"Well," cried Elizabeth, "have it your way. _He_ shall be mercenary, and _she_ shall be foolish."
"No, Lizzy, that is what I do _not_ want. I would be sorry, you know, to think badly of a young man who has lived so long in Derbyshire."

"Oh, if that is all, I have a very poor opinion of young men who live in Derbyshire—and their close friends who live in Hertfordshire are not much better. I am sick of them all. Thank heaven! Tomorrow I am going somewhere I shall find a man who has not one agreeable quality, who has neither manners nor sense to recommend him. Stupid men are the only ones worth knowing, after all."
"Be careful, Lizzy—that remark has a strong taste of disappointment."
Before they were separated by the end of the play, she had the unexpected happiness of an invitation to accompany her uncle and aunt on a pleasure trip they were planning for the summer.
"We haven't quite decided how far it will take us," said Mrs. Gardiner, "but perhaps to the Lake District."

No plan could have been more appealing to Elizabeth, and her acceptance was immediate and grateful. "My dear, dear aunt," she cried rapturously, "what delight! What joy! You give me new life and energy. Goodbye to disappointment and gloom. What are men compared to rocks and mountains? Oh, what hours of bliss we shall have! And when we _do_ return, it will not be like other travelers, unable to describe a single thing accurately. We _will_ know where we have been—we _will_ remember what we have seen. Lakes, mountains, and rivers will not be jumbled together in our imaginations, and when we try to describe a particular scene, we will not start arguing about where it was. Let _our_ first impressions be less unbearable than those of the average tourist."

chapters.title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Everything on the next day's journey was new and interesting to Elizabeth, and her spirits were high. She had seen her sister looking well enough to banish all fear for her health, and the prospect of her summer tour to the north was a constant source of delight.

When they turned off the main road onto the lane to Hunsford, every eye searched for the parsonage, and every turn was expected to bring it into view. The fence of Rosings Park formed their boundary on one side. Elizabeth smiled at the memory of everything she had heard about its inhabitants.

At last the parsonage came into sight. The garden sloping to the road, the house standing in it, the green fence and the laurel hedge—everything announced their arrival. Mr. Collins and Charlotte appeared at the door, and the carriage stopped at the small gate, which led by a short gravel walk to the house, amid the nods and smiles of the entire group. In a moment they were all out of the carriage, delighted to see each other. Mrs. Collins welcomed her friend with the warmest pleasure, and Elizabeth was more and more glad she had come when she found herself so affectionately received. She saw at once that her cousin's manners had not been changed by marriage—his formal politeness was exactly as it had been—and he kept her at the gate for several minutes to hear and satisfy his inquiries about every member of her family. They were then brought into the house, with no other delay than his pointing out the neatness of the entrance. As soon as they were in the parlor, he welcomed them a second time, with showy formality, to his humble home, and precisely repeated all his wife's offers of refreshment.

Elizabeth was prepared to see him in his element, and she could not help thinking that in showing off the good proportions of the room, its view, and its furniture, he was speaking particularly to her, as if wanting to make her feel what she had lost by refusing him. But though everything seemed tidy and comfortable, she could not gratify him with any sigh of regret, and instead looked with wonder at her friend, marveling that she could be so cheerful with such a companion. When Mr. Collins said something his wife might reasonably be embarrassed by—which was certainly not rare—she could not help glancing at Charlotte. Once or twice she caught a faint blush, but in general Charlotte wisely did not listen. After sitting long enough to admire every piece of furniture in the room, from the sideboard to the fireplace screen, and to give an account of their journey and everything that had happened in London, Mr. Collins invited them to stroll through the garden, which was large and well laid out, and to which he devoted much personal attention. Working in his garden was one of his most respectable pleasures, and Elizabeth admired the composure with which Charlotte spoke of the healthfulness of the exercise and admitted she encouraged it as much as possible. Here, leading the way through every path and cross-path, barely allowing them a moment to offer the praise he was fishing for, every view was pointed out with a thoroughness that left beauty entirely behind. He could count the fields in every direction and tell how many trees were in the most distant clump. But of all the views his garden, or the countryside, or the entire kingdom could boast, none could compare with the view of Rosings, glimpsed through an opening in the trees that bordered the park, nearly opposite the front of his house. It was a handsome modern building, well situated on rising ground.

From his garden, Mr. Collins would have led them around his two meadows, but the ladies, not having shoes for the remains of a frost, turned back. While Sir William accompanied him, Charlotte took her sister and friend through the house, probably very pleased to have the chance to show it without her husband's help. It was rather small but well built and convenient, and everything was arranged with a neatness and consistency for which Elizabeth gave Charlotte all the credit. When Mr. Collins could be forgotten, there was really a comfortable atmosphere throughout, and from Charlotte's evident enjoyment of it, Elizabeth supposed he must be often forgotten.
She had already learned that Lady Catherine was still in the country. It was mentioned again at dinner, when Mr. Collins added:

"Yes, Miss Elizabeth, you will have the honor of seeing Lady Catherine de Bourgh at church next Sunday, and I need not say you will be delighted with her. She is all friendliness and graciousness, and I have no doubt you will be honored with some share of her attention after the service. I have scarcely any hesitation in saying that she will include you and my sister Maria in every invitation with which she honors us during your stay here. Her behavior toward my dear Charlotte is charming. We dine at Rosings twice every week and are never allowed to walk home—her Ladyship's carriage is always sent for us. I _should_ say, one of her Ladyship's carriages, for she has several."
"Lady Catherine is a very respectable, sensible woman indeed," added Charlotte, "and a most attentive neighbor."
"Very true, my dear—that is exactly what I say. She is the kind of woman one cannot show too much respect."

The evening was spent mainly talking over Hertfordshire news and repeating what had already been written in letters. When it ended, Elizabeth, in the privacy of her room, had to consider Charlotte's degree of contentment, to admire her skill in managing and her patience in enduring her husband, and to acknowledge that it was all done very well. She also had to anticipate how her visit would pass—the quiet routine of their daily activities, the annoying interruptions of Mr. Collins, and the excitement of their visits to Rosings. Her lively imagination soon settled it all.

Around the middle of the next day, as she was in her room getting ready for a walk, a sudden commotion below seemed to throw the whole house into confusion. After listening for a moment, she heard someone running upstairs in a great hurry and calling loudly for her. She opened the door and found Maria on the landing, who, breathless with excitement, cried out:
"Oh, my dear Eliza! Please hurry and come to the dining room—there is such a sight! I won't tell you what it is. Hurry—come down this minute."

Elizabeth asked questions in vain—Maria would say no more—and they ran down together to the dining room, which faced the lane, in search of this wonder. It was two ladies, stopped in a small open carriage at the garden gate.
"And is this all?" cried Elizabeth. "I expected at least that the pigs had gotten into the garden, and here is nothing but Lady Catherine and her daughter!"

"Oh my!" said Maria, quite shocked at the mistake. "It's not Lady Catherine. The older lady is Mrs. Jenkinson, who lives with them. The other is Miss de Bourgh. Just look at her. She's such a tiny little thing. Who would have thought she could be so thin and small!"
"She is terribly rude to keep Charlotte standing outside in all this wind. Why doesn't she come in?"
"Oh, Charlotte says she hardly ever does. It's the greatest favor when Miss de Bourgh comes inside."
"I like her appearance," said Elizabeth, struck by other thoughts. "She looks sickly and irritable. Yes, she will do for him very well. She will make him a very suitable wife."

Mr. Collins and Charlotte were both standing at the gate talking with the ladies, and Sir William, to Elizabeth's great amusement, was stationed in the doorway, in earnest contemplation of the grandeur before him, and bowing constantly whenever Miss de Bourgh looked his way.

At last there was nothing more to be said. The ladies drove on, and the others went back inside. Mr. Collins no sooner saw the two girls than he began congratulating them on their good fortune, which Charlotte explained by telling them that the whole party was invited to dine at Rosings the next day.

chapters.title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Mr. Collins's triumph following this invitation was complete. The chance to display the grandeur of his patroness to his impressed visitors, and to let them see her graciousness toward himself and his wife, was exactly what he had wished for. That such an opportunity should come so soon was an example of Lady Catherine's condescension that he could not admire enough.

"I confess," he said, "that I would not have been at all surprised by her Ladyship inviting us on Sunday for tea and the evening at Rosings. I rather expected it, from my knowledge of her friendliness. But who could have foreseen such attention as this? Who could have imagined we would receive an invitation to _dine_ there—an invitation including the entire party—so soon after your arrival?"

"I am less surprised at what has happened," replied Sir William, "because of the knowledge of the manners of the great that my position in life has allowed me to acquire. At court, such examples of refined breeding are not uncommon."

Hardly anything else was talked about the whole day or next morning but their visit to Rosings. Mr. Collins was carefully instructing them in what to expect, so that the sight of such rooms, so many servants, and so magnificent a dinner would not completely overwhelm them.
When the ladies were separating to get dressed, he said to Elizabeth:

"Do not worry, my dear cousin, about your clothes. Lady Catherine is far from requiring of us the elegance of dress that suits herself and her daughter. I would simply advise you to put on whatever is your best outfit—there is no need for anything more. Lady Catherine will not think less of you for being simply dressed. She likes the distinction of rank to be maintained."

While they were dressing, he came two or three times to their doors to urge them to hurry, as Lady Catherine very much disliked being kept waiting for dinner. Such intimidating descriptions of her Ladyship and her way of life quite frightened Maria Lucas, who was not used to grand company. She looked forward to her introduction at Rosings with as much dread as her father had felt before his presentation at the royal court.

Since the weather was fine, they had a pleasant walk of about half a mile across the park. Every park has its beauty and its views, and Elizabeth saw much to admire, though she could not be in the raptures Mr. Collins expected the scene to inspire, and was only mildly impressed by his counting of the windows across the front of the house and his report of what the glazing had originally cost Sir Lewis de Bourgh.

When they climbed the steps to the entrance hall, Maria's anxiety was growing by the moment, and even Sir William did not look entirely calm. Elizabeth's courage did not fail her. She had heard nothing about Lady Catherine that suggested she was formidable on account of any extraordinary talent or remarkable virtue, and the mere grandeur of wealth and rank she thought she could face without fear.

From the entrance hall—the fine proportions and finished details of which Mr. Collins pointed out with a rapturous air—they followed the servants through an anteroom to the room where Lady Catherine, her daughter, and Mrs. Jenkinson were sitting. Her Ladyship rose graciously to receive them. Since Mrs. Collins had arranged with her husband that the introductions would be her job, they were performed properly, without any of the apologies and thanks he would have considered necessary.

Despite having been at the royal court, Sir William was so completely awed by the grandeur surrounding him that he barely had the courage to make a deep bow and take his seat without saying a word. His daughter, nearly frightened out of her wits, sat on the edge of her chair, not knowing where to look. Elizabeth found herself perfectly equal to the scene and could observe the three ladies before her with composure. Lady Catherine was a tall, large woman with strong features that might once have been handsome. Her manner was not warm, and her way of receiving them was not such as to let her visitors forget their lower rank. She was not made formidable by silence—but everything she said was spoken in so authoritative a tone that it proclaimed her self-importance and immediately brought Mr. Wickham to Elizabeth's mind. From her observations that day, she believed Lady Catherine to be exactly as he had described.

After studying the mother, in whose face and manner she soon detected some resemblance to Mr. Darcy, she turned her eyes to the daughter, and could almost have shared Maria's astonishment at how thin and small she was. There was no likeness between the two ladies in either figure or face. Miss de Bourgh was pale and sickly—her features, though not ugly, were unremarkable—and she spoke very little, except in a low voice to Mrs. Jenkinson, whose appearance had nothing noteworthy about it and who was entirely occupied with listening to what she said and positioning a screen to shade her eyes properly.

After sitting for a few minutes, they were all sent to one of the windows to admire the view, with Mr. Collins accompanying them to point out its beauties and Lady Catherine kindly informing them that it was much more worth seeing in the summer.

The dinner was extremely lavish, with all the servants and all the silverware Mr. Collins had promised. And as he had also predicted, he took his seat at the foot of the table at her Ladyship's direction, looking as though life could offer nothing greater. He carved and ate and praised with delighted enthusiasm, and every dish was commended first by him, then echoed by Sir William, who had recovered enough to repeat whatever his son-in-law said—in a manner that Elizabeth wondered Lady Catherine could bear. But Lady Catherine seemed pleased by their excessive admiration and bestowed most gracious smiles, especially when any dish on the table was new to them. The party did not provide much conversation. Elizabeth was ready to speak whenever there was an opening, but she was seated between Charlotte and Miss de Bourgh—the former busy listening to Lady Catherine, the latter not saying a word to her throughout dinner. Mrs. Jenkinson was mainly occupied watching how little Miss de Bourgh ate, urging her to try another dish and worrying she was unwell. Maria thought speaking was out of the question, and the gentlemen did nothing but eat and admire.

When the ladies returned to the drawing room, there was little to do but listen to Lady Catherine talk, which she did without pause until coffee arrived, delivering her opinion on every subject in so decisive a manner as showed she was not used to having her judgment questioned. She inquired into Charlotte's household matters in great detail and gave her a great deal of advice on managing everything. She told her how everything should be run in a household as small as hers and instructed her on the care of her cows and poultry. Elizabeth found that nothing was beneath this great lady's attention that could give her an opportunity to tell others what to do. In the breaks between her conversations with Mrs. Collins, she addressed various questions to Maria and Elizabeth, but especially to Elizabeth, about whom she knew the least, and who, she remarked to Mrs. Collins, was a very well-mannered, pretty sort of girl. She asked her at different times how many sisters she had, whether they were older or younger than herself, whether any of them were likely to marry, whether they were pretty, where they had been educated, what carriage her father kept, and what her mother's maiden name was. Elizabeth felt the full impertinence of her questions but answered them all calmly. Lady Catherine then observed:

"Your father's estate is entailed on Mr. Collins, I believe? For your sake," turning to Charlotte, "I am glad of it. But otherwise I see no reason for entailing estates away from the female line. It was not considered necessary in Sir Lewis de Bourgh's family. Do you play and sing, Miss Bennet?"
"A little."
"Oh, then—sometime we shall be glad to hear you. Our instrument is a superb one, probably better than—you shall try it one day. Do your sisters play and sing?"
"One of them does."
"Why didn't you all learn? You all should have learned. The Miss Webbs all play, and their father has not as good an income as yours. Do you draw?"
"No, not at all."
"What, none of you?"
"Not one."
"That is very strange. But I suppose you had no opportunity. Your mother should have taken you to London every spring for proper instruction."
"My mother would have had no objection, but my father hates London."
"Has your governess left you?"
"We never had a governess."
"No governess! How was that possible? Five daughters raised at home without a governess! I never heard of such a thing. Your mother must have been quite a slave to your education."
Elizabeth could hardly keep from smiling as she assured her that had not been the case.
"Then who taught you? Who looked after you? Without a governess, you must have been neglected."

"Compared with some families, I believe we were. But those of us who wished to learn never lacked the means. We were always encouraged to read, and had all the tutors we needed. Those who chose to be lazy certainly could be."

"Yes, no doubt—but that is what a governess would prevent. And if I had known your mother, I would have strongly advised her to hire one. I always say that nothing can be accomplished in education without steady and regular instruction, and nobody but a governess can provide it. It is remarkable how many families I have helped by finding them one. I am always glad to get a young person well placed. Four nieces of Mrs. Jenkinson are most delightfully situated through my efforts. And just the other day I recommended another young person who was merely mentioned to me in passing, and the family is absolutely delighted with her. Mrs. Collins, did I tell you that Lady Metcalfe called yesterday to thank me? She finds Miss Pope a treasure. 'Lady Catherine,' she said, 'you have given me a treasure.' Are any of your younger sisters out in society, Miss Bennet?"
"Yes, ma'am, all of them."
"All! What, all five out at once? Very odd! And you only the second. The younger ones out before the elder ones are married! Your younger sisters must be very young?"

"Yes, my youngest is not yet sixteen. Perhaps _she_ is too young to be much in society. But really, ma'am, I think it would be very unfair to the younger sisters if they were denied their share of society and entertainment simply because the elder ones may not have the means or inclination to marry early. The youngest has as much right to the pleasures of youth as the eldest. And to be held back for _such_ a reason! I think it would hardly promote sisterly affection or delicacy of feeling."
"Upon my word," said her Ladyship, "you give your opinion very decidedly for such a young person. Tell me, what is your age?"
"With three younger sisters grown up," replied Elizabeth, smiling, "your Ladyship can hardly expect me to reveal it."
Lady Catherine seemed quite astonished at not receiving a direct answer, and Elizabeth suspected she was the first person who had ever dared to trifle with such grand impertinence.
"You cannot be more than twenty, I am sure—so there is no need to hide your age."
"I am not yet twenty-one."

When the gentlemen had joined them and tea was over, the card tables were set up. Lady Catherine, Sir William, and Mr. and Mrs. Collins sat down to quadrille. Since Miss de Bourgh chose to play casino, the two girls had the honor of helping Mrs. Jenkinson make up her table. Their game was supremely dull. Scarcely a word was spoken that did not relate to the cards, except when Mrs. Jenkinson expressed her fears that Miss de Bourgh was too hot or too cold, or had too much or too little light. Much more happened at the other table. Lady Catherine was generally speaking—pointing out the other three players' mistakes or telling some story about herself. Mr. Collins was busy agreeing with everything her Ladyship said, thanking her for every hand he won, and apologizing if he thought he won too many. Sir William said little. He was storing up anecdotes and noble names in his memory.

When Lady Catherine and her daughter had played as long as they wished, the tables were broken up, the carriage was offered to Mrs. Collins, gratefully accepted, and immediately ordered. The party then gathered around the fire to hear Lady Catherine announce what weather they were to have the next day. They were called from these instructions by the arrival of the coach, and with many speeches of gratitude from Mr. Collins and as many bows from Sir William, they departed. As soon as they had driven from the door, Elizabeth was called upon by her cousin to give her opinion of everything she had seen at Rosings—which, for Charlotte's sake, she made more favorable than it really was. But her praise, though costing her some effort, could by no means satisfy Mr. Collins, and he was very soon obliged to take up her Ladyship's praise himself.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Sir William stayed only a week at Hunsford, but his visit was long enough to convince him that his daughter was very comfortably settled, and that she had a husband and a neighbor not often found. While Sir William was with them, Mr. Collins devoted his mornings to driving him around the area in his carriage and showing him the countryside. But when he left, the whole family returned to their usual routines, and Elizabeth was grateful to find that this change did not mean seeing more of her cousin. For most of the time between breakfast and dinner he was now either working in the garden, or reading and writing in his own study, which faced the road, and looking out the window. The room where the ladies sat was at the back. Elizabeth had at first wondered why Charlotte did not prefer the dining room for everyday use—it was bigger and had a nicer view—but she soon saw that her friend had an excellent reason. Mr. Collins would undoubtedly have spent much less time in his own room had they been sitting in one equally pleasant, and she gave Charlotte full credit for the arrangement.

From the drawing room they could see nothing of the lane, and depended on Mr. Collins for news of what carriages passed—and how often, especially, Miss de Bourgh drove by in her little carriage, which he never failed to come and report, though it happened almost every day. She fairly often stopped at the parsonage and had a few minutes' conversation with Charlotte, but could rarely be persuaded to come inside.

Very few days passed without Mr. Collins walking over to Rosings, and not many without his wife feeling it necessary to do the same. Until Elizabeth remembered that there might be other parish appointments to be gained, she could not understand the sacrifice of so many hours. Now and then they were honored with a visit from her Ladyship, and nothing going on in the room escaped her observation during these calls. She examined their occupations, looked at their work, and told them to do it differently. She found fault with the furniture arrangement and caught the maid being negligent. And if she accepted any refreshment, she seemed to do so only to point out that Mrs. Collins's cuts of meat were too large for her family.

Elizabeth soon realized that though this great lady held no official position of authority in the county, she was the most active magistrate in her own parish. Mr. Collins brought every tiny concern to her, and whenever any of the villagers were inclined to be quarrelsome, dissatisfied, or too poor, she marched into the village to settle their disputes, silence their complaints, and scold them into peace and prosperity.

The pleasure of dining at Rosings was repeated about twice a week, and allowing for the loss of Sir William and there being only one card table in the evening, each such dinner was a copy of the first. Their other engagements were few, as the social life of the neighborhood was generally beyond the Collinses' means. This, however, was no hardship for Elizabeth, and on the whole she spent her time comfortably enough. There were half hours of pleasant conversation with Charlotte, and the weather was so fine for the time of year that she often had great enjoyment outdoors. Her favorite walk, where she often went while the others were visiting Lady Catherine, was along the open grove that bordered that side of the park, where there was a nice sheltered path that no one seemed to appreciate but herself, and where she felt beyond the reach of Lady Catherine's curiosity.

In this quiet way the first two weeks of her visit passed. Easter was approaching, and the week before it was to bring an addition to the family at Rosings—which in so small a circle must be important. Elizabeth had heard, soon after her arrival, that Mr. Darcy was expected there within a few weeks. And though there were not many of her acquaintances she did not prefer to him, his coming would provide a relatively new face at their Rosings parties, and she might be amused by seeing how hopeless Miss Bingley's pursuit of him was, judging by his behavior toward his cousin—the woman Lady Catherine had clearly destined for him. Lady Catherine talked of his coming with the greatest satisfaction, spoke of him in terms of the highest admiration, and seemed almost annoyed to learn that Miss Lucas and Elizabeth had already seen him several times.
His arrival was soon known at the parsonage, for Mr. Collins spent the whole morning walking within sight of the gates opening onto Hunsford Lane, in order to have

the earliest confirmation of it. After bowing as the carriage turned into the park, he hurried home with the great news. The following morning he rushed to Rosings to pay his respects. There were two nephews of Lady Catherine requiring them, for Mr. Darcy had brought with him a Colonel Fitzwilliam, the younger son of his uncle, a lord. And to the great surprise of the whole household, when Mr. Collins returned, the gentlemen came with him. Charlotte had seen them from her husband's study crossing the road, and immediately ran into the other room to tell the girls what an honor they could expect, adding:
"I may thank you, Eliza, for this courtesy. Mr. Darcy would never have come so soon to visit me."

Elizabeth had barely time to deny any claim to the compliment before their approach was announced by the doorbell, and shortly afterward the three gentlemen entered the room. Colonel Fitzwilliam, who led the way, was about thirty, not handsome, but in appearance and manner every inch the gentleman. Mr. Darcy looked just as he always had in Hertfordshire, paid his respects to Mrs. Collins with his usual reserve, and whatever his feelings toward her friend might be, greeted her with every appearance of composure. Elizabeth merely curtsied to him without saying a word.

Colonel Fitzwilliam struck up a conversation immediately, with the ease and confidence of a well-bred man, and talked very pleasantly. But his cousin, after making a brief remark about the house and garden to Mrs. Collins, sat for some time without speaking to anyone. At last, however, his politeness stirred enough for him to ask Elizabeth about the health of her family. She answered in the usual way, and after a moment's pause, added:
"My eldest sister has been in town these three months. Have you never happened to see her there?"

She knew perfectly well he never had, but she wanted to see whether he would betray any awareness of what had passed between the Bingleys and Jane. She thought he looked a little uncomfortable as he answered that he had never been fortunate enough to meet Miss Bennet. The subject was dropped, and the gentlemen soon left.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: Colonel Fitzwilliam's manners were much admired at the parsonage, and the ladies all felt he would considerably enhance the pleasure of their visits to Rosings. It was some days, however, before they received any invitation there, for while there were visitors in the house they were not needed. It was not until Easter Sunday, nearly a week after the gentlemen's arrival, that they were honored with such an attention—and then they were merely asked, on leaving church, to come that evening. For the past week they had seen very little of either Lady Catherine or her daughter. Colonel Fitzwilliam had called at the parsonage more than once during that time, but Mr. Darcy they had seen only at church.

The invitation was accepted, of course, and at a suitable hour they joined the party in Lady Catherine's drawing room. Her Ladyship received them politely, but it was clear that their company was not nearly as welcome as when she could get no one else. She was, in fact, almost entirely absorbed by her nephews, talking to them—especially to Darcy—much more than to anyone else in the room.

Colonel Fitzwilliam seemed genuinely glad to see them—anything was a welcome relief to him at Rosings—and Mrs. Collins's pretty friend had caught his eye considerably. He now sat beside her and talked so agreeably about Kent and Hertfordshire, about traveling and staying home, about new books and music, that Elizabeth had never been half so well entertained in that room before. They conversed with so much energy and flow that they drew the attention of Lady Catherine herself, as well as Mr. Darcy. _His_ eyes had been quickly and repeatedly turned toward them with a look of curiosity, and that her Ladyship eventually shared the feeling was more openly shown, for she did not hesitate to call out:
"What is that you are saying, Fitzwilliam? What are you talking about? What are you telling Miss Bennet? Let me hear."
"We were talking about music, madam," he said, when he could no longer avoid answering.

"About music! Then please speak louder. It is of all subjects my favorite. I must have my share of the conversation if you are discussing music. There are few people in England, I suppose, who have more true enjoyment of music than I do, or a better natural taste. If I had ever learned, I should have been highly accomplished. And so would Anne, if her health had allowed her to practice. I am confident she would have played beautifully. How is Georgiana getting on, Darcy?"
Mr. Darcy spoke with warm praise of his sister's skill.
"I am very glad to hear such a good report of her," said Lady Catherine, "and please tell her from me that she cannot expect to excel if she does not practice a great deal."
"I assure you, madam," he replied, "she does not need such advice. She practices very regularly."

"So much the better. It cannot be done too much. And when I next write to her, I shall insist that she not neglect it on any account. I often tell young ladies that no excellence in music can be achieved without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play really well unless she practices more. And though Mrs. Collins has no piano, she is very welcome, as I have often told her, to come to Rosings every day and play the one in Mrs. Jenkinson's room. She would be in nobody's way in that part of the house."
Mr. Darcy looked somewhat embarrassed by his aunt's rudeness and made no reply.

When coffee was over, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him, and she sat down at the piano immediately. He drew a chair near her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, then resumed talking to her other nephew—until Darcy walked away from her and, moving with his usual deliberation toward the piano, positioned himself so as to have a full view of the performer's face. Elizabeth saw what he was doing and, at the first convenient pause, turned to him with a knowing smile and said:

"You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming over in such state to listen. But I will not be intimidated, even though your sister _does_ play so well. There is a stubbornness in me that cannot bear to be scared by other people's wishes. My courage always rises with every attempt to bully me."

"I shall not say you are wrong," he replied, "because you could not truly believe I intend to alarm you. And I have had the pleasure of knowing you long enough to realize that you enjoy occasionally expressing opinions that are not actually your own."

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this picture of herself, and said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, "Your cousin will give you a very unflattering impression of me, and teach you not to believe a word I say. I am particularly unlucky to meet with someone so capable of exposing my real character, in a part of the world where I had hoped to pass myself off with some credit. Really, Mr. Darcy, it is very unfair of you to mention everything you knew against me in Hertfordshire—and, let me say, very unwise too—for you are provoking me to retaliate, and things may come out that would shock your relatives."
"I am not afraid of you," he said, smiling.
"Please let me hear what you accuse him of," cried Colonel Fitzwilliam. "I would like to know how he behaves among strangers."

"You shall hear—but prepare for something truly dreadful. The first time I ever saw him in Hertfordshire, you must know, was at a ball—and at this ball, what do you think he did? He danced only four dances! I am sorry to shock you, but it's true. He danced only four dances, though gentlemen were scarce, and to my certain knowledge, more than one young lady was sitting without a partner. Mr. Darcy, you cannot deny the fact."
"I did not at that time have the honor of knowing any lady at the assembly beyond my own group."
"True—and nobody can ever be introduced at a ball. Well, Colonel Fitzwilliam, what shall I play next? My fingers await your orders."
"Perhaps," said Darcy, "I should have done better to seek an introduction. But I am not good at making myself agreeable to strangers."

"Shall we ask your cousin the reason?" said Elizabeth, still addressing Colonel Fitzwilliam. "Shall we ask him why a man of sense and education, who has lived in the world, is unable to make himself agreeable to strangers?"
"I can answer that," said Fitzwilliam, "without asking him. It is because he won't make the effort."

"I certainly do not have the talent that some people possess," said Darcy, "of conversing easily with people I have never met before. I cannot pick up their tone of conversation or seem interested in their concerns, the way I often see others do."

"My fingers," said Elizabeth, "do not move over this instrument with the mastery I see in so many other women. They do not have the same strength or speed, and do not produce the same expression. But I have always supposed it to be my own fault—because I would not take the trouble to practice. It is not that I don't believe _my_ fingers are as capable as any other woman's of superior performance."
Darcy smiled and said, "You are perfectly right. You have spent your time much better. No one privileged to hear you can think anything is missing. Neither of us performs for strangers."

Here they were interrupted by Lady Catherine, who called out to know what they were talking about. Elizabeth immediately began playing again. Lady Catherine approached, and after listening for a few minutes, said to Darcy:

"Miss Bennet would not play at all badly if she practiced more and had the benefit of a London teacher. She has a very good sense of technique, though her taste is not equal to Anne's. Anne would have been a wonderful performer, had her health allowed her to learn."

Elizabeth looked at Darcy to see how warmly he endorsed his cousin's praise, but neither at that moment nor at any other could she detect any sign of love. And from his whole manner toward Miss de Bourgh she drew this comfort for Miss Bingley: that he might just as easily have married _her_, had she been his relative.

Lady Catherine continued her comments on Elizabeth's playing, mixing in many instructions on technique and taste. Elizabeth received them with all the patience of politeness, and at the gentlemen's request remained at the piano until her Ladyship's carriage was ready to take them all home.

chapters.title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Elizabeth was sitting alone the next morning, writing to Jane, while Mrs. Collins and Maria were out in the village on errands, when she was startled by a ring at the door—the sure sign of a visitor. Since she had heard no carriage, she thought it might be Lady Catherine, and under that assumption was putting away her half-finished letter to avoid impertinent questions, when the door opened and, to her very great surprise, Mr. Darcy—and Mr. Darcy alone—entered the room.
He seemed astonished too at finding her alone, and apologized for his intrusion, explaining that he had been told all the ladies were at home.

They sat down, and after her inquiries about Rosings were made, seemed in danger of sinking into complete silence. It was absolutely necessary to think of something, and in this emergency, remembering _when_ she had last seen him in Hertfordshire and feeling curious to know what he would say about their sudden departure, she observed:

"How very suddenly you all left Netherfield last November, Mr. Darcy! It must have been a pleasant surprise for Mr. Bingley to see you all follow him so quickly—for, if I remember correctly, he left only the day before. He and his sisters were well, I hope, when you left London?"
"Perfectly, thank you."
She found that she was to get no other answer, and after a short pause, added:
"I think I have understood that Mr. Bingley has little idea of ever returning to Netherfield?"

"I have never heard him say so, but it is likely that he may spend very little time there in the future. He has many friends, and at his time of life, friends and engagements are constantly multiplying."

"If he means to be there so little, it would be better for the neighborhood if he gave up the place entirely, for then we might possibly get a settled family there. But perhaps Mr. Bingley did not take the house so much for the neighborhood's convenience as for his own, and we must expect him to keep or give it up on the same basis."
"I would not be surprised," said Darcy, "if he were to give it up as soon as a suitable property comes along to buy."
Elizabeth made no answer. She was afraid of talking longer about his friend, and having nothing else to say, was now determined to leave the effort of finding a topic to him.
He took the hint and soon began with, "This seems a very comfortable house. Lady Catherine, I believe, did a great deal to it when Mr. Collins first came to Hunsford."
"I believe she did—and I'm sure she could not have bestowed her kindness on a more grateful recipient."
"Mr. Collins seems very fortunate in his choice of wife."

"Yes, indeed. His friends may well be glad he found one of the very few sensible women who would have accepted him, or who could have made him happy if they had. My friend has excellent understanding—though I am not sure I consider her marrying Mr. Collins the wisest thing she ever did. She seems perfectly happy, however, and from a practical standpoint, it is certainly a very good match for her."
"It must be very pleasant for her to be settled within such easy distance of her own family and friends."
"An easy distance, you call it? It is nearly fifty miles."
"And what is fifty miles of good road? Little more than half a day's journey. Yes, I call it a very easy distance."
"I would never have considered the distance one of the _advantages_ of the match," cried Elizabeth. "I would never have said Mrs. Collins was settled _near_ her family."
"It is proof of your own attachment to Hertfordshire. Anything beyond the immediate neighborhood of Longbourn, I suppose, would seem far to you."
As he spoke, there was a sort of smile that Elizabeth thought she understood—he must be thinking she was referring to Jane and Netherfield—and she blushed as she answered:

"I do not mean to say that a woman cannot be settled too near her family. Near and far must be relative, and depend on many different circumstances. Where there is enough wealth to make the cost of traveling unimportant, distance is no problem. But that is not the case _here_. Mr. and Mrs. Collins have a comfortable income, but not one that allows frequent travel—and I am sure my friend would not call herself _near_ her family at anything less than _half_ the present distance."
Mr. Darcy drew his chair a little closer to her and said, "_You_ cannot have a right to such strong local attachment. _You_ cannot have always been at Longbourn."
Elizabeth looked surprised. The gentleman seemed to experience some change of feeling; he drew back his chair, picked up a newspaper from the table, and, glancing over it, said in a cooler voice:
"Are you enjoying Kent?"

A brief, calm conversation about the area followed, cut short by the entrance of Charlotte and her sister, just back from their walk. The private meeting surprised them. Mr. Darcy explained the mistake that had led to his intruding on Miss Bennet, and after sitting a few minutes more, without saying much to anyone, he left.
"What can this mean?" said Charlotte, as soon as he was gone. "My dear Eliza, he must be in love with you, or he would never have called on us in this casual way."

But when Elizabeth described his silence, it did not seem very likely, even to Charlotte's hopeful mind. After various guesses, they could only conclude that his visit was the result of having nothing else to do—which was more plausible given the time of year. All outdoor sports were over. Indoors there was Lady Catherine, books, and a billiard table, but gentlemen cannot always stay inside. And whether because of the nearness of the parsonage, the pleasantness of the walk, or the company of the people who lived there, the two cousins found a reason to walk there almost every day from this point on. They called at various times in the morning, sometimes separately, sometimes together, and now and then accompanied by their aunt. It was clear to everyone that Colonel Fitzwilliam came because he enjoyed their company—a conviction that naturally recommended him further—and Elizabeth was reminded, by her own pleasure in being with him and by his obvious admiration, of her former favorite, George Wickham. Though in comparing them she saw less of that captivating gentleness in Colonel Fitzwilliam's manner, she believed he might have the better-informed mind.

But why Mr. Darcy came so often to the parsonage was harder to understand. It could not be for the company, since he frequently sat there for ten minutes without opening his mouth. And when he did speak, it seemed forced by necessity rather than chosen—a sacrifice to politeness, not a pleasure to himself. He rarely seemed truly engaged. Mrs. Collins did not know what to make of him. Colonel Fitzwilliam's occasional laughter at his dullness proved that he was usually different, which her own limited knowledge of him could not have told her. And since she would have liked to believe this change was the effect of love—with the object of that love being her friend Eliza—she set herself seriously to investigating. She watched him whenever they were at Rosings and whenever he came to Hunsford, but without much success. He certainly looked at her friend a great deal, but the expression in that look was debatable. It was an earnest, steady gaze, but she often doubted whether it contained much admiration, and sometimes it seemed like nothing more than absent-mindedness.

She had once or twice suggested to Elizabeth the possibility of his being interested in her, but Elizabeth always laughed at the idea. Mrs. Collins did not think it right to press the point, for fear of raising hopes that might end in disappointment—for in her opinion, there was not the slightest doubt that all her friend's dislike would vanish if she could believe him to be in her power.

In her kind plans for Elizabeth, she sometimes imagined her marrying Colonel Fitzwilliam. He was, beyond comparison, the more pleasant man; he certainly admired her; and his position in life was most suitable. But to offset these advantages, Mr. Darcy had considerable power to grant church appointments, and his cousin had none at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: More than once, Elizabeth unexpectedly ran into Mr. Darcy during her walks in the park. She felt the full perversity of the bad luck that should bring him where no one else came. To prevent it happening again, she took care to inform him at first that this was a favorite spot of hers. How it could happen a second time, therefore, was very strange! Yet it did—and even a third time. It seemed like deliberate bad luck or voluntary penance, for on these occasions it was not merely a few formal questions and an awkward pause before moving on—he actually thought it necessary to turn back and walk with her. He never said much, and she did not trouble herself to talk or listen much either. But during their third encounter, it struck her that he was asking some oddly disconnected questions—about whether she was enjoying Hunsford, her love of solitary walks, and her opinion of Mr. and Mrs. Collins's happiness. And in speaking of Rosings, and her not having fully explored the house, he seemed to assume that whenever she came to Kent again she would be staying _there_ too. His words seemed to imply it. Could he have Colonel Fitzwilliam in mind? She supposed, if he meant anything, he must be hinting at what might develop in that direction. It unsettled her a little, and she was quite glad to reach the gate opposite the parsonage.

She was occupied one day, as she walked, in rereading Jane's latest letter and lingering over passages that showed Jane had not written in good spirits, when, instead of being surprised again by Mr. Darcy, she looked up and saw Colonel Fitzwilliam coming toward her. Putting the letter away immediately and forcing a smile, she said:
"I didn't know you ever walked this way."
"I have been making the circuit of the park," he replied, "as I generally do every year, and I intended to finish with a call at the parsonage. Are you going much farther?"
"No, I was about to turn back."
And so she did, and they walked toward the parsonage together.
"Are you definitely leaving Kent on Saturday?" she asked.
"Yes—if Darcy doesn't postpone it again. But I'm at his disposal. He arranges things just as he pleases."

"And if he can't please himself with the arrangement, he at least takes great pleasure in the power of choice. I don't know anyone who seems to enjoy the power of doing what he likes more than Mr. Darcy."

"He does like to have his own way," replied Colonel Fitzwilliam. "But then, so do we all. It's just that he has better means of getting it than most, because he is rich and many others are poor. I speak from experience. A younger son, you know, must learn self-denial and dependence."

"In my opinion, the younger son of an earl can know very little of either. Now, seriously, what have you ever known of self-denial and dependence? When have you been prevented by lack of money from going wherever you wanted or buying whatever you fancied?"

"Those are pointed questions—and perhaps I cannot say I have experienced many hardships of that kind. But in matters of greater weight, I may suffer from a lack of money. Younger sons cannot marry where they like."
"Unless they happen to like women of fortune, which I think they very often do."
"Our expensive habits make us too dependent, and there are not many people in my rank of life who can afford to marry without some attention to money."

"Is this," thought Elizabeth, "meant for me?" She colored at the idea, but recovering herself, said lightly, "And tell me, what is the going rate for an earl's younger son? Unless the elder brother is very sickly, I suppose you wouldn't ask more than fifty thousand pounds."
He answered her in the same tone, and the subject was dropped. To break a silence that might make him think she was affected by what had been said, she soon remarked:

"I imagine your cousin brought you down with him mainly to have someone at his disposal. I'm surprised he doesn't marry, to secure a permanent convenience of that sort. But perhaps his sister serves the purpose for now—and since she is under his sole care, he can do what he likes with her."
"No," said Colonel Fitzwilliam, "that is a privilege he must share with me. I am joint guardian of Miss Darcy."

"Are you really? And what sort of guardian are you? Does your charge give you much trouble? Young ladies of her age are sometimes a little difficult to manage, and if she has the true Darcy spirit, she may like to have her own way."

As she spoke, she noticed him looking at her intently, and the way he immediately asked why she supposed Miss Darcy would give them any trouble convinced her that she had somehow gotten very close to the truth. She replied directly:

"You needn't worry. I never heard anything bad about her, and I dare say she is one of the most easygoing young women in the world. She is a great favorite with some ladies I know—Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley. I think I've heard you say you know them."
"I know them a little. Their brother is a pleasant, gentlemanly man—he is a great friend of Darcy's."
"Oh yes," said Elizabeth drily, "Mr. Darcy is uncommonly kind to Mr. Bingley, and takes a tremendous amount of care of him."

"Care of him! Yes, I really believe Darcy _does_ take care of him in those areas where he most needs it. From something he told me on our journey here, I have reason to think Bingley is very much in his debt. But I should beg his pardon—I have no right to assume Bingley was the person he meant. It was all guesswork."
"What do you mean?"
"It is something Darcy would naturally not want widely known, because if it got back to the lady's family, it would be unpleasant."
"You can count on my not mentioning it."

"And remember, I have little reason for thinking it was Bingley. What he told me was simply this: that he congratulated himself on having recently saved a friend from the difficulties of a very unwise marriage—but without naming names or giving any other details. I only guessed it was Bingley because he seemed the kind of young man to get into that sort of situation, and because I knew they had been together all last summer."
"Did Mr. Darcy give you his reasons for this interference?"
"I understood there were some very strong objections to the lady."
"And what methods did he use to separate them?"
"He didn't describe his own methods," said Fitzwilliam, smiling. "He only told me what I have now told you."
Elizabeth made no answer and walked on, her heart swelling with indignation. After watching her for a moment, Fitzwilliam asked why she was so thoughtful.
"I am thinking about what you have been telling me," she said. "Your cousin's behavior doesn't sit well with me. Why should he be the judge?"
"You are inclined to call his interference meddlesome?"

"I don't see what right Mr. Darcy had to decide on the appropriateness of his friend's feelings, or why, on his own judgment alone, he should determine and direct how that friend was to be happy. But," she continued, collecting herself, "since we don't know all the details, it is not fair to condemn him. It is not to be supposed there was much love in the case."
"That is not an unreasonable guess," said Fitzwilliam, "but it considerably diminishes the honor of my cousin's triumph."

This was said jokingly, but it seemed to her such an accurate picture of Mr. Darcy that she did not trust herself to respond. She therefore abruptly changed the subject and talked of unrelated matters until they reached the parsonage. There, shut in her own room as soon as their visitor left, she could think without interruption about everything she had heard. It was impossible to suppose any other people were meant than those she was connected to. There could not exist in the world _two_ men over whom Mr. Darcy had such unlimited influence. That he had been involved in the efforts to separate Mr. Bingley and Jane she had never doubted, but she had always assumed Miss Bingley was the chief planner and orchestrator. If his own vanity was not misleading him, however, _he_ was the cause—his pride and caprice were the cause—of all that Jane had suffered, and still continued to suffer. He had destroyed, for a time, every hope of happiness for the most loving, generous heart in the world—and no one could say how lasting the damage might be.

"There were some very strong objections to the lady" were Colonel Fitzwilliam's words—and these strong objections probably were that she had one uncle who was a country lawyer and another who was in business in London.

"Against Jane herself," she exclaimed, "there could not possibly be any objection—as lovely and good as she is! Her understanding excellent, her mind well-informed, and her manners captivating. Nor could anything be said against my father, who, though with some eccentricities, has abilities that Mr. Darcy himself need not look down on, and a respectability he will probably never achieve." When she thought of her mother, admittedly, her confidence wavered a little—but she would not allow that any objections _there_ carried real weight with Mr. Darcy, whose pride, she was convinced, would be more deeply wounded by his friend's connections lacking social importance than by their lacking sense. She was quite certain, in the end, that he had been partly driven by this worst kind of pride, and partly by the wish to keep Mr. Bingley for his sister.

The agitation and tears this subject brought on gave her a headache, and it grew so much worse toward the evening that, combined with her unwillingness to see Mr. Darcy, she decided not to accompany her cousins to Rosings, where they were invited for tea. Mrs. Collins, seeing she was genuinely unwell, did not press her to go, and did her best to prevent her husband from pressing her. But Mr. Collins could not hide his worry that Lady Catherine might be rather displeased by her staying home.

chapters.title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: When they were gone, Elizabeth, as if trying to work herself up against Mr. Darcy as much as possible, chose to spend her time rereading all the letters Jane had written since she had been in Kent. They contained no outright complaints, no rehashing of past events, and no mention of present suffering. But in all of them, in almost every line, there was an absence of the cheerfulness that had always characterized her writing—cheerfulness that came from a mind at peace with itself and well-disposed toward everyone, and that had rarely been dimmed. Elizabeth noticed every sentence that hinted at unhappiness, with an attention she had barely given them on first reading. Mr. Darcy's shameful boast about the misery he had been able to inflict gave her a sharper sense of her sister's pain. It was some comfort to know that his visit to Rosings would end the day after next, and an even greater comfort that in less than two weeks she herself would be with Jane again, able to help restore her spirits with all the affection she could give.

She could not think of Darcy leaving Kent without remembering that his cousin would go with him. But Colonel Fitzwilliam had made it clear that he had no intentions at all, and agreeable as he was, she did not mean to be unhappy about him.

While settling this point, she was suddenly startled by the sound of the doorbell. Her spirits fluttered a little at the thought that it might be Colonel Fitzwilliam himself, who had once before called late in the evening and might now be coming to check on her. But this idea was quickly dismissed, and her feelings were very differently affected when, to her utter amazement, she saw Mr. Darcy walk into the room. In a hurried manner he immediately asked after her health, explaining his visit as a wish to hear that she was better. She answered him with cool politeness. He sat down for a few moments, then stood up and walked about the room. Elizabeth was surprised but said nothing. After several minutes of silence, he approached her in an agitated state and began:
"I have struggled with this in vain. It will not do. My feelings will not be suppressed. You must allow me to tell you how deeply I admire and love you."

Elizabeth's astonishment was beyond words. She stared, blushed, hesitated, and was silent. He took this as sufficient encouragement, and a full confession of everything he felt and had long felt for her immediately followed. He spoke well, but there were feelings besides those of the heart to be expressed, and he was no more eloquent on the subject of love than of pride. His sense of her inferiority, of it being beneath him, of the family obstacles that his judgment had always raised against his inclination—all were dwelt on with a passion that seemed appropriate to the dignity he was sacrificing, but was hardly likely to win her over.

Despite her deep-rooted dislike, she could not be unmoved by the compliment of such a man's affection, and though her intentions did not waver for an instant, she was at first sorry for the pain he was about to feel—until his subsequent words roused her to resentment, and she lost all sympathy in anger. She tried, however, to compose herself to answer him patiently when he was done. He concluded by impressing on her the strength of an attachment that, despite all his efforts, he had found impossible to conquer, and by expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand. As he said this, she could easily see that he had no doubt of a favorable answer. He _spoke_ of worry and anxiety, but his face showed real confidence. This could only provoke her further, and when he stopped, the color rose in her cheeks and she said:

"In cases like this, I believe the accepted thing is to express a sense of gratitude for the feelings declared, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that gratitude should be felt, and if I _could_ feel grateful, I would now thank you. But I cannot—I have never wanted your good opinion, and you have certainly given it most reluctantly. I am sorry to have caused anyone pain. It was done entirely without my knowledge, however, and I hope it will be short-lived. The feelings that you say have long prevented you from acknowledging your regard should have little difficulty overcoming it after this explanation."

Mr. Darcy, who was leaning against the mantelpiece with his eyes fixed on her face, seemed to take in her words with no less resentment than surprise. His face went pale with anger, and the disturbance of his mind was visible in every feature. He was struggling for the appearance of composure and would not open his mouth until he believed he had achieved it. The pause was agonizing for Elizabeth. At last, in a voice of forced calm, he said:
"And this is the entire reply I am to have the honor of receiving! I might perhaps wish to be told why, with so little _effort_ at civility, I am rejected like this. But it is of little importance."
