"I might just as well ask," she replied, "why, with such an obvious intention of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was that not some excuse for rudeness, if I _was_ rude? But I have other reasons. You know I do. Had my own feelings not already decided against you—had they been neutral, or even favorable—do you think any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?"
As she spoke these words, Mr. Darcy's color changed. But the emotion was brief, and he listened without trying to interrupt while she continued:

"I have every reason in the world to think badly of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and cruel part you played _there_. You dare not, you cannot deny that you were the principal, if not the only, means of separating them from each other—of exposing one to the world's blame for fickleness and instability, the other to its mockery for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in the sharpest misery."

She paused, and saw with considerable indignation that he was listening with an air that showed he was completely unmoved by any feeling of remorse. He even looked at her with a smile of affected disbelief.
"Can you deny that you have done it?" she repeated.

With studied calm he then replied, "I have no wish to deny that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am glad I succeeded. Toward _him_ I have been kinder than toward myself."
Elizabeth refused to dignify this self-serving remark with a response, but its meaning did not escape her, nor was it likely to soften her feelings.

"But it is not merely this affair," she continued, "that my dislike is based on. Long before it happened, my opinion of you was formed. Your character was revealed to me months ago by Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you possibly say? What imaginary act of friendship can you point to in your defense? Or what lie can you use to deceive others?"
"You take a very eager interest in that gentleman's affairs," said Darcy in a less calm tone, his color rising.
"Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help being interested in him?"
"His misfortunes!" repeated Darcy contemptuously. "Yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed."

"And of your making," cried Elizabeth with force. "You have reduced him to his present state of poverty—comparative poverty. You have withheld the advantages that you must know were intended for him. You have deprived the best years of his life of the independence that was no less his right than his due. You have done all this! And yet you can treat the mention of his misfortunes with contempt and ridicule."

"And this," cried Darcy, pacing quickly across the room, "is your opinion of me! This is how you regard me! I thank you for explaining it so fully. My faults, by this accounting, are heavy indeed! But perhaps," he added, stopping and turning toward her, "these offenses might have been overlooked, had your pride not been hurt by my honest confession of the doubts that had long prevented me from forming any serious intention. These bitter accusations might have been suppressed, had I been more calculating and concealed my inner struggles, and flattered you into believing that I was driven by pure, uncomplicated love—by reason, by reflection, by everything. But dishonesty of every kind is hateful to me. Nor am I ashamed of the feelings I described. They were natural and just. Could you expect me to celebrate the inferiority of your connections? To congratulate myself on the hope of relatives whose position in life is so clearly beneath my own?"
Elizabeth felt herself growing angrier by the moment, yet she tried with all her might to speak calmly when she said:

"You are mistaken, Mr. Darcy, if you think that the way you declared yourself affected me in any way except to spare me the regret I might have felt in refusing you, had you behaved in a more gentlemanly fashion."
She saw him flinch at this, but he said nothing, and she continued:
"You could not have made me the offer of your hand in any possible way that would have tempted me to accept it."
Again his astonishment was obvious, and he looked at her with an expression of mingled disbelief and humiliation. She went on:

"From the very beginning—from the first moment, I may almost say, of my acquaintance with you—your manners, impressing me with the fullest belief in your arrogance, your conceit, and your selfish contempt for the feelings of others, laid the groundwork of a disapproval on which subsequent events have built such an unshakeable dislike that I had not known you a month before I felt you were the last man in the world I could ever be persuaded to marry."

"You have said quite enough, madam. I perfectly understand your feelings, and have now only to be ashamed of what my own have been. Forgive me for having taken up so much of your time, and accept my best wishes for your health and happiness."

And with these words he quickly left the room, and Elizabeth heard him the next moment open the front door and leave the house. The turmoil in her mind was now painfully intense. She did not know how to support herself, and from actual weakness, sat down and cried for half an hour. Her astonishment, as she reflected on what had happened, grew with every review of it. That she should receive a proposal from Mr. Darcy! That he should have been in love with her for so many months! So much in love as to wish to marry her despite all the objections that had made him prevent his friend from marrying her sister, and that must seem at least equally powerful in his own case—it was almost unbelievable! It was gratifying to have unconsciously inspired such a strong attachment. But his pride, his hateful pride, his shameless admission of what he had done to Jane, his unforgivable confidence in confessing what he could not justify, and the callous manner in which he had spoken of Mr. Wickham—whose cruel treatment he had not even tried to deny—soon overwhelmed the pity that the thought of his love had briefly stirred.
She continued in these agitated reflections until the sound of Lady Catherine's carriage made her realize how unfit she was for Charlotte's observation, and she hurried to her room.

chapters.title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: Elizabeth woke the next morning to the same thoughts that had finally closed her eyes. She could not yet recover from the shock of what had happened—it was impossible to think of anything else—and, entirely unable to settle to any task, she decided soon after breakfast to refresh herself with fresh air and exercise. She was heading straight for her favorite walk when the memory of Mr. Darcy's sometimes coming there stopped her, and instead of entering the park, she turned up the lane that led her farther from the main road. The park fence was still the boundary on one side, and she soon passed one of the gates into the grounds.

After walking two or three times along that stretch of lane, she was tempted by the pleasant morning to stop at the gates and look into the park. The five weeks she had now spent in Kent had made a great difference to the landscape, and every day was adding to the greenness of the early trees. She was about to continue her walk when she caught a glimpse of a gentleman within the grove that bordered the park. He was moving her way, and fearing it might be Mr. Darcy, she turned to retreat at once. But the approaching figure was now close enough to see her, and stepping forward eagerly, called her name. She had turned away, but hearing herself called—though in a voice she recognized as Mr. Darcy's—she moved back toward the gate. He had reached it at the same time and, holding out a letter, which she instinctively took, said with a look of proud composure, "I have been walking in the grove for some time, hoping to meet you. Will you do me the honor of reading this letter?" And then, with a slight bow, he turned back into the trees and was soon out of sight.

Expecting no pleasure but feeling the strongest curiosity, Elizabeth opened the letter and, to her growing astonishment, found an envelope containing two sheets of letter paper, written all the way through in a very small hand. The envelope itself was also full. Continuing along the lane, she began to read. It was dated from Rosings, at eight o'clock in the morning, and read as follows:

"Do not be alarmed, madam, on receiving this letter, by any fear that it contains a repetition of the feelings, or a renewal of the offers, that were so repugnant to you last night. I write with no intention of causing you pain, or humbling myself, by dwelling on wishes that, for both our sakes, cannot be forgotten soon enough. The effort involved in writing and reading this letter should have been spared, had my honor not required it to be written and read. You must therefore forgive the liberty I take in asking for your attention; your feelings, I know, will give it reluctantly, but I ask it in the name of fairness.

"Two offenses of a very different nature, and by no means equal in seriousness, you charged me with last night. The first was that, without regard for the feelings of either party, I had separated Mr. Bingley from your sister. The second was that I had, in defiance of every claim and in defiance of honor and decency, ruined the present welfare and future prospects of Mr. Wickham. To have deliberately and cruelly cast off the companion of my youth, the acknowledged favorite of my father, a young man with scarcely any other support than our patronage, and who had been raised to expect it, would be a wickedness to which the separation of two young people whose attachment had developed over only a few weeks could bear no comparison. But I hope to be cleared hereafter of the severity of the blame so freely given last night, once the following account of my actions and their motives has been read. If, in the explanation that I owe to myself, I am forced to relate feelings that may offend yours, I can only say I am sorry. The necessity must be obeyed, and further apology would be absurd. I had not been long in Hertfordshire before I saw, along with others, that Bingley preferred your elder sister to every other young woman in the area. But it was not until the evening of the dance at Netherfield that I had any concern about a serious attachment. I had often seen him in love before. At that ball, while I had the honor of dancing with you, I first learned from Sir William Lucas's casual remark that Bingley's attentions to your sister had given rise to a general expectation of their marriage. He spoke of it as a certainty, with only the timing undecided. From that moment I watched my friend's behavior carefully, and I could see that his preference for Miss Bennet went beyond anything I had ever witnessed in him. Your sister I watched too. Her look and manners were open, cheerful, and engaging as ever, but without any sign of special feeling in return. And I remained convinced, from that evening's observation, that though she received his attentions with pleasure, she did not invite them by returning the sentiment. If _you_ have not been mistaken about this, _I_ must have been wrong. Your greater knowledge of your sister makes the latter more likely. If it is so—if I was misled by this error into causing her pain—then your resentment has not been unreasonable. But I will not hesitate to say that the composure of your sister's face and manner was such as might have convinced the sharpest observer that, however sweet her temperament, her heart was not likely to be easily touched. That I _wanted_ to believe her indifferent is certain, but I venture to say that my judgments are not usually swayed by my hopes or fears. I did not believe her indifferent because I wished it; I believed it from honest conviction, as truly as I wished it on rational grounds. My objections to the marriage were not merely those I admitted last night—objections that required the strongest passion to overcome in my own case. The lack of important connections could not matter as much to my friend as to me. But there were other reasons for disapproval—reasons that, though they still exist and exist equally in both cases, I had tried to forget because they were not immediately in front of me. These reasons must be stated, though briefly. The position of your mother's family, though not ideal, was nothing compared to the complete lack of propriety so frequently—so almost constantly—displayed by your mother herself, by your three younger sisters, and occasionally even by your father. Forgive me—it pains me to offend you. But amid your own concern for the faults of your closest relatives, and your displeasure at this account of them, let it comfort you to know that you and your eldest sister have conducted yourselves so as to escape any share of this criticism—praise that is as widely given as it is deserved by the good sense and character of you both. I will only add that the events of that evening confirmed my opinion of all parties and strengthened every reason I already had for saving my friend from what I considered a very unhappy match. He left Netherfield for London the next day, as you certainly remember, intending to return soon. My own part must now be explained. His sisters' anxiety had been aroused as much as my own. Our shared feelings were quickly discovered, and recognizing that there was no time to lose in drawing their brother away, we soon decided to follow him directly to London. We went accordingly, and I readily took on the task of pointing out to my friend the certain dangers of such a choice. I described and pressed them seriously. But however much this argument might have shaken or delayed his decision, I do not think it would ultimately have prevented the marriage, had it not been supported by my assurance—which I did not hesitate to give—of your sister's indifference. He had believed she returned his feelings with sincere, if not equal, regard. But Bingley has great natural humility, with a stronger reliance on my judgment than on his own. Convincing him that he had been mistaken was therefore not very difficult. Persuading him not to return to Hertfordshire, once that conviction was established, was hardly the work of a moment. I cannot blame myself for having done this much. There is only one part of my behavior in the whole affair that I do not look back on with satisfaction: that I stooped to being deceptive enough to hide from him the fact that your sister was in London. I knew it myself, as did Miss Bingley, but her brother is still unaware of it. That they might have met without harm is perhaps likely, but his feelings did not seem to me extinguished enough for him to see her without some risk. Perhaps this concealment was beneath me. It is done, however, and it was done for the best. On this subject I have nothing more to say, no other apology to make. If I have hurt your sister's feelings, it was done unknowingly; and though the motives that guided me may naturally seem insufficient to you, I have not yet learned to condemn them. Regarding that other, more serious accusation—of having wronged Mr. Wickham—I can only refute it by laying before you the full history of his connection with my family. I do not know what he has specifically accused me of, but I can summon more than one witness of unquestionable honesty to verify what I shall relate. Mr. Wickham is the son of a very respectable man who for many years managed all the Pemberley estates, and whose faithful service naturally inclined my father to help him. On George Wickham, who was his godson, my father's generosity was therefore freely lavished. My father paid for his schooling and later for Cambridge—crucial support, since Wickham's own father, always poor due to his wife's extravagance, would have been unable to give him a gentleman's education. My father was not only fond of this young man's company—his manners were always charming—he also had the highest opinion of him, and hoping he would enter the clergy, intended to provide for him in it. As for myself, it is many, many years since I first began to see him very differently. The vicious tendencies and lack of principle that he was careful to hide from his best patron could not escape the notice of a young man nearly his own age, who had chances to observe him in unguarded moments that Mr. Darcy never had. Here again I shall cause you pain—to what degree, only you can tell. But whatever feelings Mr. Wickham may have created in you, a suspicion of their nature shall not prevent me from revealing his true character. It only adds another reason to do so. My excellent father died about five years ago, and his attachment to Mr. Wickham was steadfast to the end—in his will he specifically asked me to advance Wickham's career as his profession allowed, and if he entered the clergy, to give him a valuable family parish as soon as it became vacant. There was also a legacy of one thousand pounds. Wickham's own father did not long survive mine, and within six months of these events, Mr. Wickham wrote to tell me that, having finally decided against entering the clergy, he hoped I would not think it unreasonable of him to expect some more immediate financial benefit in place of the parish appointment, from which he could not benefit. He had some intention, he said, of studying law, and I must realize that the interest on one thousand pounds would be very inadequate support for that. I hoped more than believed he was sincere, but was perfectly willing to agree to his proposal. I knew Mr. Wickham should not be a clergyman. The matter was quickly settled. He gave up all claim to help in the church, should he ever be in a position to receive it, and accepted three thousand pounds in return. All connection between us seemed dissolved. I thought too badly of him to invite him to Pemberley or accept his company in London. In London, I believe, he mainly lived, but his study of law was merely a pretense, and being now free from all restraint, his life was one of laziness and excess. For about three years I heard little of him, but when the incumbent of the parish that had been intended for him died, he wrote to me again to request the appointment. His circumstances, he assured me—and I had no difficulty believing it—were extremely bad. He had found law a most unprofitable study and was now absolutely determined to be ordained, if I would grant him the position—which he trusted I could hardly refuse, since he was sure I had no one else to provide for, and could not have forgotten my late father's wishes. You will hardly blame me for refusing this request, or for resisting every repetition of it. His resentment was proportional to his desperation, and he was doubtless as vicious in his abuse of me to others as in his reproaches to me directly. After this period, all pretense of acquaintance was dropped. How he lived, I do not know. But last summer he was again most painfully forced on my attention. I must now mention something I would prefer to forget—something that nothing less than the present obligation would induce me to reveal to anyone. Having said this much, I have no doubt of your discretion. My sister, who is more than ten years younger than I, was left to the joint guardianship of my mother's nephew, Colonel Fitzwilliam, and myself. About a year ago she was taken from school and a household was established for her in London. Last summer she went with the woman who ran her household to Ramsgate, and there Mr. Wickham also went—undoubtedly by design. It turned out there was a prior connection between him and Mrs. Younge, in whose character we were most unfortunately deceived. With her help and encouragement, he so far ingratiated himself with Georgiana—whose loving heart still held a strong memory of his kindness to her as a child—that she was persuaded to believe herself in love and agreed to an elopement. She was only fifteen, which must be her excuse. And after stating her foolishness, I am happy to add that I learned of it from her own confession. I joined them unexpectedly a day or two before the planned elopement, and Georgiana, unable to bear the thought of grieving and offending a brother she almost looked up to as a father, told me everything. You can imagine what I felt and how I acted. Concern for my sister's reputation and feelings prevented any public exposure, but I wrote to Mr. Wickham, who left immediately, and Mrs. Younge was of course dismissed. Mr. Wickham's chief motive was undoubtedly my sister's fortune, which is thirty thousand pounds, but I cannot help thinking that the hope of revenge against me was a strong incentive. His revenge would have been complete indeed. This, madam, is a truthful account of every event that has connected us, and if you do not absolutely reject it as false, I hope you will from now on acquit me of cruelty toward Mr. Wickham. I do not know in what way, or with what falsehoods, he has deceived you, but his success is perhaps not surprising, given how ignorant you were of everything concerning either of us. You could not possibly have detected him, and you certainly were not inclined to suspect him. You may wonder why all this was not told you last night. But I was not enough in command of myself then to know what should or could be revealed. For the truth of everything related here, I can appeal especially to the testimony of Colonel Fitzwilliam, who, from our close family ties and constant friendship—and even more as one of the executors of my father's will—has necessarily been informed of every detail of these matters. If your hatred of _me_ should make _my_ word worthless, you cannot be prevented by the same reason from trusting my cousin. And so that you may have the chance to consult him, I shall try to find an opportunity to put this letter in your hands this morning. I will only add, God bless you.
"FITZWILLIAM DARCY."

chapters.title: Chapter 36
paragraphs: When Mr. Darcy gave Elizabeth the letter, she didn't expect it to contain a renewed proposal—she had formed no expectations at all about its contents. But whatever they might be, it's easy to imagine how eagerly she read through them, and what a turmoil of conflicting emotions they stirred up. Her feelings as she read could hardly be described. She was astonished to discover that he believed he had any apology to make, and she was firmly convinced that he could offer no explanation that wouldn't be better concealed out of decent shame. With a strong prejudice against everything he might say, she began reading his account of what had happened at Netherfield. She read with an eagerness that hardly left her the ability to understand, and in her impatience to know what the next sentence would bring, she couldn't take in the meaning of the one before her eyes. She instantly decided his claim about her sister's indifference must be false, and his account of the real—the worst—objections to the match made her too angry to want to be fair to him. The regret he expressed for what he'd done didn't satisfy her; his tone wasn't apologetic but arrogant. It was all pride and insolence.

But when this subject gave way to his account of Mr. Wickham—when she read, with somewhat clearer attention, a story of events which, if true, must overturn every opinion she'd cherished about his worth, and which bore such an alarming resemblance to Wickham's own version of himself—her feelings were even more sharply painful and harder to define. Astonishment, dread, and even horror overwhelmed her. She wanted to dismiss it entirely, repeatedly exclaiming, "This must be false! This can't be! This must be the most outrageous lie!"—and when she had finished the whole letter, though she'd barely taken in the last page or two, she thrust it away, insisting she wouldn't give it any credit, that she would never look at it again.

In this agitated state of mind, with thoughts that couldn't settle on anything, she walked on; but it was no use—within half a minute the letter was unfolded again, and pulling herself together as best she could, she began the humiliating task of rereading everything about Wickham, forcing herself to examine the meaning of every sentence. The account of his connection with the Pemberley family was exactly what he himself had told her, and the kindness of the late Mr. Darcy, though she hadn't previously known its full extent, matched his own words equally well. So far each account confirmed the other; but when she came to the will, the difference was enormous. What Wickham had said about the living was fresh in her memory, and as she recalled his very words, it was impossible not to feel that there was gross dishonesty on one side or the other; for a few moments she flattered herself that her own judgment wasn't wrong. But when she read and reread, with the closest attention, the details of Wickham's giving up all claim to the living, and his receiving instead the considerable sum of three thousand pounds, she was forced to hesitate again. She put down the letter, weighed every circumstance with what she intended to be impartiality—considered the likelihood of each claim—but with little success. On both sides it was only assertion. Again she read on. But every line proved more clearly that the affair, which she had believed impossible to misrepresent in any way that could make Mr. Darcy's conduct less than disgraceful, was capable of an interpretation that made him entirely blameless throughout the whole matter.

The extravagance and general misconduct he didn't hesitate to lay at Mr. Wickham's door shocked her deeply—all the more because she could produce no evidence against the charges. She had never heard of him before he joined the ——shire militia, which he'd entered at the urging of the young man who, meeting him by chance in London, had renewed a slight acquaintance. Of his previous way of life, nothing had been known in Hertfordshire except what he'd told

them himself. As to his real character, even if she'd had the means to investigate, she had never felt the slightest urge to do so. His face, his voice, and his manner had immediately established him in possession of every virtue. She tried to recall some example of goodness, some distinguished mark of integrity or kindness, that might rescue him from Mr. Darcy's accusations; or at least, through the weight of virtue, make up for those minor failings she would try to classify Mr. Darcy's description of years of idleness and vice as being. But no such memory came to her aid. She could see him instantly before her, with all the charm of his bearing and address, but she could remember nothing more substantial than the general approval of the neighborhood and the regard his social skills had earned him in the officers' mess. After pausing on this point for a considerable while, she continued reading once more. But the story that followed, of his designs on Miss Darcy, was confirmed to some extent by what had passed between Colonel Fitzwilliam and herself only the morning before; and she was finally directed to Colonel Fitzwilliam himself for the truth of every detail—the very man from whom she had already heard of his close involvement in all his cousin's affairs, and whose character she had no reason to question. At one point she had almost decided to ask him directly, but the awkwardness of such a request held her back, and the idea was finally banished altogether by the certainty that Mr. Darcy would never have risked such a claim if he hadn't been sure of his cousin's confirmation.

She remembered perfectly everything that had passed between Wickham and herself in their first evening at Mr. Philips's. Many of his exact words were still fresh in her memory. She was now struck by the impropriety of such disclosures to a stranger, and wondered how it had escaped her notice before. She saw the indelicacy of putting himself forward as he had done, and the inconsistency between what he professed and how he actually behaved. She remembered that he had boasted of having no fear of seeing Mr. Darcy—that Mr. Darcy might leave the country, but he would stand his ground; yet he had avoided the Netherfield ball the very next week. She also remembered that until the Netherfield family had left the area, he had told his story to no one but herself; but after their departure, it had been discussed everywhere; that he'd then had no restraint, no scruples about destroying Mr. Darcy's reputation, though he had assured her that respect for the father would always prevent him from exposing the son.

How differently everything now appeared where he was concerned! His attentions to Miss King were now clearly the result of purely mercenary motives, and the modesty of her fortune proved not the moderation of his desires but his eagerness to grab at anything. His behavior toward Elizabeth herself could now have had no decent motive: he had either been mistaken about her fortune, or had been flattering his vanity by encouraging the preference she believed she had shown all too clearly. Every lingering impulse to defend him grew fainter and fainter; and in further justification of Mr. Darcy, she had to admit that Mr. Bingley, when questioned by Jane, had long ago confirmed his blamelessness in the affair—that, proud and off-putting as his manners were, she had never, in the whole course of their acquaintance (an acquaintance which had lately brought them together often, giving her a sort of familiarity with his ways) seen anything that betrayed him as unprincipled or unjust—anything that suggested irreligious or immoral habits—that among his own circle he was respected and valued—that even Wickham had granted him credit as a brother, and she had often heard him speak so affectionately of his sister as to prove him capable of genuine feeling—that had his actions been what Wickham claimed, such a gross violation of everything right could hardly have been hidden from the world; and that friendship between a man capable of such things and someone as decent as Mr. Bingley was simply impossible to explain.
She grew absolutely ashamed of herself. She couldn't think of either Darcy or Wickham without feeling that she had been blind, biased, prejudiced, and absurd.

"How shamefully I've behaved!" she cried. "I, who prided myself on my judgment! I, who valued myself on my abilities! who often scorned the generous openness of my sister, and satisfied my vanity with useless or pointless suspicion. How humiliating this discovery is! And yet, how deserved the humiliation! If I had been in love, I couldn't have been more wretchedly blind. But vanity, not love, has been my downfall. Pleased by one man's preference and offended by the other's neglect, right from the very start of our acquaintance, I courted bias and ignorance, and pushed reason aside wherever either of them was concerned. Until this moment, I never truly knew myself."

From herself to Jane, from Jane to Bingley, her thoughts followed a line which soon reminded her that Mr. Darcy's explanation on that score had seemed very inadequate; and she read it again. The effect of a second reading was entirely different. How could she deny credit to his claims in one case when she had been forced to accept them in the other? He declared himself to have been completely unaware of her sister's feelings, and she couldn't help remembering that Charlotte's opinion had always been the same. Nor could she deny the accuracy of his description of Jane. She felt that Jane's feelings, though deep, were rarely displayed, and that there was a habitual composure in her manner not often combined with great depth of feeling.

When she came to the part of the letter where her family was mentioned, in tones of such mortifying yet deserved criticism, her sense of shame was intense. The justice of the charge struck her too powerfully to deny; and the specific incidents he referred to at the Netherfield ball, which confirmed all his initial disapproval, couldn't have made a stronger impression on his mind than they now made on hers.

The compliment to herself and her sister was not unappreciated. It was soothing, but it couldn't console her for the contempt their behavior had brought upon the rest of her family; and as she considered that Jane's disappointment had, in fact, been the work of their closest relations, and reflected how seriously the reputation of both sisters must be damaged by such improper conduct, she felt more depressed than she had ever known.

After wandering along the lane for two hours, giving way to every kind of thought—reconsidering events, weighing probabilities, and reconciling herself as well as she could to a change so sudden and so significant—fatigue and the realization of her long absence finally made her turn for home. She entered the house determined to appear as cheerful as usual, and resolved to suppress the kind of reflections that would make her unfit for conversation.

She was immediately told that the two gentlemen from Rosings had each called during her absence; Mr. Darcy only for a few minutes, to say goodbye, but Colonel Fitzwilliam had been sitting with them for at least an hour, hoping she would return, and had nearly decided to go looking for her. Elizabeth could only pretend to be sorry she'd missed him; she was actually relieved. Colonel Fitzwilliam was no longer of any interest to her. She could think of nothing but the letter.

chapters.title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: The two gentlemen left Rosings the next morning, and Mr. Collins, having been waiting near the gate to give them his parting bow, was able to bring home the pleasant news that they appeared to be in very good health, and in as tolerable spirits as could be expected after the sad scene so recently endured at Rosings. He then hurried to Rosings to console Lady Catherine and her daughter, and on his return brought back, with great satisfaction, a message from her Ladyship saying that she felt so bored she very much wanted them all to dine with her.

Elizabeth couldn't see Lady Catherine without remembering that, had she chosen differently, she might by now have been presented as her future niece; nor could she think without a smile of what her Ladyship's outrage would have been. "What would she have said? How would she have reacted?" were the questions she amused herself with.

Their first topic was the reduced size of the Rosings party. "I assure you, I feel it terribly," said Lady Catherine. "I believe nobody feels the loss of friends as much as I do. But I am particularly attached to these young men, and I know them to be equally attached to me! They were enormously sorry to go! But they always are. The dear Colonel kept his spirits up tolerably well until the very end; but Darcy seemed to feel it most deeply—more, I think, than last year. His attachment to Rosings certainly grows stronger."
Mr. Collins had a compliment and a subtle reference to offer here, which were kindly smiled upon by both mother and daughter.
Lady Catherine remarked, after dinner, that Miss Bennet seemed out of spirits, and immediately explaining it to herself by supposing that she didn't want to go home so soon, added—
"But if that is the case, you must write to your mother and ask to stay a little longer. Mrs. Collins will be very glad of your company, I'm sure."
"I'm very grateful to your Ladyship for the kind invitation," replied Elizabeth, "but it's not in my power to accept. I must be in London next Saturday."

"At that rate, you'll have only been here six weeks. I expected you to stay two months. I told Mrs. Collins so before you came. There's no need for you to leave so soon. Mrs. Bennet could certainly spare you for another two weeks."
"But my father can't. He wrote last week to hurry my return."

"Oh, your father can certainly spare you if your mother can. Daughters are never of much importance to a father. And if you'll stay another full month, I'll be able to take one of you as far as London, since I'm going there in early June for a week. And since Dawson doesn't mind riding on top, there will be plenty of room for one of you—and if the weather happens to be cool, I wouldn't object to taking you both, since neither of you is particularly large."
"You are all kindness, madam, but I believe we must stick to our original plan."

Lady Catherine seemed resigned. "Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I can't bear the idea of two young women traveling by post alone. It's highly improper. You must arrange to send somebody. I have the strongest objection to that sort of thing. Young women should always be properly guarded and accompanied, according to their station in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted she have two men-servants with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, couldn't properly have appeared in any other style. I'm extremely attentive to all these things. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I'm glad I thought to mention it; for it would really be a discredit to you to let them go alone."
"My uncle is sending a servant for us."

"Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a man-servant, does he? I'm very glad you have someone who thinks of these things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you mention my name at the Bell, you'll be well looked after."

Lady Catherine had many more questions about their journey, and since she didn't answer them all herself, some attention was required—which Elizabeth felt was lucky for her, since with a mind so preoccupied, she might have forgotten where she was. Reflection would have to wait for solitary hours; whenever she was alone, she gave way to it as the greatest relief, and not a day went by without a solitary walk in which she could indulge in the full pleasure of unpleasant memories.

She was well on her way to knowing Mr. Darcy's letter by heart. She studied every sentence, and her feelings toward its author varied wildly from one moment to the next. When she remembered the tone of his declaration, she was still full of indignation; but when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and berated him, her anger turned against herself, and his disappointed feelings became an object of compassion. His attachment stirred her gratitude, his general character her respect; but she couldn't approve of him, nor could she for a moment regret her refusal, or feel the slightest wish to ever see him again. In her own past behavior there was a constant source of frustration and regret, and in the unfortunate failings of her family, a subject of even heavier distress. They were beyond remedy. Her father, content to laugh at them, would never make the effort to restrain his youngest daughters' wild behavior; and her mother, with manners so far from right herself, was entirely blind to the problem. Elizabeth had frequently joined with Jane in trying to curb the recklessness of Catherine and Lydia; but while they were encouraged by their mother's indulgence, what chance was there of improvement? Catherine, weak-spirited, irritable, and completely under Lydia's influence, had always resented their advice; and Lydia, headstrong and careless, would barely give them a hearing. They were ignorant, idle, and vain. As long as there was an officer in Meryton, they would flirt with him; and as long as Meryton was within walking distance of Longbourn, they would be going there constantly.

Worry about Jane was another persistent concern; and Mr. Darcy's explanation, by restoring Bingley to all her former good opinion, sharpened the sense of what Jane had lost. His affection had been proven sincere, and his conduct cleared of all blame, unless some could be attached to his too-implicit trust in his friend. How painful then was the thought that Jane had been denied a situation so desirable in every way, so full of advantage, so promising of happiness—all because of the foolishness and impropriety of her own family!

When these reflections were combined with the revelation of Wickham's true character, it's easy to imagine that the high spirits which had seldom been depressed before were now so deeply affected that it was almost impossible for her to appear even tolerably cheerful.

Their engagements at Rosings were as frequent during the last week of her stay as they had been at first. The very last evening was spent there, and her Ladyship again inquired in detail about the particulars of their journey, gave them directions on the best method of packing, and was so insistent about the only correct way to fold gowns, that Maria felt obliged, on returning home, to undo all the morning's work and repack her trunk from scratch.

When they parted, Lady Catherine, with great condescension, wished them a good journey and invited them to come to Hunsford again next year; and Miss de Bourgh made the effort of curtsying and holding out her hand to both of them.

chapters.title: Chapter 38
paragraphs: On Saturday morning Elizabeth and Mr. Collins met at breakfast a few minutes before the others appeared, and he took the opportunity to deliver the farewell courtesies he considered absolutely essential.

"I don't know, Miss Elizabeth," he said, "whether Mrs. Collins has yet expressed her appreciation for your kindness in visiting us, but I'm quite certain you won't leave the house without her thanks for it. The favor of your company has been deeply felt, I assure you. We know how little there is to attract anyone to our humble home. Our plain way of living, our small rooms, few servants, and the little we see of society must make Hunsford terribly dull for a young lady like yourself; but I hope you'll believe us grateful for the honor, and that we've done everything in our power to keep you from spending your time unpleasantly."

Elizabeth was eager with her thanks and assurances of happiness. She had spent six weeks with great enjoyment, and the pleasure of being with Charlotte, and the kind attention she had received, must make her feel the grateful one. Mr. Collins was gratified, and with a more smiling solemnity replied—

"It gives me the greatest pleasure to hear that you haven't found your time disagreeable. We have certainly done our best; and most fortunately, having the ability to introduce you to very superior society, and from our connection with Rosings, the frequent opportunity to vary the humble domestic scene, I think we may flatter ourselves that your Hunsford visit has not been entirely tedious. Our position with regard to Lady Catherine's family is, indeed, an extraordinary advantage and blessing that few can boast. You see what footing we're on. You see how constantly we're engaged there. In truth, I must acknowledge that, with all the drawbacks of this humble parsonage, I wouldn't think anyone living in it deserving of pity while they share our closeness with Rosings."
Words were insufficient for the height of his feelings, and he was forced to pace about the room while Elizabeth tried to combine politeness with truth in a few short sentences.

"You may, in fact, carry a very favorable report of us back to Hertfordshire, my dear cousin. I flatter myself that you'll be able to do so. Lady Catherine's great attention to Mrs. Collins you have witnessed daily; and on the whole, I trust it's clear that your friend has not drawn an unfortunate—but on that point I'd better say nothing. Only let me assure you, my dear Miss Elizabeth, that I can most sincerely wish you equal happiness in marriage. My dear Charlotte and I have but one mind and one way of thinking. There is in everything a most remarkable similarity of character and ideas between us. We seem to have been designed for each other."

Elizabeth could safely say that it was a great happiness when that was the case, and with equal sincerity could add that she truly believed in and was glad of his domestic comforts. She wasn't sorry, however, to have the recital interrupted by the entrance of the lady who was its subject. Poor Charlotte! It was sad to leave her to such company! But she had chosen it with her eyes open; and though she clearly regretted that her visitors were leaving, she didn't seem to be asking for pity. Her home and her housekeeping, her parish and her poultry, and all related concerns had not yet lost their charm.

At last the carriage arrived, the trunks were fastened on, the parcels placed inside, and it was declared ready. After an affectionate parting between the friends, Elizabeth was escorted to the carriage by Mr. Collins; and as they walked down the garden, he commissioned her with his best regards to all her family, not forgetting his thanks for the kindness he had received at Longbourn last winter, and his compliments to Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner, though he'd never met them. He then helped her in, Maria followed, and the door was about to be closed when he suddenly reminded them, with some alarm, that they had so far forgotten to leave any message for the ladies at Rosings.
"But," he added, "you will of course want your humble respects delivered to them, with your grateful thanks for their kindness during your stay."
Elizabeth made no objection; the door was then allowed to shut, and the carriage drove off.
"Good gracious!" cried Maria, after a few minutes' silence. "It seems like only a day or two since we first arrived! And yet how much has happened!"
"A great deal indeed," said her companion, with a sigh.
"We've dined nine times at Rosings, besides having tea there twice! How much I'll have to tell!"
Elizabeth privately added, "And how much I'll have to conceal!"
They completed the journey without much conversation or any incidents, and within four hours of leaving Hunsford they reached Mr. Gardiner's house, where they were to stay for a few days.

Jane looked well, and Elizabeth had little opportunity to study her spirits amid the various engagements her aunt had planned for them. But Jane was coming home with her, and at Longbourn there would be plenty of time for observation.

It took some effort, meanwhile, for her to wait even for Longbourn before telling her sister about Mr. Darcy's proposal. To know that she had the power to reveal something that would utterly astonish Jane, and must at the same time gratify whatever of her own vanity she hadn't yet managed to reason away, was such a temptation to openness that nothing could have overcome it—except her uncertainty about how much she should share, and her fear that if she once began, she might be drawn into repeating something about Bingley that would only cause her sister further pain.

chapters.title: Chapter 39
paragraphs: It was the second week of May when the three young ladies set out together from Gracechurch Street for the town of —— in Hertfordshire; and as they drew near the inn where Mr. Bennet's carriage was to meet them, they quickly spotted both Kitty and Lydia looking out from a dining room upstairs. These two girls had been there for over an hour, happily occupied in browsing the milliner's shop across the street, watching the soldier on guard duty, and preparing a salad.
After welcoming their sisters, they proudly displayed a table set out with whatever cold meat an inn kitchen typically has to offer, exclaiming, "Isn't this nice? Isn't this a lovely surprise?"

"And we're treating you all," added Lydia, "but you'll have to lend us the money, because we just spent ours at the shop over there." Then showing off her purchases—"Look here, I bought this bonnet. I don't think it's very pretty, but I figured I might as well buy it. I'll take it apart as soon as I get home and see if I can make it look better."

And when her sisters criticized it as ugly, she added with perfect indifference, "Oh, but there were two or three much uglier ones in the shop; and once I've bought some prettier satin to retrim it with, I think it'll be perfectly fine. Besides, it won't much matter what anyone wears this summer after the ——shire have left Meryton, and they're leaving in two weeks."
"Are they really?" cried Elizabeth, with the greatest satisfaction.

"They're going to be camped near Brighton, and I so want Papa to take us all there for the summer! It would be such a wonderful plan, and I'm sure it would hardly cost anything at all. Mama would love to go too, more than anything! Just think what a miserable summer we'll have otherwise!"

"Yes," thought Elizabeth, "that would be a delightful plan indeed, and would finish us off completely. Good heavens! Brighton, and an entire camp full of soldiers, for us—who have already been undone by one measly regiment of militia and the monthly balls of Meryton!"
"Now I have some news for you," said Lydia, as they sat down at the table. "What do you think? It's excellent news, wonderful news, and about a certain person we all like."
Jane and Elizabeth looked at each other, and the waiter was told he needn't stay. Lydia laughed, and said—

"Ha, that's just like your formality and discretion. You thought the waiter shouldn't hear, as if he cared! I'm sure he hears worse things than what I'm going to say. But he's an ugly fellow! I'm glad he's gone. I never saw such a long chin in my life. Well, now for my news: it's about dear Wickham—too good for the waiter, isn't it? There's no danger of Wickham marrying Mary King anymore—how do you like that! She's gone to stay with her uncle in Liverpool. Wickham is safe."
"And Mary King is safe!" added Elizabeth. "Safe from a match that would have been unwise as far as money goes."
"She's a great fool for going away, if she liked him."
"But I hope there's no strong attachment on either side," said Jane.
"I'm sure there isn't on his. I'll answer for it—he never cared a bit about her. Who could, about such a plain little freckled thing?"

Elizabeth was shocked to realize that, however incapable she herself was of such crude language, the crudeness of the sentiment was hardly different from what she had once felt and considered perfectly reasonable!

As soon as they had all eaten and the older ones had paid, the carriage was ordered; and after some arranging, the whole party, with all their boxes, workbags, parcels, and the unwelcome addition of Kitty's and Lydia's purchases, were squeezed into it.

"How nicely we're crammed in!" cried Lydia. "I'm glad I brought my bonnet, even if only for the fun of having another hatbox! Well, now let's be comfortable and cozy, and talk and laugh all the way home. First of all, tell us what's happened to you since you went away. Have you seen any good-looking men? Have you done any flirting? I was really hoping one of you would have caught a husband before coming back. Jane will be quite an old maid soon, I swear. She's almost twenty-three! Lord! How embarrassed I'd be not to be married before twenty-three! My aunt Philips wants you to find husbands so badly, you have no idea. She says Lizzy should have taken Mr. Collins; but I don't see how there would have been any fun in it. Lord! How I'd love to be married before any of you! And then I'd chaperone you to all the balls. Oh my! We had such a good time the other day at Colonel Forster's! Kitty and I were to spend the day there, and Mrs. Forster promised a little dance in the evening—by the way, Mrs. Forster and I are such friends!—and so she invited the two Harringtons, but Harriet was sick, so Pen had to come alone; and then, what do you think we did? We dressed up Chamberlayne in women's clothes, so he'd pass for a lady—just think what fun! Nobody knew about it except Colonel and Mrs. Forster, and Kitty and me, except my aunt, because we had to borrow one of her gowns; and you can't imagine how good he looked! When Denny, and Wickham, and Pratt, and two or three more of the men came in, they didn't recognize him at all. Lord! How I laughed! And so did Mrs. Forster. I thought I'd die. And that's what made the men suspicious, and then they soon figured out what was going on."

With these kinds of stories about their parties and jokes, Lydia, with Kitty's hints and additions, tried to amuse her companions all the way to Longbourn. Elizabeth listened as little as she could, but there was no escaping the constant mention of Wickham's name.
Their reception at home was most kind. Mrs. Bennet was delighted to see Jane looking as beautiful as ever; and more than once during dinner Mr. Bennet said voluntarily to Elizabeth—
"I'm glad you're back, Lizzy."

The dinner party was large, since almost all the Lucases came to meet Maria and hear the news, and the subjects that occupied them were varied: Lady Lucas was asking Maria, across the table, about the well-being and poultry of her eldest daughter; Mrs. Bennet was doubly occupied, on one side gathering an account of the latest fashions from Jane, who sat some distance below her, and on the other, relaying them all to the younger Miss Lucases; and Lydia, in a voice louder than anyone else's, was listing all the pleasures of the morning to whoever would listen.

"Oh, Mary," she said, "I wish you'd come with us, because we had such fun! As we went along, Kitty and I pulled up all the carriage blinds and pretended no one was inside; and I would have kept it up the whole way if Kitty hadn't gotten carsick. And when we reached the George, I think we behaved beautifully, because we treated the other three to the nicest cold lunch in the world, and if you'd been there, we would have treated you too. And then when we left, it was such fun! I thought we'd never get into the carriage. I was ready to die of laughing. And then we were so merry all the way home! We talked and laughed so loud that anyone could have heard us for miles!"

To this, Mary replied very gravely, "Far be it from me, dear sister, to look down on such pleasures. They would no doubt appeal to the majority of young women. But I must confess they would hold no attraction for me. I would infinitely prefer a book."
But Lydia didn't hear a word of this answer. She rarely listened to anybody for more than half a minute, and she never listened to Mary at all.

That afternoon Lydia was insistent that the rest of the girls walk to Meryton to see how everyone was doing; but Elizabeth firmly opposed the idea. It shouldn't be said that the Miss Bennets couldn't be at home half a day before they were chasing after the officers. There was another reason too for her opposition. She dreaded seeing Wickham again and was determined to avoid it as long as possible. The comfort of the regiment's approaching departure was truly beyond words. In two weeks they would be gone, and once they were, she hoped there would be nothing more to trouble her on his account.

She hadn't been many hours at home before she discovered that the Brighton scheme, which Lydia had hinted at during lunch at the inn, was a frequent subject of debate between her parents. Elizabeth saw at once that her father had no intention whatsoever of giving in; but his answers were so vague and noncommittal that her mother, though often discouraged, hadn't yet given up hope of eventually getting her way.

chapters.title: Chapter 40
paragraphs: Elizabeth's impatience to tell Jane what had happened could no longer be contained; and having resolved to suppress every detail involving her sister, and preparing her to be surprised, she told her the next morning the main events of the scene between Mr. Darcy and herself.

Miss Bennet's astonishment was soon lessened by her strong sisterly loyalty, which made any admiration of Elizabeth seem perfectly natural; and all surprise was quickly overtaken by other feelings. She was sorry that Mr. Darcy had expressed his feelings in a way so unlikely to recommend them; but she was even more sorry for the unhappiness her sister's rejection must have caused him.
"His being so sure of success was wrong," she said, "and certainly shouldn't have shown; but think how much it must increase his disappointment."
"Indeed," replied Elizabeth, "I am truly sorry for him; but he has other feelings which will probably soon drive away his regard for me. You don't blame me for refusing him, though?"
"Blame you! Oh, no."
"But you blame me for speaking so harshly about Wickham?"
"No—I don't know that you were wrong in what you said."
"But you will know it when I tell you what happened the very next day."

She then spoke of the letter, repeating its entire contents as far as they concerned George Wickham. What a blow this was for poor Jane, who would gladly have gone through life without believing that so much wickedness existed in the whole human race as was collected here in one individual! Nor could Darcy's vindication, though welcome to her feelings, console her for such a discovery. She tried hard to prove the possibility of error, and to clear one man without condemning the other.

"This won't work," said Elizabeth. "You'll never be able to make them both into good men. Pick one, but you'll have to settle for only one. There's only a certain amount of merit between them—just enough for one decent man; and lately it's been shifting around quite a bit. For my part, I'm inclined to give it all to Mr. Darcy, but you can do as you like."
It was some time before a smile could be coaxed from Jane.

"I don't know when I've been more shocked," she said. "Wickham so bad! It's almost impossible to believe. And poor Mr. Darcy! Dear Lizzy, just think what he must have suffered. Such a disappointment! And knowing of your poor opinion of him too! And having to tell such a thing about his sister! It really is too distressing. I'm sure you must feel it."

"Oh no, my regret and compassion are all used up from seeing you so full of both. I know you'll do him such thorough justice that I'm becoming more unconcerned and indifferent by the moment. Your abundance makes me stingy; and if you go on feeling sorry for him much longer, my heart will be as light as a feather."
"Poor Wickham! There's such an expression of goodness in his face! Such openness and gentleness in his manner."
"There was certainly some serious mismanagement in the upbringing of those two young men. One got all the goodness, and the other all the appearance of it."
"I never thought Mr. Darcy as lacking in the appearance of it as you used to."

"And yet I thought I was being terribly clever in taking such a strong dislike to him without any real reason. It's such a spur to one's wit, such an opportunity for cleverness, to have a dislike of that kind. You can be constantly insulting without saying anything fair; but you can't always be mocking a man without occasionally stumbling onto something genuinely funny."
"Lizzy, when you first read that letter, I'm sure you couldn't treat the matter as you do now."

"Indeed I couldn't. I was uncomfortable enough—I was very uncomfortable—I might say unhappy. And with no one to talk to about what I felt, no Jane to comfort me and tell me I hadn't been quite so vain and foolish and absurd as I knew I had! Oh, how I needed you!"
"How unfortunate that you used such strong language about Wickham to Mr. Darcy, because now those words do seem entirely undeserved."

"Certainly. But the misfortune of speaking bitterly is a natural consequence of the prejudice I'd been nursing. There's one point where I want your advice. I want to know whether I should let our acquaintances generally understand Wickham's true character."
Miss Bennet paused a moment, then replied, "Surely there's no need to expose him so dreadfully. What's your own opinion?"

"That it shouldn't be attempted. Mr. Darcy hasn't authorized me to make his letter public. On the contrary, everything about his sister was meant to be kept as private as possible; and if I try to change people's minds about the rest of his behavior, who would believe me? The general prejudice against Mr. Darcy is so strong that it would kill half the good people of Meryton to try to put him in a favorable light. I'm not up to it. Wickham will be gone soon, and so it won't matter to anyone here what he really is. Sooner or later it will all come out, and then we can laugh at their stupidity in not knowing it before. For now, I'll say nothing about it."
"You're quite right. Making his faults public might ruin him forever. He may be sorry now for what he's done, and anxious to rebuild his reputation. We mustn't drive him to desperation."

The turmoil of Elizabeth's mind was calmed by this conversation. She had unburdened herself of two of the secrets that had weighed on her for a fortnight, and was assured of a willing listener in Jane whenever she might want to discuss either subject again. But there was still something she was holding back, which prudence forbade her from disclosing. She didn't dare reveal the other half of Mr. Darcy's letter, or explain to her sister how deeply Bingley had valued her. This was knowledge no one could share; and she was certain that nothing less than a complete understanding between the two parties could justify her in lifting this last layer of secrecy. "And then," she said to herself, "if that very unlikely event ever takes place, I'll simply be able to tell what Bingley can tell in a much more pleasant way himself. The freedom to share this information can't be mine until it has lost all its value!"

She was now, being settled at home, free to observe the true state of her sister's feelings. Jane was not happy. She still cherished a very tender affection for Bingley. Never having imagined herself in love before, her feelings had all the warmth of a first attachment, and from her age and temperament, greater steadiness than first attachments usually have; and she valued his memory so deeply, and preferred him to every other man, that all her good sense and all her consideration for her family's feelings were needed to keep her from dwelling on regrets that could only have been bad for her health and their peace.

"Well, Lizzy," said Mrs. Bennet one day, "what's your opinion now of this sad business with Jane? For my part, I've resolved never to speak of it again to anyone. I told my sister Philips so the other day. But I can't find out that Jane saw anything of him in London. Well, he's a very undeserving young man—and I don't suppose there's the slightest chance of her getting him now. There's no talk of his coming to Netherfield again this summer; and I've asked everyone who might know."
"I don't believe he'll ever live at Netherfield again."

"Oh, well! He can do as he pleases. Nobody wants him to come—though I shall always say he treated my daughter very badly; and if I were her, I wouldn't have stood for it. Well, my comfort is that Jane will surely die of a broken heart, and then he'll be sorry for what he's done."
But since Elizabeth couldn't find any comfort in that expectation, she said nothing.

"Well, Lizzy," her mother continued shortly afterward, "and so the Collinses are living very comfortably, are they? Well, well, I only hope it lasts. And what sort of table do they keep? Charlotte is an excellent manager, I'm sure. If she's half as shrewd as her mother, she saves plenty. There's nothing extravagant in their housekeeping, I imagine."
"No, nothing at all."

"A great deal of good management, no doubt. Yes, yes. They'll be careful not to outspend their income. They'll never be short of money. Well, much good may it do them! And so, I suppose they often talk about having Longbourn when your father is dead. They consider it quite their own, I dare say, whenever that happens."
"That was a subject they couldn't mention in front of me."

"No, it would have been strange if they had. But I have no doubt they often discuss it between themselves. Well, if they can feel easy about an estate that isn't rightfully theirs, so much the better. I should be ashamed of having one that was only entailed on me."

chapters.title: Chapter 41
paragraphs: The first week of their return was soon gone. The second began. It was the regiment's last week in Meryton, and all the young ladies in the neighborhood were wilting fast. The gloom was nearly universal. Only the elder Miss Bennets could still eat, drink, sleep, and go about their usual activities. They were frequently scolded for this lack of feeling by Kitty and Lydia, whose own misery was extreme and who couldn't understand such hard-heartedness in any member of the family.
"Good heavens! What's to become of us? What are we to do?" they would often cry in the bitterness of grief. "How can you be smiling, Lizzy?"
Their affectionate mother shared all their sorrow; she remembered what she herself had endured in a similar situation twenty-five years ago.
"I'm sure," she said, "I cried for two solid days when Colonel Miller's regiment went away. I thought my heart would break."
"I'm sure mine will break," said Lydia.
"If only one could go to Brighton!" observed Mrs. Bennet.
"Oh yes!—if only one could go to Brighton! But Papa is so disagreeable."
"A little sea-bathing would set me up forever."
"And my aunt Philips is sure it would do me a great deal of good," added Kitty.

Such were the laments echoing endlessly through Longbourn House. Elizabeth tried to be amused by them, but any pleasure was lost in shame. She felt anew the justice of Mr. Darcy's objections, and never before had she been so inclined to excuse his interference in his friend's affairs.

But the cloud over Lydia's future was soon lifted; for she received an invitation from Mrs. Forster, the wife of the regiment's colonel, to accompany her to Brighton. This invaluable friend was a very young woman, only recently married. A shared love of high spirits and good humor had drawn her and Lydia together, and out of their three months' acquaintance they had been intimate for two.

The rapture of Lydia on this occasion, her adoration of Mrs. Forster, the delight of Mrs. Bennet, and the mortification of Kitty can scarcely be described. Completely oblivious to her sister's feelings, Lydia flew about the house in restless ecstasy, demanding everyone's congratulations, and laughing and talking more wildly than ever; while the unfortunate Kitty sat in the parlor lamenting her fate in terms as unreasonable as her tone was whiny.

"I can't see why Mrs. Forster shouldn't ask me as well as Lydia," she said, "even though I'm not her particular friend. I have just as much right to be asked as she does, and more, because I'm two years older."

Elizabeth tried in vain to make her see reason, and Jane to make her accept it. As for Elizabeth herself, this invitation was so far from exciting the same feelings as it did in her mother and Lydia that she saw it as the death sentence for any hope of common sense in Lydia; and as deplorable as such a step would make her look, she couldn't help privately advising her father not to let her go. She laid out for him all the problems with Lydia's general behavior, the little benefit she could get from the friendship of a woman like Mrs. Forster, and the likelihood of her becoming even more reckless with such a companion in Brighton, where the temptations would be far greater than at home. He heard her carefully, and then said—

"Lydia will never be satisfied until she's embarrassed herself in some public place, and we can never expect her to do it with so little expense or trouble to the family as under the present circumstances."

"If you understood," said Elizabeth, "the very serious harm to us all that must come from Lydia's reckless and imprudent behavior—harm which, in fact, has already come from it—I'm sure you would judge the matter differently."

"Already come from it!" repeated Mr. Bennet. "What! Has she frightened away some of your admirers? Poor little Lizzy! But don't worry. Squeamish young men who can't bear to be connected with a bit of absurdity aren't worth regretting. Come, let me see the list of pitiful fellows who've been scared off by Lydia's foolishness."

"You're mistaken. I have no such injuries to complain about. It's not personal but general harm I'm talking about. Our standing, our respectability in the world, must be affected by the wild recklessness, the arrogance and contempt for all restraint that define Lydia's character. Forgive me—for I must speak plainly. If you, my dear father, won't take the trouble to check her wild spirits and teach her that her current pursuits can't be the business of her life, she'll soon be beyond the reach of correction. Her character will be set, and she will, at sixteen, be the most determined flirt who ever made herself and her family ridiculous—a flirt, too, of the worst and cheapest kind; with no attraction beyond youth and a decent appearance; and from the ignorance and emptiness of her mind, completely unable to fend off any of the universal contempt that her desperate need for attention will provoke. Kitty is in the same danger. She'll follow wherever Lydia leads. Vain, ignorant, idle, and utterly uncontrolled! Oh, my dear father, can you possibly think they won't be criticized and despised wherever they are known, and that their sisters won't constantly be dragged into the disgrace?"
Mr. Bennet saw that her whole heart was in the matter; and, taking her hand affectionately, replied—

"Don't upset yourself, my love. Wherever you and Jane are known, you'll be respected and valued; and you won't look any worse for having a couple of—or I might say three—very silly sisters. We'll have no peace at Longbourn if Lydia doesn't go to Brighton. Let her go, then. Colonel Forster is a sensible man and will keep her out of any real trouble; and she's fortunately too poor to be worth anyone's pursuit. In Brighton she'll be of even less importance as a common flirt than she's been here. The officers will find women better worth their notice. Let's hope that being there will teach her how insignificant she is. At any rate, she can hardly get much worse without giving us the right to lock her up for the rest of her life."

Elizabeth had to be content with this answer, but her own opinion remained unchanged, and she left him disappointed and sad. It wasn't in her nature, however, to make her problems worse by dwelling on them. She was confident she had done her duty; and to fret over unavoidable troubles, or multiply them through anxiety, was no part of her disposition.

Had Lydia and her mother known what Elizabeth had discussed with her father, their outrage would have been hard to contain. In Lydia's imagination, a trip to Brighton encompassed every possible form of earthly happiness. She saw, with the creative eye of fantasy, the streets of that fashionable seaside town filled with officers. She saw herself the center of attention for dozens of them, all currently unknown to her. She saw all the splendors of the camp: its tents stretched out in beautiful uniform rows, crowded with the young and the lively, and dazzling in scarlet; and to complete the picture, she saw herself sitting beneath a tent, tenderly flirting with at least six officers at once.

Had she known her sister had tried to tear her from such prospects and such realities, what would she have felt? Only her mother, who might have felt much the same, could have understood. Lydia going to Brighton was all that consoled Mrs. Bennet for the depressing certainty that her husband would never go there himself.
But they were entirely ignorant of what had been said, and their excitement continued, with little interruption, right up until the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Having been frequently in his company since her return, her earlier agitation was mostly gone; the excitement of her former partiality had vanished entirely. She had even learned to detect, in the very charm that had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness that now bored and repelled her. In his current behavior toward her, moreover, she found a fresh source of irritation; for his obvious intention to revive the attention he'd shown early in their acquaintance could only serve, after what she now knew, to annoy her. She lost all concern for him when she found herself singled out for such idle and shallow flirtation; and while she firmly discouraged it, she couldn't help feeling the insult contained in his assumption that, however long and for whatever reason his attentions had been withdrawn, her vanity would be gratified and her preference secured by their mere renewal.

On the very last day of the regiment's stay in Meryton, he dined with other officers at Longbourn; and Elizabeth was so little disposed to part from him on good terms that she mentioned Colonel Fitzwilliam's and Mr. Darcy's having both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, alarmed; but after a moment's thought, and with a returning smile, replied that he had formerly seen him often; and after observing that he was a very gentlemanly man, asked how she had liked him. Her answer was warmly in his favor. With an air of indifference, he soon added, "How long did you say he was at Rosings?"
"Nearly three weeks."
"And you saw him often?"
"Yes, almost every day."
"His manners are very different from his cousin's."
"Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves on closer acquaintance."

"Indeed!" cried Wickham, with a look that didn't escape her. "And may I ask—" but catching himself, he added in a lighter tone, "Is it in politeness that he improves? Has he condescended to add some civility to his usual manner? Because I hardly dare hope," he continued more seriously, "that he has improved in what really matters."
"Oh, no!" said Elizabeth. "In essentials, I believe he's very much what he always was."

While she spoke, Wickham looked as if he hardly knew whether to be pleased by her words or suspicious of their meaning. There was something in her expression that made him listen with anxious attention as she added—
"When I said that he improves on closer acquaintance, I didn't mean that his mind or his manners had improved, but that knowing him better made his character better understood."
Wickham's alarm now showed in his heightened color and agitated look; for a few minutes he was silent. Then, shaking off his embarrassment, he turned to her again and said in the gentlest tone—

"You, who know so well how I feel about Mr. Darcy, will understand how sincerely I must be glad that he's wise enough to at least put on an appearance of doing what's right. His pride, in that direction, may serve some purpose, if not for himself, then for many others, since it must deter him from the kind of shameful conduct I've suffered from. I only worry that the sort of caution you seem to be describing is merely a performance he puts on for his aunt, whose good opinion and judgment he greatly fears. That fear has always influenced him when they're together, I know; and much of it can be traced to his desire to promote the match with Miss de Bourgh, which I'm certain he has very much at heart."

Elizabeth couldn't suppress a smile at this, but she answered only with a slight nod. She could see that he wanted to draw her into the old subject of his grievances, and she was in no mood to indulge him. The rest of the evening passed with the appearance, on his side, of his usual cheerfulness, but with no further attempt to single out Elizabeth; and they parted at last with mutual politeness, and possibly a mutual wish to never meet again.

When the party broke up, Lydia left with Mrs. Forster for Meryton, from where they were to set out early the next morning. The separation between her and her family was more noisy than emotional. Kitty was the only one who shed tears, but she wept from frustration and envy. Mrs. Bennet was effusive in her wishes for her daughter's happiness, and forceful in her instructions that she not miss any opportunity to enjoy herself—advice there was every reason to believe would be followed. And amid the loud and cheerful farewells of Lydia herself, the quieter goodbyes of her sisters went unheard.

chapters.title: Chapter 42
paragraphs: Had Elizabeth's views been drawn entirely from her own family, she could not have formed a very flattering picture of married happiness or domestic comfort. Her father, captivated by youth and beauty and that appearance of good humor which youth and beauty generally give, had married a woman whose weak understanding and narrow mind had very early put an end to any real affection for her. Respect, esteem, and trust had vanished forever, and all his visions of domestic happiness had collapsed. But Mr. Bennet was not the sort of man to seek comfort for his own poor judgment in the pleasures that too often console the unfortunate for their foolishness or vice. He was fond of the countryside and of books, and from these interests came his chief enjoyments. To his wife he was hardly indebted at all, except that her ignorance and foolishness had contributed to his amusement. This is not the sort of happiness a man would generally wish to owe to his wife; but where other forms of entertainment are lacking, the true philosopher will make the best of what's available.

Elizabeth, however, had never been blind to the problems in her father's behavior as a husband. She had always seen it with pain; but respecting his abilities, and grateful for his affectionate treatment of herself, she had tried to forget what she couldn't overlook, and to push from her thoughts the constant breach of marital duty and decency which, by exposing his wife to the contempt of her own children, was so deeply wrong. But she had never felt as strongly as now the disadvantages facing the children of such an unsuitable marriage, nor been so fully aware of the harm arising from such a misguided use of talent—talent which, properly applied, might at least have preserved the respectability of his daughters, even if it couldn't have broadened his wife's mind.

When Elizabeth had finished being relieved about Wickham's departure, she found little else to be glad about in the regiment's loss. Their social engagements were less varied than before; and at home she had a mother and sister whose constant complaining about the dullness of everything cast a real shadow over the household. And though Kitty might in time regain her natural level of sense now that the sources of her distraction were removed, her other sister—from whose character greater trouble might be expected—was likely to be only hardened in all her folly and boldness by the double danger of a seaside resort and a military camp. On the whole, she found, as others have found before, that an event she had looked forward to with impatient longing did not, when it arrived, bring all the satisfaction she had promised herself. It was therefore necessary to fix on some other milestone for the beginning of real happiness; to have some other goal for her wishes and hopes, and by enjoying the pleasure of anticipation, console herself for the present and prepare for another disappointment. Her tour to the Lakes was now what her happiest thoughts centered on; it was her best comfort against all the miserable hours that her mother's and Kitty's discontentment made inevitable; and if only Jane could have been included, every part of it would have been perfect.

"But it's lucky," she thought, "that I have something to wish for. If everything were arranged perfectly, my disappointment would be guaranteed.
