But here, by carrying with me one constant source of regret in my sister's absence, I may reasonably hope to have all my expectations of pleasure fulfilled. A plan where every part promises delight can never succeed; and general disappointment is only prevented by the safeguard of some particular annoyance."

When Lydia went away she promised to write very often and in great detail to her mother and Kitty; but her letters were always long awaited and always very short. Those to her mother contained little besides the fact that they had just returned from the library, where various officers had accompanied them, and where she had seen such beautiful accessories as made her wild; that she had a new dress or a new parasol, which she would have described more fully but had to dash off because Mrs. Forster was calling her and they were heading to the camp. And from her correspondence with Kitty, even less could be learned, since her letters to her sister, though somewhat longer, were far too full of underlined words to be read aloud.

After the first two or three weeks of her absence, health, good humor, and cheerfulness began to return to Longbourn. Everything wore a happier aspect. The families who had been in London for the winter came back, and summer fashions and summer plans emerged. Mrs. Bennet was restored to her usual complaining contentment; and by mid-June Kitty had recovered enough to be able to enter Meryton without tears—an achievement so promising that Elizabeth dared to hope that by the following Christmas she might be reasonable enough to mention an officer no more than once a day, unless, by some cruel arrangement at the War Office, another regiment should be stationed in Meryton.

The date set for their northern tour was now fast approaching, and only two weeks remained when a letter arrived from Mrs. Gardiner that both delayed its start and shortened its scope. Mr. Gardiner would be held up by business and couldn't leave until two weeks later in July, and had to be back in London within a month. Since that left too little time to go as far and see as much as they had planned, or at least to see it with the leisure and comfort they had counted on, they were forced to give up the Lakes and settle for a shorter tour. According to the revised plan, they would go no farther north than Derbyshire. There was enough to see in that county to fill most of their three weeks; and for Mrs. Gardiner it held a particularly strong attraction. The town where she had once spent several years of her life, and where they were now to stay for a few days, was probably as much an object of her curiosity as all the famous beauties of Matlock, Chatsworth, Dovedale, or the Peak.

Elizabeth was extremely disappointed; she had set her heart on seeing the Lakes and still thought there might have been time enough. But it was her duty to be satisfied—and certainly her nature to be happy; and soon everything was right again.

The mention of Derbyshire brought many associations. It was impossible for her to see the word without thinking of Pemberley and its owner. "But surely," she said, "I may enter his county without incident, and steal a few petrified stones without him noticing me."

The waiting period was now doubled. Four weeks had to pass before her uncle and aunt's arrival. But they did pass, and Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner, with their four children, finally appeared at Longbourn. The children—two girls of six and eight and two younger boys—were to be left in the care of their cousin Jane, who was the general favorite, and whose steady temperament and sweetness made her perfectly suited for looking after them in every way—teaching them, playing with them, and loving them.

The Gardiners stayed only one night at Longbourn and set off the next morning with Elizabeth in search of novelty and amusement. One pleasure was guaranteed: their suitability as traveling companions—a suitability that included the health and temperament to bear inconveniences, the cheerfulness to enhance every pleasure, and the affection and good sense which could supply enjoyment among themselves if there were disappointments along the way.

It is not the purpose of this story to describe Derbyshire, nor any of the remarkable places on their route—Oxford, Blenheim, Warwick, Kenilworth, Birmingham, and the rest are sufficiently well known. Only a small part of Derbyshire concerns us now. To the little town of Lambton, the scene of Mrs. Gardiner's former residence, where she had recently learned that some old friends still remained, they directed their steps, having already seen all the principal wonders of the area. And within five miles of Lambton, Elizabeth learned from her aunt that Pemberley was situated. It wasn't directly on their route, nor more than a mile or two out of the way. While discussing their itinerary the evening before, Mrs. Gardiner mentioned a desire to see the place again. Mr. Gardiner was happy to go, and Elizabeth was asked for her opinion.

"My love, wouldn't you like to see a place you've heard so much about?" said her aunt. "A place, too, with which so many of your acquaintances are connected. Wickham spent his whole youth there, you know."

Elizabeth was distressed. She felt she had no business at Pemberley, and was forced to pretend she had no interest in seeing it. She had to claim she was tired of grand houses: after seeing so many, she really took no pleasure in fine carpets or satin curtains.

Mrs. Gardiner dismissed her excuse. "If it were merely a fine house with expensive furnishings," she said, "I wouldn't care about it either; but the grounds are delightful. They have some of the finest woods in the country."

Elizabeth said no more, but her mind wouldn't rest. The possibility of running into Mr. Darcy while touring the property immediately occurred to her. That would be dreadful! She blushed at the very idea, and thought it would be better to speak openly to her aunt than to risk such a meeting. But there were objections to that course too; and she finally decided that it would be a last resort, if her private inquiries about the family's absence got an unfavorable answer.

Accordingly, when she retired that night, she asked the chambermaid whether Pemberley was a very fine place, what was the name of its owner, and—with no small anxiety—whether the family were there for the summer. A most welcome "No" followed that last question; and with her fears now removed, she was free to feel a great deal of curiosity about seeing the house herself. When the subject came up again the next morning and she was asked once more, she could readily answer, with a suitable air of indifference, that she had no real objection to the plan.
To Pemberley, therefore, they were to go.

chapters.title: Chapter 43
paragraphs: As they drove along, Elizabeth watched for the first appearance of Pemberley Woods with some nervousness; and when they finally turned in at the lodge, her spirits were in a high flutter.
The park was very large and contained a great variety of landscape. They entered at one of its lowest points and drove for some time through beautiful woods stretching over a wide expanse.

Elizabeth's mind was too full for conversation, but she took in and admired every remarkable view. They gradually climbed for half a mile, and then found themselves at the top of a considerable rise where the woods ended, and the eye was instantly caught by Pemberley House, situated on the opposite side of the valley, into which the road descended with some abruptness. It was a large, handsome stone building, well positioned on rising ground and backed by a ridge of high wooded hills; in front, a stream of some natural size had been widened, but without any artificial appearance. Its banks were neither formal nor elaborately decorated. Elizabeth was delighted. She had never seen a place where nature had done more, or where natural beauty had been so little spoiled by bad taste. They were all warm in their admiration; and at that moment she felt that to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!

They descended the hill, crossed the bridge, and drove to the door; and as Elizabeth examined the nearer aspect of the house, all her dread of meeting its owner returned. She feared the chambermaid had been wrong. When they applied to see the place, they were admitted into the hall; and while waiting for the housekeeper, Elizabeth had time to wonder at finding herself where she was.

The housekeeper arrived—a respectable-looking elderly woman, far less grand and far more civil than Elizabeth had expected. They followed her into the dining room. It was a large, well-proportioned room, handsomely furnished. Elizabeth, after briefly looking around, went to a window to enjoy the view. The hill they had descended, crowned with woods and appearing even steeper from this distance, was a beautiful sight. Every feature of the landscape was pleasing, and she gazed with delight at the whole scene—the river, the trees scattered along its banks, and the winding of the valley as far as she could trace it. As they passed through other rooms, these elements shifted position, but from every window there were beauties to admire. The rooms were spacious and handsome, their furnishings suited to the fortune of their owner; but Elizabeth noticed, with admiration for his taste, that nothing was gaudy or pointlessly ornate—less showy and more genuinely elegant than the rooms at Rosings.

"And I might have been mistress of this place," she thought. "These rooms might have been familiar to me by now! Instead of viewing them as a stranger, I might have taken joy in them as my own, and welcomed my uncle and aunt here as visitors. But no," she caught herself, "that could never have been; my uncle and aunt would have been lost to me; I would never have been allowed to invite them."
This was a fortunate thought—it saved her from something like regret.

She longed to ask the housekeeper whether her master was truly away, but didn't have the nerve. At last, however, her uncle asked the question, and she turned away in alarm while Mrs. Reynolds confirmed he was—adding, "But we expect him tomorrow with a large party of friends." How glad Elizabeth was that their own journey hadn't been delayed by even a day!

Her aunt now called her to look at a picture. She approached and saw a portrait of Mr. Wickham hanging among several other miniatures over the fireplace. Her aunt asked with a smile how she liked it. The housekeeper stepped forward and told them it was the picture of a young gentleman, the son of her late master's steward, who had been raised by him at his own expense. "He's gone into the army now," she added, "but I'm afraid he's turned out quite wild."
Mrs. Gardiner looked at her niece with a smile, but Elizabeth couldn't return it.
"And that," said Mrs. Reynolds, pointing to another miniature, "is my master—and a very good likeness. It was painted at the same time as the other—about eight years ago."
"I've heard a great deal about your master's fine appearance," said Mrs. Gardiner, studying the picture. "It's a handsome face. But Lizzy, you can tell us whether it's a good likeness or not."
Mrs. Reynolds's respect for Elizabeth seemed to increase at this hint that she knew her master.
"Does that young lady know Mr. Darcy?"
Elizabeth colored and said, "A little."
"And don't you think him a very handsome gentleman, ma'am?"
"Yes, very handsome."

"I'm sure I know no one so handsome; but in the gallery upstairs you'll see a finer, larger picture of him. This room was my late master's favorite, and these miniatures are just as they were in his time. He was very fond of them."
This explained to Elizabeth why Mr. Wickham's portrait was among them.
Mrs. Reynolds then directed their attention to a portrait of Miss Darcy, painted when she was only eight years old.
"And is Miss Darcy as handsome as her brother?" asked Mr. Gardiner.

"Oh yes—the handsomest young lady you ever saw, and so accomplished! She plays and sings all day long. In the next room there's a new instrument just arrived for her—a present from my master. She comes here tomorrow with him."

Mr. Gardiner, whose manners were easy and pleasant, encouraged her chattiness with his questions and remarks; Mrs. Reynolds, whether from pride or affection, clearly took great pleasure in talking about her master and his sister.
"Is your master at Pemberley much during the year?"
"Not as much as I'd like, sir; but I'd say he spends about half his time here, and Miss Darcy is always here for the summer months."
"Except," thought Elizabeth, "when she goes to Ramsgate."
"If your master married, you might see more of him."
"Yes, sir; but I don't know when that will be. I don't know who would be good enough for him."
Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner smiled. Elizabeth couldn't help saying, "It's very much to his credit that you should think so."

"I say no more than the truth, and what everyone who knows him would say," replied the housekeeper. Elizabeth thought this was going rather far; and she listened with growing astonishment as Mrs. Reynolds added, "I've never had a cross word from him in my life, and I've known him since he was four years old."

This was praise of the most extraordinary kind, completely opposite to Elizabeth's ideas. That he was not a good-tempered man had been her firmest belief. Her keenest attention was awakened; she longed to hear more, and was grateful to her uncle for saying—
"There are very few people of whom so much can be said. You're lucky to have such a master."

"Yes, sir, I know I am. If I searched the whole world, I couldn't find a better one. But I've always noticed that those who are good-natured as children are good-natured when they grow up; and he was always the sweetest-tempered, most generous boy in the world."
Elizabeth nearly stared at her. "Can this be Mr. Darcy?" she thought.
"His father was an excellent man," said Mrs. Gardiner.
"Yes, ma'am, that he was indeed; and his son is just like him—just as kind to the poor."

Elizabeth listened, wondered, doubted, and wanted more. Mrs. Reynolds could hold her interest on no other topic. She described the subjects of the paintings, the dimensions of the rooms, and the price of the furniture to no effect. Mr. Gardiner, highly amused by what he saw as natural family loyalty, soon led her back to the subject; and she spoke with great energy about his many virtues as they proceeded together up the grand staircase.

"He is the best landlord and the best master that ever lived. Not like the wild young men nowadays, who think of nothing but themselves. There isn't one of his tenants or servants who won't speak well of him. Some people call him proud, but I've never seen anything of it. To my mind, it's only because he doesn't chatter on like other young men."
"What a favorable light this puts him in!" thought Elizabeth.
"This glowing account of him," her aunt whispered as they walked, "doesn't quite match his behavior toward our poor friend."
"Perhaps we were wrong about that."
"That's not very likely; our source was too reliable."

When they reached the spacious landing above, they were shown into a very pretty sitting room, recently redecorated with more elegance and lightness than the rooms downstairs. They were told it had just been done to please Miss Darcy, who had taken a liking to the room on her last visit to Pemberley.
"He's certainly a good brother," said Elizabeth, walking to one of the windows.

Mrs. Reynolds anticipated Miss Darcy's delight when she would see the room. "And that's always the way with him," she added. "Whatever can give his sister pleasure is done in a moment. There's nothing he wouldn't do for her."

The picture gallery and two or three of the principal bedrooms were all that remained to see. In the gallery there were many fine paintings, but Elizabeth knew nothing of art; and from those already visible downstairs she had gladly turned to look at some drawings by Miss Darcy, in crayon, whose subjects were usually more interesting and more accessible.

In the gallery there were many family portraits, but they held little to capture a stranger's attention. Elizabeth walked on, looking for the only face whose features would be familiar to her. At last it caught her eye—and she found herself looking at a striking likeness of Mr. Darcy, with a smile on his face that she remembered having occasionally seen when he looked at her. She stood several minutes before the painting in earnest study, and returned to it again before they left the gallery. Mrs. Reynolds told them it had been painted during his father's lifetime.

There was certainly at this moment, in Elizabeth's mind, a gentler feeling toward the original than she had ever experienced at the height of their acquaintance. The praise bestowed on him by Mrs. Reynolds was no trivial matter. What recommendation is more valuable than the praise of a perceptive servant? As a brother, a landlord, a master, she considered how many people's happiness was in his care! How much pleasure or pain he had the power to give! How much good or harm he could do! Every impression the housekeeper had conveyed was favorable to his character; and as she stood before the canvas where he was portrayed, his eyes seeming to rest on her, she thought of his affection with a deeper gratitude than it had ever stirred before. She remembered its warmth, and softened the memory of its improper expression.

When everything in the house that was open to the public had been seen, they went back downstairs and, taking leave of the housekeeper, were handed over to the gardener, who met them at the front door.

As they walked across the lawn toward the river, Elizabeth turned back to look at the house once more; her uncle and aunt stopped too, and while Mr. Gardiner was guessing at the date of the building, the owner himself suddenly appeared from the road that led behind the house to the stables.

They were within twenty yards of each other, and his appearance was so sudden that it was impossible to avoid being seen. Their eyes met instantly, and both their faces flushed deeply. He absolutely started, and for a moment seemed frozen with surprise; but quickly recovering, he walked toward the group and spoke to Elizabeth with—if not perfect composure—at least perfect civility.

She had instinctively turned away, but stopping as he approached, she received his greetings with an embarrassment impossible to overcome. Had his sudden appearance, or his resemblance to the portrait they had just been studying, been insufficient to tell her uncle and aunt that this was Mr. Darcy, the gardener's expression of surprise at seeing his master would have told them everything. They stood slightly apart while he spoke to their niece, who, astonished and confused, barely dared look at his face and hardly knew what answers she gave to his polite questions about her family. Amazed at the change in his manner since they had last parted, every sentence he spoke increased her embarrassment; and the thought that it was improper for her to be found here kept recurring, making those few minutes among the most uncomfortable of her life. He seemed no more at ease himself; when he spoke, his voice lacked its usual steadiness, and he repeated his questions about when she had left Longbourn and how long she had been in Derbyshire so often and in such a hurried way as to plainly reveal how distracted his thoughts were.
At last every topic seemed to fail him, and after standing for a few moments without speaking, he suddenly collected himself and took his leave.

The others then joined her and expressed their admiration of his appearance; but Elizabeth heard not a word, and entirely absorbed in her own feelings, followed them in silence. She was overwhelmed by shame and embarrassment. Coming here had been the most unfortunate, the most ill-judged thing in the world! How strange it must look to him! In what an unflattering light it might strike so proud a man! It might seem as if she had purposely thrown herself in his path again! Oh, why had she come? Or why had he arrived a day early? Had they been only ten minutes sooner, they would have been beyond his reach; for it was clear he had just that moment arrived, just that moment dismounted from his horse or stepped out of his carriage. She blushed again and again at the perversity of this meeting. And his behavior, so strikingly changed—what could it mean? That he should even speak to her was astonishing!—but to speak with such courtesy, to ask about her family! Never in her life had she seen his manners so little dignified, never had he spoken with such gentleness as at this unexpected encounter. What a contrast to his last speech in Rosings Park, when he put his letter into her hand! She didn't know what to think or how to account for it.

They had now entered a beautiful walk along the water's edge, and every step revealed a finer stretch of the woods ahead; but it was some time before Elizabeth noticed any of it. Though she answered mechanically when her uncle and aunt pointed things out, she took in nothing of the scenery. Her thoughts were all fixed on that one spot of Pemberley House, wherever it might be, where Mr. Darcy now was. She longed to know what was passing through his mind; how he was thinking of her; and whether, in spite of everything, she still mattered to him. Perhaps he had been polite only because he felt comfortable; yet there had been something in his voice that didn't sound comfortable. Whether he had felt more pain or pleasure in seeing her, she couldn't tell, but he certainly hadn't seen her with composure.
At last, however, her companions' remarks about her distraction roused her, and she felt she must make an effort to appear more like herself.

They entered the woods and, leaving the river for a while, climbed to higher ground, where openings in the trees offered charming views of the valley, the opposite hills with their long range of woods, and glimpses of the stream. Mr. Gardiner expressed a wish to walk around the whole park, but feared it might be too far. With a triumphant smile, the gardener told them it was ten miles around. That settled the matter, and they followed the usual circuit, which eventually brought them down through hanging woods to the water's edge at one of its narrowest points. They crossed by a simple bridge in keeping with the natural character of the scene: it was a spot less adorned than any they had yet visited, and the valley, narrowing here into a glen, allowed room only for the stream and a narrow path through the rough undergrowth along its banks. Elizabeth longed to explore its twists and turns, but after crossing the bridge they realized how far they were from the house, and Mrs. Gardiner, who was not a great walker, could go no farther and wanted only to get back to the carriage as quickly as possible. Elizabeth had to give in, and they made their way toward the house on the opposite side of the river by the most direct route; but their progress was slow, since Mr. Gardiner, who seldom got the chance to indulge his love of fishing, was so absorbed in watching the occasional trout in the water and talking to the gardener about them that he barely moved. While they wandered along at this slow pace, they were again surprised—and Elizabeth's astonishment was as great as before—by the sight of Mr. Darcy approaching them, at no great distance. The path being less sheltered here, they saw him before they met. Elizabeth, however startled, was at least better prepared than before, and resolved to appear calm if he really intended to approach them. For a few moments she thought he might take another path. The idea lasted while a turn in the walk hid him from view; but after the turn, he was immediately before them. With a glance she saw that he had lost none of his recent civility; and to match his politeness, she began as they met to admire the beauty of the place. But she had barely gotten beyond "delightful" and "charming" when some unfortunate associations intruded, and she worried that praise of Pemberley from her might be awkwardly interpreted. Her color changed, and she said no more.

Mrs. Gardiner was standing a little behind, and when Elizabeth paused, he asked if she would do him the honor of introducing him to her friends. This was a courtesy she was entirely unprepared for; and she could hardly suppress a smile at his now seeking the acquaintance of the very people whose existence his pride had rejected when he proposed to her. "What will his surprise be," she thought, "when he finds out who they are! He takes them for fashionable people."

The introduction, however, was made at once; and as she named their relationship to herself, she stole a glance at him to see how he took it, half expecting him to flee from such embarrassing connections. That he was surprised was obvious; but he bore it well, and far from retreating, turned back with them and struck up a conversation with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth couldn't help being pleased—couldn't help feeling a small triumph. It was comforting to know she had some relatives who would not cause embarrassment. She listened carefully to everything they said and took pride in every remark of her uncle's that showed his intelligence, his good taste, or his fine manners.

The conversation soon turned to fishing, and she heard Mr. Darcy invite him, with the greatest civility, to fish there whenever he liked during his stay in the area, offering to lend him tackle and pointing out where the best fishing was. Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look of amazement. Elizabeth said nothing, but it pleased her enormously; the compliment must be all for her sake. Her astonishment, however, was extreme, and she kept thinking, "Why is he so changed? What's behind it? It can't be for me—it can't be for my sake that his manners have softened like this. My criticisms at Hunsford couldn't have produced such a change. It's impossible that he should still love me."

After walking some time in this way—the two ladies in front, the two gentlemen behind—they changed positions when they went down to the riverbank to examine some unusual water plant. The rearrangement was Mrs. Gardiner's doing: tired from the morning's exercise, she found Elizabeth's arm an inadequate support and preferred her husband's. Mr. Darcy took her place beside Elizabeth, and they walked on together. After a brief silence, Elizabeth spoke first. She wanted him to know she had been told he was away before she came, and so she began by saying that his arrival had been very unexpected—"because your housekeeper told us you definitely wouldn't be here until tomorrow, and before we left Bakewell, we understood you weren't expected in the area at all." He confirmed this was true, and said that business with his steward had brought him ahead of the rest of his party. "They'll join me early tomorrow," he continued, "and among them are some people you know—Mr. Bingley and his sisters."

Elizabeth answered with only a slight nod. Her thoughts were instantly carried back to the last time Mr. Bingley's name had been mentioned between them; and if she could judge from his complexion, his mind was similarly occupied.

"There is also someone else in the party," he continued after a pause, "who particularly wishes to meet you. Will you allow me—or am I asking too much—to introduce my sister to you during your stay at Lambton?"

The surprise of such a request was enormous; it was too great for her to know how she accepted it. She immediately realized that whatever desire Miss Darcy might have to meet her must be her brother's doing, and without looking further, it was satisfying—it was gratifying to know that his resentment hadn't made him think badly of her.

They now walked on in silence, each deep in thought. Elizabeth was not comfortable—that was impossible—but she was flattered and pleased. His wish to introduce his sister was a compliment of the highest order. They soon outpaced the others, and when they reached the carriage, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner were still a good distance behind.

He then invited her to come into the house, but she said she wasn't tired, and they stood together on the lawn. At such a moment much might have been said, and the silence was very awkward. She wanted to talk, but every subject seemed off-limits. At last she remembered that she had been traveling, and they discussed Matlock and Dovedale with determined persistence. Yet time and her aunt moved slowly—and her patience and her conversation topics were nearly exhausted before the awkward tête-à-tête was over.

When Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner arrived, they were all invited to come inside for refreshment, but the offer was declined, and they parted on each side with the greatest politeness. Mr. Darcy handed the ladies into the carriage, and as it drove away, Elizabeth saw him walking slowly back toward the house.
Her uncle and aunt's observations now began, and each of them declared him far superior to anything they had expected.
"He's perfectly well-mannered, polite, and unpretentious," said her uncle.

"There is something a little stately about him, to be sure," replied her aunt, "but it's only in his bearing and isn't unbecoming. I can say now, with the housekeeper, that though some people may call him proud, I've seen nothing of it."

"I was never more surprised than by his behavior toward us. It was more than polite; it was genuinely attentive. And there was no need for such attention. His acquaintance with Elizabeth was very slight."

"Well, Lizzy," said her aunt, "he's not as handsome as Wickham—or rather, he doesn't have Wickham's kind of face, though his features are perfectly fine. But why did you tell us he was so unpleasant?"
Elizabeth made the best excuses she could; she said she had liked him better when they met in Kent than before, and that she had never seen him so pleasant as this morning.

"But he may just be putting on a show of civility," replied her uncle. "Important men often do that. So I won't take him at his word about the fishing, since he might change his mind and throw me off his property."
Elizabeth felt they had entirely misjudged his character, but said nothing.

"From what we've seen of him," continued Mrs. Gardiner, "I really wouldn't have thought he could treat anyone as cruelly as he's treated poor Wickham. He doesn't look unkind. On the contrary, there's something pleasing about his mouth when he speaks. And there's a dignity in his expression that wouldn't give you a bad impression of his heart. But the good woman who showed us the house certainly gave him a glowing recommendation! I could hardly keep from laughing aloud at times. But I suppose he's a generous master, and to a servant, that covers every virtue."

Elizabeth now felt called upon to say something in defense of his treatment of Wickham, and so gave them to understand, as carefully as she could, that from what she had heard from his relatives in Kent, his actions were open to a very different interpretation, and that his character was by no means as flawed—nor Wickham's as admirable—as they had been considered in Hertfordshire. To support this, she related the details of all the financial dealings between them, without actually naming her source, but saying it was one that could be relied upon.

Mrs. Gardiner was surprised and troubled; but as they were now approaching the scene of her former pleasures, every other thought gave way to the charm of old memories, and she was too busy pointing out familiar spots to her husband to think of anything else. Tired as she had been from the morning's walk, they had no sooner finished dinner than she set off again to look up old friends, and the evening was spent in the satisfactions of a renewed acquaintance after many years' absence.

The day's events were too interesting to leave Elizabeth much attention for any of these new friends; and she could do nothing but think, and think with wonder, of Mr. Darcy's civility, and above all, of his wish that she should meet his sister.

chapters.title: Chapter 44
paragraphs: Elizabeth had assumed that Mr. Darcy would bring his sister to visit her the day after she arrived at Pemberley, and had therefore resolved not to leave the inn the whole morning. But she was wrong; for on the very morning after their own arrival at Lambton, the visitors came. They had been walking around the town with some of their new friends and had just returned to the inn to change for dinner with the same family, when the sound of a carriage drew them to the window, and they saw a gentleman and lady in a light open carriage driving up the street. Elizabeth immediately recognized the livery, guessed what it meant, and surprised her relatives considerably by telling them about the honor she expected. Her uncle and aunt were all amazement; and the embarrassment of her manner, combined with the visit itself and many details from the day before, opened up a new possibility in their minds. Nothing had ever suggested it before, but they now felt there was no other way to explain such attention from such a source than by supposing he was attracted to their niece. While these newly formed ideas were forming in their heads, Elizabeth's agitation was growing by the moment. She was amazed at her own nervousness; but among other causes for unease, she worried that the brother might have said too much in her favor, and more than usually anxious to make a good impression, she naturally feared she would fail completely.
She retreated from the window, afraid of being seen; and as she paced up and down the room, trying to compose herself, the curious looks from her uncle and aunt only made everything worse.

Miss Darcy and her brother appeared, and the dreaded introduction took place. Elizabeth was astonished to find that her new acquaintance was at least as embarrassed as herself. Since arriving in Lambton, she had heard that Miss Darcy was extremely proud; but a few minutes' observation convinced her that she was only extremely shy. It was hard to get even a single word from her beyond a monosyllable.

Miss Darcy was tall and of a larger build than Elizabeth; and though barely sixteen, her figure was mature and her appearance womanly and graceful. She was less handsome than her brother, but there was intelligence and good humor in her face, and her manners were perfectly modest and gentle. Elizabeth, who had expected to find an observer as keen and assured as Mr. Darcy himself, was much relieved to discover such different qualities.

They hadn't been together long before Darcy told her that Bingley was also coming to pay his respects, and she had barely time to express her pleasure and prepare herself before Bingley's quick step was heard on the stairs, and in a moment he entered the room. Any anger Elizabeth had ever felt toward him had long since disappeared; but even if it hadn't, it could hardly have withstood the unaffected warmth with which he greeted her. He asked in a friendly, though general, way about her family, and looked and spoke with the same good-natured ease as always.

To Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner he was hardly less interesting than to Elizabeth herself. They had long wanted to meet him. The entire group, in fact, held their keen attention. Their suspicions about Mr. Darcy and their niece directed their observation toward each with careful but discreet scrutiny, and they soon became convinced that at least one of the pair knew what it was to be in love. They remained slightly uncertain about the lady's feelings, but there was no question the gentleman was overflowing with admiration.

Elizabeth, for her part, had plenty to manage. She wanted to read each visitor's feelings, she wanted to control her own, and she wanted to be agreeable to everyone. In this last goal—where she feared most to fail—she was most likely to succeed, since those she was trying to please were already well disposed toward her. Bingley was ready, Georgiana was eager, and Darcy determined, to be pleased.

In watching Bingley, her thoughts naturally flew to her sister; and oh, how intensely she longed to know whether any of his thoughts were similarly directed. Sometimes she fancied he talked less than on previous occasions, and once or twice imagined that, as he looked at her, he was trying to trace a resemblance. But though this might be imaginary, she could not be mistaken about his behavior toward Miss Darcy, who had been set up as Jane's rival. There was nothing on either side to suggest particular affection. Nothing passed between them that could justify his sister's hopes. On this point she was soon reassured; and two or three small incidents before they parted, which in her anxious interpretation suggested memories of Jane—not untouched by tenderness—and a wish to say more that might lead to mentioning her, had he dared. He remarked to her, in a quiet moment when the others were talking, with something of real regret in his tone, that "it had been a very long time since he'd had the pleasure of seeing her." And before she could reply, he added, "It's been over eight months. We haven't met since November 26th, when we were all dancing together at Netherfield."

Elizabeth was pleased to find his memory so precise; and he afterward took the chance to ask her, when no one else was listening, whether all her sisters were at Longbourn. There wasn't much in the question, or in his earlier remark; but there was a look and a manner that gave them meaning.

She seldom turned her eyes toward Mr. Darcy himself; but whenever she did steal a glance, she saw an expression of general warmth, and in everything he said she heard a tone so completely free of the arrogance or disdain of his companions that she was convinced the improved manners she had seen yesterday—however temporary they might prove—had at least lasted more than one day. When she saw him actively seeking the acquaintance and courting the good opinion of people whose company, only a few months ago, he would have considered beneath him; when she saw him so civil not only to herself but to the very relatives he had openly looked down upon, and when she remembered their last lively scene at Hunsford Parsonage—the difference, the change, was so great that it struck her forcibly, and she could hardly keep her astonishment from showing. Never, even among his close friends at Netherfield or his grand relatives at Rosings, had she seen him so eager to please, so free from self-importance or stiffness, as now—when nothing could be gained from the effort, and when the very acquaintance of those he was being attentive to would be mocked by the ladies of both Netherfield and Rosings.

Their visitors stayed for over half an hour, and when they rose to leave, Mr. Darcy asked his sister to join him in inviting Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner and Miss Bennet to dinner at Pemberley before they left the area. Miss Darcy, though with a shyness that showed she wasn't used to giving invitations, readily agreed. Mrs. Gardiner looked at her niece, wanting to know how she—the one the invitation most concerned—felt about accepting, but Elizabeth had turned away. Assuming, however, that this deliberate avoidance came from momentary embarrassment rather than actual reluctance, and seeing in her husband—who was fond of company—a perfect willingness to accept, she ventured to say yes for all of them, and the day after next was fixed.

Bingley was openly delighted at the certainty of seeing Elizabeth again, having much still to say to her and many questions to ask about their Hertfordshire friends. Elizabeth, reading all this as a desire to hear her talk about her sister, was pleased; and between this and other considerations, she found herself, after the visitors left, able to look back on the last half hour with some satisfaction—though while it was happening, she had barely enjoyed it. Eager to be alone and afraid of questions or hints from her uncle and aunt, she stayed with them only long enough to hear their favorable opinion of Bingley, and then hurried away to change.

But she had no reason to fear her relatives' curiosity; it was not their wish to press her for information. It was clear she knew Mr. Darcy much better than they had suspected, and clear that he was very much in love with her. They saw much to interest them but nothing to justify asking questions.

As for Mr. Darcy, it was now a matter of some importance to Elizabeth to think well of him; and as far as their acquaintance went, there was nothing to criticize. They couldn't help being struck by his politeness, and had they judged his character from their own experience and his servant's report alone, ignoring all other accounts, nobody in Hertfordshire would have recognized the description. There was now a reason to believe the housekeeper, and they soon came to feel that the authority of a servant who had known him since he was four years old, and whose own manners showed respectability, was not to be lightly dismissed. Nor had anything they heard from their Lambton friends undermined it. The only charge against him was pride; and he probably did have pride—if not, it would certainly be attributed to him by the inhabitants of a small market town where the family didn't mix socially. It was acknowledged, however, that he was a generous man who did much good among the poor.

As for Wickham, the travelers soon discovered that he was not highly regarded there; for although the details of his dealings with the Darcy family were not fully known, it was a well-established fact that when he left Derbyshire, he had left many debts behind him, which Mr. Darcy had afterward paid.

As for Elizabeth, her thoughts were at Pemberley that evening even more than the night before; and the evening, though it seemed long as it passed, was not long enough to sort out her feelings about one particular person in that house. She lay awake for two full hours trying to understand them. She certainly didn't hate him. No—hatred had vanished long ago, and she had been almost as long ashamed of ever having felt a dislike strong enough to deserve that name. The respect born from recognizing his genuine qualities, though initially resisted, had for some time ceased to be unwelcome; and it was now heightened into something friendlier by the testimony so strongly in his favor, casting his character in such a good light, that yesterday had produced. But above all—above respect and esteem—there was a feeling of goodwill that couldn't be ignored. It was gratitude: gratitude not merely for having once loved her, but for loving her still enough to forgive all the rudeness and bitterness of her manner in rejecting him, and all the unfair accusations that had accompanied her rejection. He, whom she had been certain would avoid her as his greatest enemy, seemed—at this accidental meeting—most eager to continue their acquaintance. And without any showy display of affection, or any special manner when the two of them were alone, he was seeking the good opinion of her friends and determined to introduce her to his sister. Such a change in a man of so much pride stirred not only astonishment but gratitude—for it could only be explained by deep, genuine love; and as such, its effect on her was of a kind to be encouraged, by no means unpleasant, though she couldn't quite define it. She respected him, she esteemed him, she was grateful to him, she felt a real interest in his wellbeing; and she only wanted to know how far she wished that wellbeing to depend on herself, and how far it would be for the happiness of both if she were to use the power—which she had a feeling she still possessed—to encourage him to propose again.

It had been agreed between aunt and niece that evening that such a striking courtesy as Miss Darcy's—visiting them on the very day of her arrival at Pemberley, when she had only gotten there in time for a late breakfast—ought to be repaid, though it couldn't be matched, by some effort of politeness on their side; and consequently, they would visit her at Pemberley the following morning. They were therefore to go. Elizabeth was pleased—though when she asked herself why, she had very little to say in reply.
Mr. Gardiner left them soon after breakfast. The fishing plan had been revived the day before, and a definite arrangement made for him to meet some of the gentlemen at Pemberley by noon.

chapters.title: Chapter 45
paragraphs: Convinced as Elizabeth now was that Miss Bingley's dislike of her had originated in jealousy, she couldn't help wondering how coldly or civilly that lady would treat her now.

When they reached the house, they were shown through the hall into a drawing room whose north-facing windows made it delightfully cool in summer. The tall windows, opening to the ground, offered a refreshing view of the high wooded hills behind the house and of the beautiful oaks and Spanish chestnuts scattered across the lawn between.

In this room they were received by Miss Darcy, who was sitting there with Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley, and the lady who lived with her in London. Georgiana greeted them politely, but with all the embarrassment that, though it came from shyness and the fear of doing something wrong, could easily give those who felt themselves inferior the impression of pride and coldness. Mrs. Gardiner and her niece, however, understood the truth and pitied her.

Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley acknowledged them with nothing more than a curtsy; and once they were seated, an awkward pause followed for several moments. It was first broken by Mrs. Annesley, a well-bred, agreeable-looking woman whose efforts to start a conversation showed her to be far better mannered than either of the others. Between her and Mrs. Gardiner, with occasional help from Elizabeth, the talk was kept going. Miss Darcy looked as if she wished she had the courage to join in, and sometimes ventured a short sentence when there was the least chance of its being heard.

Elizabeth soon noticed she was being closely watched by Miss Bingley, and that she couldn't say a word, especially to Miss Darcy, without drawing her attention. This wouldn't have stopped Elizabeth from trying to talk to the younger girl, had they not been seated too far apart; but she was just as glad to be spared the effort. Her own thoughts were keeping her occupied. She expected every moment that some of the gentlemen would come in; she hoped and feared that the master of the house might be among them; and whether she hoped or feared it more, she couldn't decide. After a quarter of an hour of this, without hearing Miss Bingley's voice, Elizabeth was startled by a cold inquiry from her about the health of her family. She answered with equal coolness and brevity, and the other said no more.

The next development was the entrance of servants with cold meat, cake, and a variety of the finest seasonal fruits; but this didn't happen until Mrs. Annesley had given Miss Darcy several pointed looks and smiles to remind her of her duties as hostess. Now everyone had something to do: though they couldn't all talk, they could all eat; and the beautiful displays of grapes, peaches, and nectarines soon gathered them around the table.

While they were eating, Elizabeth had a perfect opportunity to settle whether she more feared or wished for Mr. Darcy's appearance—judging by how she felt when he walked in. And though only a moment before she had believed her wishes were stronger, she now began to regret that he'd come.

He had been with Mr. Gardiner and two or three other gentlemen by the river, and had only left them on learning that the ladies of the family planned to visit Georgiana that morning. No sooner did he appear than Elizabeth wisely resolved to be perfectly relaxed and natural—a resolution all the more necessary because she could see that every eye in the room was watching his behavior. In no face was eager curiosity more plainly visible than in Miss Bingley's, despite the smiles she put on whenever she spoke to either Darcy or his sister; for jealousy had not yet made her desperate, and her pursuit of Mr. Darcy was far from over. Miss Darcy, on her brother's entrance, made a much greater effort to join the conversation; and Elizabeth saw that he was anxious for his sister and herself to become friends, and encouraged every attempt at conversation on either side. Miss Bingley saw all this too; and in the recklessness of anger, she seized the first chance to say, with sneering politeness—
"Tell me, Miss Eliza, isn't the ——shire militia gone from Meryton? They must be a great loss to your family."

In Darcy's presence she didn't dare say Wickham's name; but Elizabeth instantly understood who she was referring to, and the various memories connected with him caused a moment's pain. But gathering herself to repel the mean-spirited attack, she answered the question in a reasonably composed tone. While she spoke, an involuntary glance showed her Darcy with a heightened color, looking at her intently, and his sister overcome with confusion, unable to raise her eyes. Had Miss Bingley known what pain she was causing her beloved friend, she would certainly have held back; but she had only meant to embarrass Elizabeth by bringing up a man she believed Elizabeth was attracted to, hoping to make her betray a sensitivity that might damage her in Darcy's eyes—and perhaps remind him of all the foolishness by which some of her family were connected to that regiment. Not a whisper had ever reached her of Miss Darcy's near-elopement. It had been kept secret from everyone possible, except Elizabeth; and from all of Bingley's connections, Darcy was particularly anxious to conceal it, because of his very hope that those connections might one day become his own. He had certainly formed such a plan; and though he didn't intend it to influence his efforts to separate Bingley from Miss Bennet, it probably added to his concern for his friend's welfare.

Elizabeth's composed behavior, however, quickly calmed his distress; and as Miss Bingley, frustrated and disappointed, didn't dare go any further toward mentioning Wickham, Georgiana also recovered in time, though not enough to speak again. Her brother, whose eye she was afraid to meet, barely remembered her connection to the matter; and the very trick designed to turn his thoughts away from Elizabeth seemed to fix them on her more firmly and more warmly.

Their visit didn't last much longer after this exchange; and while Mr. Darcy walked them to their carriage, Miss Bingley was giving vent to her feelings by criticizing Elizabeth's appearance, behavior, and dress. But Georgiana wouldn't join in. Her brother's praise was enough to ensure her goodwill: his judgment couldn't be wrong, and he had spoken of Elizabeth in terms that left Georgiana unable to see her as anything but lovely and charming. When Darcy returned to the room, Miss Bingley couldn't resist repeating some of what she had said to his sister.

"How terribly unwell Eliza Bennet looks this morning, Mr. Darcy," she cried. "I never saw anyone so changed since last winter. She's become so brown and coarse! Louisa and I were agreeing we wouldn't have recognized her."
However little Mr. Darcy may have liked this, he contented himself with coolly replying that he noticed no change other than a slight tan—an unsurprising result of traveling in summer.

"For my own part," she continued, "I must say I never could see any beauty in her. Her face is too thin; her complexion has no glow; and her features are not at all handsome. Her nose has no character; there's nothing distinctive about it. Her teeth are acceptable but nothing special; and as for her eyes, which have sometimes been called fine, I never could see anything extraordinary about them. They have a sharp, shrewd look that I don't like at all; and in her whole bearing there's a self-assurance without elegance that's intolerable."

Sure as Miss Bingley was that Darcy admired Elizabeth, this was not the best way to recommend herself; but angry people are not always wise, and seeing him at last look somewhat irritated, she got exactly the result she expected. He remained resolutely silent, however; and from a determination to make him speak, she continued—

"I remember when we first met her in Hertfordshire, how amazed we all were to hear she was considered a beauty; and I particularly remember your saying one night, after they'd dined at Netherfield, 'Her a beauty! I might as well call her mother a wit.' But she seemed to grow on you afterward, and I believe at one point you thought her rather pretty."

"Yes," replied Darcy, who could restrain himself no longer, "but that was only when I first knew her. It is many months now since I have considered her one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance."
He then walked away, and Miss Bingley was left with the full satisfaction of having forced him to say something that gave no one any pain but herself.

Mrs. Gardiner and Elizabeth talked of everything that had happened during their visit as they returned—except the one thing that had most interested them both. They discussed the looks and behavior of everyone they had seen, except the person who had most engaged their attention. They talked of his sister, his friends, his house, his fruit—everything but himself; yet Elizabeth was longing to know what Mrs. Gardiner thought of him, and Mrs. Gardiner would have been delighted if her niece had raised the subject.

chapters.title: Chapter 46
paragraphs: Elizabeth had been quite disappointed not to find a letter from Jane when they first arrived at Lambton; and this disappointment had been renewed each morning since. But on the third day her patience was rewarded by the arrival of two letters at once, one of which was marked as having been misdirected. Elizabeth wasn't surprised, since Jane had addressed it remarkably badly.

They had just been getting ready for a walk when the letters came, and her uncle and aunt left her to enjoy them in peace, setting off by themselves. The misdirected one had to be read first; it had been written five days earlier. The beginning contained an account of all their little social events and engagements, along with whatever local news there was; but the second half, dated a day later and written in obvious agitation, brought more important news. It went like this:

"Since writing the above, dearest Lizzy, something has happened of a most unexpected and serious nature; but I'm afraid of alarming you—rest assured that we are all well. What I have to say concerns poor Lydia. An express messenger came at midnight, just as we had all gone to bed, from Colonel Forster, to inform us that she had run off to Scotland with one of his officers; to tell the truth, with Wickham! Imagine our surprise. To Kitty, however, it doesn't seem entirely unexpected. I am very, very sorry. Such an imprudent match on both sides! But I'm willing to hope for the best, and that his character has been misunderstood. I can easily believe him thoughtless and irresponsible, but this step (and let us take comfort from it) suggests nothing truly wicked at heart. His choice is at least disinterested, since he must know my father can give her nothing. Our poor mother is dreadfully upset. My father is handling it better. How grateful I am that we never told them what had been said against him; we must forget it ourselves. They left Saturday night around midnight, as far as anyone can tell, but weren't missed until yesterday morning at eight. The express was sent immediately. My dear Lizzy, they must have passed within ten miles of us. Colonel Forster expects to be here soon. Lydia left a few lines for his wife, telling her what they intended. I must stop, because I can't be away from our poor mother for long. I'm afraid you won't be able to make out what I've written, but I hardly know what I'm saying."

Without pausing to think, and barely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth immediately seized the other letter and opened it with the greatest impatience. It had been written a day later than the end of the first.

"By now, my dearest sister, you've received my hurried letter; I hope this one will be more coherent, but though I'm not rushed for time, my head is so confused that I can't promise to make sense. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to write, but I have bad news that can't be delayed. Imprudent as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we now desperately hope it has taken place, because there's too much reason to fear they haven't gone to Scotland after all. Colonel Forster came yesterday, having left Brighton the day before, just hours after the express. Though Lydia's short note to Mrs. Forster said they were going to Gretna Green, something Denny let slip suggested he believed Wickham never meant to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. This was reported to Colonel Forster, who immediately set out from Brighton to trace their route. He tracked them easily to Clapham, but no farther; for there they switched from their hired carriage to a hackney coach and sent the first one back to Epsom. All that's known after that is they were seen continuing toward London. I don't know what to think. After making every possible inquiry in that part of London, Colonel Forster came on to Hertfordshire, checking at every turnpike and inn along the way, but with no success—nobody matching their description had been seen. With the kindest concern, he came to Longbourn and broke his fears to us in the most tactful way possible. I feel deeply sorry for him and Mrs. Forster, but no one can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I can't think so badly of him. There are many reasons it might have been more practical for them to marry privately in London rather than follow their original plan; and even if he could form such a design against a girl from Lydia's family—which is surely unlikely—can I believe she's so lost to everything? Impossible! I'm sorry to find, however, that Colonel Forster doesn't expect them to have married; he shook his head when I expressed my hopes, and said he feared Wickham was not a man to be trusted. My poor mother is really ill and keeps to her room. Could she exert herself, it would be better, but that's not to be expected; and as for my father, I never in my life saw him so affected. Poor Kitty is furious at having been sworn to secrecy about their attachment, but since it was told in confidence, one can't blame her. I'm truly glad, dearest Lizzy, that you've been spared these awful scenes; but now that the first shock is over, shall I admit that I long for your return? I'm not so selfish as to press for it if it's inconvenient. Goodbye! I pick up my pen again to do what I just said I wouldn't; but the situation is such that I must earnestly beg you all to come here as soon as possible. I know my dear uncle and aunt well enough to ask this without hesitation, though I have something more to request of the former. My father has gone to London with Colonel Forster to try to find her. What he means to do, I have no idea; but his extreme distress won't allow him to take the best or safest course, and Colonel Forster must be back in Brighton by tomorrow evening. In such an emergency, my uncle's advice and help would mean everything in the world; he will immediately understand what I must be feeling, and I rely on his goodness."

"Oh! Where, where is my uncle?" cried Elizabeth, leaping from her seat as she finished the letter, desperate to find him without losing a precious moment; but as she reached the door, it was opened by a servant, and Mr. Darcy appeared. Her pale face and agitated manner made him start, and before he could recover enough to speak, she—whose mind was completely consumed by Lydia's situation—burst out, "I beg your pardon, but I must leave you. I must find Mr. Gardiner this instant on business that can't wait; I haven't a moment to lose."

"Good God! What's the matter?" cried he, with more feeling than formality; then collecting himself, "I won't keep you a minute; but let me, or let the servant, go after Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner. You're not well enough—you can't go yourself."

Elizabeth hesitated, but her knees were trembling and she saw how little would be gained by trying to go after them. Calling back the servant, she sent him—though in such a breathless voice as to be almost unintelligible—to fetch his master and mistress home immediately.

When he left the room, she sat down, unable to support herself, and looking so miserably ill that it was impossible for Darcy to leave her, or to stop himself from saying, in a tone of gentleness and sympathy, "Let me call your maid. Is there nothing you could take for relief? A glass of wine—shall I get you one? You look very ill."
"No, thank you," she replied, trying to pull herself together. "There's nothing wrong with me. I'm perfectly well. I'm only upset by some dreadful news I've just received from Longbourn."
She burst into tears as she spoke, and for several minutes couldn't say another word. Darcy, in miserable suspense, could only murmur something indistinct about his

concern, and watch her in sympathetic silence. At last she spoke again. "I've just had a letter from Jane with such awful news. It can't be kept from anyone. My youngest sister has abandoned all her friends—has eloped—has thrown herself into the power of—of Mr. Wickham. They've run off together from Brighton. You know him too well to doubt the rest. She has no money, no connections, nothing that could tempt him to—she is lost forever."
Darcy was frozen in astonishment.

"When I think," she added in an even more agitated voice, "that I might have prevented it! I, who knew what he was. If I had only explained some part of it—even some part of what I'd learned—to my own family! If his true character had been known, this could never have happened. But it's all, all too late now."
"I'm grieved, truly grieved," cried Darcy. "Grieved—shocked. But is it certain? Absolutely certain?"
"Oh yes! They left Brighton together on Sunday night and were traced almost to London, but not beyond. They've certainly not gone to Scotland."
"And what has been done—what has been tried—to find her?"

"My father has gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's immediate help. We'll be leaving within the half hour, I hope. But nothing can be done—I know perfectly well that nothing can be done. How can such a man be influenced? How can they even be found? I haven't the slightest hope. It's horrible in every way!"
Darcy shook his head in silent agreement.
"When my eyes were opened to his real character—oh! if I had known what I should have done, what I dared to do! But I didn't know—I was afraid of doing too much. What a wretched, wretched mistake!"

Darcy said nothing. He seemed barely to hear her, and was pacing the room in deep thought, his brow furrowed, his expression grim. Elizabeth soon noticed and instantly understood. Her influence was fading; everything must collapse under such proof of family weakness, such a guarantee of the deepest disgrace. She could neither wonder at it nor blame him; but the belief that he was giving her up brought no comfort—instead, it was precisely what made her understand her own feelings. Never had she so honestly felt that she could have loved him, as now, when all love must be in vain.

But self-pity, though it intruded, couldn't dominate. Lydia—the humiliation, the misery she was bringing on them all—soon swallowed up every private concern; and covering her face with her handkerchief, Elizabeth was soon lost to everything else. After a pause of several minutes, she was recalled to her situation only by the voice of her companion, who, in a manner that conveyed both sympathy and restraint, said—

"I'm afraid you've been wanting me to leave for some time, and I have nothing to offer as an excuse for staying except genuine, though useless, concern. Would to God that anything could be said or done on my part to offer comfort in such distress! But I won't torment you with hollow wishes that might seem like an attempt to fish for your thanks. This unfortunate affair will, I fear, prevent my sister from having the pleasure of seeing you at Pemberley today."
"Oh yes! Please apologize for us to Miss Darcy. Say that urgent business calls us home immediately. Keep the unhappy truth hidden as long as possible. I know it can't be hidden for long."

He assured her of his secrecy, expressed his sorrow for her distress once more, wished for a happier outcome than there was presently reason to hope for, and—with only one serious, lingering look—left the room.

As he went, Elizabeth felt how unlikely it was that they would ever see each other again on such friendly terms as had marked their several meetings in Derbyshire; and as she cast a look back over the whole of their acquaintance—so full of contradictions and reversals—she sighed at the perversity of feelings that now wished to continue what she had formerly been glad to see ending.

If gratitude and esteem are good foundations for affection, then Elizabeth's change of heart will seem neither unlikely nor wrong. But if otherwise—if love that springs from such sources is unreasonable or unnatural compared to what is so often described as arising at first sight, before two words have even been exchanged—then nothing can be said in her defense, except that she had given the latter method something of a trial in her partiality for Wickham, and that its failure might reasonably lead her to try the less dramatic approach. Be that as it may, she watched him go with regret; and in this early demonstration of what Lydia's scandal must produce, she found additional anguish. Not for a moment since reading Jane's second letter had she entertained any hope that Wickham meant to marry Lydia. No one but Jane, she thought, could flatter herself with such an expectation. Surprise was the least of her feelings. While the first letter's contents were still on her mind, she had been all surprise and disbelief that Wickham would marry a girl with no money. How Lydia could have attracted him had seemed incomprehensible. But now it all made too much sense. For the kind of attraction this was, she might have been appealing enough; and though Elizabeth didn't imagine Lydia had deliberately planned an elopement without intending marriage, she had no trouble believing that neither her virtue nor her judgment would protect her from becoming an easy target.

She had never noticed, while the regiment was in Hertfordshire, that Lydia had any particular interest in Wickham; but she was sure Lydia had needed only the slightest encouragement to attach herself to anyone. Sometimes one officer, sometimes another had been her favorite, as their attentions raised them in her esteem. Her affections had constantly shifted, but never without an object. The damage caused by neglect and misguided indulgence toward such a girl—oh, how painfully she felt it now!

She was wild to be home—to hear, to see, to be there to share with Jane the burdens that must now fall entirely on her, in a family so disrupted: a father gone, a mother unable to function and requiring constant care. And though she was almost certain nothing could be done for Lydia, her uncle's involvement seemed absolutely essential. Until he entered the room, the agony of waiting was severe. Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner had hurried back in alarm, assuming from the servant's account that their niece had been taken suddenly ill; but Elizabeth quickly reassured them and eagerly explained why she had sent for them, reading both letters aloud and dwelling on the postscript of the second with trembling energy. Though Lydia had never been a favorite with them, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner couldn't help being deeply affected. Not just Lydia but the whole family was involved; and after the first exclamations of surprise and horror, Mr. Gardiner readily promised every assistance in his power. Elizabeth, though expecting nothing less, thanked him through tears of gratitude; and all three, driven by the same urgency, quickly settled everything about their journey. They would leave as soon as possible. "But what about Pemberley?" cried Mrs. Gardiner. "John told us Mr. Darcy was here when you sent for us—was that true?"
"Yes; and I told him we couldn't keep our engagement. That's all taken care of."
"What's all taken care of?" repeated her aunt as she ran to her room to pack. "And are they on such terms that she could tell him the real truth? Oh, if only I knew how things stood!"

But wishes were pointless—or at best could only distract her during the frantic hour that followed. Had Elizabeth been free to be idle, she would have been certain that all activity was impossible for someone as wretched as herself; but she had her share of tasks, and among them were notes to be written to all their friends in Lambton, with invented excuses for their sudden departure. An hour, however, saw everything done; and Mr. Gardiner, having settled the account at the inn, there was nothing left but to go. Elizabeth, after all the morning's misery, found herself in less time than she would have thought possible seated in the carriage and on the road to Longbourn.

chapters.title: Chapter 47
paragraphs: "I've been thinking it over again, Elizabeth," said her uncle as they drove from the town, "and on serious reflection, I'm much more inclined than I was to agree with your eldest sister. It seems so very unlikely that any young man would deliberately target a girl who is by no means friendless or unprotected, and who was actually staying with his Colonel's family, that I'm strongly inclined to hope for the best. Could he expect her friends wouldn't step in? Could he expect to be tolerated by the regiment after such an insult to Colonel Forster? The reward isn't worth the risk."
"Do you really think so?" cried Elizabeth, brightening for a moment.

"I do, indeed," said Mrs. Gardiner. "I'm coming around to your uncle's view. It would be too great a violation of decency, honor, and self-interest for him to be guilty of it. I can't think so badly of Wickham. Can you, Lizzy? Can you really give up on him entirely and believe him capable of it?"

"Not perhaps of ignoring his own interests. But of every other kind of neglect I can believe him capable. If only it were true! But I don't dare hope. Why wouldn't they have gone on to Scotland if that were the case?"
"In the first place," replied Mr. Gardiner, "there's no absolute proof they haven't gone to Scotland."
"Oh, but their switching from a hired carriage to a hackney coach is such strong evidence against it! And besides, no trace of them was found on the road to Barnet."

"Well then—suppose they're in London. They may be there for privacy, not for anything worse. Neither of them is likely to have much money, and it might have occurred to them that they could be married more cheaply, if less quickly, in London than in Scotland."

"But why all this secrecy? Why any fear of being found? Why must their marriage be private? Oh, no—this isn't likely. His closest friend, as Jane's letter says, was convinced he never intended to marry her. Wickham will never marry a woman without money. He can't afford it. And what does Lydia have to offer beyond youth, health, and high spirits that could make him sacrifice every chance of bettering himself through a good marriage? As for whatever restraint the threat of disgrace in the regiment might put on a dishonorable elopement, I'm not in a position to judge, since I know nothing about the military consequences. But as for your other argument, I'm afraid it won't hold. Lydia has no brothers to defend her honor, and from my father's behavior—from his laziness and the little attention he's ever seemed to pay to what was happening in his family—Wickham might well have calculated that he would do as little and think as little about it as any father could."
"But can you believe Lydia is so lost to everything but her feelings for him that she'd agree to live with him on any terms other than marriage?"

"It does seem—and it's truly shocking," replied Elizabeth, with tears in her eyes, "that a sister's sense of decency and virtue should even be in question. But honestly, I don't know what to say. Perhaps I'm being unfair to her. But she's very young; she's never been taught to think about serious things; and for the last year or more, she's been given over to nothing but amusement and vanity. She's been allowed to spend her time in the most idle and frivolous way, and to adopt whatever opinions crossed her path. Since the ——shire first arrived in Meryton, nothing but love, flirtation, and officers have been in her head. She has been doing everything in her power, by thinking and talking about it constantly, to make her feelings even more—what shall I call it?—susceptible than they naturally are. And we all know that Wickham has every charm of appearance and manner that can captivate a woman."
"But you see that Jane," said her aunt, "doesn't think so badly of Wickham as to believe him capable of this."

"When does Jane ever think badly of anyone? And who is there, regardless of their past behavior, that she'd believe capable of such a thing until it was proven? But Jane knows, as well as I do, what Wickham really is. We both know he's been dishonest in every sense of the word; that he has neither integrity nor honor; that he is as false and deceitful as he is charming."
"And do you really know all this?" cried Mrs. Gardiner, whose curiosity about the source of this knowledge was thoroughly aroused.

"I do, indeed," replied Elizabeth, coloring. "I told you the other day about his outrageous behavior toward Mr. Darcy; and you yourself, when you were last at Longbourn, heard how he spoke of the man who had shown him such patience and generosity. And there are other circumstances I'm not free to share—which aren't worth going into—but his lies about the entire Pemberley family are endless. From what he told me about Miss Darcy, I was fully prepared to meet a proud, cold, unpleasant girl. Yet he knew the opposite was true. He must have known she was as sweet and unassuming as we found her to be."
"But does Lydia know none of this? Can she be ignorant of what you and Jane seem to understand so well?"

"Oh yes!—that's the worst of it. Until I went to Kent and saw so much of both Mr. Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam, I didn't know the truth myself. And when I got home, the ——shire was leaving Meryton in a week or two. Since that was the case, neither Jane—to whom I'd told everything—nor I thought it necessary to make our knowledge public; for what good would it apparently do anyone to destroy the favorable opinion the whole neighborhood had of him? And even when it was decided that Lydia should go with Mrs. Forster, it never occurred to me that she needed to be warned about his character. It never entered my head that she could be in any danger from his deception. That something like this would result, you can easily believe, was the farthest thing from my mind."
"So when they all went to Brighton, you had no reason to believe they were fond of each other?"

"Not the slightest. I can't recall any sign of attraction on either side; and had there been any, you must know that ours is not a family where such things go unnoticed. When he first joined the regiment, she was ready enough to admire him; but so were we all. Every girl in or near Meryton was wild about him for the first two months; but he never singled her out for any special attention, and so, after a reasonable period of excessive and wild admiration, her infatuation faded, and others in the regiment who treated her with more attention became her new favorites."

It's easy to imagine that however little new could be added to their fears, hopes, and speculations on this absorbing subject by going over it again and again, no other topic could hold their attention for long during the entire journey. Elizabeth's thoughts never strayed from it. Fixed there by the sharpest of all pain—self-reproach—she could find no moment of relief or forgetfulness.

They traveled as fast as possible; and after spending one night on the road, they reached Longbourn by dinnertime the next day. It was a comfort to Elizabeth to think that Jane hadn't been left waiting in anxious suspense.

The little Gardiners, attracted by the sight of the carriage, were standing on the steps of the house as they entered the grounds; and when the carriage pulled up to the door, the delighted surprise that lit up their faces and animated their whole bodies in a burst of jumping and dancing was the first pleasant sign of welcome.
Elizabeth jumped out and, after giving each of them a quick kiss, hurried into the entrance hall, where Jane, who had come running downstairs from their mother's room, immediately met her.
Elizabeth, embracing her affectionately while tears filled both their eyes, didn't waste a moment before asking whether anything had been heard of the runaways.
"Not yet," replied Jane. "But now that my dear uncle is here, I hope everything will be all right."
"Is my father in London?"
"Yes, he left on Tuesday, as I wrote you."
"And have you heard from him often?"

"Only once. He wrote me a few lines on Wednesday to say he had arrived safely and to give me his address, which I'd specifically asked him to do. He just added that he wouldn't write again until he had something important to report."
"And our mother—how is she? How are you all?"

"Mother is fairly well, I think, though her nerves are badly shaken. She's upstairs and will be very glad to see you all. She still hasn't left her dressing room. Mary and Kitty, thank heaven, are perfectly well."
"But you—how are you?" cried Elizabeth. "You look pale. How much you must have been through!"

Her sister, however, assured her she was perfectly well; and their conversation, which had been going on while Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner were occupied with their children, was now ended by the approach of the whole group. Jane ran to her uncle and aunt, welcoming and thanking them both with alternating smiles and tears.

When they were all in the drawing room, the questions Elizabeth had already asked were naturally repeated by the others, and they soon learned that Jane had no news to share. Her hopeful nature, however, had not yet deserted her; she still expected everything to end well, and that every morning would bring a letter—from Lydia or from their father—explaining what had happened and perhaps announcing the marriage.

Mrs. Bennet, whose room they all went to after a few minutes' conversation, received them exactly as expected: with tears and laments, attacks on Wickham's villainous behavior, and complaints about her own suffering and mistreatment—blaming everyone but the person whose irresponsible indulgence was mostly responsible for her daughter's mistakes.

"If I had been able," she said, "to get my way about going to Brighton with the whole family, this wouldn't have happened. But poor dear Lydia had nobody to look after her. Why did the Forsters ever let her out of their sight? I'm sure there was some terrible neglect on their part, because she's not the kind of girl to do such a thing if she'd been properly supervised. I always thought they were completely unfit to have charge of her; but I was overruled, as I always am. Poor dear child!
