And now Mr. Bennet has gone away, and I know he'll fight Wickham wherever he finds him, and then he'll be killed, and what's to become of us all? The Collinses will throw us out before he's cold in his grave; and if you're not kind to us, brother, I don't know what we shall do."

They all protested against such terrifying ideas; and Mr. Gardiner, after general assurances of his affection for her and all her family, told her he meant to be in London the very next day and would help Mr. Bennet in every effort to find Lydia.

"Don't give in to useless panic," he added. "Though it's right to be prepared for the worst, there's no reason to assume it. It's not quite a week since they left Brighton. In a few days we may have news of them; and until we know they're not married and have no intention of marrying, let's not give up hope. As soon as I get to London, I'll go to my brother-in-law and bring him home with me to Gracechurch Street, and then we can decide what to do."

"Oh, my dear brother," replied Mrs. Bennet, "that's exactly what I most wish for! And now, when you get to London, find them, wherever they are; and if they're not married already, make them marry. And as for wedding clothes, don't let them wait for that—tell Lydia she can have as much money as she likes to buy them after they're married. And above all, keep Mr. Bennet from fighting. Tell him what a dreadful state I'm in—that I'm frightened out of my mind, and have such trembling and fluttering all over me, such pains in my side and my head, and such pounding in my heart that I can get no rest day or night. And tell my dear Lydia not to order any clothes until she's seen me, because she doesn't know which are the best shops. Oh, brother, how kind you are! I know you'll manage everything."

But Mr. Gardiner, though he promised again to do his utmost, couldn't help advising her to be moderate, in her hopes as well as her fears; and after talking with her this way until dinner, they left her to pour out all her feelings on the housekeeper, who was attending her in place of her daughters.

Though her brother and sister-in-law were convinced there was no real need for such seclusion from the family, they didn't try to oppose it, knowing she couldn't be trusted to hold her tongue in front of the servants during meals, and judging it better that only one member of the household—and the one they could most trust—should hear all her fears and anxieties.

In the dining room they were soon joined by Mary and Kitty, who had been too busy in their own rooms to appear earlier. One came from her books, the other from her dressing table. The faces of both were fairly calm, and no change was visible in either, except that the loss of her favorite sister—or the anger she had brought on herself—had given Kitty's voice an even more irritable edge than usual. As for Mary, she was composed enough to whisper to Elizabeth, with an expression of solemn reflection, soon after they sat down—
"This is a most unfortunate affair, and will probably be much talked about. But we must resist the tide of gossip, and pour into each other's wounded hearts the balm of sisterly comfort."

Then, seeing that Elizabeth had no inclination to reply, she added, "Unhappy as this event must be for Lydia, we may draw from it a useful lesson: that the loss of virtue in a woman is irreversible, that one false step plunges her into endless ruin, that her reputation is as fragile as it is beautiful, and that she cannot be too careful in her behavior toward unworthy men."
Elizabeth looked up in amazement, but was too weighed down to make any reply. Mary, however, continued to console herself with such moral observations drawn from the trouble before them.

In the afternoon, the two elder Miss Bennets were able to be alone for half an hour; and Elizabeth immediately took the opportunity to make the inquiries that Jane was equally eager to answer. After joining in general laments over the terrible outcome of the affair—which Elizabeth considered all but certain, and which Jane couldn't declare entirely impossible—Elizabeth pressed for more details. "But tell me everything I don't already know. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they had no suspicion of anything before the elopement? They must have seen them together constantly."

"Colonel Forster did admit he had often suspected some attraction, especially on Lydia's side, but nothing to alarm him. I feel so sorry for him. His behavior was attentive and kind to the utmost. He was already on his way to us to express his concern before he had any idea they hadn't gone to Scotland; when that fear first arose, it only made him travel faster."
"And was Denny convinced Wickham wouldn't marry her? Did he know about their plan to run off? Had Colonel Forster spoken to Denny himself?"

"Yes; but when questioned, Denny denied knowing anything about their plan and wouldn't give his real opinion about it. He didn't repeat his belief that they wouldn't marry, and from that I'm inclined to hope he was misunderstood before."
"And until Colonel Forster came himself, none of you had any doubt they were really married?"

"How could such an idea have entered our minds? I felt a little uneasy—a little worried about my sister's happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his behavior hadn't always been quite right. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only saw how imprudent such a match would be. Kitty then admitted, with obvious triumph at knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia's last letter she had been prepared for something like this. She had known, it turns out, about their being in love for weeks."
"But not before they went to Brighton?"
"No, I don't think so."
"And did Colonel Forster seem to think badly of Wickham himself? Does he know his real character?"

"I must admit he didn't speak as well of Wickham as he used to. He believed him to be careless and extravagant; and since this sad affair has come to light, it's said he left Meryton heavily in debt. But I hope that may be false."
"Oh Jane, if we'd been less secretive—if we'd told what we knew about him—this couldn't have happened!"
"Perhaps it would have been better," replied her sister.
"But to expose someone's past faults without knowing what their present feelings were seemed wrong."
"We acted with the best intentions."
"Could Colonel Forster repeat the details of Lydia's note to his wife?"
"He brought it with him for us to see."
Jane then took it from her pocket-book and gave it to Elizabeth. These were the contents:
"My dear Harriet,

"You will laugh when you know where I've gone, and I can't help laughing myself at the surprise you'll get tomorrow morning when you find me missing. I'm going to Gretna Green, and if you can't guess with whom, I'll think you a simpleton, because there's only one man in the world I love, and he's an angel. I'd never be happy without him, so don't think it wrong of me to go. You needn't send word to Longbourn of my leaving if you'd rather not, since it'll make the surprise even better when I write to them and sign my name Lydia Wickham. What a good joke it will be! I can hardly write for laughing. Please make my excuses to Pratt for not keeping my engagement to dance with him tonight. Tell him I hope he'll forgive me when he knows all, and tell him I'll dance with him with great pleasure at the next ball we attend. I'll send for my clothes when I get to Longbourn; but I wish you'd tell Sally to mend a big tear in my embroidered muslin dress before they're packed up. Goodbye. Give my love to Colonel Forster. I hope you'll drink to our safe journey.
"Your affectionate friend,
"LYDIA BENNET."

"Oh, thoughtless, thoughtless Lydia!" cried Elizabeth when she had finished. "What a letter to write at such a moment! But at least it shows that she was serious about what she intended. Whatever he might have persuaded her to afterward, it was not a deliberate plan of dishonor on her part. My poor father! How he must have felt it!"
"I never saw anyone so shattered. He couldn't speak a word for a full ten minutes. Mother was taken ill immediately, and the whole house was in confusion!"
"Oh Jane," cried Elizabeth, "was there a servant in the house who didn't know the whole story before the day was out?"

"I don't know; I hope not. But it's very hard to be careful at such a time. Mother was in hysterics, and though I did everything I could for her, I'm afraid I didn't do as much as I should have. The horror of what might be happening nearly overwhelmed me."
"The strain of looking after her has been too much for you. You don't look well. Oh, if only I'd been here! You've had every worry and responsibility to yourself."

"Mary and Kitty have been very kind and would have shared every burden, I'm sure, but I didn't think it right for either of them. Kitty is slight and delicate, and Mary studies so much that her rest shouldn't be disturbed. My aunt Philips came to Longbourn on Tuesday, after my father left, and was kind enough to stay until Thursday. She was a great help and comfort to us all. And Lady Lucas has been very kind too; she walked over on Wednesday morning to offer sympathy and said we could call on her or any of her daughters if they could be of use."

"She would have been better off staying home," cried Elizabeth. "Perhaps she meant well, but in a misfortune like this, the less one sees of one's neighbors the better. Help is impossible; sympathy is unbearable. Let them gloat from a distance and be satisfied."
She then asked about the steps their father had planned to take in London to find his daughter.

"He meant, I believe," replied Jane, "to go to Epsom, the last place where they changed horses, and try to get information from the drivers. His main goal was to find out the number of the hackney coach they took from Clapham. It had come from London with a fare, and since he thought a gentleman and lady transferring between carriages might have been noticed, he planned to make inquiries at Clapham. If he could somehow discover which house the coachman had previously dropped off his fare at, he intended to investigate there, hoping he might find the stand and number of the coach. I don't know what other plans he had; but he was in such a hurry to leave, and so distressed, that I had difficulty learning even this much."

chapters.title: Chapter 48
paragraphs: The whole household hoped for a letter from Mr. Bennet the next morning, but the post came without a single line from him. His family knew he was, in ordinary circumstances, a most neglectful and slow correspondent; but at such a time they had hoped for effort. They were forced to conclude he had no good news to send; but even knowing that for certain would have been something. Mr. Gardiner had waited only for the post before setting off.

When he was gone, they were at least sure of receiving regular updates on what was happening; and their uncle promised, as he left, to persuade Mr. Bennet to return to Longbourn as soon as possible—to the great comfort of his sister, who saw this as the only way to keep her husband from being killed in a duel.

Mrs. Gardiner and the children were to remain in Hertfordshire a few days longer, as she thought her presence might be useful to her nieces. She helped look after Mrs. Bennet and was a great comfort to them in their free hours. Their other aunt also visited frequently, always claiming her purpose was to cheer them up—though since she never came without reporting some fresh instance of Wickham's extravagance or misbehavior, she rarely left without making them more depressed than she'd found them.

All of Meryton seemed determined to blacken the man who, only three months before, had been almost an angel of light. He was declared to be in debt to every shopkeeper in the place, and his romantic exploits—all now dignified with the word "seduction"—were said to have extended into every tradesman's family. Everyone declared he was the worst young man in the world; and everyone suddenly realized they had always mistrusted his apparent goodness. Elizabeth, though she didn't believe half of what was said, believed enough to confirm her certainty of her sister's ruin; and even Jane, who believed still less, had nearly given up hope—especially since the time had now come when, if they had gone to Scotland (which she had never entirely ruled out), they should have heard some news.

Mr. Gardiner left Longbourn on Sunday; on Tuesday his wife received a letter. He reported that on arriving he had immediately found Mr. Bennet and persuaded him to come to Gracechurch Street; that Mr. Bennet had already been to Epsom and Clapham without finding anything useful; and that he was now determined to check all the major hotels in London, thinking it possible they might have gone to one on first arriving before finding lodgings. Mr. Gardiner himself didn't expect this to succeed, but since his brother-in-law was keen on it, he intended to help. He added that Mr. Bennet seemed completely unwilling to leave London for the time being, and promised to write again soon. There was also a postscript:

"I've written to Colonel Forster asking him to find out, if possible, from some of the young man's associates in the regiment whether Wickham has any relatives or connections who might know which part of London he's hiding in. If there were someone we could ask, with a reasonable chance of getting such a lead, it could be crucial. At present we have nothing to guide us. Colonel Forster will, I'm sure, do everything he can to help us on this point. But on second thought, perhaps Lizzy could tell us what living relatives he has better than anyone else."
Elizabeth understood perfectly where this confidence in her knowledge came from, but she was unfortunately unable to provide the kind of information the compliment deserved.

She had never heard of his having any relatives except a father and mother, both of whom had been dead for many years. It was possible, however, that some of his former companions in the ——shire might have more information; and though she wasn't very hopeful, the inquiry was at least something to look forward to.

Every day at Longbourn was now a day of anxiety; but the most anxious part was when the post was expected. The arrival of letters was the first great hope of every morning. Through letters, whatever good or bad news there was would be delivered; and each new day was expected to bring something important.

But before they heard again from Mr. Gardiner, a letter arrived for their father from a different quarter: from Mr. Collins. Since Jane had been instructed to open all mail that came for him in his absence, she read it accordingly; and Elizabeth, who knew what curiosities his letters always were, read it over her shoulder. It went as follows:
"My dear Sir,

"I feel it my duty, given our family connection and my position in life, to offer condolences on the terrible affliction you are now suffering, of which we were informed yesterday by a letter from Hertfordshire. Please be assured, my dear sir, that Mrs. Collins and I sincerely sympathize with you and all your respectable family in your present distress, which must be of the most bitter kind, since it arises from a cause that no amount of time can remedy. No argument shall be lacking on my part that might lessen so severe a misfortune, or that might comfort you in a circumstance that must be, above all others, most painful to a parent's heart. The death of your daughter would have been a blessing in comparison. And it is all the more to be lamented because there is reason to believe, as my dear Charlotte informs me, that this moral

depravity in your daughter has resulted from an excessive degree of indulgence; though, at the same time, for the comfort of yourself and Mrs. Bennet, I am inclined to think her own nature must be fundamentally bad, or she could not have been guilty of such an outrage at so young an age. However that may be, you are deeply to be pitied; an opinion shared not only by Mrs. Collins but also by Lady Catherine and her daughter, to whom I have related the matter. They agree with me that this disgraceful step by one daughter will damage the prospects of all the others; for who, as Lady Catherine herself graciously observes, would want to be connected with such a family? And this consideration leads me to reflect, with heightened satisfaction, on a certain event of last November; for had things gone otherwise, I would have been caught up in all your sorrow and disgrace. Let me advise you, then, my dear sir, to console yourself as much as possible, to cast off your unworthy child from your affection forever, and leave her to suffer the consequences of her own terrible sin.
"I am, dear sir," etc., etc.

Mr. Gardiner didn't write again until he had received a reply from Colonel Forster; and then he had nothing pleasant to report. It wasn't known that Wickham had a single relative with whom he was still in contact, and it was certain he had no close family living. His former acquaintances had been numerous, but since joining the militia he didn't appear to have been on close terms with any of them. There was no one, therefore, who could be expected to have news of him. And in the wretched state of his finances, there was a very strong motive for secrecy, in addition to his fear of being found by Lydia's family; for it had just come out that he had left gambling debts behind him to a very considerable amount. Colonel Forster believed that more than a thousand pounds would be needed to settle his expenses at Brighton. He owed a great deal in the town, but his gambling debts were even more alarming. Mr. Gardiner didn't try to hide these details from the Longbourn family. Jane heard them with horror. "A gambler!" she cried. "This is completely unexpected; I had no idea."

Mr. Gardiner added, in his letter, that they could expect to see their father home the following day, Saturday. Made spiritless by the failure of all their efforts, he had given in to his brother-in-law's urging that he return to his family and leave it to Mr. Gardiner to do whatever seemed advisable. When Mrs. Bennet was told of this, she didn't express as much satisfaction as her children expected, considering how anxious she had been about his safety.
"What! He's coming home without poor Lydia?" she cried. "Surely he won't leave London before he's found them. Who is to fight Wickham and make him marry her, if he comes away?"

Since Mrs. Gardiner wanted to get home, it was arranged that she and her children would leave for London at the same time Mr. Bennet returned. The carriage therefore took them for the first leg of their journey and brought its master back to Longbourn.

Mrs. Gardiner departed still entirely puzzled about Elizabeth and her Derbyshire friend. His name had never been voluntarily mentioned by her niece, and the vague expectation Mrs. Gardiner had formed—of a letter from him following them home—had come to nothing. Elizabeth had received no correspondence since her return that could have come from Pemberley.

The family's present unhappy state made any other explanation for her low spirits unnecessary; nothing, therefore, could be accurately guessed on that subject. Though Elizabeth—who was by now fairly well acquainted with her own feelings—was perfectly aware that, had she known nothing of Darcy, she could have borne the dread of Lydia's disgrace somewhat better. It would have spared her, she thought, one sleepless night out of two.

When Mr. Bennet arrived, he had all the appearance of his usual detached calm. He said as little as ever; made no mention of the business that had taken him away; and it was some time before his daughters had the courage to raise the subject.

It wasn't until the afternoon, when he joined them at tea, that Elizabeth ventured to bring it up; and when she briefly expressed her sorrow for what he must have endured, he replied, "Say nothing of that. Who should suffer but me? It's been my own doing, and I deserve to feel it."
"You mustn't be too hard on yourself," replied Elizabeth.

"You're right to warn me against that tendency. Human nature is so prone to it! No, Lizzy, let me for once in my life feel how much I've been to blame. I'm not afraid of being overwhelmed by the feeling. It'll pass soon enough."
"Do you think they're in London?"
"Yes; where else could they hide so well?"
"And Lydia always did want to go to London," added Kitty.
"She's happy, then," said her father drily, "and her stay there will probably be lengthy."

Then, after a short silence, he continued, "Lizzy, I bear you no grudge for being proven right in the advice you gave me last May, which—considering how things turned out—shows a certain greatness of character."
They were interrupted by Jane, who came to fetch their mother's tea.

"This is quite a production," he said. "It gives such elegance to misfortune! Another day I'll do the same: I'll sit in my library in my nightcap and dressing gown, and cause as much trouble as I can—or perhaps I'll wait until Kitty runs away."
"I'm not going to run away, Papa," said Kitty, hurt. "If I ever went to Brighton, I would behave better than Lydia."

"You go to Brighton! I wouldn't trust you within fifty miles of it! No, Kitty, I have at least learned to be cautious, and you will feel the effects of it. No officer is ever to enter my house again, or even pass through the village. Balls will be absolutely forbidden unless you dance with one of your sisters. And you're never to set foot outside the door until you can prove you've spent ten minutes of every day doing something sensible."
Kitty, who took all these threats seriously, began to cry.
"Well, well," he said, "don't make yourself miserable. If you're a good girl for the next ten years, I'll take you to a military review at the end of them."

chapters.title: Chapter 49
paragraphs: Two days after Mr. Bennet's return, as Jane and Elizabeth were walking together in the garden behind the house, they saw the housekeeper coming toward them. Assuming she was coming to call them to their mother, they went to meet her; but instead of the expected summons, she said to Miss Bennet, "I beg your pardon, ma'am, for interrupting you, but I was hoping you might have received some good news from London, so I took the liberty of coming to ask."
"What do you mean, Hill? We've heard nothing from London."
"Dear ma'am," cried Mrs. Hill in great astonishment, "don't you know there's an express messenger come for master from Mr. Gardiner? He's been here this half hour, and master has had a letter."

The girls ran off, too excited to speak. They ran through the hall into the breakfast room; from there to the library—their father was in neither; and they were about to look for him upstairs when they were met by the butler, who said—
"If you're looking for my master, ma'am, he's walking toward the little copse."
On hearing this, they instantly dashed through the hall again and ran across the lawn after their father, who was deliberately making his way toward a small wood on the edge of the grounds.
Jane, who was not as light on her feet or as used to running as Elizabeth, soon fell behind, while her sister, gasping for breath, caught up with him and eagerly cried out—
"Oh, Papa, what news? What news? Have you heard from my uncle?"
"Yes, I've had a letter from him by express."
"Well, and what news does it bring—good or bad?"
"What good is there to expect?" he said, taking the letter from his pocket. "But perhaps you'd like to read it."
Elizabeth impatiently snatched it from his hand. Jane now caught up.
"Read it aloud," said their father, "because I hardly know myself what it's about."
"Gracechurch Street, Monday, August 2.
"My dear Brother,

"At last I am able to send you some news of my niece, and such as, on the whole, I hope will give you satisfaction. Soon after you left me on Saturday, I was fortunate enough to discover what part of London they were in. The details I'll save until we meet. It's enough to know they've been found: I have seen them both—"
"Then it's as I always hoped," cried Jane. "They are married!"

Elizabeth read on: "I have seen them both. They are not married, nor can I find there was ever any intention of it; but if you are willing to honor the commitments I have ventured to make on your behalf, I hope it will not be long before they are. All that is required of you is to guarantee your daughter, by legal settlement, her equal share of the five thousand pounds secured among your children after the death of yourself and my sister; and moreover, to commit to allowing her, during your lifetime, one hundred pounds per year. These are conditions which, considering everything, I had no hesitation in agreeing to, as far as I felt authorized. I shall send this by express so that no time is lost in getting your reply. You will easily understand from these details that Mr. Wickham's financial situation is not so hopeless as generally believed. The world has been deceived on that point; and I am happy to say there will be some money remaining, even after all his debts are cleared, to settle on my niece in addition to her own share. If, as I expect, you send me full authority to act on your behalf throughout this matter, I will immediately instruct Haggerston to prepare a proper settlement. There will be no need whatever for you to come to London again; so stay quietly at Longbourn and trust in my diligence and care. Send your reply as soon as you can, and make sure to write clearly. We have judged it best that my niece be married from this house, which I hope you will approve. She comes to us today. I shall write again as soon as anything more is settled. Yours, etc.
"EDW. GARDINER."
"Is it possible?" cried Elizabeth when she had finished. "Can it really be that he'll marry her?"
"Wickham is not so undeserving as we thought him, then," said her sister. "My dear father, congratulations!"
"And have you answered the letter?" said Elizabeth.
"No; but it must be done soon."
She then earnestly begged him to waste no more time before writing.
"Oh, my dear father," she cried, "come back and write immediately. Think how important every moment is in a case like this!"
"Let me write for you," said Jane, "if you'd rather not do it yourself."
"I would rather not," he replied, "but it must be done."
And turning back with them, he walked toward the house.
"And—may I ask?" said Elizabeth. "But the terms, I suppose, must be accepted."
"Accepted! I'm only ashamed he asked so little."
"And they must marry! Yet he is such a man."

"Yes, yes, they must marry. There's nothing else to be done. But there are two things I very much want to know: first, how much money your uncle has put up to make this happen; and second, how I'm ever to repay him."
"Money! My uncle!" cried Jane. "What do you mean, sir?"
"I mean that no man in his right mind would marry Lydia on as small an incentive as a hundred pounds a year during my life, and fifty after I'm gone."

"That's very true," said Elizabeth, "though it hadn't occurred to me before. His debts to be paid, and still something left over! Oh, it must be my uncle's doing! Generous, good man—I'm afraid he's strained his own finances. A small sum couldn't have done all this."
"No," said her father. "Wickham's a fool if he takes her for a penny less than ten thousand pounds. I'd be sorry to think so badly of him this early in our family relationship."
"Ten thousand pounds! Heaven forbid! How is even half that sum to be repaid?"

Mr. Bennet made no answer, and each of them, deep in thought, walked in silence until they reached the house. Their father then went to the library to write, and the girls went into the breakfast room.

"And they really are to be married!" cried Elizabeth as soon as they were alone. "How strange this is! And for this we're supposed to be thankful. That they should marry, slim as their chances of happiness are and wretched as his character is, we're forced to rejoice! Oh, Lydia!"

"I comfort myself with thinking," replied Jane, "that he certainly wouldn't marry Lydia if he didn't have real feelings for her. Though our kind uncle has clearly done something to help, I can't believe ten thousand pounds or anything like it has been put up. He has children of his own and may have more. How could he spare half that amount?"

"If we ever find out how much Wickham's debts were," said Elizabeth, "and how much has been settled on our sister, we'll know exactly what Mr. Gardiner has done for them—because Wickham hasn't a penny of his own. The kindness of my uncle and aunt can never be repaid. Taking her into their home and giving her their personal protection and respectability is such a sacrifice for her benefit that years of gratitude won't be enough. By now she's actually with them! If such goodness doesn't make her ashamed now, she'll never deserve to be happy! What a moment for her, when she first sees my aunt!"

"We must try to forget everything that's happened on either side," said Jane. "I hope and trust they will be happy. His agreeing to marry her is proof, I want to believe, that he's come to see things differently. Their love for each other will give them stability; and I flatter myself they will settle down quietly and live so sensibly that in time their past recklessness will be forgotten."
"Their behavior has been such," replied Elizabeth, "that neither you, nor I, nor anyone, can ever forget it. It's useless to talk about it."

It now occurred to the girls that their mother was very likely completely unaware of what had happened. They went to the library, therefore, and asked their father whether he wanted them to tell her. He was writing and, without raising his head, coolly replied—
"Whatever you like."
"May we take my uncle's letter to read to her?"
"Take whatever you want, and go away."

Elizabeth took the letter from his writing desk, and they went upstairs together. Mary and Kitty were both with Mrs. Bennet, so one announcement would do for all. After a brief preparation for good news, the letter was read aloud. Mrs. Bennet could hardly contain herself. As soon as Jane read Mr. Gardiner's hope that Lydia would soon be married, her joy burst out, and every following sentence added to her excitement. She was now in a state of agitation as extreme from delight as she had ever been from anxiety and distress. To know her daughter would be married was enough. She wasn't troubled by any concern for Lydia's future happiness or any shame over her misconduct.

"My dear, dear Lydia!" she cried. "This is wonderful! She will be married! I shall see her again! She will be married at sixteen! My good, kind brother! I knew how it would be—I always said he would manage everything. How I long to see her! And dear Wickham too! But the clothes, the wedding clothes! I must write to my sister Gardiner about them right away. Lizzy, dear, run down to your father and ask how much he'll give her. Wait—I'll go myself. Ring the bell, Kitty, for Hill. I'll get dressed in a moment. My dear, dear Lydia! How merry we'll be when we're together!"
Her eldest daughter tried to calm the violence of these outbursts by turning her thoughts to the debt they all owed Mr. Gardiner.
"For we must credit this happy outcome," she added, "in large part to his kindness. We believe he has pledged his own money to help Mr. Wickham."

"Well," cried her mother, "that's quite right; who should do it but her own uncle? If he hadn't had a family of his own, my children and I would have had all his money, you know; and this is the first time we've ever gotten anything from him besides a few presents. Well! I am so happy! Soon I'll have a married daughter. Mrs. Wickham! How well it sounds! And she was only sixteen last June. My dear Jane, I'm so flustered I'm sure I can't write; so I'll dictate and you write for me. We'll settle the money question with your father later; but the things should be ordered immediately."

She was then proceeding to all the specifics of cotton, muslin, and cambric, and would have dictated some very generous orders had not Jane, with some difficulty, persuaded her to wait until their father could be consulted. A day's delay, she pointed out, would make little difference; and her mother was too happy to be as stubborn as usual. Other schemes also came to mind.

"I'll go to Meryton," she said, "as soon as I'm dressed, and tell the good news to my sister Philips. And on the way back I can call on Lady Lucas and Mrs. Long. Kitty, run down and order the carriage. A drive would do me a world of good, I'm sure. Girls, is there anything I can do for you in Meryton? Oh! Here comes Hill. My dear Hill, have you heard the good news? Miss Lydia is going to be married; and you shall all have a bowl of punch to celebrate at her wedding."

Mrs. Hill immediately expressed her joy. Elizabeth received her congratulations along with the rest, and then, sick of all this foolishness, took refuge in her own room so she could think in peace. Poor Lydia's situation was, at best, bad enough; but that it wasn't worse, she had reason to be grateful. She felt it deeply; and though, looking ahead, neither genuine happiness nor worldly prosperity could reasonably be expected for her sister, looking back at what they had feared only two hours ago, she appreciated the full value of what they had gained.

chapters.title: Chapter 50
paragraphs: Mr. Bennet had often wished, before this point in his life, that instead of spending his entire income, he had put aside an annual sum for the better provision of his children and his wife, should she survive him. He wished it now more than ever. Had he done his duty in that regard, Lydia wouldn't have needed to depend on her uncle for whatever honor or credit could now be purchased for her. The satisfaction of persuading one of the most worthless young men in Great Britain to become her husband might then have rested where it belonged.

He was deeply troubled that a matter bringing so little benefit to anyone should have been handled at his brother-in-law's sole expense; and he was determined, if possible, to discover the full extent of the assistance and repay the obligation as soon as he could.

When Mr. Bennet had first married, saving had seemed completely unnecessary; for of course they were going to have a son. This son would join in breaking the entail as soon as he came of age, and the widow and younger children would thereby be provided for. Five daughters entered the world one after another, but the son was still expected; and Mrs. Bennet had been certain he would come for many years after Lydia's birth. By the time that hope was finally abandoned, it was too late to start saving. Mrs. Bennet had no talent for economy, and only her husband's love of independence had prevented them from spending beyond their income.

Five thousand pounds had been settled on Mrs. Bennet and the children by the marriage agreement. But how it should be divided among the children depended on the parents' wishes. This was one point that now needed to be settled regarding Lydia at least, and Mr. Bennet had no hesitation in accepting the proposal before him. In terms of grateful acknowledgment for his brother's kindness, though expressed as briefly as possible, he then set down on paper his complete approval of everything that had been done and his willingness to fulfill the commitments made on his behalf. He had never imagined that, if Wickham could be persuaded to marry his daughter, it would be done with so little inconvenience to himself as the current arrangement required. He would be scarcely ten pounds a year worse off by the hundred that was to be paid them; for, what with her room and board, her pocket money, and the constant gifts of cash that passed to her through her mother, Lydia's expenses had always nearly reached that amount.

That it would require so little effort on his part was another welcome surprise; for his chief wish at present was to have as little trouble as possible. When the first burst of rage that had spurred his activity in searching for her subsided, he naturally returned to all his former laziness. His letter was soon dispatched; for though slow to start business, he was quick to finish it. He asked for further details about what he owed his brother; but was too angry with Lydia to send her any message.

The good news quickly spread through the house, and with equal speed through the neighborhood. It was received in the latter with decent composure. To be sure, it would have made for better gossip if Miss Lydia Bennet had ended up on the streets, or alternatively been hidden away on some remote farm. But there was plenty to discuss in the marriage itself; and the well-meaning wishes for her happiness that had come from all the spiteful old ladies of Meryton lost little of their spirit with this change of circumstances, since with such a husband her misery was considered a certainty.

It was two weeks since Mrs. Bennet had been downstairs, but on this happy day she again took her seat at the head of the table, in oppressively high spirits. No feeling of shame dampened her triumph. The marriage of a daughter, which had been her chief goal since Jane turned sixteen, was now about to be achieved, and her thoughts and words ran entirely on the accessories of an elegant wedding—fine fabrics, new carriages, and servants. She was busy searching the neighborhood for a suitable home for her daughter, and without knowing or considering what their income might be, rejected many as too small or too unimportant.

"Haye Park might do," she said, "if the Gouldings would leave, or the big house at Stoke, if the drawing room were larger; but Ashworth is too far away. I couldn't bear to have her ten miles from me; and as for Purvis Lodge, the attics are dreadful."

Her husband let her talk on without interruption while the servants were present. But when they had left, he said, "Mrs. Bennet, before you claim any or all of these houses for your son and daughter, let us understand each other. They will never be admitted into any house in this neighborhood. I will not encourage the recklessness of either of them by receiving them at Longbourn."

A long argument followed this declaration, but Mr. Bennet was firm. It soon led to another dispute; and Mrs. Bennet discovered, with amazement and horror, that her husband would not contribute a single penny toward buying clothes for his daughter. He insisted she would receive from him no token of affection whatever on this occasion. Mrs. Bennet could hardly believe it. That his anger could reach such a point of unimaginable stubbornness as to deny his daughter a privilege without which her marriage would hardly seem real exceeded everything she thought possible. She was more upset about the disgrace that a lack of new clothes would bring to her daughter's wedding than by any shame over the elopement or the weeks of living with Wickham before the ceremony.

Elizabeth was now deeply sorry that, in the distress of the moment, she had told Mr. Darcy about their fears for her sister; for since the marriage would soon put a proper end to the elopement, they might hope to hide its unfortunate beginning from everyone who wasn't directly involved.

She had no fear of the secret spreading through him. There were few people whose discretion she would have trusted more; but at the same time there was no one whose knowledge of a sister's downfall would have mortified her so deeply. Not, however, from any fear of personal harm to herself; for in any case there seemed to be an impassable gulf between them. Had Lydia's marriage been concluded on the most honorable terms, Mr. Darcy would surely never connect himself with a family to whose existing objections would now be added an alliance with the man he most justly despised.

From such a connection she couldn't blame him for recoiling. The interest in her that she had been sure he felt in Derbyshire could not, by any rational expectation, survive such a blow. She was humbled and grieved; she repented, though she hardly knew of what. She became possessive of his good opinion at the very moment she could no longer hope to benefit from it. She wanted news of him when there seemed the least chance of hearing any. She was convinced she could have been happy with him, just when it was no longer likely they would ever meet.

What a triumph for him, she often thought, if he could know that the proposal she had so proudly rejected only four months ago would now have been gladly and gratefully accepted! He was, she had no doubt, as generous as any man could be. But while he was human, there would have to be a sense of triumph.

She began now to understand that he was exactly the man who, in temperament and abilities, would most suit her. His understanding and character, though different from her own, would have answered all her wishes. It was a union that must have benefited both: her ease and liveliness would have softened his mind and improved his manners; and from his judgment, knowledge, and experience of the world, she would have gained advantages of far greater importance.

But no such happy marriage could now teach the admiring public what married happiness really was. A union of a very different kind, one that made the other impossible, was soon to be formed in their family.

How Wickham and Lydia were to be supported in any kind of independence she couldn't imagine. But how little lasting happiness could belong to a couple brought together only because their passions were stronger than their principles—that she could easily predict.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. To Mr. Bennet's grateful thanks he replied briefly, with assurances of his eagerness to help any member of the family, and concluded by asking that the subject never be mentioned to him again. The main purpose of his letter was to inform them that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

"It was very much my wish that he should do so," he added, "as soon as the marriage was settled. And I think you'll agree that a move from that regiment is highly advisable for both his sake and my niece's. It is Mr. Wickham's intention to join the Regular Army; and among his former friends there are still some able and willing to assist him. He has the promise of a commission in General ——'s regiment, now stationed in the north. It's an advantage to have it so far from this part of the country. He gives fair promises; and I hope that among different people, where they each have a reputation to maintain, they will both be more sensible. I have written to Colonel Forster to inform him of our arrangements and to ask him to settle Wickham's various debts in and near Brighton, for which I have pledged myself. And would you take the trouble to make similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton, of whom I am enclosing a list based on his information? He has declared all his debts; I hope at least he hasn't deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be completed within a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and I understand from Mrs. Gardiner that my niece very much wants to see you all before she leaves the south. She is well, and sends her dutiful regards to you and her mother.—Yours, etc.
"E. GARDINER."

Mr. Bennet and his daughters saw all the advantages of Wickham's leaving the ——shire as clearly as Mr. Gardiner did. But Mrs. Bennet was less pleased with it. Lydia being settled in the north, just when she had expected the most pleasure and pride in her company—for she had by no means given up her plan of having them live in Hertfordshire—was a bitter disappointment. Besides, it was such a shame that Lydia should be taken from a regiment where she knew everyone and had so many favorites.
"She's so fond of Mrs. Forster," she said. "It will be awful to send her away! And there are several of the young men she likes very much. The officers may not be as nice in General ——'s regiment."

His daughter's request—for such it might be considered—to be welcomed back into the family before heading north was initially met with a flat refusal. But Jane and Elizabeth, who agreed that for their sister's sake and dignity she should be acknowledged by her parents on her marriage, urged him so earnestly yet so reasonably to receive her and her husband at Longbourn as soon as they were married, that he was eventually persuaded. And their mother had the satisfaction of knowing she would be able to show off her married daughter in the neighborhood before she was banished to the north. When Mr. Bennet wrote again to his brother, therefore, he sent his permission for them to come; and it was settled that, as soon as the ceremony was over, they would proceed to Longbourn. Elizabeth was surprised, however, that Wickham would agree to such a plan; and had she consulted only her own wishes, seeing him again would have been the last thing she wanted.

chapters.title: Chapter 51
paragraphs: Their sister's wedding day arrived; and Jane and Elizabeth probably felt more on her behalf than she felt herself. The carriage was sent to meet them at ——, and they were to return in it by dinnertime. Their arrival was dreaded by the elder Miss Bennets—Jane especially, who imagined Lydia would feel the shame that she herself would have felt in the same situation, and was wretched thinking about what her sister must be enduring.

They came. The family was assembled in the breakfast room to receive them. Smiles covered Mrs. Bennet's face as the carriage pulled up to the door; her husband looked impenetrably serious; her daughters were alarmed, anxious, and uneasy.

Lydia's voice was heard in the hall; the door was thrown open, and she ran into the room. Her mother stepped forward, embraced her, and welcomed her with delight; offered her hand to Wickham with an affectionate smile as he followed his wife; and wished them both joy with an eagerness that showed no doubt of their happiness.

Their reception from Mr. Bennet, to whom they then turned, was not nearly as warm. His expression actually grew more stern, and he barely opened his mouth. The brazen confidence of the young couple was, in fact, enough to provoke him.

Elizabeth was disgusted, and even Jane was shocked. Lydia was still Lydia—unrestrained, unembarrassed, wild, loud, and fearless. She turned from sister to sister, demanding their congratulations; and when they all finally sat down, she looked eagerly around the room, noticed some small change in it, and laughed, saying it had been ages since she'd been there.

Wickham was no more troubled than she was; but his manners were always so pleasant that, had his character and marriage been what they should have been, his smiles and his easy warmth as he claimed their family connection would have charmed them all. Elizabeth had not previously believed him capable of such brazenness; but she sat down, resolving to set no further limits on the shamelessness of a shameless man. She blushed, and Jane blushed; but the faces of the two who caused their embarrassment showed not the slightest change of color.

There was no shortage of conversation. The bride and her mother could neither of them talk fast enough; and Wickham, who happened to be sitting near Elizabeth, began asking about his acquaintances in the neighborhood with a cheerful ease that she found impossible to match in her replies. They both seemed to have only the happiest memories. Nothing from the past was recalled with any pain; and Lydia voluntarily raised subjects her sisters wouldn't have mentioned for anything.

"Just think—it's been three months since I went away!" she cried. "It feels like only two weeks, I swear; and yet so much has happened. Good gracious! When I left, I had no more idea of getting married before I came back! Though I thought it would be great fun if I did."
Her father raised his eyes; Jane looked distressed; Elizabeth gave Lydia a pointed look; but Lydia, who never noticed or saw anything she chose to ignore, gaily continued—

"Oh, Mama, do the people around here know I was married today? I was afraid they might not; and when we passed William Goulding in his carriage, I was determined he should know, so I lowered the window, took off my glove, and let my hand rest on the window frame so he could see the ring—and then I bowed and smiled like anything."

Elizabeth could bear it no longer. She got up and ran out of the room, and didn't return until she heard them passing through the hall to the dining room. She then joined them just in time to see Lydia, with proud ceremony, walk up to her mother's right hand and say to her eldest sister—
"Ah, Jane, I take your place now, and you must go lower, because I'm a married woman."

It was not to be expected that time would produce in Lydia any of the embarrassment she had been entirely free of from the start. Her ease and high spirits only increased. She longed to see Mrs. Philips, the Lucases, and all their other neighbors, and to hear herself called "Mrs. Wickham" by each of them; and in the meantime, after dinner, she went to show her ring and boast about being married to Mrs. Hill and the two housemaids.

"Well, Mama," she said when they were all back in the breakfast room, "and what do you think of my husband? Isn't he charming? I'm sure my sisters must all envy me. I only hope they'll have half my good luck. They should all go to Brighton. That's the place to get husbands. What a shame, Mama, that we didn't all go!"
"Very true; and if I'd had my way, we would have. But, my dear Lydia, I don't like your going so far away. Must it really be?"

"Oh, Lord! Yes—there's nothing to worry about. I shall love it. You and Papa and my sisters must come visit us. We'll be at Newcastle all winter, and I'm sure there'll be some balls, and I'll make sure to find good dance partners for everyone."
"I should like that beyond anything!" said her mother.
"And when you leave, you can leave one or two of my sisters behind; and I dare say I'll have husbands for them before the winter is over."
"I appreciate the offer," said Elizabeth, "but I don't particularly care for your method of finding husbands."
Their visitors were to stay no more than ten days. Mr. Wickham had received his commission before leaving London and was to join his regiment in two weeks.

No one but Mrs. Bennet regretted that their stay would be so short; and she made the most of the time by visiting around with her daughter and hosting frequent parties at home. These gatherings were welcome to everyone; avoiding the family circle was even more desirable for those who were capable of thought than for those who were not.

Wickham's affection for Lydia was exactly what Elizabeth had expected: not equal to Lydia's for him. She had scarcely needed fresh observation to confirm what common sense already told her—that their elopement had been driven by the strength of her love rather than his. She would have wondered why, without deeply caring for Lydia, he had chosen to elope with her at all, had she not been certain that his flight was forced by desperate financial circumstances; and in that case, he was not the man to pass up a willing companion.

Lydia was wildly fond of him. He was her dear Wickham on every occasion; no one was to be compared with him. He did everything best in the world; and she was sure he would shoot more birds on the first of September than anyone in the county.
One morning, soon after their arrival, as she was sitting with her two elder sisters, she said to Elizabeth—
"Lizzy, I never told you about my wedding, did I? You weren't there when I told Mama and the others all about it. Aren't you curious to hear how it went?"
"No, really," replied Elizabeth. "I think the less said about it the better."

"Goodness! You're so strange! But I must tell you how it went. We were married at St. Clement's, you know, because Wickham's lodgings were in that parish. And it was arranged that we should all be there by eleven o'clock. My uncle and aunt and I were to go together, and the others were to meet us at the church.

"Well, Monday morning came and I was in such a state! I was so afraid something would happen to prevent it, and then I would have gone completely mad. And there was my aunt, the whole time I was dressing, lecturing and going on as if she were reading a sermon. I didn't hear more than one word in ten, though, because I was thinking—you can imagine—of my dear Wickham. I was dying to know whether he'd be married in his blue coat.

"Well, and so we had breakfast at ten as usual. I thought it would never end. By the way, you should know my uncle and aunt were horribly unpleasant the whole time I was with them. Would you believe, I didn't once set foot outside the door, though I was there for two weeks. Not one party, not one outing, not a single thing! London was rather empty, of course, but the Little Theatre was open.

"Well, and just as the carriage came to the door, my uncle was called away on business to that dreadful man Mr. Stone. And then, you know, once they start talking there's no end to it. I was so frightened—I didn't know what to do, because my uncle was to give me away, and if we were past the hour we couldn't be married at all that day. But luckily he came back within ten minutes, and off we all went. Though I remembered afterward that if he had been prevented from going, the wedding needn't have been postponed—because Mr. Darcy could have done just as well."
"Mr. Darcy!" repeated Elizabeth, in utter amazement.

"Oh yes! He was there with Wickham, you know. But good gracious! I completely forgot! I wasn't supposed to say a word about it. I promised them faithfully! What will Wickham say? It was supposed to be such a secret!"
"If it was meant to be a secret," said Jane, "say nothing more about it. You may be sure I won't ask any questions."
"Oh, certainly," said Elizabeth, though burning with curiosity, "we won't ask you anything."
"Thank you," said Lydia, "because if you did, I'd certainly tell you everything, and then Wickham would be so angry."
With such an encouragement to ask, Elizabeth was forced to put it out of her power by walking away.

But to remain ignorant on such a point was impossible; or at least it was impossible not to try for information. Mr. Darcy had been at her sister's wedding. It was exactly the kind of scene, and exactly among the kind of people, where he seemed to have the least reason to be and the least desire to go. Theories about what it meant, rapid and wild, rushed through her mind; but she was satisfied with none. The explanations that pleased her most, as putting his conduct in the noblest light, seemed the most unlikely. She couldn't bear such suspense; and hastily grabbing a sheet of paper, she wrote a short letter to her aunt, asking for an explanation of what Lydia had let slip, if such an explanation was compatible with the secrecy that had apparently been intended.

"You can easily understand," she added, "how curious I must be to know how a person unconnected with any of us, and comparatively a stranger to our family, should have been among you at such a time. Please write immediately and help me understand—unless there are very strong reasons for the secrecy that Lydia seems to think necessary; in which case I must try to be satisfied with not knowing."
"Not that I shall be," she added to herself as she finished the letter, "and, my dear aunt, if you don't tell me honestly, I shall certainly resort to tricks and schemes to find it out."

Jane's delicate sense of honor wouldn't allow her to mention to Elizabeth what Lydia had let slip; and Elizabeth was glad of it—until she knew whether her questions would be answered, she'd rather not have a confidante.

chapters.title: Chapter 52
paragraphs: Elizabeth had the satisfaction of receiving a reply to her letter as soon as she possibly could. The moment she had it in hand, she hurried to the little copse where she was least likely to be disturbed, sat down on one of the benches, and prepared to be happy; for the length of the letter assured her it didn't contain a refusal.
"Gracechurch Street, September 6.
"My dear Niece,

"I have just received your letter and shall devote this entire morning to answering it, since I foresee that a little writing won't cover what I have to tell you. I must say I'm surprised by your question; I didn't expect it from you. But don't think me angry—I only mean to let you know I hadn't imagined such inquiries would be necessary on your side. If you genuinely don't understand me, forgive my frankness. Your uncle is as surprised as I am; and nothing but the belief that you were personally involved would have allowed him to act as he did. But if you truly are innocent and uninformed, I must be more explicit. On the very day I returned home from Longbourn, your uncle had a most unexpected visitor. Mr. Darcy called and was closeted with him for several hours. It was all over before I arrived, so my curiosity wasn't quite as horribly tested as yours seems to have been. He came to tell Mr. Gardiner that he had discovered where your sister and Mr. Wickham were, and that he had seen and spoken with them both—Wickham repeatedly, Lydia once. From what I can gather, he left Derbyshire only one day after we did, and came to London determined to find them. His stated reason was his conviction that Wickham's worthlessness had not been made known widely enough to prevent any young woman of good character from trusting him. He generously blamed the whole situation on his own mistaken pride, and confessed that he had previously thought it beneath him to make his private dealings public. His character, he felt, should speak for itself. He therefore called it his duty to step forward and try to remedy a problem he had helped to create. If he had another motive, I'm sure it would do him no discredit. He had been in London several days before he could find them, but he had a lead that we lacked, and knowing this was another reason he resolved to follow us. There was a woman, it seems—a Mrs. Younge—who had once been Miss Darcy's governess and was dismissed for some reason he didn't specify. She had taken a large house in Edward Street and was making her living by letting rooms. This Mrs. Younge was, he knew, closely connected with Wickham, and he went to her for information as soon as he arrived in London. But it was two or three days before he could get what he needed from her. She wouldn't betray her friend, I suppose, without being bribed, since she really did know where he was. Wickham had gone to her on their first arrival in London, and had she been able to take them in, they would have stayed with her. At last, however, our kind friend obtained the address. They were in —— Street. He saw Wickham, and then insisted on seeing Lydia. His first aim, he admitted, was to persuade her to leave her current disgraceful situation and return to her family, offering his help as far as it could go. But he found Lydia absolutely determined to stay. She cared nothing for any of her friends; she wanted no help from him; she refused to hear of leaving Wickham. She was sure they'd be married sooner or later, and it didn't much matter when. Since those were her feelings, the only option, he felt, was to secure and expedite a marriage which—as he easily learned from his very first conversation with Wickham—had never been Wickham's intention. Wickham admitted he'd been forced to leave the regiment because of pressing debts of honor, and didn't hesitate to blame the entire mess on Lydia's foolishness alone. He intended to resign his commission immediately; as for his future, he could guess very little. He had to go somewhere, but didn't know where, and knew he'd have nothing to live on. Mr. Darcy asked why he didn't simply marry Lydia. Though Mr. Bennet wasn't thought to be wealthy, he could have done something for his son-in-law, and Wickham's situation could only have been improved by marriage. But in response, Wickham revealed he still hoped to make his fortune through a more advantageous marriage elsewhere. Under the circumstances, however, he wasn't likely to resist the temptation of immediate relief. They met several times, as there was much to negotiate. Wickham naturally wanted more than he could get, but was eventually brought to see reason. Once everything was settled between them, Mr. Darcy's next step was to inform your uncle, and he first called at Gracechurch Street the evening before I came home. But Mr. Gardiner wasn't available, and Mr. Darcy learned that your father was still with him but would leave London the next morning. He didn't think your father was the right person to consult, preferring your uncle, and therefore easily delayed the meeting until after your father's departure. He didn't leave his name, and until the next day it was only known that a gentleman had called on business. On Saturday he came again. Your father was gone, your uncle was home, and, as I said before, they had a great deal to discuss. They met again on Sunday, and then I saw him too. It wasn't all settled until Monday; as soon as it was, the express was sent to Longbourn. But our visitor was very stubborn. I suspect, Lizzy, that stubbornness is the real fault in his character. He has been accused of many things at different times, but this is the true one. Nothing was to be done that he didn't do himself; though I'm sure (and I don't say this to be thanked, so please say nothing about it) your uncle would have been perfectly willing to handle the whole thing. They argued about it for a long time, longer than either the gentleman or lady concerned deserved. But at last your uncle was forced to give in, and instead of being allowed to help his niece, had to settle for merely getting the credit for it—which went very much against the grain. I truly believe your letter this morning gave him great pleasure, because it called for an explanation that would strip him of his borrowed glory and give the praise where it was due. But, Lizzy, this must go no further than yourself, or Jane at most. You know fairly well, I suppose, what has been done for the young people. His debts are to be paid—amounting, I believe, to considerably more than a thousand pounds—another thousand in addition to her own share settled on her, and his commission purchased. The reason all this was to be done by him alone is what I've described above. It was owing to him, to his reticence and lack of proper openness, that Wickham's character had been so misunderstood, and consequently that he had been received and welcomed as he was. Perhaps there's some truth in this, though I doubt whether his reserve, or anyone's reserve, can truly be held responsible for what happened. But in spite of all this noble talk, my dear Lizzy, you may rest perfectly assured that your uncle would never have given in if we hadn't credited him with another interest in the affair. When all this was resolved, Mr. Darcy returned to his friends at Pemberley; but it was agreed he would be in London again when the wedding took place, and all financial matters were to be finalized then. I believe I've now told you everything. It is a story which you tell me will greatly surprise you; I hope at least it won't displease you. Lydia came to us, and Wickham was a constant visitor. He was exactly as he'd been when I knew him in Hertfordshire; but I won't tell you how little I was satisfied with her behavior while she stayed with us, except that I saw from Jane's letter last Wednesday that her conduct since returning home has been equally bad, so what I say now can't cause you any fresh pain. I spoke to her repeatedly in the most serious way, pointing out the wickedness of what she'd done and all the unhappiness she'd brought on her family. If she heard me, it was by luck, because I'm sure she wasn't listening. I was sometimes quite exasperated; but then I remembered my dear Elizabeth and Jane, and for their sakes I was patient. Mr. Darcy was punctual in his return and, as Lydia told you, attended the wedding. He dined with us the following day and was to leave London again on Wednesday or Thursday. Will you be very angry with me, my dear Lizzy, if I take this opportunity to say (what I was never brave enough to say before) how much I like him? His behavior toward us has been, in every way, as pleasing as it was in Derbyshire. His intelligence and opinions all appeal to me; he needs only a little more liveliness, and that, if he marries wisely, his wife may teach him. I thought him very reserved; he hardly ever mentioned your name. But reserve seems to be the fashion. Please forgive me if I've been too forward, or at least don't punish me by banning me from Pemberley. I'll never be quite happy until I've been all around the park. A low carriage with a nice little pair of ponies would be the very thing. But I must stop writing. The children have been wanting me for the last half hour.
"Yours, very sincerely,
"M. GARDINER."

The contents of this letter threw Elizabeth into a whirl of emotions in which it was hard to tell whether pleasure or pain was greater. The vague and unsettled suspicions she'd had—about what Mr. Darcy might have done to facilitate her sister's marriage, which she'd been afraid to encourage as too great an act of kindness to be likely, and at the same time dreaded to be true because of the burden of obligation—were now confirmed beyond their greatest extent. He had followed them to London on purpose; he had taken on himself all the trouble and humiliation of such a search, in which he'd had to beg for help from a woman he must despise, and been forced to meet, argue with, persuade, and ultimately bribe the man he most wished to avoid, and whose very name it was painful for him to speak. He had done all this for a girl he could neither care about nor respect. Her heart whispered that he had done it for her. But that hope was quickly checked by other thoughts; and she soon felt that even her vanity was insufficient to sustain it—to believe that his affection for a woman who had already refused him could overcome such a natural feeling as disgust at being related to Wickham. Brother-in-law of Wickham! Every kind of pride must recoil from such a connection. He had certainly done a great deal. She was ashamed to think how much. But he had given a reason for his involvement that required no extraordinary leap of faith. It was reasonable that he should feel he'd been wrong; he had the generosity, and he had the means, to act on it. And though she wouldn't consider herself his primary motivation, she could perhaps believe that his lingering feelings for her had contributed to his efforts in a cause where her peace of mind was deeply affected. It was painful—exceedingly painful—to know they were indebted to someone who could never be repaid. They owed the rescue of Lydia—her reputation, everything—to him. Oh, how bitterly she regretted every ungracious thought she had ever harbored, every sharp word she had ever aimed at him! For herself, she was humbled; but she was proud of him—proud that, in a cause of compassion and honor, he had been able to overcome his own feelings. She read her aunt's praise of him again and again. It was barely adequate, but it pleased her. She was even pleased, though it was mixed with regret, to discover how firmly both her aunt and uncle had believed there was a real understanding between Mr. Darcy and herself.
She was roused from her seat and her reflections by someone approaching; and before she could take another path, she was overtaken by Wickham.
"I'm afraid I'm interrupting your solitary walk, my dear sister?" he said as he joined her.
"You certainly are," she replied with a smile, "but that doesn't mean the interruption is unwelcome."
"I'd be sorry if it were. We were always good friends, and now we're better."
"True. Are the others coming out?"
"I don't know. Mrs. Bennet and Lydia are going to Meryton in the carriage. And so, my dear sister, I understand from our uncle and aunt that you've actually seen Pemberley."
She confirmed that she had.

"I almost envy you the experience, and yet I think it would be too much for me—though I could take it in on my way to Newcastle. And you saw the old housekeeper, I suppose? Poor Reynolds—she was always very fond of me. But of course she didn't mention my name to you."
"Yes, she did."
"And what did she say?"
"That you had gone into the army, and she was afraid had—not turned out well. At such a distance, you know, things get strangely distorted."
"Certainly," he replied, biting his lip. Elizabeth hoped she had silenced him; but he soon added—
"I was surprised to see Darcy in London last month. We ran into each other several times. I wonder what he could be doing there."
"Perhaps preparing for his marriage to Miss de Bourgh," said Elizabeth. "It must be something unusual to bring him there at this time of year."
"No doubt. Did you see him while you were at Lambton? I thought I gathered from the Gardiners that you had."
"Yes; he introduced us to his sister."
"And do you like her?"
"Very much."
"I've heard she's greatly improved in the last year or two. When I last saw her, she wasn't very promising. I'm very glad you liked her. I hope she'll turn out well."
"I'm sure she will; she's past the most difficult age."
"Did you go through the village of Kympton?"
"I don't recall that we did."
"I mention it because that's the living I ought to have had. A most delightful place! Excellent rectory house! It would have suited me in every way."
"How would you have liked writing sermons?"

"Very much. I would have considered it part of my duty, and the effort would soon have been nothing. One shouldn't complain; but it would have been so perfect for me! The peace, the quiet retirement of such a life would have matched all my dreams of happiness! But it wasn't to be. Did you ever hear Darcy mention the matter when you were in Kent?"
"I did hear, from a source I considered just as reliable, that the living was left to you only conditionally, at the discretion of the current patron."
"You did! Yes, there was something in that. I told you so from the start, you may remember."

"I did also hear that there was a time when the idea of being a clergyman wasn't as appealing to you as it seems to be now—that you actually declared your intention of never taking orders, and that a financial settlement was reached accordingly."
"You did! And there was not no truth in that. You may remember what I told you about it when we first discussed it."
They were now almost at the door, for she had been walking fast to get rid of him; and unwilling, for her sister's sake, to provoke him, she only said in reply, with a good-natured smile—
"Come, Mr. Wickham, we are brother and sister now, you know. Let's not quarrel about the past. In the future, I hope we'll always be of one mind."
She held out her hand; he kissed it with gallant courtesy, though he hardly knew where to look, and they entered the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 53
paragraphs: Mr. Wickham was so thoroughly satisfied with this conversation that he never again troubled himself or provoked his dear sister Elizabeth by bringing up the subject; and she was pleased to find she had said enough to keep him quiet.

The day of his and Lydia's departure soon came, and Mrs. Bennet was forced to endure a separation that—since her husband refused to entertain her plan of all of them going to Newcastle—was likely to last at least a year.
"Oh, my dear Lydia," she cried, "when shall we see each other again?"
"Oh, Lord! I don't know. Not for two or three years, probably."
"Write to me very often, dear."
"As often as I can. But you know, married women never have much time for writing. My sisters can write to me. They'll have nothing else to do."
Mr. Wickham's farewells were much more affectionate than his wife's. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many charming things.

"He is as fine a fellow," said Mr. Bennet, as soon as they were out of the house, "as I ever saw. He smirks and simpers and charms us all. I am enormously proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas himself to produce a more valuable son-in-law."
The loss of her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very gloomy for several days.
"I often think," she said, "that there's nothing so bad as parting from one's friends. One feels so lost without them."
"This is the consequence, you see, madam, of marrying off a daughter," said Elizabeth. "It should make you more content that your other four are still single."
"It's nothing of the sort. Lydia doesn't leave me because she's married, but only because her husband's regiment happens to be so far away. If it were closer, she wouldn't have gone so soon."

But her depressed state was soon relieved, and her mind opened again to the excitement of hope, by a piece of news that began circulating. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to prepare for her master's arrival; he was coming in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was in a perfect flutter. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head, by turns.

"Well, well, and so Mr. Bingley is coming back, sister"—for Mrs. Philips had first brought her the news. "Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He's nothing to us, you know, and I'm sure I never want to see him again. But he's very welcome to come to Netherfield if he likes. And who knows what may happen? But that's nothing to us. You know, sister, we agreed long ago never to say a word about it. And so, is it quite certain he's coming?"

"You may depend on it," replied the other, "for Mrs. Nichols was in Meryton last night; I saw her passing by and went out myself to ask. She told me it was definitely true. He's coming Thursday at the latest, probably Wednesday. She was on her way to the butcher's to order meat for Wednesday, she told me, and she's got three pairs of ducks just ready to be killed."
Miss Bennet hadn't been able to hear of his coming without changing color. It was many months since she had mentioned his name to Elizabeth; but now, as soon as they were alone, she said—

"I saw you looking at me today, Lizzy, when my aunt told us the news; and I know I looked flustered. But don't imagine it was for any foolish reason. I was only embarrassed for a moment, because I felt I was being watched. I assure you the news affects me with neither pleasure nor pain. I'm glad of one thing—that he comes alone; we'll see less of him that way. Not that I'm afraid of myself, but I dread other people's comments."

Elizabeth didn't know what to make of it. Had she not seen him in Derbyshire, she might have supposed he was coming with no intention beyond what was openly stated; but she still thought him attracted to Jane, and wavered between thinking he was coming with his friend's permission or being bold enough to come without it.
"Yet it's hard," she sometimes thought, "that this poor man can't visit a house he's legally rented without causing all this speculation! I will leave him alone."

Despite what her sister declared and genuinely believed her feelings to be, Elizabeth could easily see that her spirits were affected. They were more unsteady and more agitated than she had often seen them.
The subject that had been so hotly debated between their parents about a year ago was now raised again.
"As soon as Mr. Bingley arrives, my dear," said Mrs. Bennet, "you will call on him, of course."
"No, no. You forced me into visiting him last year, and promised that if I went to see him he'd marry one of my daughters. But it came to nothing, and I won't be sent on a fool's errand again."
His wife argued that such a courtesy was absolutely required of every gentleman in the neighborhood when Bingley returned to Netherfield.

"That's an etiquette I despise," he said. "If he wants our company, let him come to us. He knows where we live. I will not spend my time running after my neighbors every time they leave and come back."

"Well, all I know is it will be horribly rude if you don't call on him. But that won't stop me from inviting him to dinner. We must have Mrs. Long and the Gouldings soon. That will make thirteen with ourselves, so there will be just room at the table for him."

Consoled by this plan, she was better able to bear her husband's rudeness; though it was very annoying to know that her neighbors might all see Mr. Bingley before they did. As the day of his arrival drew near—

"I'm starting to be sorry he's coming at all," said Jane to her sister. "It wouldn't matter; I could see him with perfect indifference; but I can hardly bear to hear it talked about constantly. Mama means well, but she doesn't know—no one can know—how much I suffer from what she says. I'll be happy when his stay at Netherfield is over!"

"I wish I could say something to comfort you," replied Elizabeth, "but it's entirely beyond my power. You must feel it; and the usual satisfaction of preaching patience to a sufferer is denied me, because you always have so much of it already."

Mr. Bingley arrived. Mrs. Bennet, with the help of servants, managed to be the first to hear of it, ensuring her period of anxious anticipation was as long as possible. She counted the days before they could send their invitation—convinced she wouldn't see him before then. But on the third morning after his arrival, she saw him from her dressing room window riding across the grounds toward the house.

Her daughters were eagerly called to share her excitement. Jane firmly kept her place at the table; but Elizabeth, to satisfy her mother, went to the window. She looked—she saw Mr. Darcy with him—and sat down again by her sister.
"There's a gentleman with him, Mama," said Kitty. "Who can it be?"
"Some friend or other, my dear, I suppose. I'm sure I don't know."
"Goodness!" replied Kitty. "It looks just like that man who used to be with him before. Mr.—what's his name—that tall, proud man."
"Good gracious! Mr. Darcy!—and so it does, I declare. Well, any friend of Mr. Bingley's will always be welcome here, to be sure; but otherwise I must say I hate the very sight of him."

Jane looked at Elizabeth with surprise and concern. She knew little of their meeting in Derbyshire, and so felt for the awkwardness her sister must experience in seeing him almost for the first time since receiving his letter. Both sisters were uncomfortable enough. Each felt for the other, and of course for themselves; and their mother went on about her dislike of Mr. Darcy and her resolution to be civil to him only as Mr. Bingley's friend, without being heard by either of them. But Elizabeth had sources of anxiety that Jane couldn't yet suspect—Jane, to whom she had never yet had the courage to show Mrs. Gardiner's letter or reveal her changed feelings toward him. To Jane, he could only be a man whose proposal she had rejected and whose worth she had undervalued; but to Elizabeth, with her fuller knowledge, he was the person to whom the whole family was indebted for the greatest of services, and whom she herself regarded with a feeling that was—if not quite as tender—at least as reasonable and justified as what Jane felt for Bingley. Her astonishment at his coming—coming to Netherfield, to Longbourn, and voluntarily seeking her out again—was almost equal to what she had felt on first seeing his changed behavior in Derbyshire.
