The color that had drained from her face returned for half a minute with an extra glow, and a smile of delight added brightness to her eyes, as she thought for that brief moment that his feelings and wishes must still be unchanged. But she wouldn't let herself be sure.
"Let me first see how he behaves," she said. "It will be soon enough then for expectations."

She sat intently at her work, trying to stay calm, and without daring to look up until anxious curiosity carried her eyes to her sister's face as the servant approached the door. Jane looked a little paler than usual but more composed than Elizabeth had expected. When the gentlemen appeared, her color deepened; yet she received them with reasonable ease and a manner equally free of resentment or excessive warmth.

Elizabeth said as little to either of them as politeness allowed and sat down again to her work, with an intensity she didn't usually show. She had ventured only one glance at Darcy. He looked serious as usual—more like his old Hertfordshire manner, she thought, than how he'd been at Pemberley. But perhaps he couldn't be the same in her mother's house as before her uncle and aunt. It was a painful thought, but not an unlikely one.

Bingley she had also glimpsed briefly, and in that short moment saw him looking both pleased and embarrassed. He was received by Mrs. Bennet with a degree of civility that made her two daughters cringe, especially when compared with the cold and ceremonious politeness she showed his friend.
Elizabeth in particular, who knew that the latter had saved her mother's favorite daughter from permanent disgrace, was pained and embarrassed by such misplaced distinction.

Darcy, after asking how Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner were—a question she couldn't answer without blushing—said almost nothing. He wasn't seated near her; perhaps that was why he was silent. But it hadn't been so in Derbyshire. There he had talked to her friends when he couldn't talk to her. But now several minutes passed without his speaking at all; and when occasionally, unable to resist her curiosity, she raised her eyes to his face, she found him looking at Jane as often as at herself, and frequently at nothing but the floor. More thoughtfulness and less effort to please than at their last meeting were plainly visible. She was disappointed, and angry with herself for being so.
"Could I have expected anything else?" she said to herself. "Yet why did he come?"
She was in no mood for conversation with anyone but him; and toward him she could hardly muster the courage to speak.
She asked after his sister, but could manage no more.
"It's been a long time since you went away, Mr. Bingley," said Mrs. Bennet.
He readily agreed.

"I was starting to think you'd never come back. People did say you meant to leave the place entirely at Michaelmas; but I hope that's not true. A great many changes have happened in the neighborhood since you left. Miss Lucas is married and settled, and one of my own daughters too. I suppose you've heard of it; you must have seen it in the papers. It was in the Times and the Courier, I know; though it wasn't printed as it ought to have been. It only said, 'Lately, George Wickham, Esq., to Miss Lydia Bennet,' without a syllable about her father, or where she lived, or anything. It was my brother Gardiner's work, and I wonder how he made such a mess of it. Did you see it?"
Bingley said he had, and offered his congratulations. Elizabeth didn't dare look up. How Mr. Darcy looked, therefore, she couldn't tell.

"It's a delightful thing, to be sure, to have a daughter well married," her mother continued, "but at the same time, Mr. Bingley, it's very hard to have her taken away. They've gone to Newcastle, a place quite far north it seems, and there they're to stay, I don't know how long. His regiment is there; for I suppose you've heard he's left the ——shire and joined the Regulars. Thank heavens he has some friends, though perhaps not so many as he deserves."

Elizabeth, who knew this last remark was aimed at Mr. Darcy, was in such agony of embarrassment that she could barely stay in her seat. It did, however, force her to speak, which nothing else had managed to do; and she asked Bingley whether he planned to stay long in the country. A few weeks, he thought.

"When you've shot all your own birds, Mr. Bingley," said her mother, "I hope you'll come here and shoot as many as you please on Mr. Bennet's land. I'm sure he'd be delighted, and will save the best coveys for you."

Elizabeth's misery increased at such unnecessary, such intrusive attention! If the same promising situation were to arise now as had flattered them a year ago, everything, she was sure, would rush toward the same disastrous conclusion. At that moment she felt that years of happiness couldn't make up to Jane or herself for moments of such painful embarrassment.
"My dearest wish," she said to herself, "is never to be in the same room with either of them again. Their company can offer no pleasure worth this misery! Let me never see either one again!"

Yet the suffering for which years of happiness supposedly couldn't compensate received considerable relief soon afterward, from watching the beauty of her sister rekindle the admiration of her former suitor. When he first arrived, he had spoken to Jane only briefly; but every five minutes seemed to bring her more of his attention. He found her as beautiful as the year before, as good-natured and as natural, though not quite as talkative. Jane was determined that no difference should be noticed, and truly believed she talked as much as ever; but her mind was so occupied that she didn't always realize when she was silent.
When the gentlemen rose to leave, Mrs. Bennet remembered her planned civility and they were invited to dine at Longbourn in a few days.

"You owe us quite a visit, Mr. Bingley," she added. "When you went to London last winter, you promised to take a family dinner with us as soon as you returned. I haven't forgotten, you see; and I was very disappointed that you didn't come back and keep your word."
Bingley looked slightly sheepish at this reproach and said something about having been prevented by business. They then left.

Mrs. Bennet had been strongly tempted to ask them to stay for dinner that day; but though she always kept a generous table, she didn't think anything less than two courses would be good enough for a man she had such ambitious designs on, or would satisfy the appetite and pride of one who had ten thousand a year.

chapters.title: Chapter 54
paragraphs: As soon as they were gone, Elizabeth walked out to recover her spirits—or in other words, to dwell without interruption on the very subjects that would crush them further. Mr. Darcy's behavior astonished and frustrated her.
"Why, if he came only to be silent, serious, and distant," she said, "did he come at all?"
She couldn't make sense of it in any way that satisfied her.

"He could still be warm and pleasant to my uncle and aunt when he was in London—so why not to me? If he's afraid of me, why come here? If he no longer cares for me, why be silent? Infuriating, infuriating man! I will think no more about him."
Her resolution was briefly enforced by the approach of her sister, who joined her with a cheerful expression that showed she was more satisfied with their visitors than Elizabeth was.

"Now," she said, "that this first meeting is over, I feel perfectly at ease. I know my own strength, and I shall never be embarrassed again by his coming. I'm glad he's dining here on Tuesday. It will then be publicly clear that we meet only as ordinary, indifferent acquaintances."
"Yes, very indifferent indeed," said Elizabeth, laughing. "Oh, Jane! Be careful."
"My dear Lizzy, you can't think me so weak as to be in danger now."
"I think you're in very great danger of making him as much in love with you as ever."

They didn't see the gentlemen again until Tuesday; and Mrs. Bennet, in the meantime, was giving way to all the happy schemes that Bingley's good humor and common courtesy, in a half hour's visit, had revived.

On Tuesday a large party gathered at Longbourn; and the two who were most anxiously awaited arrived, to the credit of their punctuality as sportsmen, in very good time. When they moved to the dining room, Elizabeth eagerly watched to see whether Bingley would take the seat that, at all their previous parties, had been next to her sister. Her calculating mother had the same idea and refrained from inviting him to sit by herself. On entering the room, he seemed to hesitate; but Jane happened to look around and happened to smile; and that decided it. He sat down beside her.

Elizabeth, with a triumphant feeling, looked toward his friend. He appeared nobly indifferent; and she would have imagined Bingley had received Darcy's blessing to be happy, had she not seen his eyes also turn toward Mr. Darcy with an expression of half-amused alarm.

His behavior toward Jane during dinner showed an admiration which, though more guarded than before, persuaded Elizabeth that if left to himself, Jane's happiness and his own would soon be settled. Though she dared not count on the outcome, she took pleasure from observing his manner. It gave her all the energy her spirits could muster; for she herself was far from cheerful. Mr. Darcy was nearly as far from her as the table allowed. He was on one side of her mother. She knew how little pleasure that arrangement would give either of them, or allow either to appear to advantage. She was too far away to hear their conversation, but she could see how seldom they spoke, and how formal and cold they were when they did. Her mother's rudeness made the weight of their debt to him all the more painful to Elizabeth; and she would, at times, have given anything to be allowed to tell him that his kindness was neither unknown nor unappreciated by the whole family.

She hoped the evening would provide some chance to bring them together—that the entire visit wouldn't pass without something more than the polite greeting that had accompanied his entrance. Anxious and restless, the period in the drawing room before the gentlemen arrived was tedious and dull to a degree that almost made her rude. She looked forward to their entrance as the moment on which all her chances of enjoying the evening depended.
"If he doesn't come to me then," she said, "I shall give him up forever."

The gentlemen came; and she thought he looked as if he would have come to her—but alas, the ladies had crowded so closely around the table where Jane was making tea and Elizabeth pouring coffee that there wasn't a single empty seat near her. And as the gentlemen approached, one of the girls moved even closer and whispered—
"The men aren't going to separate us. I'm determined. We don't want any of them, do we?"

Darcy had walked to another part of the room. She followed him with her eyes, envied everyone he spoke to, could barely concentrate on serving coffee, and then was furious with herself for being so silly!

"A man who has already been refused! How could I ever be foolish enough to expect a renewed proposal? Is there a man alive who wouldn't resist the indignity of proposing twice to the same woman? There is no insult more offensive to their pride."
She was slightly cheered, however, when he brought back his coffee cup himself; and she seized the opportunity to say—
"Is your sister still at Pemberley?"
"Yes; she'll stay there until Christmas."
"And quite alone? Have all her friends left?"
"Mrs. Annesley is with her. The others have been in Scarborough for three weeks."

She could think of nothing more to say; but if he wanted to talk, he might have done better. He stood by her for some minutes in silence; and at last, when the young lady whispered to Elizabeth again, he walked away.

When the tea things were cleared and the card tables set up, the ladies all rose; and Elizabeth was hoping to be joined by him when all her hopes collapsed—she saw him fall victim to her mother's desperate need for whist players, and within moments he was seated at a card table with the rest. She had now lost all expectation of pleasure. They were stuck at different tables for the evening, and she had nothing to hope for except that his eyes were turned so often toward her side of the room as to make him play as badly as she did.
Mrs. Bennet had planned to keep both Netherfield gentlemen for supper; but their carriage was, unfortunately, ordered before anyone else's, and she had no chance to detain them.

"Well, girls," she said as soon as they were alone, "what do you think of the day? I think everything went wonderfully well. The dinner was as beautifully prepared as any I've ever seen. The venison was cooked to perfection—and everyone said they'd never seen such a fat piece. The soup was fifty times better than what we had at the Lucases' last week; and even Mr. Darcy admitted that the partridges were remarkably well done—and I suppose he has at least two or three French chefs. And, my dear Jane, I never saw you looking more beautiful. Mrs. Long said so too, because I asked her. And do you know what else she said? 'Ah, Mrs. Bennet, we shall have her at Netherfield at last!' She did indeed. I think Mrs. Long is as good a soul as ever lived—and her nieces are very well-behaved girls, and not at all pretty. I like them enormously."

Mrs. Bennet, in short, was in very high spirits. She had seen enough of Bingley's behavior toward Jane to be convinced she would get him in the end; and her expectations for the family's advantage, when she was in a happy mood, went so far beyond reason that she was quite disappointed he didn't come back the next day to propose.
"It's been a very pleasant day," said Jane to Elizabeth. "The party seemed so well chosen, so well matched. I hope we may often meet again."
Elizabeth smiled.

"Lizzy, you must not do that. You must not suspect me. It hurts me. I assure you I have now learned to enjoy his conversation as that of a pleasant, sensible young man, without any wishes beyond that. I am perfectly satisfied from his manners now that he never had any intention of winning my heart. It's only that he's blessed with greater charm and a stronger desire to please than any other man."
"You are very cruel," said her sister. "You won't let me smile, and you're provoking me to it every moment."
"How hard it is in some cases to be believed! And how impossible in others! But why should you want to persuade me that I feel more than I admit?"

"That is a question I hardly know how to answer. We all love to give advice, though we can only teach what isn't worth knowing. Forgive me; and if you insist on indifference, don't make me your confidante."

chapters.title: Chapter 55
paragraphs: A few days after this visit, Mr. Bingley called again, and alone. His friend had left for London that morning but was to return in ten days. He sat with them for over an hour and was in remarkably good spirits. Mrs. Bennet invited him to dinner, but with many expressions of regret, he confessed he was already engaged elsewhere.
"Next time you call," she said, "I hope we'll be more fortunate."
He said he would be particularly happy at any time, etc., etc.; and if she would give him permission, would visit again soon.
"Can you come tomorrow?"
Yes, he had nothing planned for tomorrow; and her invitation was accepted eagerly.
He came, and so early that none of the ladies were dressed. Mrs. Bennet ran into her daughters' room in her dressing gown, her hair half done, crying out—
"My dear Jane, hurry and come downstairs. He's here—Mr. Bingley is here. He is, truly. Hurry, hurry. Here, Sarah, come help Miss Bennet with her dress this instant. Never mind Miss Lizzy's hair."
"We'll be down as soon as we can," said Jane, "but I'm sure Kitty is ahead of us—she went upstairs half an hour ago."
"Oh, forget Kitty! What does she matter? Come, be quick! Where is your sash, dear?"
But when her mother had gone, Jane wouldn't go down without one of her sisters.

The same eagerness to get everyone else out of the room was visible again in the evening. After tea, Mr. Bennet retired to the library as usual, and Mary went upstairs to her piano. With two of the five obstacles removed, Mrs. Bennet sat winking and gesturing at Elizabeth and Kitty for a considerable time, without making any impression. Elizabeth refused to notice; and when Kitty finally did, she said innocently, "What's the matter, Mama? Why do you keep winking at me? What am I supposed to do?"
"Nothing, child, nothing. I didn't wink at you." She sat still for five more minutes; but unable to waste such a precious opportunity, she suddenly got up and, saying to Kitty—

"Come here, dear, I want to talk to you"—took her out of the room. Jane instantly gave Elizabeth a look that conveyed her distress at such scheming and her plea not to give in to it. Within minutes, Mrs. Bennet half-opened the door and called—
"Lizzy, dear, I want to speak with you."
Elizabeth was forced to go.
"We might as well leave them alone, you know," said her mother as soon as she was in the hall. "Kitty and I are going upstairs to sit in my dressing room."
Elizabeth made no attempt to argue with her mother but stayed quietly in the hall until she and Kitty were out of sight, then returned to the drawing room.

Mrs. Bennet's plans for that day failed. Bingley was everything that was charming, except the declared lover of her daughter. His ease and cheerfulness made him a most agreeable addition to the evening; and he endured the mother's heavy-handed interference and heard all her foolish remarks with a patience and composure particularly grateful to the daughter.
He hardly needed an invitation to stay for supper; and before he left, an arrangement was made—mostly through his own and Mrs. Bennet's efforts—for him to come shoot with Mr. Bennet the next morning.

After this day, Jane said no more about her indifference. Not a word passed between the sisters about Bingley; but Elizabeth went to bed happily certain that everything must soon be settled, unless Mr. Darcy returned later than planned. She did seriously believe, however, that all this must be happening with that gentleman's approval.

Bingley was punctual to his appointment; and he and Mr. Bennet spent the morning together as agreed. The latter was much more agreeable than his companion had expected. There was nothing foolish or presumptuous about Bingley to provoke his ridicule or put him off; and he was more talkative and less eccentric than Mr. Bennet had ever seen him. Bingley naturally returned with him to dinner; and in the evening Mrs. Bennet's ingenuity was again at work clearing everyone from the room. Elizabeth, who had a letter to write, went to the breakfast room for that purpose soon after tea; for since the others were all going to play cards, she wouldn't be missed to counteract her mother's plots.

But when she returned to the drawing room, her letter finished, she saw, to her astonishment, that there was reason to fear her mother had been too clever for her own good. Opening the door, she found her sister and Bingley standing together by the fireplace, clearly in the middle of an earnest conversation; and had this not been enough to arouse suspicion, the faces of both, as they hastily turned and moved apart, would have told everything. Their situation was awkward enough; but hers, she felt, was worse. Not a word was spoken by either; and Elizabeth was about to leave again when Bingley, who like the others had sat down, suddenly stood, whispered a few words to her sister, and rushed from the room.
Jane could keep nothing from Elizabeth when sharing it would bring happiness; and instantly embracing her, she acknowledged, with the deepest emotion, that she was the happiest person in the world.
"It's too much!" she added. "Far too much. I don't deserve it. Oh, why isn't everyone as happy?"

Elizabeth's congratulations were given with a sincerity, a warmth, and a delight that words could only poorly express. Every kind word was a fresh source of happiness to Jane. But she wouldn't let herself stay or say even half of what she wanted, for the moment.

"I must go to our mother immediately," she cried. "I wouldn't dream of trifling with her affectionate concern, or letting her hear it from anyone but me. He's gone to our father already. Oh, Lizzy, to know that what I have to tell will give such pleasure to all my dear family! How shall I bear so much happiness?"
She then hurried away to her mother, who had purposely broken up the card party and was sitting upstairs with Kitty.
Elizabeth, left alone, smiled at the speed and ease with which a matter that had given them so many months of suspense and frustration had been finally settled.
"And this," she said, "is the end of all his friend's anxious meddling! Of all his sister's dishonesty and scheming! The happiest, wisest, and most reasonable conclusion!"
In a few minutes she was joined by Bingley, whose meeting with her father had been brief and to the point.
"Where is your sister?" he said eagerly, opening the door.
"Upstairs with my mother. She'll be down in a moment, I'm sure."

He then closed the door and, coming up to her, claimed the good wishes and affection of a sister. Elizabeth honestly and warmly expressed her delight at the prospect of their relationship. They shook hands with great warmth; and then, until her sister came down, she had to listen to everything he wanted to say about his own happiness and Jane's perfections. And despite his being a man in love, Elizabeth really believed all his expectations of happiness were well founded, because they rested on the excellent understanding and wonderful disposition of Jane, and on a genuine similarity of feeling and taste between them.

It was an evening of uncommon delight for them all. The joy in Miss Bennet's heart gave her face such a glow of sweet radiance that she looked more beautiful than ever. Kitty giggled and smiled, hoping her turn would come soon. Mrs. Bennet couldn't give her blessing or express her approval warmly enough to match her feelings, though she talked to Bingley of nothing else for half an hour. And when Mr. Bennet joined them at supper, his voice and manner plainly showed how truly happy he was.
Not a word, however, did he say about it until their visitor had left for the night; but as soon as he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said—
"Jane, congratulations. You will be a very happy woman."
Jane went to him at once, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

"You are a good girl," he replied, "and I have great pleasure in thinking you'll be so happily settled. I have no doubt you'll do very well together. Your temperaments are not at all unlike. You're each so agreeable that nothing will ever be decided; so easy-going that every servant will cheat you; and so generous that you will always spend more than your income."
"I hope not. Carelessness with money would be unforgivable in me."

"Spend more than their income! My dear Mr. Bennet," cried his wife, "what are you talking about? He has four or five thousand a year, and very likely more." Then to her daughter, "Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I'm sure I won't sleep a wink tonight. I knew it would happen. I always said it must. I was sure you couldn't be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, the very first moment I saw him when he came into Hertfordshire last year, I thought how likely it was you'd end up together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man that ever was seen!"

Wickham, Lydia—all were forgotten. Jane was now far and away her favorite child. At that moment she cared for no other. Her younger sisters soon began trying to extract from her whatever future benefits she might be able to provide.
Mary asked for the use of the library at Netherfield; and Kitty begged hard for a few balls there every winter.

Bingley, from this point on, was naturally a daily visitor at Longbourn; arriving frequently before breakfast and always staying past supper—unless some inconsiderate neighbor, who deserved nothing but scorn, had given him a dinner invitation he felt obliged to accept.

Elizabeth now had little time for conversation with her sister; for when Bingley was present, Jane had no attention to spare for anyone else. But she found herself very useful to both of them in those periods of separation that sometimes had to occur. When Jane was absent, Bingley always attached himself to Elizabeth for the pleasure of talking about Jane; and when Bingley was gone, Jane always sought the same relief.
"He made me so happy," she said one evening, "by telling me he had no idea I was in London last spring! I hadn't believed it possible."
"I suspected as much," replied Elizabeth. "But how did he explain it?"

"It must have been his sisters' doing. They certainly didn't encourage his acquaintance with me, which I can't wonder at, since he could have chosen so much more advantageously. But when they see, as I trust they will, that their brother is happy with me, they'll learn to accept it, and we'll be on good terms again—though we can never be what we once were."
"That is the most unforgiving speech I've ever heard you make," said Elizabeth. "Good for you! It would truly bother me to see you duped by Miss Bingley's pretended friendship again."
"Would you believe it, Lizzy—that when he went to London last November, he really loved me, and only a belief that I was indifferent kept him from coming back?"
"He made a little mistake, to be sure; but it speaks well of his modesty."
This naturally led to a burst of praise from Jane for his humility and the little value he placed on his own good qualities.

Elizabeth was glad to learn he hadn't revealed his friend's interference; for although Jane had the most generous and forgiving heart in the world, this was a detail that would certainly have prejudiced her against Darcy.

"I am definitely the most fortunate person who ever existed!" cried Jane. "Oh, Lizzy, why am I so singled out from my family, and blessed above them all? If only I could see you as happy! If there were another man just like him for you!"

"If you gave me forty such men, I could never be as happy as you. Until I have your temperament and goodness, I can never have your happiness. No, no—let me manage for myself; and perhaps, if I'm very lucky, I'll find another Mr. Collins in time."

The state of affairs in the Bennet family couldn't remain a secret long. Mrs. Bennet was granted the privilege of whispering it to Mrs. Philips, who ventured, without any permission, to tell all her neighbors in Meryton.
The Bennets were quickly declared the luckiest family in the world; though only a few weeks earlier, when Lydia first ran away, they had been universally judged as marked for misfortune.

chapters.title: Chapter 56
paragraphs: One morning, about a week after Bingley's engagement to Jane had been announced, as he and the women of the family were sitting together in the dining room, their attention was suddenly drawn to the window by the sound of a carriage; and they saw a chaise and four driving up to the house. It was too early for visitors, and the carriage didn't belong to any of their neighbors. The horses were hired post-horses, and neither the carriage nor the servant's livery was familiar. Since someone was clearly coming, however, Bingley immediately persuaded Jane to escape the intrusion and walk out with him into the garden. They both left; and the remaining three continued to speculate, with little satisfaction, until the door was thrown open and their visitor entered. It was Lady Catherine de Bourgh.
They were all prepared to be surprised, but their astonishment exceeded all expectations; and on the part of Mrs. Bennet and Kitty—though they had never met her—it was even greater than Elizabeth's.

She entered the room with an air more than usually unpleasant, gave no reply to Elizabeth's greeting beyond a slight nod, and sat down without a word. Elizabeth had mentioned her name to her mother when her Ladyship appeared, though no introduction had been requested.

Mrs. Bennet, completely bewildered but flattered by a guest of such importance, received her with the utmost politeness. After sitting in silence for a moment, Lady Catherine said very stiffly to Elizabeth—
"I hope you are well, Miss Bennet. That lady, I suppose, is your mother?"
Elizabeth replied briefly that she was.
"And that, I suppose, is one of your sisters?"

"Yes, madam," said Mrs. Bennet, delighted to be speaking to a Lady Catherine. "She is my youngest but one. My youngest is recently married, and my eldest is somewhere on the grounds, walking with a young man who, I believe, will soon become part of the family."
"You have a very small park here," returned Lady Catherine after a short silence.
"It's nothing compared to Rosings, my Lady, I'm sure; but I assure you, it's much larger than Sir William Lucas's."
"This must be a most inconvenient sitting room for summer evenings; the windows face due west."
Mrs. Bennet assured her they never sat there after dinner, and then added—
"May I ask whether you left Mr. and Mrs. Collins well?"
"Yes, very well. I saw them the night before last."
Elizabeth now expected she would produce a letter from Charlotte, as that seemed the only likely reason for her visit. But no letter appeared, and she was completely baffled.
Mrs. Bennet, with great politeness, offered her Ladyship some refreshment; but Lady Catherine very firmly, and not very politely, declined everything. Then, standing up, she said to Elizabeth—
"Miss Bennet, there seemed to be a rather pretty little wilderness on one side of your lawn. I should like to take a turn in it, if you will come with me."
"Go, my dear," cried her mother, "and show her Ladyship around the different paths. I think she'll enjoy the hermitage."

Elizabeth obeyed; and running to her room for her parasol, accompanied her noble guest downstairs. As they passed through the hall, Lady Catherine opened the doors to the dining room and drawing room, pronounced them, after a brief inspection, to be decent-looking rooms, and walked on.

Her carriage remained at the door, and Elizabeth saw that her lady's maid was waiting inside it. They proceeded in silence along the gravel path leading to the copse; Elizabeth was determined to make no effort at conversation with a woman who was now more than usually arrogant and disagreeable.
"How could I ever have thought her like her nephew?" she said to herself, looking at her face.
As soon as they entered the copse, Lady Catherine began—
"You can be in no doubt, Miss Bennet, as to the reason for my journey. Your own heart, your own conscience must tell you why I have come."
Elizabeth looked at her with genuine surprise.
"Indeed, you are mistaken, madam. I have been entirely unable to account for the honor of seeing you here."

"Miss Bennet," replied her Ladyship angrily, "you should know that I am not to be trifled with. But however insincere you may choose to be, you will not find me so. My character has always been celebrated for its honesty and directness, and in a matter of such importance I shall certainly not abandon them. A report of a most alarming nature reached me two days ago. I was told that not only was your sister about to be most advantageously married, but that you—that Miss Elizabeth Bennet—would in all likelihood soon be united with my nephew—my own nephew, Mr. Darcy. Though I know this must be a scandalous falsehood—though I would not insult him so much as to suppose it true—I immediately set out for this place, to make my feelings known to you."
"If you believed it to be impossible," said Elizabeth, coloring with astonishment and contempt, "I wonder you took the trouble of coming so far. What could your Ladyship hope to achieve?"
"To insist that such a report be universally denied."
"Your coming to Longbourn to see me and my family," said Elizabeth coolly, "will more likely confirm it—if such a report even exists."
"If! Do you pretend to be ignorant of it? Has it not been deliberately spread by yourselves? Do you not know that such a report is circulating?"
"I never heard that it was."
"And can you also declare that there is no foundation for it?"
"I do not claim to be as blunt as your Ladyship. You may ask questions that I shall choose not to answer."
"This is intolerable. Miss Bennet, I insist on being satisfied. Has he—has my nephew—made you an offer of marriage?"
"Your Ladyship has declared it to be impossible."

"It ought to be; it must be, while he has the use of his reason. But your arts and charms may, in a moment of weakness, have made him forget what he owes to himself and his family. You may have lured him in."
"If I have, I shall be the last to admit it."
"Miss Bennet, do you know who I am? I am not accustomed to such language. I am almost his nearest living relative and have every right to know his most important concerns."
"But you have no right to know mine; nor will behavior like this ever make me willing to share them."
"Let me be perfectly clear. This match, which you have the presumption to aspire to, can never take place. Never. Mr. Darcy is engaged to my daughter. Now, what have you to say?"
"Only this: that if he is, you have no reason to think he would make an offer to me."
Lady Catherine hesitated a moment, then replied—

"The engagement between them is of a special kind. From infancy they have been intended for each other. It was the dearest wish of his mother, as well as mine. While they were still in their cradles, we planned the union; and now, at the moment when the wishes of both sisters would be fulfilled, is their marriage to be prevented by a young woman of inferior birth, of no importance in the world, and with no connection to the family? Have you no regard for the wishes of his friends—for his understanding with Miss de Bourgh? Are you lost to all sense of propriety and decency? Have you not heard me say that from his earliest days he was destined for his cousin?"

"Yes, and I had heard it before. But what is that to me? If there is no other objection to my marrying your nephew, I certainly won't be deterred by knowing that his mother and aunt wanted him to marry Miss de Bourgh. You both did your best to arrange the match. But its completion depended on others. If Mr. Darcy is bound to his cousin by neither honor nor personal inclination, why shouldn't he make another choice? And if I am that choice, why may I not accept him?"

"Because honor, propriety, prudence—and indeed self-interest—forbid it. Yes, Miss Bennet, self-interest; for do not expect to be recognized by his family or friends if you willfully defy everyone's wishes. You will be criticized, snubbed, and despised by everyone connected with him. Your alliance will be a disgrace; your name will never even be mentioned by any of us."

"These are heavy punishments," replied Elizabeth. "But the wife of Mr. Darcy must have such extraordinary advantages attached to her position that, on the whole, she would have no cause for complaint."

"Stubborn, headstrong girl! I am ashamed of you! Is this your gratitude for my kindness to you last spring? Do I deserve nothing for that? Let us sit down. You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here with the firm intention of getting my way, and I will not be put off. I am not used to giving in to anyone's whims. I have never tolerated disappointment."
"That will make your Ladyship's current situation all the more unpleasant; but it will have no effect on me."

"I will not be interrupted! Hear me in silence. My daughter and my nephew are made for each other. They are descended, on their mothers' side, from the same noble family; and on their fathers', from respectable, honorable, and ancient, though untitled, families. Their fortunes on both sides are magnificent. They are destined for each other by every member of their respective families; and what is to stand in the way? The upstart ambitions of a young woman without family, connections, or fortune! Is this to be tolerated? But it must not—shall not—be! If you understood your own best interests, you would not want to leave the sphere in which you were raised."
"In marrying your nephew, I would not consider myself as leaving that sphere. He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are equal."
"True. You are a gentleman's daughter. But who was your mother? Who are your uncles and aunts? Do not imagine me ignorant of their situation."
"Whatever my connections may be," said Elizabeth, "if your nephew doesn't object to them, they are nothing to you."
"Tell me, once and for all—are you engaged to him?"
Though Elizabeth would not have answered this question merely to oblige Lady Catherine, she couldn't help saying, after a moment's thought—
"I am not."
Lady Catherine seemed pleased.
"And will you promise me never to enter into such an engagement?"
"I will make no promise of the kind."

"Miss Bennet, I am shocked and astonished. I expected to find a more reasonable young woman. But do not deceive yourself into thinking I will ever back down. I will not leave until you give me the assurance I require."

"And I certainly never shall. I will not be bullied into anything so utterly unreasonable. Your Ladyship wants Mr. Darcy to marry your daughter; but would my giving you the promise you want make their marriage any more likely? Supposing he were attached to me, would my refusing his hand make him want to offer it to his cousin? Allow me to say, Lady Catherine, that the arguments you've brought in support of this extraordinary demand have been as flimsy as the demand itself was inappropriate. You have badly mistaken my character if you think I can be manipulated by such tactics. How far your nephew might approve of your interference in his affairs I can't say, but you have certainly no right to interfere in mine. I must beg you not to raise the subject again."

"Not so fast, if you please. I have by no means finished. To all the objections I've already raised, I have yet another. I am well aware of the details of your youngest sister's disgraceful elopement. I know everything—that the young man's marrying her was a patched-up arrangement, paid for by your father and uncle. And is such a girl to be my nephew's sister? Is her husband, the son of his late father's steward, to be his brother? Heaven and earth! What are you thinking? Are the grounds of Pemberley to be so polluted?"
"You can now have nothing further to say," she answered angrily. "You have insulted me in every possible way. I must ask to return to the house."
And she rose as she spoke. Lady Catherine rose too, and they turned back. Her Ladyship was furious.
"You have no regard, then, for the honor and reputation of my nephew! Heartless, selfish girl! Do you not see that a connection with you must disgrace him in everyone's eyes?"
"Lady Catherine, I have nothing more to say. You know my position."
"You are determined to have him, then?"
"I have said no such thing. I am only determined to act in whatever way I believe will make me happy, without reference to you or to anyone so completely unconnected with me."

"Very well. You refuse to oblige me. You refuse to obey the claims of duty, honor, and gratitude. You are determined to ruin him in the opinion of all his friends and make him the laughingstock of the world."

"Neither duty, nor honor, nor gratitude," replied Elizabeth, "has any claim on me in this matter. My marrying Mr. Darcy would violate no principle of any kind. And as for the anger of his family or the scorn of the world—if the former were caused by his marrying me, it wouldn't give me a moment's concern; and the world in general would have too much sense to join in."

"And this is your honest opinion! This is your final answer! Very well. I shall now know how to act. Do not imagine, Miss Bennet, that your ambition will ever be gratified. I came to test you. I hoped to find you reasonable; but depend upon it, I will have my way."
In this manner Lady Catherine talked on until they reached the carriage door, when she turned abruptly and added—
"I take no leave of you, Miss Bennet. I send no regards to your mother. You deserve no such courtesy. I am deeply displeased."

Elizabeth made no reply; and without trying to persuade her Ladyship to return to the house, walked quietly inside. She heard the carriage drive away as she went upstairs. Her mother met her impatiently at the door of her dressing room, wanting to know why Lady Catherine wouldn't come in again and rest.
"She didn't want to," said her daughter. "She had to go."

"She's a very fine-looking woman! And her calling here was extraordinarily kind! She only came, I suppose, to tell us the Collinses were well. She's on her way somewhere, I'm sure, and just thought she'd stop by since she was passing through Meryton. I suppose she had nothing particular to say to you, Lizzy?"
Elizabeth was forced to tell a small lie here; for to admit the substance of their conversation was impossible.

chapters.title: Chapter 57
paragraphs: The agitation this extraordinary visit threw Elizabeth into was not easily overcome; nor could she, for many hours, stop thinking about it. Lady Catherine had actually taken the trouble to travel all the way from Rosings for the sole purpose of breaking off her supposed engagement to Mr. Darcy. It was a rational plan, to be sure! But where the rumor of their engagement could have started, Elizabeth was at a loss to imagine—until she remembered that his being Bingley's close friend, and her being Jane's sister, was enough, at a time when one wedding made everyone eager for another, to plant the idea. She herself hadn't forgotten that her sister's marriage must bring them together more often. And her neighbors at Lucas Lodge—through whom the report had reached Lady Catherine via the Collinses, she concluded—had simply taken as almost certain and imminent what she had merely considered possible at some future time.

Reviewing Lady Catherine's words, however, she couldn't help feeling some unease about the possible consequences. From what she had said about her determination to prevent the match, it seemed likely she would go directly to her nephew; and how he might respond to a similar presentation of the problems with a connection to Elizabeth, she couldn't predict. She didn't know the strength of his attachment to his aunt or his respect for her judgment, but it was natural to suppose he valued her opinion more highly than Elizabeth did. And it was certain that, in listing the disadvantages of a match with someone whose immediate family was so far beneath his own, his aunt would be striking at his weakest point. With his ideas about dignity, he would probably find that arguments which had seemed weak and absurd to Elizabeth contained a great deal of good sense.

If he had been wavering—as had often seemed likely—the advice and pressure of so close a relative might settle his doubts and decide him once and for all to be as happy as his unblemished dignity would allow. In that case he would never return. Lady Catherine might catch him on her way through London, and his promise to Bingley about coming back to Netherfield would be quietly broken.

"If, therefore, an excuse for not keeping his promise reaches his friend within a few days," she added, "I shall know exactly what it means. I shall then give up all expectation, every hope of his constancy. If he is content to merely regret me, when he might have had my love and my hand, I shall soon cease to regret him at all."

The surprise of the rest of the family at learning who their visitor had been was considerable; but they satisfied their curiosity with the same kind of explanation that had appeased Mrs. Bennet, and Elizabeth was spared much questioning on the subject.
The next morning, as she was going downstairs, she was met by her father coming out of his library with a letter in his hand.
"Lizzy," he said, "I was just looking for you. Come into my room."

She followed him, and her curiosity about what he had to tell was heightened by the thought that it might be connected to the letter he held. It suddenly struck her that it might be from Lady Catherine, and she dreaded the explanations that would follow.
She followed her father to the fireplace, and they both sat down. He then said—

"I received a letter this morning that has completely astonished me. Since it mainly concerns you, you should know its contents. I had no idea I had two daughters on the brink of matrimony. Let me congratulate you on a very important conquest."

Elizabeth's face flushed instantly, certain the letter was from the nephew rather than the aunt; and she couldn't decide whether to be pleased that he was writing at all or offended that the letter wasn't addressed to her—when her father continued—

"You look as though you know something. Young ladies have great insight in these matters; but even your cleverness, I think, will fail to guess the name of your admirer. This letter is from Mr. Collins."
"From Mr. Collins! And what can he have to say?"

"Something very much to the point, naturally. He begins with congratulations on the approaching marriage of my eldest daughter, which he has apparently heard about from the helpful, gossiping Lucases. I won't bore you by reading what he says about that. What concerns you is this: 'Having offered you the sincere congratulations of Mrs. Collins and myself on this happy event, let me add a brief note on another subject, of which we have been informed by the same source. Your daughter Elizabeth, it is presumed, will not long bear the name of Bennet after her elder sister has given it up; and the chosen partner of her fate may reasonably be looked up to as one of the most distinguished personages in this land.' Can you possibly guess, Lizzy, who is meant? 'This young gentleman is blessed, in a special way, with everything the heart of mortal can most desire—magnificent property, noble family, and powerful connections. Yet, despite all these enticements, let me warn my cousin Elizabeth, and yourself, of the dangers you may face by too hastily accepting this gentleman's proposals, which you will of course be eager to do.' Have you any idea, Lizzy, who this gentleman is? But now it comes out. 'My reason for cautioning you is as follows: we have reason to believe that his aunt, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, does not look on the match with a friendly eye.' Mr. Darcy, you see, is the man! Now, Lizzy, I think I have surprised you. Could he, or the Lucases, have picked any man in our entire circle of acquaintance whose name would have more completely contradicted what they claimed? Mr. Darcy, who never looks at any woman except to find a flaw, and who probably never looked at you in his life! It's priceless!"
Elizabeth tried to join in her father's amusement, but could only force one very reluctant smile. Never had his wit been aimed in a way so unpleasant to her.
"Aren't you entertained?"
"Oh, yes. Please read on."

"'After mentioning the likelihood of this marriage to her Ladyship last night, she immediately, with her usual graciousness, expressed her feelings; and it became clear that, on the basis of certain family objections on my cousin's side, she would never consent to what she called so disgraceful a match. I felt it my duty to inform my cousin at once, so that she and her noble admirer may know what they're doing, and not rush into a marriage that has not been properly sanctioned.' Mr. Collins adds, 'I am truly glad that my cousin Lydia's sad business has been so well hushed up, and am only concerned that their living together before the marriage should have been so widely known. I must not, however, neglect the duties of my position, or refrain from expressing my shock that you received the young couple into your house as soon as they were married. It was an encouragement of vice; and had I been the rector of Longbourn, I should have strongly opposed it. You ought certainly to forgive them as a Christian, but never to admit them into your sight, or allow their names to be mentioned in your hearing.' That is his notion of Christian forgiveness! The rest of his letter is about dear Charlotte's condition, and his expectation of a young addition to the family. But, Lizzy, you look as if you're not enjoying this. You're not going to be prim, I hope, and pretend to be offended by a silly rumor. For what do we live, but to amuse our neighbors and laugh at them in turn?"
"Oh," cried Elizabeth, "I'm enormously diverted. But it's so strange!"

"Yes, that's what makes it funny. Had they picked any other man it would have been nothing; but his perfect indifference and your open dislike make it so delightfully absurd! Much as I hate writing, I wouldn't give up Mr. Collins's correspondence for anything. In fact, when I read one of his letters, I almost prefer him to Wickham, much as I value my son-in-law's shamelessness and hypocrisy. And tell me, Lizzy, what did Lady Catherine say about this report? Did she come to withhold her consent?"

To this question his daughter replied only with a laugh; and since it had been asked without any real suspicion, she wasn't troubled by his repeating it. Elizabeth had never been more at a loss to make her feelings appear what they were not. It was necessary to laugh when she would rather have cried. Her father had cruelly wounded her by his comments about Mr. Darcy's indifference; and she could only wonder at such a lack of perception, or fear that instead of his seeing too little, she might have been imagining too much.

chapters.title: Chapter 58
paragraphs: Instead of receiving the expected excuses from his friend, Bingley was able to bring Darcy with him to Longbourn only a few days after Lady Catherine's visit. The gentlemen arrived early, and before Mrs. Bennet had time to mention having seen his aunt—something Elizabeth dreaded every moment—Bingley, wanting to be alone with Jane, suggested they all go for a walk. It was agreed. Mrs. Bennet never walked; Mary could never spare the time; but the remaining five set off together. Bingley and Jane soon fell behind, while Elizabeth, Kitty, and Darcy were left to entertain each other. Very little was said by any of them; Kitty was too afraid of Darcy to talk; Elizabeth was secretly forming a desperate resolution; and perhaps he was doing the same.

They walked toward the Lucases' because Kitty wanted to visit Maria; and since Elizabeth saw no reason to make it a group affair, when Kitty left them she went boldly on with Darcy alone. Now was the moment to carry out her resolution, and while her courage was high, she said—

"Mr. Darcy, I am a very selfish person, and for the sake of relieving my own feelings I don't care how much I may be hurting yours. I can no longer hold back from thanking you for your extraordinary kindness to my poor sister. Ever since I learned of it, I have been desperate to tell you how grateful I am. If the rest of my family knew, it would not be only my gratitude I would have to express."

"I am sorry, extremely sorry," replied Darcy, in a tone of surprise and emotion, "that you were ever told of something that might, seen in a wrong light, have caused you distress. I didn't think Mrs. Gardiner was so little to be trusted."

"You must not blame my aunt. Lydia's carelessness first let slip that you were involved; and after that, naturally, I couldn't rest until I knew the details. Let me thank you again and again, in the name of all my family, for that generous compassion that led you to take so much trouble and endure so many humiliations in order to find them."

"If you must thank me," he replied, "let it be for yourself alone. That the wish to make you happy might have strengthened the other reasons that drove me, I won't try to deny. But your family owes me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe I was thinking only of you."

Elizabeth was too embarrassed to say a word. After a short pause, he added, "You are too generous to play games with me. If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. My affections and wishes are unchanged; but one word from you will silence me on this subject forever."

Elizabeth, feeling all the awkwardness and anxiety of his situation, now forced herself to speak; and immediately, though not very smoothly, gave him to understand that her feelings had changed so completely since the time he referred to that she received his present assurances with gratitude and pleasure. The happiness this reply produced was greater than he had probably ever known; and he expressed himself on the occasion as warmly and as sensibly as a man deeply in love can be expected to do. Had Elizabeth been able to meet his eyes, she would have seen how well the expression of heartfelt delight that spread across his face became him; but though she couldn't look, she could listen, and he told her of feelings which, in proving how important she was to him, made his love more valuable with every moment.

They walked on without knowing which direction they were going. There was too much to think, feel, and say for them to notice anything else. She soon learned that they owed their present understanding to the efforts of his aunt, who had indeed called on him on her way back through London, and told him about her visit to Longbourn—its purpose and the substance of her conversation with Elizabeth—dwelling on every word of the latter which, in her Ladyship's view, showed particular defiance and audacity, in the belief that such a report would help her obtain from her nephew the promise Elizabeth had refused to give. But, unfortunately for her Ladyship, the effect had been exactly the opposite.

"It taught me to hope," he said, "as I had scarcely ever allowed myself to hope before. I knew enough of your character to be certain that if you were absolutely, irrevocably set against me, you would have said so to Lady Catherine frankly and openly."

Elizabeth blushed and laughed as she replied, "Yes, you know enough of my bluntness to believe me capable of that. After insulting you so horribly to your face, I could have had no qualms about insulting you to all your relatives."

"What did you say of me that I didn't deserve? For though your accusations were unfounded and based on wrong assumptions, my behavior toward you at the time had earned the harshest criticism. It was unforgivable. I cannot think of it without disgust."
"We will not quarrel over who bears more blame for that evening," said Elizabeth. "Neither of us, strictly examined, behaved well; but since then we have both, I hope, improved in civility."

"I cannot be so easily reconciled to myself. The memory of what I said—my conduct, my manners, my words during that whole scene—has been, and remains, unbearably painful. Your rebuke, so justly delivered, I shall never forget: 'Had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner.' Those were your words. You cannot imagine how they have tortured me—though I admit it was some time before I was reasonable enough to accept their justice."
"I was certainly far from expecting them to make such an impression. I had no idea they would ever be felt so deeply."

"I can well believe it. You thought me entirely without feeling, I'm sure. The look on your face I shall never forget, when you said I could not have proposed to you in any way that would have made you accept."
"Oh, don't repeat what I said then. Those memories won't do at all. I assure you, I have long been deeply ashamed of it."
Darcy mentioned his letter. "Did it," he said, "did it soon make you think better of me? Did you, on reading it, give any credit to its contents?"
She described the effect it had had on her, and how gradually all her former prejudices had been removed.

"I knew," he said, "that what I wrote must cause you pain, but it was necessary. I hope you have destroyed the letter. There was one part—especially the opening—that I would dread your being able to reread. I can remember some words that might justly make you hate me."

"The letter shall certainly be burned if you think it essential to preserving my regard; but though we both have reason to think my opinions aren't entirely unchangeable, they are not, I hope, quite so easily shifted as that implies."
"When I wrote that letter," replied Darcy, "I believed myself perfectly calm and composed; but I have since realized it was written in terrible bitterness of spirit."

"The letter may have begun in bitterness, but it didn't end that way. The closing is kindness itself. But let's think no more of the letter. The feelings of the person who wrote it and the person who received it are now so entirely different from what they were then that every unpleasant detail ought to be forgotten. You must learn some of my philosophy. Think of the past only as it gives you pleasure."

"I can't credit you with any such philosophy. Your memories must be so free of self-reproach that the contentment they bring comes not from philosophy but, what is far better, from innocence. But for me, it's not so. Painful memories will intrude, and they cannot and should not be pushed away. I have been a selfish man all my life, in practice though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temperament. I was given good principles but left to follow them with pride and arrogance. Unfortunately, as an only son—for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents, who, though good people themselves (my father especially, as kind and generous as anyone), allowed, encouraged, almost taught me to be selfish and domineering, to care for no one outside my own family circle, to think poorly of the rest of the world—to wish, at least, to think poorly of their intelligence and worth compared with my own. Such I was from eight to twenty-eight; and such I might still be, but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you! You taught me a lesson, hard at first but invaluable. By you I was properly humbled. I came to you without a doubt that I would be accepted. You showed me how completely inadequate were all my claims to please a woman worth pleasing."
"Had you really persuaded yourself that I would say yes?"
"Indeed I had. What will you think of my vanity? I believed you were waiting for, expecting, my proposal."

"My manner must have been at fault, but not intentionally, I assure you. I never meant to mislead you, but my high spirits may often have given the wrong impression. How you must have hated me after that evening!"
"Hate you! I was angry, perhaps, at first, but my anger soon found its proper target."
"I'm almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. You blamed me for coming?"
"No indeed. I felt nothing but surprise."
"Your surprise couldn't have been greater than mine at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no special kindness, and I confess I didn't expect more than my due."

"My aim then," replied Darcy, "was to show you, by every courtesy in my power, that I wasn't so petty as to resent the past; and I hoped to earn your forgiveness, to lessen your poor opinion, by showing you that I had taken your criticisms to heart. How soon other wishes crept in, I can hardly say, but I believe it was about half an hour after seeing you."

He then told her of Georgiana's delight in meeting her, and her disappointment at its sudden interruption—which naturally led to the cause of that interruption, and she soon learned that his decision to follow her from Derbyshire in pursuit of her sister had been made before he left the inn, and that his gravity and preoccupation there had come from no other struggle than what such a purpose required.
She expressed her gratitude again, but it was too painful a subject for either of them to dwell on.
After walking several miles at a leisurely pace, too absorbed to notice their surroundings, they found at last, on checking their watches, that it was time to go home.

"What can have happened to Mr. Bingley and Jane?" was a question that introduced a discussion of their affairs. Darcy was delighted with their engagement; his friend had told him at the first opportunity.
"I have to ask—were you surprised?" said Elizabeth.
"Not at all. When I left, I felt it would happen soon."
"That is to say, you had given your permission. I guessed as much." And though he protested at the word, she found that was pretty much the case.

"On the evening before I left for London," he said, "I made a confession to Bingley that I should have made long ago. I told him everything that had happened to make my earlier interference in his affairs absurd and inappropriate. His surprise was enormous—he had never had the slightest suspicion. I also told him that I believed I had been wrong to think, as I had, that your sister was indifferent to him; and since I could easily see that his feelings for her were unchanged, I had no doubt they would be happy together."
Elizabeth couldn't help smiling at his easy way of directing his friend.
"Did you speak from your own observation," she asked, "when you told him my sister loved him, or merely from what I said last spring?"
"From my own observation. I had watched her closely during the two recent visits I had made here, and I was convinced of her affection."
"And your assurance, I suppose, immediately convinced him."

"It did. Bingley is genuinely modest. His lack of confidence had prevented him from trusting his own judgment in something so important, but his faith in mine made everything easy. I was obliged to confess one thing, which for a time, and not unjustly, angered him. I couldn't bring myself to hide the fact that your sister had been in London for three months last winter, that I had known about it, and had deliberately kept it from him. He was angry. But his anger, I'm sure, lasted no longer than his doubt about your sister's feelings. He has now forgiven me wholeheartedly."

Elizabeth wanted to point out that Mr. Bingley was a most delightful friend—so easily led that his value was priceless—but she held back. She remembered that he had yet to learn to be teased, and it was rather too early to start. In anticipating the happiness of Bingley, which of course could only be surpassed by his own, he continued their conversation until they reached the house. In the hall they parted.

chapters.title: Chapter 59
paragraphs: "My dear Lizzy, where can you have been walking?" was the question Elizabeth received from Jane as soon as she entered the room, and from everyone else when they sat down to dinner. She had only to say they had wandered about until she lost track of where they were. She blushed as she spoke, but neither that nor anything else aroused a suspicion of the truth.

The evening passed quietly, without anything remarkable. The acknowledged lovers talked and laughed; the unacknowledged were silent. Darcy was not the kind of man whose happiness overflows in laughter; and Elizabeth, agitated and confused, was more aware that she was happy than she actually felt it. Besides the immediate embarrassment, there were other worries ahead. She anticipated the family's reaction when her situation became known; she was aware that no one liked him except Jane; and she even feared that, with the others, their dislike might not be overcome by all his wealth and importance.
That night she confided in Jane. Though suspicion was far from Miss Bennet's usual nature, she was absolutely incredulous.
"You're joking, Lizzy. This can't be! Engaged to Mr. Darcy! No, no, you won't fool me. I know it's impossible."

"This is a terrible beginning, indeed! My one hope was you; and I'm sure no one else will believe me if you don't. Yet I am in earnest. I'm telling nothing but the truth. He still loves me, and we are engaged."
Jane looked at her doubtfully. "Oh, Lizzy! It can't be. I know how much you dislike him."

"You know nothing about it. That's all to be forgotten. Perhaps I didn't always love him as well as I do now; but in cases like these, a good memory is unforgivable. This is the last time I shall ever think of it myself."
Miss Bennet still looked amazed. Elizabeth again, and more seriously, assured her it was true.

"Good heavens! Can it really be?" cried Jane. "Yet now I must believe you. My dear, dear Lizzy, I do congratulate you—but are you certain—forgive the question—are you quite certain you can be happy with him?"
"There can be no doubt of it. It's settled between us that we are to be the happiest couple in the world. But are you pleased, Jane? Will you like having such a brother?"

"Very, very much. Nothing could give Bingley or me more delight. But we had considered it impossible—we had even discussed it. And do you really love him enough? Oh, Lizzy! Do anything rather than marry without love. Are you quite sure you feel what you should?"
"Oh yes! You'll only think I feel more than I should when I tell you everything."
"What do you mean?"
"Well, I must confess that I love him better than I love Bingley. I'm afraid you'll be angry."
"Dearest sister, now please be serious. I want to talk very seriously. Let me know everything without delay. Will you tell me how long you have loved him?"
"It's been coming on so gradually that I hardly know when it began. But I think I must date it from my first sight of his beautiful grounds at Pemberley."
Another plea for seriousness produced the desired effect, and she soon satisfied Jane with solemn assurances of her attachment. Once convinced on that point, Jane had nothing more to wish for.

"Now I am truly happy," she said, "for you will be as happy as I am. I always valued him. Were it for nothing but his love for you, I should always have esteemed him; but now, as Bingley's friend and your husband, only Bingley and yourself can be dearer to me. But, Lizzy, you have been very secretive with me. How little you told me of what happened at Pemberley and Lambton! Everything I know about it came from someone else, not from you."

Elizabeth explained her reasons for secrecy. She had been unwilling to mention Bingley; and the unsettled state of her own feelings had made her equally avoid mentioning his friend. But now she would no longer hide from Jane his role in Lydia's marriage. Everything was acknowledged, and half the night was spent talking.

"Good gracious!" cried Mrs. Bennet, standing at the window the next morning. "If that unpleasant Mr. Darcy isn't coming here again with our dear Bingley! What can he mean by being such a nuisance, always showing up? I had no idea he'd do anything but go shooting or something and leave us in peace. What shall we do with him? Lizzy, you must walk out with him again so he won't get in Bingley's way."
Elizabeth could hardly help laughing at such a convenient suggestion; yet she was genuinely annoyed that her mother kept using such unflattering terms about him.

As soon as they arrived, Bingley looked at her so meaningfully and shook hands so warmly as to leave no doubt he knew; and he soon said aloud, "Mrs. Bennet, have you no more lanes around here where Lizzy might lose her way again today?"
"I suggest Mr. Darcy and Lizzy and Kitty walk to Oakham Mount this morning," said Mrs. Bennet. "It's a nice long walk, and Mr. Darcy has never seen the view."
"It may be fine for the others," replied Bingley, "but I'm sure it'll be too much for Kitty. Won't it, Kitty?"
Kitty said she'd rather stay home. Darcy expressed great curiosity about the view, and Elizabeth silently agreed. As she went upstairs to get ready, Mrs. Bennet followed, saying—

"I'm quite sorry, Lizzy, that you should be stuck with that unpleasant man all to yourself; but I hope you won't mind it. It's all for Jane's sake, you know; and there's no need to talk to him except now and then. So don't go to any trouble."

During their walk, it was decided that Mr. Bennet's consent should be sought that evening. Elizabeth reserved her mother's reaction for herself. She couldn't predict how her mother would take it—sometimes doubting whether all his wealth and status would be enough to overcome her dislike of the man; but whether she was violently opposed or violently delighted, her manner would be equally unsuitable. Elizabeth could no more bear to have Mr. Darcy witness the first outburst of her mother's joy than the first blast of her disapproval.

That evening, soon after Mr. Bennet withdrew to the library, she saw Mr. Darcy stand and follow him, and her anxiety at seeing it was extreme. She didn't fear her father's opposition, but he was about to be made unhappy—and that it should be through her, his favorite child, distressing him with her choice, filling him with fears and regrets—was a wretched thought. She sat in misery until Mr. Darcy reappeared, and looking at him, was slightly reassured by his smile. In a few minutes he came to the table where she sat with Kitty and, while pretending to admire her needlework, whispered, "Go to your father; he wants you in the library." She went at once.
Her father was pacing the room, looking serious and anxious. "Lizzy," he said, "what are you doing? Are you out of your mind, accepting this man? Haven't you always hated him?"

How earnestly she wished that her earlier opinions had been more reasonable, her words more measured! It would have spared her from explanations and professions that were extremely awkward to make. But they were necessary now, and she assured him, with some confusion, of her attachment to Mr. Darcy.
"Or, in other words, you're determined to have him. He is rich, to be sure, and you may have more fine clothes and carriages than Jane. But will they make you happy?"
"Have you any other objection," said Elizabeth, "besides your belief that I'm indifferent?"
"None at all. We all know him to be a proud, unpleasant sort of man; but that would be nothing if you really liked him."

"I do, I do like him," she replied with tears in her eyes. "I love him. He has no improper pride. He is perfectly good. You don't know what he really is; so please don't hurt me by speaking of him like that."

"Lizzy," said her father, "I have given him my consent. He is the kind of man to whom I could never dare refuse anything he asked. I now give my consent to you, if you are determined to have him. But let me advise you to think carefully. I know your nature, Lizzy. I know you could be neither happy nor respectable unless you truly respected your husband—unless you looked up to him. Your lively mind would put you in the greatest danger in an unequal marriage. You could scarcely escape unhappiness and disgrace. My child, do not let me suffer the grief of seeing you unable to respect your partner in life. You don't know what you're doing."

Elizabeth, even more moved, was earnest and solemn in her reply; and at last, by repeated assurances that Mr. Darcy was truly the man she had chosen, by explaining the gradual change her estimation of him had undergone, by declaring her absolute certainty that his love was no passing fancy but had withstood many months of uncertainty, and by passionately listing all his good qualities, she conquered her father's disbelief and reconciled him to the match.
"Well, my dear," he said when she finished, "I have no more to say. If this is the case, he deserves you. I could not have given you up, my Lizzy, to anyone less worthy."
To complete the favorable impression, she then told him what Mr. Darcy had voluntarily done for Lydia. He heard her with astonishment.

"This is an evening of wonders, indeed! So—Darcy did everything: arranged the marriage, put up the money, paid the man's debts, and got him his commission! So much the better. It will save me a world of trouble and expense. Had it been your uncle's doing, I would have had to repay him; but these passionate young lovers insist on having their way. I shall offer to pay him tomorrow; he'll rant and carry on about his love for you, and that will be the end of it."

He then remembered her embarrassment a few days ago when he read Mr. Collins's letter; and after laughing at her for some time, finally let her go, saying as she left the room, "If any young men come for Mary or Kitty, send them in—I'm quite free."

Elizabeth's mind was now freed from a very heavy burden; and after half an hour's quiet thought in her own room, she was able to rejoin the others with reasonable composure. Everything was too fresh for high spirits, but the evening passed peacefully; there was no longer anything serious to fear, and the comfort of ease and familiarity would come in time.

When her mother went to her dressing room that night, Elizabeth followed and made the important announcement. Its effect was extraordinary: on first hearing it, Mrs. Bennet sat perfectly still, unable to utter a syllable. Nor was it until many, many minutes had passed that she could take in what she'd heard—though she was generally not slow to believe anything that benefited her family, or that came in the form of a suitor for one of her daughters. She gradually recovered and began fidgeting in her chair, standing up, sitting down again, exclaiming and blessing herself.

"Good gracious! Lord bless me! Only think! Dear me! Mr. Darcy! Who would have thought it? And is it really true? Oh, my sweetest Lizzy! How rich and how grand you will be! What pin-money, what jewels, what carriages you will have! Jane's match is nothing to it—nothing at all. I am so pleased—so happy! Such a charming man! So handsome! So tall! Oh, my dear Lizzy! Please apologize for my having disliked him so much before. I hope he will overlook it. Dear, dear Lizzy. A house in London! Everything that is wonderful! Three daughters married! Ten thousand a year! Oh, Lord! What will become of me? I shall go mad."

This was enough to prove her approval wasn't in doubt; and Elizabeth, glad that such an outburst had been heard by no one but herself, soon left. But before she had been three minutes in her own room, her mother followed.

"My dearest child," she cried, "I can think of nothing else. Ten thousand a year, and very likely more! As good as a lord! And a special license—you must be married by special license. But, my dearest love, tell me what dish Mr. Darcy is particularly fond of, so I can have it tomorrow."

This was an ominous preview of how her mother might behave toward the gentleman himself; and Elizabeth found that, though she was now certain of his deepest love and assured of her family's consent, there was still something to be wished for. But the next day went much better than expected, because Mrs. Bennet was so much in awe of her future son-in-law that she hardly dared speak to him unless she could offer some attention or show deference to his opinion.
Elizabeth had the satisfaction of seeing her father make an effort to get to know him; and Mr. Bennet soon assured her that his esteem for Darcy was growing by the hour.
"I admire all three of my sons-in-law greatly," he said. "Wickham is perhaps my favorite; but I think I shall like your husband quite as well as Jane's."

chapters.title: Chapter 60
paragraphs: Elizabeth's spirits soon rising to playfulness again, she wanted Mr. Darcy to explain how he had ever fallen in love with her. "How could you begin?" she said. "I can understand your falling deeper in love once you'd started; but what first set you off?"
"I cannot fix on the hour, or the spot, or the look, or the words that laid the foundation. It was too long ago. I was in the middle before I knew I had begun."

"My beauty you had early resisted, and as for my manners—my behavior toward you was at least always bordering on rudeness, and I never spoke to you without rather wanting to hurt you than not. Now, be honest: did you admire me for my impertinence?"
"For the liveliness of your mind, I did."

"You might as well call it impertinence outright. It was barely anything less. The fact is, you were tired of civility, of deference, of people fawning over you. You were fed up with women who were always speaking and looking and thinking only for your approval. I intrigued you because I was so different. Had you not been genuinely good, you would have hated me for it; but despite all your efforts to disguise yourself, your instincts were always noble and fair, and in your heart you thoroughly despised those who courted you so eagerly. There—I've saved you the trouble of explaining it; and really, all things considered, I'm beginning to think it perfectly reasonable. Of course, you knew nothing actually good about me—but nobody thinks about that when they fall in love."
"Wasn't there good in your devoted care of Jane while she was ill at Netherfield?"

"Dearest Jane! Who could have done less for her? But by all means make it a virtue. My good qualities are under your protection, and you must exaggerate them as much as possible; and in return, it falls to me to find occasions for teasing and quarreling with you as often as may be. And I'll start right now, by asking what made you so reluctant to come to the point. What made you so shy of me when you first called, and afterward when you dined here? And especially—when you called—why did you look as if you didn't care about me?"
"Because you were serious and silent, and gave me no encouragement."
"But I was embarrassed."
"And so was I."
"You might have talked to me more when you came to dinner."
"A man who felt less might have."

"How annoying that you should have such a reasonable answer, and that I should be reasonable enough to accept it! But I wonder how long you would have gone on if left to yourself. I wonder when you would have spoken if I hadn't brought it up! My resolution to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly had a great effect. Too much, I fear; for what becomes of the moral if our happiness springs from a broken promise? I shouldn't have mentioned the subject at all. This will never do."

"Don't trouble yourself. The moral is perfectly sound. Lady Catherine's outrageous attempt to separate us was what removed all my doubts. I'm not indebted for my present happiness to your eagerness to express gratitude. I wasn't willing to wait for you to make an opening. My aunt's report had given me hope, and I was determined to learn everything at once."

"Lady Catherine has been enormously useful—which ought to make her happy, since she does love to be useful. But tell me, what did you come to Netherfield for? Was it merely to ride to Longbourn and be embarrassed? Or did you have more serious intentions?"

"My real purpose was to see you, and to judge, if I could, whether I might ever hope to make you love me. My stated purpose—or what I told myself—was to see whether your sister still cared for Bingley, and if so, to make the confession I have since made."
"Shall you ever have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what's in store for her?"
"I'm more likely to lack the time than the courage, Elizabeth. But it ought to be done; and if you'll give me a sheet of paper, I'll do it right now."

"And if I didn't have a letter of my own to write, I could sit beside you and admire the evenness of your handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt who must not be neglected any longer."

Reluctant to admit how much her closeness to Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had never yet answered Mrs. Gardiner's long letter; but now, having news she knew would be most welcome, she was almost ashamed to find that her uncle and aunt had already lost three days of happiness, and wrote at once—
