"I would have thanked you before, my dear aunt, as I ought to have done, for your long, kind, wonderfully detailed letter; but to tell the truth, I was too cross to write. You assumed more than was actually the case. But now assume as much as you like; give your imagination free rein; and unless you believe me actually married, you can hardly go wrong. You must write again very soon and praise him a great deal more than you did last time. I thank you again and again for not going to the Lakes. How silly of me to have wished it! Your idea about the ponies is delightful. We'll drive around the park every day. I am the happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so before, but no one with such justice. I am happier even than Jane; she only smiles—I laugh. Mr. Darcy sends you all the love in the world that can be spared from me. You are all to come to Pemberley at Christmas. Yours, etc."
Mr. Darcy's letter to Lady Catherine was in a different style; and different from either was what Mr. Bennet sent to Mr. Collins in reply to his last.
"Dear Sir,

"I must trouble you once more for congratulations. Elizabeth will soon be the wife of Mr. Darcy. Console Lady Catherine as well as you can. But, if I were you, I would side with the nephew. He has more to give.
"Yours sincerely," etc.

Miss Bingley's congratulations to her brother on his approaching marriage were as affectionate as they were insincere. She even wrote to Jane to express her delight and repeat all her old claims of friendship. Jane was not fooled, but she was touched; and though she put no faith in it, she couldn't help writing a much kinder reply than she knew was deserved.

The joy Miss Darcy expressed on receiving the same news was as genuine as her brother's in sending it. Four pages were not enough to contain all her delight and her earnest wish to be loved by her new sister.

Before any reply could come from Mr. Collins, or any congratulations to Elizabeth from his wife, the Longbourn family heard that the Collinses had come to Lucas Lodge in person. The reason for this sudden move was soon clear. Lady Catherine had been made so furious by her nephew's letter that Charlotte, who was genuinely happy about the match, wanted to get away until the storm blew over. At such a moment, the arrival of her friend was a real pleasure to Elizabeth; though in the course of their meetings she sometimes felt the pleasure was dearly bought, seeing Mr. Darcy subjected to all the fawning and obsequious politeness of her husband. He bore it, however, with remarkable calm. He could even listen to Sir William Lucas complimenting him on carrying off the brightest jewel of the county, and expressing hopes of their all meeting frequently at St. James's, with very decent composure. If he did shrug his shoulders, it wasn't until Sir William was out of sight.

Mrs. Philips's vulgarity was another, and perhaps greater, test of his patience; and though Mrs. Philips, like her sister, stood in too much awe of him to speak with the familiarity that Bingley's good nature encouraged, whenever she did speak she was inevitably coarse. Nor was her respectfulness, though it made her quieter, at all likely to make her more refined. Elizabeth did everything she could to shield him from the frequent attention of either aunt, and was always anxious to keep him to herself and to those members of her family whose company wouldn't cause him embarrassment. And though the uncomfortable feelings arising from all this took away much of the pleasure of courtship, they added to her hopes for the future; and she looked forward with delight to the time when they would be removed from a social circle so unpleasant to either of them, to all the comfort and elegance of their family life at Pemberley.

chapters.title: Chapter 61
paragraphs: Happy for all her maternal feelings was the day on which Mrs. Bennet got rid of her two most deserving daughters. With what delighted pride she afterward visited Mrs. Bingley and talked of Mrs. Darcy may be imagined. I wish I could say, for the sake of her family, that the achievement of her lifelong ambition in seeing so many of her children well established produced so happy an effect as to make her a sensible, pleasant, well-informed woman for the rest of her life; though perhaps it was fortunate for her husband, who might not have enjoyed domestic happiness in so unfamiliar a form, that she remained occasionally nervous and permanently foolish.
Mr. Bennet missed his second daughter enormously; his love for her drew him away from home more than anything else could. He delighted in visiting Pemberley, especially when he was least expected.

Mr. Bingley and Jane stayed at Netherfield only a year. Being so close to her mother and the Meryton relations proved too much even for his easy temperament and her affectionate heart. His sisters' fondest wish was then granted: he bought an estate in a neighboring county to Derbyshire, and Jane and Elizabeth, in addition to every other source of happiness, were within thirty miles of each other.

Kitty, to her great benefit, spent most of her time with her two elder sisters. In such superior company, her improvement was considerable. She was not as ungovernable as Lydia, and once removed from Lydia's influence, she became, with proper care and attention, less irritable, less ignorant, and less vapid. She was, of course, carefully kept from Lydia's company; and though Mrs. Wickham frequently invited her to visit, with promises of balls and young men, her father would never consent to her going.

Mary was the only daughter who remained at home; and she was necessarily drawn away from her books by Mrs. Bennet's inability to sit alone. Mary was forced to mix more with society, but she could still moralize over every morning call; and since she was no longer humiliated by comparisons between her sisters' beauty and her own, it was suspected by her father that she accepted the change without much reluctance.

As for Wickham and Lydia, their characters suffered no transformation from her sisters' marriages. He bore with philosophical calm the certainty that Elizabeth must now learn of all his ingratitude and dishonesty that had previously been unknown to her; and despite everything, he was not entirely without hope that Darcy might still be persuaded to advance his career. The congratulatory letter Elizabeth received from Lydia on her marriage showed that, by his wife at least if not by himself, such a hope was alive. The letter went like this:
"My dear Lizzy,

"I wish you joy. If you love Mr. Darcy half as well as I love my dear Wickham, you must be very happy. It's a great comfort to have you so rich; and when you have nothing else to do, I hope you will think of us. I'm sure Wickham would love a position at court, and I don't think we shall have quite enough money to live on without some help. Any position would do, of about three or four hundred a year; but don't mention it to Mr. Darcy if you'd rather not.
"Yours, etc."

As it happened, Elizabeth very much would rather not, and she tried in her reply to put an end to every such appeal. Such relief as she could provide, however, through careful economy in her own private spending, she frequently sent them. It had always been obvious that an income like theirs, managed by two people so extravagant and careless about the future, must be woefully insufficient; and whenever they moved, either Jane or Elizabeth could be sure of being asked for some small help in paying their bills. Their way of life, even after peace was restored and they were settled in a home, was thoroughly unstable. They were always moving from place to place in search of a cheap situation, and always spending more than they should. His affection for her soon faded into indifference; hers lasted a little longer; and despite her youth and her behavior, she retained all the social standing that marriage had given her. Though Darcy would never receive Wickham at Pemberley, he helped him further in his career, for Elizabeth's sake. Lydia was an occasional visitor when her husband was off enjoying himself in London or Bath; and with the Bingleys they both frequently stayed so long that even Bingley's good nature was strained, and he went so far as to talk of hinting they should leave.

Miss Bingley was deeply mortified by Darcy's marriage; but since she thought it wise to keep her visiting privileges at Pemberley, she dropped all her resentment, was fonder than ever of Georgiana, nearly as attentive to Darcy as before, and paid off every last debt of civility to Elizabeth.

Pemberley was now Georgiana's home, and the bond between the two sisters was exactly what Darcy had hoped to see. They were able to love each other as well as they had intended. Georgiana had the highest opinion in the world of Elizabeth; though at first she was often startled to the point of alarm by her lively, playful way of talking to her brother. He, who had always inspired in Georgiana a respect that almost overpowered her affection, was now the target of open teasing. Her mind received a lesson it had never encountered before. Through Elizabeth's example, she began to understand that a woman may take liberties with her husband that a brother will not always tolerate from a much younger sister.

Lady Catherine was extremely indignant at her nephew's marriage; and since she gave free rein to all the genuine frankness of her character in her reply to the letter announcing the engagement, she used language so abusive—especially of Elizabeth—that all communication between them ceased for some time. But at last, through Elizabeth's persuasion, he was brought to overlook the insult and seek a reconciliation; and after a little further resistance, his aunt gave way, either from affection for him or curiosity to see how his wife conducted herself. She even condescended to visit them at Pemberley, despite the pollution its woods had received not merely from the presence of such a mistress but from the visits of her uncle and aunt from the city.

With the Gardiners they were always on the closest terms. Darcy, as well as Elizabeth, truly loved them; and both were forever grateful to the people who, by bringing her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them.
